title: Introduction to Programming Concepts Quiz
description: A comprehensive quiz assessing fundamental programming concepts including variables, data types, control structures, and basic problem-solving skills using pseudocode and Python syntax.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and use appropriate data types (integers, strings, booleans, lists)
Demonstrate understanding of variables and assignment operations
Apply conditional statements (if/else) to solve basic problems
Implement simple loops (for and while) for repetitive tasks
Read and interpret basic Python code snippets
Write pseudocode to outline problem-solving approaches
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Variables (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, understands variable assignment, demonstrates knowledge of naming conventions and scope
Control Structures (25 points): Accurately uses if/else statements, understands boolean logic, correctly implements decision-making processes
Loops and Iteration (25 points): Properly implements for and while loops, understands loop termination conditions, applies loops to solve repetitive tasks
Code Reading and Problem Solving (25 points): Correctly interprets existing code, traces through program execution, writes clear pseudocode solutions
instructions:
This quiz consists of 20 questions covering fundamental programming concepts. You have 45 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully before answering.

SECTION A - Multiple Choice (Questions 1-10, 2 points each): Select the best answer for each question. Only one answer is correct per question.

SECTION B - Code Analysis (Questions 11-15, 4 points each): Examine the provided code snippets and answer questions about their output, functionality, or identify errors. Show your work by tracing through the code step-by-step.

SECTION C - Problem Solving (Questions 16-20, 6 points each): Write pseudocode or simple Python code to solve the given problems. Focus on logic and structure rather than perfect syntax. Partial credit will be given for correct approaches even if minor syntax errors exist.

GENERAL GUIDELINES:
- Use clear, readable handwriting or typing
- For coding questions, include comments explaining your logic
- If you're unsure about syntax, write your solution in pseudocode
- Manage your time: spend approximately 15 minutes per section
- Review your answers if time permits
- No external resources or collaboration allowed
- Submit your completed quiz before the time limit expires
grading_notes: Award full points for completely correct answers. For Section B (Code Analysis), give partial credit if student shows correct thinking process even with minor computational errors. For Section C (Problem Solving), focus on logical approach and problem decomposition - award 60% credit for correct logic with syntax errors, 80% for minor logical gaps, full credit for complete correct solutions. Common issues to watch: off-by-one errors in loops, confusion between assignment and comparison operators, incorrect indentation understanding. Expected grade distribution: 15% A's, 35% B's, 35% C's, 15% below C. Flag students scoring below 60% for additional support.

title: Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Project
description: Students will conduct a complete data science project analyzing customer churn patterns using a provided telecommunications dataset. This assessment evaluates data preprocessing, exploratory analysis, feature engineering, predictive modeling, and business communication skills through a comprehensive analysis report and model implementation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply data preprocessing techniques including handling missing values, outliers, and categorical encoding
Conduct exploratory data analysis to identify patterns and generate actionable business insights
Engineer relevant features and select appropriate variables for predictive modeling
Build, evaluate, and compare multiple machine learning models using appropriate metrics
Communicate technical findings effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing & Quality (25 points): Proper handling of missing values, outliers, data types, and categorical variables. Clear documentation of data cleaning decisions and their rationale.

Exploratory Data Analysis (25 points): Comprehensive visualization and statistical analysis revealing meaningful patterns. Identification of key churn drivers with supporting evidence and business context.

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of at least 2 different algorithms, proper train/validation/test splits, appropriate metrics (precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC), hyperparameter tuning, and model comparison with justified final selection.

Communication & Business Impact (25 points): Clear, professional report with executive summary, actionable recommendations, limitations discussion, and appropriate visualizations. Code organization and documentation quality.
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (telecom_churn.csv), develop a complete churn prediction solution. Your deliverables must include: (1) A Jupyter notebook containing all analysis code with clear markdown explanations, (2) A 4-6 page business report in PDF format targeting company executives. Your analysis should begin with thorough data exploration, identifying key patterns in customer behavior and churn rates across different segments. Implement appropriate preprocessing steps including handling missing values, encoding categorical variables, and addressing any data quality issues. Create at least 5 meaningful visualizations that reveal churn patterns. For modeling, implement and compare at least two different algorithms (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost). Use proper cross-validation, evaluate models using multiple metrics appropriate for imbalanced classification, and justify your final model selection. Your business report should include an executive summary, key findings, model performance summary, and specific recommendations for reducing churn with estimated business impact. Submit both files via the course portal by 11:59 PM on the due date. Ensure your code runs completely without errors and includes comments explaining key decisions.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should target 15% A grades, 35% B grades, 35% C grades, 15% D/F grades. Common issues to watch for: inadequate data exploration (students jumping straight to modeling), improper handling of data leakage, using inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data, overly technical business reports, and poor code organization. Award partial credit for incomplete sections if methodology is sound. Deduct points for code that doesn't run, missing visualizations, or failure to address business context. Strong projects will demonstrate clear thinking progression from data understanding through modeling to business recommendations, with particular attention to practical implementation considerations and model limitations.

rubric_criteria: Problem-Solving Methodology (25 points): Demonstrates systematic approach to complex problems, shows clear work progression, uses appropriate mathematical techniques, and applies theorems correctly

instructions:
This exam consists of 6 problems worth varying point values totaling 100 points. You have 3 hours to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and justify your reasoning. Partial credit will be awarded for correct methodology even if final answers are incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation throughout.

Problem 1 (15 points): Find and classify all critical points of f(x,y) = x³ - 3xy² + y³, then determine absolute maximum and minimum values on the region bounded by x² + y² ≤ 4.

Problem 2 (20 points): Use Lagrange multipliers to optimize f(x,y,z) = xyz subject to the constraint x² + 2y² + 3z² = 6. Interpret your results geometrically.

Problem 3 (15 points): Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix A = [[2,-1,0],[-1,2,-1],[0,-1,2]]. Determine if A is diagonalizable and find the diagonal form if possible.

Problem 4 (20 points): A population model involves the system x'(t) = Ax(t) where A is the matrix from Problem 3. Given initial condition x(0) = [1,0,1]ᵀ, find the general solution and describe long-term behavior.

Problem 5 (15 points): Evaluate the surface integral ∬_S (x² + y² + z²) dS where S is the portion of the sphere x² + y² + z² = 4 above the plane z = 1.

Problem 6 (15 points): Prove that if A is a symmetric n×n matrix, then eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Calculators are permitted. Clearly label your final answers. If you cannot complete a problem, explain your approach for partial credit.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct methodology. Look for: proper setup of problems (5-10% of problem value), correct application of techniques (60-70% of problem value), and accurate final results (20-30% of problem value). Common issues include: sign errors in eigenvalue calculations, forgetting to check second-order conditions in optimization, incomplete constraint analysis in Lagrange multiplier problems, and unclear geometric interpretations. Expect grade distribution: A (15-20%), B (25-30%), C (30-35%), D/F (15-20%). Deduct points for poor mathematical notation or unclear presentation. Give full credit for alternative valid solution methods.

description: Students will analyze and design a comprehensive distributed system architecture for a real-world scenario, demonstrating expertise in scalability, fault tolerance, consistency models, and modern distributed computing paradigms.

Discussion Engagement and Communication (25 points): Provides substantive feedback on peer designs, asks insightful technical questions, clearly articulates complex concepts, and contributes meaningfully to collaborative problem-solving
instructions:
You are tasked with designing a distributed system architecture for a global ride-sharing platform that handles 10 million daily active users across multiple continents. Your system must support real-time driver-passenger matching, dynamic pricing, payment processing, and trip tracking.

Phase 1 - Initial Design (48 hours): Create a comprehensive architectural proposal including: (1) High-level system architecture diagram with all major components, (2) Database design strategy addressing geographical distribution and consistency requirements, (3) Technology stack justification for each system layer, (4) Scalability and fault tolerance mechanisms, (5) Security considerations for payment and user data.

Phase 2 - Peer Review (24 hours): Review two peer submissions and provide detailed technical feedback addressing: architectural strengths/weaknesses, potential scalability bottlenecks, alternative design approaches, and specific implementation concerns.

Phase 3 - Discussion Forum (72 hours): Engage in threaded discussions addressing: consensus algorithm trade-offs for different system components, database partitioning strategies, microservices vs. monolithic considerations, and disaster recovery planning. Respond substantively to at least 5 peer posts with technical insights, questions, or alternative perspectives.

Submission Requirements: Initial architecture document (3-5 pages with diagrams), peer review reports (1-2 pages each), and active participation in forum discussions. All technical claims must be supported with relevant research or industry examples. Use proper computer science terminology and cite distributed systems literature where appropriate.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical accuracy against established distributed systems principles from Tanenbaum, van Steen, and Kleppmann texts. Look for evidence of understanding CAP theorem implications, appropriate use of eventual consistency vs. strong consistency, and realistic scalability projections. Common issues include: oversimplified fault tolerance mechanisms, unrealistic consistency guarantees, inappropriate technology choices for scale requirements, and superficial peer engagement. Expect 15-20% A grades for designs demonstrating novel solutions or exceptional trade-off analysis. Deduct points for generic responses lacking specific technical justification or failure to engage meaningfully with peer work.

Section 1 - Programming Concepts (25 points): Answer multiple choice and short answer questions about variables, data types, and operators. Define key programming terms and explain their usage.

Section 2 - Control Structures (25 points): Complete code segments using if/else statements and loops. Write small programs that use conditional logic and iteration to solve given problems.

Section 3 - Functions (25 points): Write function definitions based on provided specifications. Include proper parameter handling and return values. Write code that calls these functions correctly.

Section 4 - Code Analysis (25 points): Trace through provided code segments step-by-step and determine the output. Identify syntax errors, logical errors, and runtime errors in buggy code samples. Provide corrected versions.

General Requirements: Use proper Python syntax throughout. Show intermediate steps for code tracing problems. Partial credit will be awarded for partially correct solutions. If you're unsure about syntax, focus on demonstrating logical understanding. No external resources or collaboration permitted.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for logical thinking even with minor syntax errors. For code tracing, give credit for correct methodology even if final answer is wrong due to early mistake. Common issues include: incorrect indentation (major point deduction), confusion between = and == operators, off-by-one errors in loops, and missing return statements in functions. Grade distribution should target: 85-100 (A), 75-84 (B), 65-74 (C), 55-64 (D). Students scoring below 60% likely need additional foundational support before advancing.

Section 3: Function Writing (25 points, 25 minutes) - Create functions according to specified requirements. Each function should include proper parameter handling, return statements, and docstrings describing the function's purpose.

grading_notes: Grade each section independently using the point allocations specified. For coding sections, award partial credit for correct logic even if syntax is imperfect - focus on understanding over perfect syntax. Common issues to watch: incorrect indentation (deduct 1-2 points), missing return statements in functions (deduct 3-5 points), logical errors in loop conditions (deduct 5-10 points). Section C (25 points): Function-related tasks including writing function definitions, making function calls, and explaining parameter passing. You may be asked to debug existing functions or create new ones from specifications.

title: Advanced Mathematical Modeling: Real-World Optimization Problem Analysis and Presentation
description: Students will identify a real-world optimization problem, develop multiple mathematical models to solve it, analyze the effectiveness of different approaches, and present their findings in a comprehensive 15-minute presentation with visual aids and mathematical justification.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced calculus concepts (derivatives, integrals, multivariable optimization) to solve real-world problems
Construct and compare multiple mathematical models for complex scenarios
Analyze the validity, limitations, and assumptions of mathematical solutions
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences
Demonstrate proficiency in mathematical software tools and visualization techniques
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of advanced mathematical concepts, accurate calculations, appropriate use of optimization techniques, proper handling of constraints and variables

Model Development and Analysis (25 points): Creation of multiple viable models, comparison of approaches, identification of assumptions and limitations, validation of results against real-world context

Presentation Quality and Communication (25 points): Clear explanation of mathematical concepts, effective use of visual aids, logical flow of ideas, appropriate pacing, professional delivery, engagement with audience questions

Problem Selection and Real-World Application (25 points): Choice of sufficiently complex and relevant problem, demonstration of practical impact, connection between mathematical solution and real-world implementation, discussion of broader implications
instructions: Select a real-world optimization problem from fields such as engineering, economics, logistics, environmental science, or operations research. Your problem must involve at least three variables and multiple constraints. Develop a minimum of two different mathematical approaches to solve the problem (e.g., linear programming vs. calculus-based optimization, or analytical vs. numerical methods). Your presentation must include: (1) Clear problem statement with background context and stakeholder impact, (2) Mathematical formulation showing variables, objective function, and constraints, (3) Step-by-step solution process for each approach with all calculations shown or clearly referenced, (4) Comparison of methods including computational complexity and accuracy, (5) Sensitivity analysis examining how changes in parameters affect the solution, (6) Real-world validation and implementation considerations. Create visual aids including graphs, charts, and mathematical diagrams using software such as MATLAB, Python, R, or Mathematica. Prepare to answer questions about your methodology, alternative approaches, and practical limitations. Submit your slides and supporting calculations 24 hours before presentation. Include a brief abstract (150 words) and bibliography of at least 5 scholarly sources.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical sophistication - look for use of advanced techniques beyond basic optimization. Common weaknesses include oversimplified problems, computational errors in complex calculations, and failure to validate results. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90+), 35% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70%. Deduct points for presentations under 12 or over 18 minutes. Award bonus consideration for innovative approaches or exceptional real-world research. Pay special attention to handling of Q&A - this reveals depth of understanding. Students should demonstrate mastery of both theoretical concepts and practical application.

title: Advanced Mathematical Modeling: Real-World Optimization Problem Analysis and Presentation - Students Will
description: Students will research, analyze, and present a comprehensive solution to a complex real-world optimization problem using advanced mathematical techniques including calculus, linear programming, or differential equations. learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced calculus concepts (optimization, derivatives, integrals) to solve complex real-world problems
Demonstrate proficiency in mathematical modeling techniques and their practical limitations
Critically analyze and interpret mathematical results within real-world contexts
Communicate complex mathematical concepts clearly to diverse audiences using appropriate terminology and visual aids
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of advanced mathematical techniques, accurate calculations, proper use of mathematical notation, clear identification of assumptions and constraints

Problem Selection and Modeling (25 points): Selection of appropriately complex real-world problem, sophisticated mathematical model development, clear justification of chosen approach, acknowledgment of model limitations

Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Thorough analysis of results, discussion of practical implications, sensitivity analysis or alternative scenarios, critical evaluation of solution feasibility and real-world applicability

Presentation Quality and Communication (25 points): Clear oral delivery, effective use of visual aids, appropriate mathematical language, engagement with audience questions, adherence to time limits, professional presentation format
instructions: Select a complex real-world optimization problem from fields such as economics, engineering, environmental science, or operations research. Your problem must require advanced mathematical techniques beyond basic algebra. Develop a comprehensive mathematical model and solution, then prepare a 15-20 minute presentation covering: (1) Problem background and significance, (2) Mathematical model development with clear variable definitions and constraints, (3) Solution methodology showing all major calculation steps, (4) Results analysis including graphical representations where appropriate, (5) Discussion of practical implications and model limitations, (6) Potential improvements or alternative approaches. Your presentation must include: a title slide, problem statement, mathematical formulation, solution process with key steps shown, results visualization (graphs, charts, tables), real-world interpretation, and conclusions. Prepare to answer 5 minutes of audience questions demonstrating deep understanding. Submit your presentation slides and a 2-page mathematical appendix with detailed calculations 24 hours before presenting. Cite at least 3 academic sources. Examples of suitable problems include: portfolio optimization with risk constraints, supply chain network optimization, resource allocation in healthcare systems, traffic flow optimization, or renewable energy system design.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical sophistication - problems should require calculus-level or higher techniques. Look for correct mathematical notation and proper problem setup. Award full points for mathematical accuracy only if major steps are correct; minor computational errors should result in 2-3 point deductions per criterion. For modeling criterion, assess whether the chosen problem genuinely requires advanced mathematics and if the model appropriately captures real-world complexity. Strong presentations will acknowledge model assumptions and limitations. Communication scores should reflect clarity for a mathematical audience - use of proper terminology is essential, but excessive jargon without explanation should be penalized. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below 70. Presentations lacking mathematical rigor or using overly simplistic problems should not exceed 75 points regardless of presentation quality.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Discussion: Real-World Applications of Basic Operations
description: Students will engage in peer discussions about solving real-world mathematical problems using basic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and explain their problem-solving strategies to classmates.
estimated_time: 45-60 minutes for initial post and responses
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic mathematical operations to solve real-world problems
Communicate mathematical thinking clearly using appropriate vocabulary
Analyze and evaluate different problem-solving approaches
Connect mathematical concepts to everyday situations
rubric_criteria: Problem Solution Accuracy (25 points): Correctly applies mathematical operations and arrives at accurate solutions with clear computational work shown
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses appropriate mathematical vocabulary and explains reasoning clearly with step-by-step explanations
Real-World Application (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of how mathematics connects to practical situations and provides relevant examples
Peer Interaction Quality (25 points): Provides constructive feedback to classmates, asks meaningful questions, and engages thoughtfully with alternative approaches
instructions: You will participate in an online discussion about solving real-world math problems. First, choose ONE of the following scenarios and solve it completely: (1) Planning a pizza party for 24 people where each pizza serves 8 people and costs $12, calculating total cost and change from $100; (2) Calculating weekly earnings from a part-time job working 15 hours at $8.50 per hour, minus $25 for transportation; (3) Determining how many bags of fertilizer are needed for a 450 square foot garden if each bag covers 75 square feet, and calculating total cost at $6.99 per bag. In your initial post (200-250 words), show all mathematical work step-by-step, explain your problem-solving strategy, and discuss why this type of calculation is important in daily life. Include at least three mathematical vocabulary terms (such as 'quotient,' 'product,' 'difference,' 'sum,' 'remainder'). After posting your solution, respond to TWO classmates' posts (75-100 words each). In your responses, compare their approach to yours, ask a thoughtful question about their strategy, or suggest an alternative method. Check their calculations respectfully and offer constructive feedback. All posts must be submitted within the discussion period, with initial posts due by the midpoint deadline and responses due by the final deadline.
grading_notes: Award full points for accuracy only when all calculations are correct and clearly shown. For communication points, look for proper use of mathematical terms and logical flow of explanation. Real-world application points should reflect genuine understanding of practical relevance, not just superficial connections. Peer interaction points require substantive engagement - simple agreement or praise without mathematical content should receive partial credit. Common issues include: incomplete work shown, incorrect order of operations, failure to include units in answers, and responses that don't demonstrate mathematical thinking. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70.

Connect mathematical concepts to everyday experiences

Communication and Explanation (25 points): Uses appropriate mathematical vocabulary, explains thinking clearly, and provides detailed reasoning that others can follow and understand

instructions: You will participate in a discussion forum exploring how mathematics appears in everyday life. Create an original word problem based on your chosen scenario that requires at least two different mathematical operations to solve. Post your problem along with a complete solution showing all steps and explaining your reasoning. Your initial post should be 150-200 words and include: (1) the word problem you created, (2) your step-by-step solution with calculations, (3) explanation of why you chose specific operations, and (4) reflection on how this type of problem relates to real experiences. After posting, read at least three classmates' problems and provide substantive responses of 75-100 words each. In your responses, verify their solutions, suggest alternative solving methods if applicable, or share similar experiences from your own life. Ask thoughtful questions that encourage deeper thinking about the mathematical concepts involved. All posts must use proper mathematical vocabulary and show respect for different problem-solving approaches. Submit your initial post by the midweek deadline and complete all peer responses by the end of the week.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for mathematical correctness first, then assess explanation quality. Look for students who show their work clearly and use terms like 'sum,' 'difference,' 'product,' and 'quotient' appropriately. Common issues include incomplete explanations, calculation errors, and superficial peer responses. Expect 80% of students to score 75+ points with proper scaffolding. Award full points for peer engagement when responses go beyond simple agreement and demonstrate genuine mathematical dialogue. Deduct points for late submissions or failure to meet word count requirements. Provide specific feedback on mathematical reasoning and suggest improvements for unclear explanations.

title: Beginner Programming Portfolio: Personal Calculator Project
description: Students will create a comprehensive portfolio documenting the development of a simple calculator program, including planning documents, code implementation, testing procedures, and reflection on their learning process.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate understanding of basic programming concepts (variables, functions, conditionals, loops)
Apply problem-solving strategies to break down programming tasks
Document code effectively using comments and external documentation
Test and debug simple programs systematically
Reflect on programming learning process and identify areas for improvement
rubric_criteria: Planning and Design (25 points): Complete project plan with pseudocode, flowchart, and feature list. Clear problem decomposition and logical design approach.
Code Implementation (25 points): Functional calculator with basic operations (+, -, *, /) and error handling. Clean, readable code with appropriate variable names and structure.
Documentation and Comments (25 points): Comprehensive README file explaining project purpose and usage. Well-commented code explaining logic. Testing log with at least 5 test cases and results.
Reflection and Learning (25 points): Thoughtful reflection essay (300-500 words) discussing challenges faced, solutions found, concepts learned, and future improvement plans.
instructions: Create a portfolio documenting your development of a personal calculator program. Your portfolio must include: 1) Planning Documents: Create a project plan with pseudocode or flowchart showing your calculator's logic, list of features to implement, and timeline. 2) Source Code: Implement a calculator that performs basic arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /) with input validation and error handling for division by zero. Code must be well-commented and use meaningful variable names. 3) Documentation: Write a README file explaining what your calculator does, how to run it, and what features it includes. Create a testing log documenting at least 5 different test cases with expected and actual results. 4) Reflection Essay: Write 300-500 words reflecting on your development process, challenges encountered, how you solved problems, key programming concepts you learned, and what you would improve next time. Submit all components in a single folder (digital) or binder (physical) with clear organization and labeling. Code should run without errors and demonstrate understanding of basic programming concepts covered in class.
grading_notes: Evaluate portfolios holistically while checking each rubric component. For Planning: Look for evidence of thinking before coding, not perfection. For Code: Focus on functionality and readability over advanced features. Expect beginner-level syntax but working programs. For Documentation: Assess completeness and clarity, not professional polish. For Reflection: Look for genuine self-assessment and learning evidence, not just project summary. Common issues: Students jumping straight to coding without planning, minimal comments, testing only 'happy path' cases, reflection focusing on what they built rather than what they learned. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 15% C-level (70-79), 5% below C. Provide specific feedback on each rubric component and highlight strengths alongside improvement areas.

title: Fundamentals of Data Science: Exploratory Data Analysis Exam
description: Students will demonstrate their understanding of basic data science concepts by performing exploratory data analysis on a provided dataset, interpreting statistical summaries, creating visualizations, and drawing preliminary insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic statistical concepts to describe and summarize datasets
Create and interpret fundamental data visualizations
Identify data quality issues and propose cleaning strategies
Formulate hypotheses based on exploratory data analysis findings
rubric_criteria: Data Summary and Statistics (25 points): Correctly calculates and interprets descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles) for numerical variables and frequency distributions for categorical variables

Data Visualization (25 points): Creates appropriate charts (histogram, box plot, scatter plot, bar chart) with proper labels, titles, and formatting; selects visualization types that effectively communicate data patterns
Data Quality Assessment (25 points): Identifies missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies; proposes reasonable data cleaning approaches; recognizes potential data collection issues or biases

Insights and Interpretation (25 points): Draws logical conclusions from analysis; identifies meaningful patterns, trends, or relationships; formulates testable hypotheses for future analysis; communicates findings clearly
instructions:
You will receive a CSV dataset containing customer information for an e-commerce company (1000 records, 8 variables including age, income, purchase amount, product category, etc.). Complete all four sections below, showing your work and reasoning.

Section 1 - Data Summary (25 points): Calculate descriptive statistics for all numerical variables. Create frequency tables for categorical variables. Interpret what these statistics tell us about the dataset.

Section 2 - Visualizations (25 points): Create four different visualizations: one histogram, one box plot, one scatter plot, and one bar chart. Each must include proper titles, axis labels, and legends where appropriate. Briefly explain what each visualization reveals.

Section 3 - Data Quality (25 points): Identify any missing values, outliers, or data inconsistencies. For each issue found, explain why it's problematic and suggest a specific remedy (remove, impute, transform, etc.).

Section 4 - Analysis Summary (25 points): Write a 200-word summary of your key findings. Include at least two specific insights about customer behavior and formulate one hypothesis for further investigation.

Submit your work as a single document (PDF preferred) containing all calculations, visualizations, and written responses. You may use any software tools (Excel, Python, R, etc.) but must show your process clearly.
grading_notes: Expect most students to score 70-85%. Award partial credit generously for correct methodology even if calculations contain minor errors. Common issues include: incorrect chart types for data, missing axis labels, failure to address obvious outliers, and overly general conclusions. Deduct 5 points for late submission. Look for evidence of critical thinking in data quality section - students should question unusual values rather than accept everything. In insights section, reward specific, data-supported observations over generic statements.

title: Fundamentals of Data Science: Exploratory Data Analysis Exam - Comprehensive Beginner-Level

learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate understanding of basic data science terminology and workflow
Apply descriptive statistics to summarize and interpret datasets
Create and interpret basic data visualizations using appropriate chart types
Identify data quality issues and propose cleaning strategies
Draw meaningful insights from exploratory data analysis

Data Visualization & Interpretation (25 points): Creates appropriate visualizations (histograms, scatter plots, bar charts) with proper labels and formatting. Correctly interprets visual patterns and trends.
Insights & Recommendations (25 points): Formulates clear, data-driven insights based on analysis. Provides actionable recommendations supported by evidence from the data exploration.
instructions: This exam consists of four sections based on the provided 'retail_sales.csv' dataset containing 1,000 records of customer transactions. You may use Excel, Google Sheets, or basic Python/R functions (no advanced libraries). Section 1: Data Exploration - Examine the dataset structure, identify data types for each column, count missing values, and describe any data quality issues you observe. Section 2: Statistical Summary - Calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for numerical variables. Create frequency tables for categorical variables and identify the distribution shapes. Section 3: Data Visualization - Create five visualizations: histogram of sales amounts, bar chart of top product categories, scatter plot of quantity vs. price, line chart of monthly sales trends, and one additional chart of your choice. Include titles, axis labels, and brief interpretations. Section 4: Business Insights - Based on your analysis, identify three key findings about customer behavior, sales patterns, or product performance. Provide specific recommendations for business improvement with supporting data evidence. Submit all work in a single PDF document with clearly labeled sections. Include any calculations, charts, and written explanations. Ensure all visualizations are readable and properly formatted.
grading_notes: Use a 4-point scale for each criterion: Excellent (23-25 pts), Good (18-22 pts), Satisfactory (13-17 pts), Needs Improvement (0-12 pts). Common issues to watch for include: incorrect statistical calculations, inappropriate chart types for data, missing axis labels or titles, unsupported conclusions, and failure to address data quality issues. Expect grade distribution of approximately 20% A's, 40% B's, 30% C's, 10% D/F. Partial credit should be given for correct methodology even with minor computational errors. Pay special attention to students' ability to connect statistical findings to business context.

title: Personal Task Manager Web Application

Implement CSS styling for responsive and visually appealing layouts

title: Quantum Mechanics Interpretation Debate: Copenhagen vs Many-Worlds vs Hidden Variables
description: Students engage in a structured academic discussion defending one of the major interpretations of quantum mechanics while critically analyzing competing interpretations. This assessment evaluates understanding of quantum mechanical principles, philosophical implications, and ability to construct rigorous scientific arguments.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate mastery of quantum mechanical postulates and mathematical formalism
Analyze the philosophical and scientific implications of quantum measurement theory
Evaluate competing scientific theories using evidence-based reasoning
Communicate complex physics concepts with precision and clarity
rubric_criteria: Theoretical Understanding (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive knowledge of quantum mechanical principles, mathematical formalism, and experimental foundations. Correctly applies concepts like wave function collapse, superposition, entanglement, and measurement theory.

Critical Analysis (25 points): Provides sophisticated evaluation of strengths and weaknesses of different interpretations. Addresses key experiments (double-slit, EPR paradox, Bell's theorem) and their implications for each interpretation.

Argumentation Quality (25 points): Constructs logical, evidence-based arguments with clear reasoning chains. Effectively counters opposing viewpoints while acknowledging limitations of their chosen interpretation. Uses appropriate scientific terminology and mathematical notation.

Discussion Engagement (25 points): Actively participates in scholarly discourse, asks probing questions, builds upon others' ideas constructively. Demonstrates intellectual flexibility and responds thoughtfully to challenges and new perspectives.
instructions:
You will participate in a structured debate defending one of three major quantum mechanics interpretations: Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, or Hidden Variables (Bohmian mechanics). Each student will be randomly assigned an interpretation to defend.

Preparation Phase: Research your assigned interpretation thoroughly. Prepare a 10-minute opening presentation covering: (1) Core principles and mathematical framework, (2) How it explains key quantum phenomena, (3) Experimental support or predictions, (4) Responses to major criticisms. Create visual aids showing relevant equations, diagrams, or experimental setups.

Discussion Phase: After all opening presentations, engage in moderated cross-examination where you must defend your interpretation while questioning others. Address specific scenarios: Schrödinger's cat, quantum tunneling, delayed-choice experiments, and quantum computing implications.

Submission Requirements: Submit your presentation slides, a 500-word reflection on insights gained from defending your assigned position, and a 300-word critique of the interpretation you found least convincing. All mathematical expressions must use proper notation and cite primary sources.

Evaluation Focus: You'll be assessed on depth of understanding, quality of reasoning, ability to handle challenges gracefully, and contribution to collective learning. Grading considers both preparation quality and live discussion performance.
grading_notes: Instructors should evaluate both prepared materials and live performance equally. Watch for students who merely repeat textbook explanations versus those demonstrating genuine understanding through novel examples or analogies. Common issues include: oversimplifying interpretations, avoiding difficult questions, or making unsupported claims. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (exceptional synthesis and original insights), 50% B-level (solid understanding with good participation), 25% C-level (basic comprehension but limited analysis), 5% below C (significant gaps in understanding). During discussion, note students' ability to adapt arguments in real-time and maintain scientific rigor under pressure.

instructions:

Step 1: Download and examine the provided dataset using your preferred analysis tool (Python, R, Excel, etc.). Document your initial observations about data structure, size, and obvious issues.

Step 2: Create a detailed data quality assessment report (500-750 words) that:
- Catalogs specific data quality issues found, organized by category
- Provides examples with actual data values where appropriate
- Estimates the scope/frequency of each problem type
- Assesses potential impact on analysis if left untreated

Step 3: Develop a systematic cleaning strategy (400-600 words) that:
- Outlines step-by-step cleaning procedures in logical order
- Justifies chosen methods for handling each issue type
- Discusses alternative approaches considered and why they were rejected
- Addresses potential risks or limitations of your approach
- Estimates expected data loss and mitigation strategies

Step 4: Participate in forum discussions by:
- Posting your complete assessment and strategy by the initial deadline
- Reading and responding to at least 2 classmates' posts with specific, constructive feedback
- Engaging in follow-up discussions about alternative approaches or challenging questions

grading_notes: Instructors should evaluate technical accuracy alongside analytical thinking. Expect 15% A grades (90-100), 25% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 20% below 70%. Deduct heavily for incomplete testing documentation. Award bonus points for advanced features like route filtering, QoS implementation, or IPv6 dual-stack.

title: Enterprise Network Design and Implementation Lab Report - Students Will
description: Students will design, configure, and document a complete enterprise network infrastructure for a multi-site organization, implementing advanced routing protocols, security features, and redundancy mechanisms while providing comprehensive technical documentation and performance analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement enterprise-grade network topologies with appropriate redundancy and scalability considerations
Configure and optimize advanced routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) for multi-area and multi-AS environments
Implement comprehensive network security policies including VLANs, ACLs, VPN tunnels, and AAA authentication
Troubleshoot complex network issues using systematic methodologies and advanced diagnostic tools
Document network infrastructure with professional-grade diagrams, configuration files, and technical reports
rubric_criteria: Network Design and Architecture (25 points): Logical network topology with proper IP addressing scheme, VLAN segmentation, redundant paths, scalable design principles, and appropriate equipment selection for a 500+ user enterprise environment

Configuration Implementation (25 points): Complete and optimized router/switch configurations including OSPF multi-area setup, inter-VLAN routing, spanning tree optimization, security hardening, and site-to-site VPN implementation with proper authentication and encryption

Testing and Troubleshooting Documentation (25 points): Comprehensive testing procedures with ping/traceroute analysis, bandwidth utilization reports, failover testing results, security penetration testing, and systematic troubleshooting methodology with root cause analysis

Technical Documentation Quality (25 points): Professional network diagrams using industry-standard symbols, complete configuration backup files, change management procedures, disaster recovery plan, and executive summary suitable for C-level presentation
instructions: Design and implement a complete enterprise network for TechCorp Industries, a growing company with headquarters (200 users), branch office (150 users), data center (50 servers), and remote workforce (100 VPN users). Your lab report must include: 1) Network topology diagram with IP addressing scheme using /24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16 range, 2) Complete router and switch configurations implementing OSPF areas 0, 1, and 2 with appropriate network types and authentication, 3) VLAN implementation separating users, servers, management, and guest networks with inter-VLAN routing, 4) Security implementation including standard/extended ACLs, port security, DHCP snooping, and site-to-site IPSec VPN between locations, 5) Redundancy features including HSRP/VRRP, EtherChannel, and spanning tree optimization, 6) Performance testing results showing end-to-end connectivity, failover times under 30 seconds, and throughput measurements, 7) Troubleshooting scenarios documenting at least three network issues with systematic resolution steps. Submit as PDF including network diagrams, configuration files in text format, test results with screenshots, and executive summary. All configurations must be tested in packet tracer or physical lab environment with verification commands documented.
grading_notes: Evaluate network designs for scalability and industry best practices - deduct points for single points of failure or poor IP allocation. Configuration syntax must be error-free and optimized - common issues include incorrect OSPF network statements, missing VLAN interfaces, and weak security implementations. Testing documentation should demonstrate thorough validation - look for comprehensive ping/traceroute tests, failover verification, and realistic troubleshooting scenarios. Professional documentation standards are critical - diagrams should use proper Cisco icons, configurations must be properly formatted, and executive summary should be business-appropriate. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades (90-100), 35% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 10% below 70. Partial credit available for each criterion, but configurations that don't compile receive maximum 50% for implementation section.

title: Fundamentals of Programming Logic and Basic Python Syntax Quiz
description: A comprehensive quiz assessing students' understanding of fundamental programming concepts including variables, data types, basic operators, conditional statements, and simple loops using Python syntax. Students will demonstrate their ability to read, trace, and write basic Python code.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and correctly use Python data types (integers, floats, strings, booleans)
Demonstrate understanding of variable assignment and naming conventions
Apply basic arithmetic and comparison operators in Python expressions
Construct and analyze simple conditional statements (if/elif/else)
Implement basic loop structures (for and while loops) for simple iterations
Trace through code execution and predict program output
Write syntactically correct Python code to solve basic problems
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Variables (25 points): Correctly identifies Python data types, demonstrates proper variable assignment, follows Python naming conventions, and understands variable scope in simple contexts

Operators and Expressions (25 points): Accurately uses arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, **), comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=), and logical operators (and, or, not) in expressions and conditional statements
Control Structures (25 points): Constructs proper if/elif/else statements with correct indentation, implements basic for and while loops, and demonstrates understanding of loop control and iteration

Code Analysis and Problem Solving (25 points): Successfully traces through code execution, predicts correct output for given code snippets, identifies and corrects basic syntax errors, and writes simple Python programs to solve specified problems
instructions:
This quiz consists of 20 questions covering fundamental Python programming concepts. You have 60 minutes to complete all questions. The quiz includes multiple-choice questions, code tracing exercises, error identification tasks, and short coding problems.

Question Types:
- Multiple Choice (8 questions): Select the best answer for questions about data types, operators, and basic syntax
- Code Tracing (5 questions): Analyze provided code snippets and determine their output
- Error Identification (4 questions): Identify and explain syntax or logical errors in given code
- Short Coding (3 questions): Write 3-5 lines of Python code to solve simple problems

General Requirements:
- All code must use proper Python syntax and indentation (4 spaces per level)
- Variable names should follow Python conventions (lowercase with underscores)
- Show your work for code tracing questions by writing intermediate values
- For coding questions, include comments explaining your logic
- Partial credit will be awarded for partially correct solutions

Submission Guidelines:
- Complete all questions before submitting
- Review your answers, especially checking for proper syntax and indentation
- Ensure all code tracing shows step-by-step execution
- Submit through the online quiz platform before the time limit expires
- No external resources, notes, or collaboration permitted during the assessment
grading_notes: Grade distribution should follow standard scale: 90-100 (A), 80-89 (B), 70-79 (C), 60-69 (D), below 60 (F). Award partial credit generously for coding questions that show correct logic but minor syntax errors. Common issues to watch: incorrect indentation (major point deduction), confusion between assignment (=) and equality (==), off-by-one errors in loops, and mixing up integer vs. float division. For code tracing, accept answers that show understanding even if intermediate steps are not fully shown. Deduct points for failure to follow Python naming conventions only if explicitly taught. Expect 70-80% of students to score above 75 points. Flag students scoring below 60 for additional support.

title: Integrated Project Recovery and Optimization Lab Report
description: Students will analyze a failing IT infrastructure project, develop a comprehensive recovery plan using advanced project management methodologies, and present evidence-based recommendations with detailed risk mitigation strategies and resource optimization solutions.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced project recovery techniques including earned value management and critical chain methodology
Synthesize stakeholder analysis with risk assessment to create comprehensive mitigation strategies
Evaluate resource allocation decisions using quantitative optimization methods and cost-benefit analysis
Design integrated project control systems incorporating agile and traditional project management frameworks
rubric_criteria: Project Analysis and Problem Identification (25 points): Demonstrates thorough analysis of project failures using multiple diagnostic tools (schedule variance analysis, stakeholder mapping, root cause analysis). Identifies critical path issues, resource constraints, and scope creep with supporting quantitative evidence.

Recovery Strategy Development (25 points): Develops comprehensive recovery plan incorporating earned value management, resource leveling, and schedule compression techniques. Integrates agile methodologies where appropriate and provides detailed implementation timeline with measurable milestones.

Risk Management and Stakeholder Integration (25 points): Creates detailed risk register with probability-impact matrices, implements Monte Carlo simulation for schedule risks, and develops stakeholder communication plan addressing resistance to change. Includes contingency planning with trigger points and escalation procedures.

Resource Optimization and Financial Justification (25 points): Applies advanced resource allocation models, conducts cost-benefit analysis of recovery options, and provides detailed budget reforecasting. Includes sensitivity analysis and ROI calculations with clear financial justification for recommended approach.
instructions: You will receive a comprehensive case study of DataTech Solutions' failed ERP implementation project, including original project charter, current status reports, stakeholder interviews, and financial data. Your task is to create a professional lab report (8-10 pages) containing: (1) Executive Summary with key findings and recommendations, (2) Detailed project diagnostic analysis using at least three PM analytical tools, (3) Comprehensive recovery strategy with specific methodologies and timelines, (4) Risk management plan with quantitative analysis, and (5) Resource optimization recommendations with financial justification. Include all calculations, charts, and supporting documentation in appendices. Use APA formatting with minimum 8 scholarly sources from project management literature. Submit your report as a PDF with Excel workbook containing all calculations and models. The case study materials will be available in the course portal 48 hours before the assignment deadline. Focus on practical, implementable solutions rather than theoretical discussions. Your recommendations should address the specific constraints outlined in the case study including limited budget flexibility, regulatory compliance requirements, and stakeholder resistance to scope changes.
grading_notes: Evaluate depth of analysis over breadth - students should demonstrate mastery of advanced PM techniques rather than superficial coverage of many topics. Look for evidence-based reasoning with quantitative support for all major recommendations. Common issues include: insufficient use of PM analytical tools, vague implementation timelines, unrealistic resource assumptions, and inadequate financial analysis. Excellent work (90-100) shows innovative application of PM methodologies with clear integration between analysis and recommendations. Good work (80-89) demonstrates competent use of tools with sound reasoning. Satisfactory work (70-79) meets basic requirements but lacks depth or integration. Below 70 indicates insufficient analysis or major methodological errors. Expect 15% A grades, 35% B grades, 40% C grades, 10% below C.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS
description: Students will design and deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS, demonstrating understanding of core services, security best practices, and cost optimization. The project involves setting up presentation, application, and database tiers using EC2, RDS, and supporting AWS services.
learning_objectives_assessed: Deploy and configure EC2 instances with proper security groups and networking
Set up and connect to RDS database instances with appropriate security configurations
Implement basic AWS security best practices including IAM roles and VPC configuration
Demonstrate understanding of AWS cost optimization strategies
Document AWS architecture decisions and deployment process
rubric_criteria: Architecture Implementation (25 points): Correctly deploys web server on EC2, application logic tier, and RDS database with proper connectivity between all tiers. All services are functional and accessible.

Security Configuration (25 points): Implements appropriate security groups, uses IAM roles instead of access keys, follows principle of least privilege, and ensures database is not publicly accessible.

Documentation and Architecture Diagram (25 points): Provides clear architecture diagram showing all components and connections, documents deployment steps, includes screenshots of working application, and explains design decisions.

Cost Optimization and Best Practices (25 points): Uses appropriate instance types, implements resource tagging, demonstrates understanding of AWS Free Tier limitations, and includes cost estimation analysis.
instructions: Deploy a three-tier web application on AWS with the following requirements: 1) Web Tier: Launch an EC2 instance running a web server (Apache/Nginx) serving a simple HTML page with a form. 2) Application Tier: Create a second EC2 instance or use the same instance to process form submissions (can use PHP, Python, or Node.js). 3) Database Tier: Set up an RDS MySQL instance to store form submissions. Your application must successfully save and retrieve data from the database. Create a VPC with public and private subnets, placing the database in the private subnet. Configure security groups to allow only necessary traffic between tiers. Use IAM roles for EC2 instances instead of hardcoded credentials. Submit: (1) Architecture diagram showing all components and data flow, (2) Screenshots proving your application works end-to-end, (3) Documentation explaining your deployment process and security decisions, (4) Cost analysis estimating monthly charges, (5) Text file with all AWS resource URLs/identifiers for verification. Ensure all resources are properly tagged with your name and project identifier. Clean up resources after submission to avoid charges, but keep screenshots and documentation for grading.
grading_notes: Verify student applications are actually functional by testing the provided URLs. Check that RDS instances are not publicly accessible and that proper security groups are configured. Look for evidence of IAM role usage rather than access keys. Common issues include: security groups blocking necessary traffic, database connection errors due to misconfigured credentials or network settings, and instances launched outside the free tier. Award partial credit for partially working implementations if documentation clearly explains what was attempted. Excellent projects may include additional features like load balancing, auto-scaling groups, or CloudFormation templates (bonus points possible). Deduct points for poor documentation, missing screenshots, or security misconfigurations that expose sensitive data.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS - Students Will

Configure S3 buckets for static content hosting
Apply cost optimization strategies for AWS resources

Security Implementation (25 points): Configure security groups with principle of least privilege, implement proper IAM roles, and secure database access

title: Basic Web Application Development Exam
description: Students will demonstrate fundamental programming concepts by building a simple personal portfolio website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This hands-on exam assesses basic syntax knowledge, problem-solving skills, and ability to implement interactive web features.
learning_objectives_assessed: Write clean, syntactically correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code
Implement basic programming constructs including variables, functions, and event handling
Create responsive web layouts using CSS fundamentals
Debug simple code errors and implement basic interactive features
Follow web development best practices and semantic markup
rubric_criteria: HTML Structure & Semantics (25 points): Proper use of semantic HTML5 elements, valid markup, appropriate document structure, and accessibility considerations
CSS Styling & Layout (25 points): Effective use of CSS properties, responsive design principles, proper selector usage, and visual appeal
JavaScript Functionality (25 points): Correct implementation of required interactive features, proper syntax, working event handlers, and error-free execution
Code Quality & Best Practices (25 points): Clean, readable code with consistent formatting, meaningful variable names, appropriate comments, and adherence to web standards
instructions: Create a personal portfolio website with the following requirements: 1) HTML: Build a single-page website with header, navigation, about section, projects section, and footer using semantic HTML5 elements. Include at least 3 placeholder project entries with titles and descriptions. 2) CSS: Style your portfolio to be visually appealing and responsive. Ensure all files are properly linked and the website functions completely when opened locally. Test your code in a web browser before submission. You may use online resources for syntax reference but all code must be your own work. Comment your JavaScript code to explain functionality.
grading_notes: Use browser developer tools to verify HTML validation and CSS functionality. Test JavaScript features by interacting with all elements. Common issues include: missing semantic elements, non-responsive CSS, JavaScript errors preventing execution, and improper file linking. Expect grade distribution: 90-100 points (A) for fully functional sites with clean code, 80-89 points (B) for mostly working sites with minor issues, 70-79 points (C) for sites with significant problems but demonstrating basic understanding, below 70 points for non-functional or incomplete submissions.

instructions:

title: E-commerce Analytics Implementation and Optimization Project

Professional Reporting and Documentation (25 points): Clear, professional presentation of findings through custom dashboards, visualizations, and written reports that effectively communicate insights to stakeholders with proper data interpretation and context
instructions: You will work with a provided e-commerce website scenario (online electronics retailer) to complete this comprehensive Google Analytics project. First, set up a GA4 property and implement tracking using Google Tag Manager, configuring enhanced e-commerce events including purchases, add-to-cart, and product views. Using the provided 6-month historical data simulation, conduct thorough analysis covering traffic acquisition, user behavior flow, product performance, and conversion funnel analysis. Identify drop-off points, high-performing content, and user engagement patterns. Create a custom dashboard displaying key KPIs and automated reports for stakeholder distribution. Deliverables include: (1) Screenshots of GA4 configuration with explanatory annotations, (2) GTM container export file, (3) Custom dashboard with 8-10 key metrics, (4) 15-page analytical report with executive summary, findings, and strategic recommendations, (5) 10-minute video presentation summarizing insights and recommendations. Ensure all tracking complies with privacy regulations and include data retention considerations in your implementation documentation.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical accuracy by reviewing GA4 configurations and GTM setups for proper implementation - look for correct event parameters, conversion tracking, and audience definitions. For data analysis, assess depth of insights beyond basic metrics - students should demonstrate understanding of attribution models, cohort analysis, and segment comparisons. instructions: Create a comprehensive portfolio documenting the design and implementation of an enterprise network for 'TechCorp,' a technology company with headquarters (500 users), two branch offices (100 users each), and remote workers. title: AWS Cloud Fundamentals Knowledge Assessment
description: A comprehensive quiz evaluating students' understanding of core AWS services, security fundamentals, pricing models, and basic cloud architecture principles. This assessment covers essential concepts needed for entry-level cloud roles and AWS certification preparation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and describe core AWS services including compute, storage, database, and networking
Explain AWS security features, shared responsibility model, and basic access management
Compare AWS pricing models and cost optimization strategies
Demonstrate understanding of cloud deployment models and basic architectural concepts
rubric_criteria: Core Services Knowledge (25 points): Accurately identifies AWS compute (EC2, Lambda), storage (S3, EBS), database (RDS, DynamoDB), and networking services with correct use cases
Security and Access Management (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of IAM, security groups, shared responsibility model, and basic security best practices
Pricing and Cost Management (25 points): Shows knowledge of on-demand, reserved, and spot pricing; understands cost factors and basic optimization strategies
Cloud Architecture Fundamentals (25 points): Correctly explains availability zones, regions, scalability concepts, and deployment models (public, private, hybrid)
instructions: Complete this 40-question multiple-choice quiz within 45 minutes. The assessment covers four main areas of AWS cloud fundamentals. Read each question carefully and select the single best answer. Questions are worth 2-3 points each based on complexity. You have one attempt to complete this quiz, and it must be finished in one session - you cannot save and return later. Ensure you have a stable internet connection before beginning. The quiz includes scenario-based questions where you'll need to recommend appropriate AWS services for given business requirements. Some questions may have 'select all that apply' formats - these will be clearly marked. Before starting, review your AWS service comparison charts and security best practices notes. Questions cover real-world applications of AWS services, so think about practical use cases rather than just memorizing definitions. Pay special attention to cost optimization scenarios and security implementation questions, as these represent common workplace decisions. If you're unsure about an answer, use elimination strategies and consider the most cost-effective or secure option when applicable. Time management is important - don't spend more than 90 seconds on any single question. Submit your completed quiz before the time limit expires to ensure all answers are recorded.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should follow: 90-100% (A), 80-89% (B), 70-79% (C), 60-69% (D), below 60% (F). Common mistakes include confusing EBS vs S3 storage use cases, misunderstanding shared responsibility boundaries, and incorrectly calculating cost scenarios. Watch for students who struggle with scenario-based questions vs factual recall - this indicates need for more practical application exercises. Partial credit not available for multiple choice format. Students scoring below 70% should be offered remedial resources on weak areas identified through question category analysis. Flag students who finish in under 20 minutes for potential academic integrity review. Provide feedback highlighting specific service categories where improvement needed.

title: AWS Three-Tier Web Application Deployment Portfolio

learning_objectives_assessed: Deploy and configure EC2 instances with proper security groups and networking

title: Project Risk Management Plan Presentation

learning_objectives_assessed: Apply risk identification techniques to recognize potential project threats and opportunities
Perform qualitative and quantitative risk analysis using PMP standard tools and techniques

rubric_criteria: Risk Identification & Documentation (25 points): Comprehensive identification of at least 15 risks using multiple techniques (brainstorming, SWOT, expert judgment), proper risk register format, clear risk categorization using RBS

Risk Response Planning (25 points): Appropriate response strategies for top 10 risks (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept), realistic implementation plans, clear assignment of risk owners, consideration of secondary and residual risks

Submit your presentation slides and a detailed risk register (Excel format) 24 hours before your scheduled presentation date via the course management system. Assume a project budget of $2-5 million and timeline of 12-18 months. Use PMI standard templates and terminology throughout your deliverables.
grading_notes: Evaluate presentations using the four-point scale: Exemplary (23-25 points), Proficient (20-22 points), Developing (17-19 points), Inadequate (0-16 points). title: Advanced Electromagnetic Induction System Design and Analysis Project
description: Students will design, build, and comprehensively analyze an electromagnetic induction system (such as a wireless charging station, electromagnetic brake, or induction heater) incorporating advanced concepts including Faraday's law, Lenz's law, eddy currents, and AC circuit analysis. The project requires theoretical modeling, practical construction, experimental validation, and optimization analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply Faraday's law and Lenz's law to predict and calculate induced EMF in complex geometries
Analyze AC circuits with impedance, phase relationships, and power considerations
Model magnetic field distributions using mathematical tools and simulation software
Design and optimize electromagnetic systems for specific performance criteria
Evaluate energy efficiency and power losses in electromagnetic devices
Integrate theoretical predictions with experimental measurements and analyze discrepancies
rubric_criteria: Theoretical Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of electromagnetic principles with accurate mathematical modeling, proper application of Faraday's and Lenz's laws, correct impedance calculations, and sophisticated understanding of magnetic field theory. Includes detailed derivations and justifications for all theoretical predictions.

System Design and Construction (25 points): Creates a functional electromagnetic induction device with appropriate component selection, innovative design features, proper safety considerations, and evidence of iterative improvement. Device must operate reliably and meet specified performance targets.

Experimental Methodology and Data Analysis (25 points): Implements rigorous experimental procedures with appropriate instrumentation, systematic data collection, statistical analysis of uncertainties, and comprehensive comparison between theoretical and experimental results. Identifies and quantifies sources of error.

Optimization and Professional Communication (25 points): Provides evidence-based recommendations for system improvements, analyzes trade-offs between competing design parameters, and presents findings through a professional technical report with clear figures, proper citations, and executive summary suitable for engineering audiences.
instructions: Select one electromagnetic induction application: wireless power transfer system, electromagnetic braking system, or induction heating device. Your project must include: (1) Theoretical modeling section deriving all relevant equations from first principles, calculating expected EMF, current, power, and efficiency. Use Maxwell's equations where appropriate and justify all approximations. (2) Design documentation with detailed schematics, component specifications, safety analysis, and cost estimation. Include CAD drawings or technical sketches with dimensions. (3) Construction of a working prototype with photographic documentation of assembly process. Device must operate safely and demonstrate key electromagnetic principles. (4) Experimental validation measuring at least 5 key parameters (EMF, current, power, efficiency, magnetic field strength) across multiple operating conditions. Include uncertainty analysis and error propagation. (5) Optimization study examining how 3+ design parameters affect performance, with recommendations for improvement backed by quantitative analysis. Submit a 15-page technical report following IEEE format, plus appendices with raw data, calculations, and construction photos. Include a 5-minute video demonstration of your working device. All theoretical work must show complete derivations, not just final equations. Cite minimum 8 peer-reviewed sources. Project timeline: Week 1-2 design and modeling, Week 3-4 construction, Week 5-6 testing and optimization, Week 7-8 report writing.
grading_notes: Look for sophisticated understanding beyond basic textbook applications - students should demonstrate ability to handle complex geometries, non-ideal components, and real-world constraints. Theoretical analysis should show original derivation work, not copied equations. Experimental section must show genuine scientific methodology with proper controls and statistical treatment. Common issues: insufficient error analysis, theoretical models that don't match experimental setup, safety violations during construction, poor quality experimental data due to inadequate instrumentation. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A grades (exceptional innovation and analysis), 40% B grades (solid competent work meeting all requirements), 30% C grades (adequate but lacking depth or rigor), 10% D/F grades (incomplete or fundamentally flawed). Deduct points for late submission: 5 points per day. Bonus points (up to 5) available for exceptional innovation, sophisticated analysis techniques, or practical applications with commercial potential.

instructions: Design and construct an electromagnetic induction system capable of generating at least 10 volts with minimum 60% efficiency. Your system must incorporate at least three advanced electromagnetic concepts (e.g., mutual inductance, eddy current minimization, magnetic flux optimization). Begin with comprehensive theoretical modeling using Maxwell's equations to predict performance. Build your system using appropriate materials and document all design decisions with scientific justification. Conduct systematic experimental testing with at least 15 data points across different operating conditions. Measure key parameters including voltage output, current, power efficiency, and magnetic field strength using calibrated instruments. Calculate uncertainties for all measurements and perform statistical analysis comparing experimental results to theoretical predictions. Submit a 15-page technical report following IEEE format standards, including: executive summary (1 page), theoretical background with mathematical derivations (3-4 pages), system design and construction details (3-4 pages), experimental methodology and results (4-5 pages), discussion and engineering analysis (2-3 pages), and conclusions with improvement recommendations (1 page). Include minimum 10 professional references. Provide complete circuit diagrams, CAD drawings or detailed sketches, data tables, and error analysis calculations. Present findings in 15-minute oral presentation with demonstration of working system. All work must be original with proper citation of sources. Late submissions penalized 10% per day.
grading_notes: Evaluate functional systems through live demonstration - non-functional systems receive maximum 15/25 for construction criterion. Mathematical modeling should show mastery beyond undergraduate level; look for proper boundary conditions, realistic assumptions, and integration of multiple physics principles. Experimental analysis must include propagated uncertainties - projects without uncertainty analysis cannot exceed 20/25 for methodology criterion. Professional documentation requires IEEE formatting, clear technical writing, and publication-quality figures. Common issues include insufficient theoretical depth, inadequate error analysis, poor documentation of design decisions, and unrealistic efficiency claims. Grade distribution typically: 15% receive 90-100 points, 40% receive 80-89 points, 35% receive 70-79 points, 10% below 70 points. Exceptional projects demonstrating innovation or achieving >80% efficiency may receive bonus points up to 105/100.

title: Distributed Systems Architecture Design Discussion and Critique
description: Students will design a distributed system architecture for a large-scale application, defend their design choices, and critically analyze peer submissions through structured discussions and technical evaluations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed system architectures considering trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Evaluate and justify technology choices for distributed systems components including databases, message queues, and load balancers
Analyze system designs for potential failure modes and propose fault tolerance mechanisms
Communicate complex technical designs effectively through documentation and peer critique
rubric_criteria: System Architecture Design (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of distributed systems principles, appropriate component selection, clear system boundaries, and realistic scalability considerations

Technical Justification (25 points): Provides well-reasoned explanations for all major design decisions, accurately identifies trade-offs, addresses CAP theorem implications, and demonstrates deep knowledge of chosen technologies

Failure Analysis & Resilience (25 points): Identifies potential failure modes, proposes appropriate fault tolerance mechanisms, considers data consistency scenarios, and designs for graceful degradation

Peer Review Quality (25 points): Provides constructive, technically accurate feedback to peers, identifies genuine design issues, suggests viable alternatives, and engages meaningfully in follow-up discussions
instructions: You will complete this assessment in two phases over two weeks. **Phase 1 (Week 1):** Design a distributed system architecture for a social media platform handling 50 million daily active users. Your submission must include: (1) A system architecture diagram showing all major components, data flow, and communication patterns; (2) A 1500-word technical specification documenting your database choices (SQL/NoSQL), caching strategies, microservices breakdown, load balancing approach, and message queue implementation; (3) A failure analysis section identifying at least 5 potential failure scenarios and your mitigation strategies. Submit your design as a PDF with embedded diagrams. **Phase 2 (Week 2):** You will be assigned 3 peer submissions to review. For each review, provide: (1) A 500-word technical critique identifying strengths and weaknesses; (2) At least 2 specific improvement suggestions with technical rationale; (3) Questions about design choices that need clarification. Post reviews in the discussion forum by Wednesday, then engage in follow-up discussions with your peers through Friday. Original authors must respond to all reviews and questions.
