Use proper technical terminology, cite relevant papers or industry examples where appropriate, and maintain professional discourse. All submissions must demonstrate graduate-level technical depth and consideration of real-world constraints including cost, maintenance, and team expertise.
grading_notes: Evaluate system designs for technical feasibility rather than theoretical perfection. Look for evidence of understanding core distributed systems concepts: eventual consistency, partitioning strategies, consensus algorithms, and service discovery. Strong submissions will acknowledge limitations and make pragmatic trade-offs. Common issues include: oversimplified database sharding strategies, unrealistic consistency guarantees, missing consideration of operational complexity. Peer reviews should be assessed on technical accuracy and constructiveness rather than length. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (90-100), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Students who fail to complete peer reviews lose 25 points regardless of design quality. Plagiarism check all submissions against common distributed systems textbooks and online resources.

title: Data Science Process and Insights Presentation
description: Students will create and deliver a 10-minute presentation analyzing a provided dataset, demonstrating their understanding of the data science workflow from exploration to insights communication
estimated_time: 6-8 hours (4-5 hours preparation, 1-2 hours presentation creation, 10 minutes presentation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply the data science process (question formulation, data exploration, analysis, interpretation)
Create effective data visualizations using appropriate chart types
Communicate data-driven insights to non-technical audiences
Identify data quality issues and limitations in analysis
rubric_criteria: Data Exploration and Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates systematic exploration of dataset, identifies key patterns/trends, shows appropriate use of summary statistics and data profiling techniques

Visualization Quality (25 points): Creates clear, appropriate, and well-labeled charts that effectively support findings; uses proper chart types for data; includes titles, axes labels, and legends where needed
Insights and Interpretation (25 points): Draws meaningful, data-supported conclusions; explains business/real-world implications; acknowledges limitations and potential biases in the data or analysis

Presentation Skills (25 points): Delivers clear, organized presentation within time limit; uses non-technical language appropriate for general audience; engages audience and handles questions effectively
instructions: You will receive a real-world dataset (e.g., retail sales, survey responses, or public health data) and must create a 10-minute presentation for a non-technical audience. Your presentation must include: 1) A brief introduction to the dataset and your main research question, 2) 3-4 key findings supported by visualizations, 3) At least one surprising or counterintuitive discovery, 4) Business recommendations or actionable insights, and 5) A discussion of data limitations. Create 8-10 slides using any presentation software. Include at least 4 different types of visualizations (bar charts, line graphs, scatter plots, etc.). Prepare to answer 2-3 audience questions. Submit your slide deck as PDF 24 hours before your presentation slot. During presentation, focus on storytelling rather than technical methods - imagine you're presenting to company executives or community stakeholders who need to make decisions based on your analysis. Practice timing to ensure you finish within the 10-minute limit while allowing time for questions.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of systematic thinking rather than just correct answers. Award full points for exploration even if students don't find earth-shattering insights - the process matters more than the findings. Common issues to watch: overly technical language, poor time management, visualizations without clear labels, conclusions not supported by data shown. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90+), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Deduct points for going significantly over time limit. Give partial credit for good process even if final insights are weak.

title: Distributed Hash Table Implementation and Performance Analysis
description: Students will implement a distributed hash table (DHT) using consistent hashing with virtual nodes, conduct comprehensive performance testing under various network conditions, and analyze the system's behavior during node failures and recovery scenarios.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems with fault tolerance mechanisms
Apply consistent hashing algorithms to achieve load balancing in distributed environments
Analyze system performance under varying network conditions and failure scenarios
Demonstrate understanding of distributed systems principles including replication, partitioning, and eventual consistency
rubric_criteria: Implementation Quality (25 points): Correct implementation of DHT with consistent hashing, virtual nodes, and replication factor of 3. Code must be well-structured, documented, and handle edge cases appropriately.

Fault Tolerance and Recovery (25 points): Proper implementation of node failure detection, data migration during joins/leaves, and recovery mechanisms. System must maintain data availability during planned and unplanned node departures.

Performance Analysis (25 points): Comprehensive testing with at least 3 different cluster sizes (5, 10, 20 nodes), measurement of lookup latency, storage distribution variance, and network overhead. Results must be presented with statistical analysis and visualizations.

Technical Communication (25 points): Clear lab report with system architecture diagrams, detailed methodology, results interpretation, limitations discussion, and professional presentation. Code must include comprehensive documentation and README with setup instructions.
instructions: Implement a distributed hash table supporting basic operations (PUT, GET, DELETE) across multiple nodes. Your implementation must use consistent hashing with virtual nodes (minimum 150 virtual nodes per physical node) and maintain a replication factor of 3. The system should handle dynamic node joins and departures gracefully. Provide a configuration file for cluster setup and implement a simple gossip protocol for failure detection with configurable heartbeat intervals. Create a test suite that simulates various scenarios: normal operations with different data loads, planned node departures, unplanned failures (simulate by killing processes), and network partitions. Measure and analyze: average lookup latency, data distribution variance across nodes, network message overhead, and recovery time after failures. Your submission must include: (1) Complete source code with build instructions, (2) Configuration files for different test scenarios, (3) Automated test scripts, (4) A detailed lab report (8-12 pages) covering system design, implementation challenges, experimental methodology, results analysis, and performance bottlenecks identified. Include system architecture diagrams and performance graphs. Submit all materials in a single ZIP file named 'LastName_DHT_Lab.zip' via the course management system. Late submissions will incur a 10% penalty per day. Schedule a 15-minute demo session during office hours to walk through your implementation and answer questions about design decisions.
grading_notes: Focus on correctness of the consistent hashing implementation - common issues include improper hash ring management and incorrect virtual node placement. Verify that replication is working correctly by testing data availability after node failures. Performance analysis should show understanding of distributed systems trade-offs; look for discussion of CAP theorem implications. Code quality assessment should consider modularity, error handling, and documentation completeness. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-range (exceptional implementations with optimizations), 60% B-range (solid implementations meeting all requirements), 20% C-range (implementations with minor issues or incomplete testing), 5% below C (significant functionality missing). Common issues to watch: improper failure detection leading to false positives, data inconsistency during network partitions, inadequate testing scenarios, and superficial performance analysis. Bonus consideration (up to 5 points) for implementations that include advanced features like merkle trees for consistency checking or adaptive replication strategies.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Assessment: Model Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization
description: Students will demonstrate expert-level understanding of machine learning pipeline design by implementing and comparing multiple algorithms with advanced hyperparameter optimization techniques on a complex, real-world dataset with class imbalance and missing values.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model validation
Apply advanced hyperparameter optimization techniques including Bayesian optimization and automated feature selection
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics for imbalanced datasets and provide statistical significance testing
Analyze and interpret model results, including feature importance, bias detection, and business impact assessment
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering (25 points): Proper handling of missing values, outliers, and categorical variables; creation of meaningful derived features; appropriate scaling and encoding techniques; documentation of preprocessing decisions

Model Implementation and Hyperparameter Optimization (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (tree-based, linear, and ensemble); use of advanced optimization techniques (GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, or Bayesian optimization); proper cross-validation strategy with appropriate scoring metrics

Model Evaluation and Statistical Analysis (25 points): Use of appropriate metrics for imbalanced classification (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR); statistical significance testing between models; analysis of confusion matrices and classification reports; consideration of business cost implications

Code Quality and Business Interpretation (25 points): Clean, well-documented, reproducible code with clear variable names and comments; professional presentation of results; actionable business recommendations based on model insights; identification of model limitations and potential biases
instructions: You are provided with a customer churn dataset containing 50,000 records with 23 features including demographic, behavioral, and transactional data. Your task is to build a comprehensive machine learning pipeline to predict customer churn with high precision while maintaining reasonable recall. Submit a Jupyter notebook containing: (1) Exploratory data analysis with at least 5 meaningful visualizations and statistical insights about churn patterns, (2) Complete data preprocessing pipeline handling missing values (12% missing), outliers, and feature engineering including interaction terms and domain-specific derived features, (3) Implementation and comparison of at least three different algorithms: one tree-based model (Random Forest or XGBoost), one linear model (Logistic Regression with regularization), and one ensemble method (Voting Classifier or Stacking), (4) Hyperparameter optimization using either Bayesian optimization (preferred) or comprehensive grid search with at least 5 hyperparameters per model, (5) Model evaluation using stratified k-fold cross-validation with business-relevant metrics, including cost-benefit analysis assuming $100 cost to retain a customer and $500 loss per churned customer, (6) Feature importance analysis and interpretation of at least top 10 predictive features with business context, (7) Model fairness analysis across different customer segments (age groups, tenure, contract types), (8) Final recommendation including model selection rationale, expected business impact, deployment considerations, and monitoring strategy. Code must be reproducible with random seeds set. Include executive summary (max 500 words) suitable for non-technical stakeholders.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should follow: 90-100 points (A): Exceptional work with innovative approaches, comprehensive analysis, and clear business value; 80-89 points (B): Solid implementation meeting all requirements with good insights; 70-79 points (C): Adequate work with minor gaps in analysis or technical implementation; Below 70 points: Significant deficiencies in core requirements. Common issues to deduct points for: hardcoded values without explanation (-5), data leakage in preprocessing (-10), inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data (-8), lack of statistical significance testing (-7), poor code documentation (-5), unrealistic business recommendations (-8), missing fairness analysis (-10). Bonus points (up to 5) for: advanced techniques like SHAP values, automated feature selection, or novel evaluation approaches. Ensure notebooks run completely without errors - deduct 10 points for execution failures.

title: Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Midterm Exam
description: A comprehensive examination testing students' understanding of fundamental data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables) and algorithm analysis including time/space complexity, searching, and sorting algorithms. Students will demonstrate both theoretical knowledge and practical problem-solving skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze time and space complexity of algorithms using Big O notation
Implement and manipulate fundamental data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, binary trees)
Design and evaluate searching and sorting algorithms
Select appropriate data structures for given problem scenarios
Trace algorithm execution and predict outcomes
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Analysis & Big O (25 points): Correctly determines time/space complexity, uses proper Big O notation, shows clear mathematical reasoning for complexity calculations
Data Structure Implementation (25 points): Demonstrates accurate understanding of data structure operations, writes syntactically correct pseudocode/code, handles edge cases appropriately
Problem Solving & Algorithm Design (25 points): Selects optimal algorithms for given problems, shows logical problem decomposition, provides efficient solutions with clear step-by-step approaches

Technical Communication & Accuracy (25 points): Uses proper computer science terminology, shows work clearly with organized presentations, provides accurate final answers with minimal computational errors
instructions:
This exam consists of 6 problems covering data structures and algorithm analysis. Read all questions carefully before beginning. Show all work for partial credit consideration. For coding problems, you may use pseudocode or any programming language covered in class (Python, Java, C++). Clearly indicate your chosen language.

Section A (Problems 1-2): Algorithm complexity analysis - determine Big O notation for given code snippets and justify your answers with step-by-step analysis.

Section B (Problems 3-4): Data structure implementation - write code to implement specific operations (e.g., insert into binary search tree, queue operations) and trace through execution examples.

Section C (Problems 5-6): Applied problem solving - design algorithms to solve real-world scenarios using appropriate data structures, then analyze their efficiency.

Submission requirements: Write legibly in blue or black ink. Cross out mistakes clearly rather than using correction fluid. Number your solutions clearly. If you need additional space, use the back of pages and indicate continuation clearly. Time management suggestion: spend approximately 20 minutes per problem. Budget time for review in the final 10 minutes.
grading_notes: Partial credit available for all problems - award points for correct approach even with minor errors. For complexity analysis, accept equivalent correct notations (e.g., O(n²) = O(2n²)). In coding sections, focus on logic over syntax perfection but deduct for major syntax errors that would prevent compilation. Common issues to watch: students confusing worst-case vs average-case complexity, off-by-one errors in array operations, incorrect tree traversal orders. Expected grade distribution: 85-100 (A range) for students showing mastery of most concepts, 70-84 (B range) for solid understanding with some gaps, below 70 (C or below) for significant conceptual misunderstandings. Provide specific feedback on major errors to guide future study.

title: Ethical AI and Algorithmic Bias in Production Systems: A Critical Analysis Discussion
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world cases of algorithmic bias in deployed machine learning systems, examining the technical causes, societal impacts, and proposing comprehensive mitigation strategies from both technical and organizational perspectives.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (initial research and post preparation: 3 hours, discussion participation: 1-2 hours)
learning_objectives_assessed: Critically evaluate ethical implications of machine learning models in real-world applications
Analyze technical sources of bias in data collection, feature engineering, and model development processes
Synthesize interdisciplinary approaches to responsible AI implementation in organizational contexts
Communicate complex technical concepts and their societal implications to diverse stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis Depth (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of bias sources (data, algorithmic, evaluation), statistical concepts (fairness metrics, confounding variables), and technical mitigation strategies with specific implementation details

Case Study Integration (25 points): Provides well-researched, current examples with quantitative evidence, connects multiple real-world cases, and draws meaningful parallels between different domains (healthcare, criminal justice, hiring, etc.)

Solution Framework Quality (25 points): Proposes comprehensive, feasible solutions addressing technical, organizational, and regulatory dimensions; considers implementation challenges, resource requirements, and stakeholder perspectives

Discussion Engagement (25 points): Responds thoughtfully to peers with evidence-based arguments, asks probing questions that advance collective understanding, builds constructively on others' ideas, and facilitates inclusive dialogue
instructions: Participate in a week-long asynchronous discussion examining algorithmic bias in production ML systems. Begin by selecting two recent cases (within last 3 years) of documented algorithmic bias from different domains. Your initial post (400-600 words) must include: (1) Technical analysis of bias sources using specific fairness metrics and statistical concepts covered in class, (2) Quantitative evidence of disparate impact with citations to peer-reviewed sources or official reports, (3) Comprehensive mitigation framework addressing data governance, model validation, monitoring systems, and organizational policies. Support arguments with at least 5 credible sources including academic papers, industry reports, or regulatory documentation. Respond substantively to minimum 3 peers' posts (150-200 words each), challenging assumptions, offering alternative perspectives, or extending their analysis. Responses should demonstrate engagement with technical details and propose specific improvements or additional considerations. Use proper data science terminology and cite sources in APA format. Submit initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM, complete peer responses by Sunday 11:59 PM. Posts must be original work with proper attribution of all sources and data.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical accuracy using standard fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, etc.) and statistical reasoning. Look for evidence of research beyond course materials - high-scoring submissions typically cite recent academic papers and industry case studies. Common weaknesses include superficial bias analysis without quantitative evidence, generic solutions lacking implementation specifics, and peer responses that merely agree without adding substantive value. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Deduct points for late submissions (5 points per day), insufficient peer engagement, or failure to use proper citations. Watch for potential academic integrity issues in case study selection - students may use same high-profile cases without adding unique analysis.

title: Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Original Proof and Applications
description: Students will conduct independent research on an open problem or recent development in advanced mathematics, develop an original proof or solution approach, and present their findings in a 20-minute formal presentation to demonstrate mastery of advanced mathematical reasoning, proof techniques, and communication skills.
estimated_time: 40-50 hours total (30-35 hours research and preparation, 20 minutes presentation, 10-15 minutes Q&A)
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate mastery of advanced proof techniques including direct proof, contradiction, induction, and constructive methods
Apply sophisticated mathematical reasoning to analyze complex problems and develop original solutions
Synthesize knowledge across multiple mathematical domains to tackle interdisciplinary problems
Communicate complex mathematical concepts clearly and precisely to expert audiences
Evaluate and critique mathematical arguments for logical consistency and completeness
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Proof Quality (25 points): Original proof or solution demonstrates advanced techniques, logical consistency, completeness, and mathematical sophistication. All steps are justified, notation is precise, and arguments are sound.

Research Depth and Innovation (25 points): Shows comprehensive understanding of relevant literature, identifies meaningful connections between concepts, presents novel insights or approaches, and demonstrates independent mathematical thinking.

Presentation Clarity and Organization (25 points): Complex ideas are explained clearly with appropriate visual aids, logical flow from motivation through conclusion, effective use of examples, and maintains audience engagement throughout.

Technical Defense and Q&A Response (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding by answering challenging questions accurately, defending methodology and conclusions effectively, acknowledging limitations appropriately, and engaging in sophisticated mathematical discourse.
instructions: Select an advanced mathematical topic from approved areas including algebraic topology, functional analysis, number theory, or differential geometry. Your presentation must include: (1) A 5-minute introduction establishing context, motivation, and stating your main theorem or conjecture; (2) A 10-minute technical section presenting your original proof, solution method, or theoretical framework with complete mathematical details; (3) A 5-minute conclusion discussing applications, implications, and future research directions. Submit a written component 48 hours before presentation including: complete proof manuscript (8-12 pages), annotated bibliography of 15+ sources, and presentation slides. Your proof must demonstrate advanced techniques beyond undergraduate level and show original thinking—extensions of known results, novel proof methods, or applications to new domains are acceptable. Visual aids should enhance understanding without replacing rigorous mathematical exposition. Prepare for 10-15 minutes of technical questioning from faculty and peers. All mathematical notation must follow standard conventions, and any computational tools used must be documented and validated.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical content independently from presentation skills initially, then consider integration. For Mathematical Rigor: A-level work shows proof techniques appropriate for graduate courses, B-level demonstrates solid undergraduate advanced methods, C-level meets basic proof standards. For Research Depth: Look for evidence of reading primary sources, understanding historical context, and making non-trivial connections. Common issues include: insufficient literature review, proof gaps disguised by presentation style, over-reliance on computational verification without theoretical insight. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations: 15-20% A grades (exceptional original contribution), 40-50% B grades (solid advanced work), remainder C or below. During Q&A, assess ability to think on feet and defend work under scrutiny—this distinguishes true mathematical maturity from memorized presentations.

title: Personal Programming Journey Portfolio
description: Students create a comprehensive portfolio documenting their learning journey in programming fundamentals, showcasing completed projects, reflection on problem-solving approaches, and demonstration of core computer science concepts through practical applications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply fundamental programming concepts (variables, loops, conditionals, functions) to solve basic problems
Demonstrate understanding of basic data structures (arrays, lists) and their practical applications
Practice systematic problem-solving and debugging techniques
Reflect on learning progress and articulate programming concepts in written form
rubric_criteria: Code Quality & Functionality (25 points): Programs run without errors, demonstrate proper syntax, show correct implementation of required concepts (variables, loops, conditionals, functions), and include meaningful variable names and basic comments

Problem-Solving Documentation (25 points): Clear explanation of approach to each problem, evidence of planning or pseudocode, documentation of debugging process, and demonstration of iterative improvement in solutions

Concept Application (25 points): Correct use of at least 3 fundamental programming concepts across projects, appropriate selection of data structures for given problems, and progressive complexity showing growth in understanding

Reflection & Communication (25 points): Thoughtful written reflection on learning process, clear explanation of challenges encountered and overcome, articulation of how concepts connect to real-world applications, and professional presentation of portfolio materials
instructions: Create a digital portfolio containing: 1) Five programming projects of increasing complexity (simple calculator, number guessing game, basic data organizer, pattern generator, and one project of your choice), 2) Written reflection (500-750 words) on your programming journey, including biggest challenges, breakthrough moments, and future learning goals, 3) Problem-solving documentation for each project showing your planning process, including pseudocode or flowcharts, 4) Code commentary explaining key decisions and learning moments. Organize your portfolio in a clear folder structure with separate files for each project. Include a README file with project descriptions and instructions for running your programs. Submit as a compressed folder or provide access to a GitHub repository. All code must be your original work, though you may reference learning resources (cite any external help). Focus on demonstrating growth and understanding rather than perfection - include examples of problems you solved through debugging and iteration.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of genuine learning progression rather than perfect code. Reward students who show clear problem-solving processes and honest reflection about struggles. Expect beginner-level syntax errors but focus on whether core concepts are correctly applied. Students should demonstrate understanding of fundamental concepts even if implementation isn't flawless. Common issues: insufficient commenting, missing reflection components, projects too simple or too advanced for skill level. Grade distribution expectation: 70-80% of students should score 75-90 points, with higher scores for those showing exceptional reflection and documentation of their learning process.

title: Advanced Multivariable Calculus and Linear Algebra Applications Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' mastery of multivariable calculus concepts including partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector fields, and their applications to optimization and linear transformations. Students will solve complex problems requiring integration of theoretical knowledge with computational skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply partial differentiation techniques to find critical points and classify extrema of multivariable functions
Evaluate double and triple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems and transformation techniques
Analyze vector fields and apply Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, or divergence theorem to solve circulation and flux problems
Solve constrained optimization problems using Lagrange multipliers and interpret results in real-world contexts
rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Mathematical Reasoning (25 points): Correctly identifies appropriate techniques, sets up equations properly, demonstrates clear understanding of underlying mathematical concepts, and shows logical progression of thought
Computational Accuracy (25 points): Executes calculations correctly, applies formulas accurately, handles algebraic manipulations without errors, and arrives at correct numerical or symbolic answers

Application of Advanced Techniques (25 points): Properly applies coordinate transformations, uses appropriate theorems (Green's, Stokes', Divergence), correctly implements Lagrange multipliers, and demonstrates mastery of integration techniques

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Shows all work clearly, uses proper mathematical notation, provides appropriate units and interpretations, and presents solutions in organized, readable format
instructions: This quiz consists of 4 comprehensive problems covering multivariable calculus and linear algebra applications. You have 120 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and use proper mathematical notation throughout your solutions. Each problem is worth 25 points and will be evaluated based on mathematical reasoning, computational accuracy, technique application, and presentation quality. For optimization problems, clearly identify critical points and justify your classification. For integration problems, show your setup including limits and any coordinate transformations. For vector field problems, state which theorem you're applying and verify all necessary conditions. When using Lagrange multipliers, set up the system of equations explicitly and solve systematically. Round final numerical answers to three decimal places where appropriate, but show exact values in intermediate steps. Partial credit will be awarded for correct approach and setup even if computational errors occur. Use separate sheets for each problem and label your solutions clearly. Calculators are permitted for basic arithmetic, but show all calculus steps by hand. Submit all work sheets with your name and student ID clearly written on each page.
grading_notes: Award full points for each criterion when students demonstrate complete mastery. For Problem Setup (25 pts): 20-25 pts for correct approach, 15-19 pts for minor conceptual gaps, 10-14 pts for significant setup errors, below 10 pts for fundamental misunderstanding. For Computational Accuracy (25 pts): Deduct 2-3 points per arithmetic error, 5 points per algebraic mistake, 8-10 points per major computational flaw. For Advanced Techniques (25 pts): Verify correct application of theorems, appropriate coordinate systems, and proper constraint handling. For Communication (25 pts): Expect clear notation, labeled diagrams where relevant, and step-by-step solutions. Common issues include: incorrect Jacobian calculations in transformations, forgetting to check boundary conditions in optimization, misapplying vector calculus theorems, and unclear presentation of final answers. Aim for class average of 75-80%. Students scoring below 60% should be advised to review fundamental concepts before proceeding to applications.

title: Distributed System Design and Implementation: Real-Time Chat Application with Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design and implement a horizontally scalable, real-time chat application using microservices architecture, demonstrating advanced concepts in distributed systems, concurrent programming, database design, and system optimization. The project requires building multiple interconnected services with proper load balancing, fault tolerance, and performance monitoring.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems with microservices architecture
Apply advanced concurrency and synchronization techniques for real-time applications
Implement fault-tolerant systems with proper error handling and recovery mechanisms
Optimize system performance through caching, load balancing, and database design
Demonstrate proficiency in system monitoring, logging, and testing strategies
rubric_criteria: System Architecture and Design (25 points): Proper microservices decomposition, API design, database schema, system diagram quality, scalability considerations, and documentation of architectural decisions

Implementation Quality and Functionality (25 points): Code quality, proper use of design patterns, real-time messaging functionality, user authentication, message persistence, error handling, and adherence to coding standards

Performance and Scalability (25 points): Load balancing implementation, caching strategies, database optimization, horizontal scaling capability, performance benchmarks, and system monitoring integration
Testing and Reliability (25 points): Comprehensive test suite (unit, integration, load tests), fault tolerance mechanisms, graceful degradation, logging implementation, and deployment automation
instructions: Develop a real-time chat application supporting multiple chat rooms and concurrent users. Your system must include: (1) User Service - authentication, user profiles, session management; (2) Chat Service - real-time messaging using WebSockets, message routing; (3) Room Service - chat room creation/management, user permissions; (4) Notification Service - push notifications, email alerts; (5) API Gateway - request routing, rate limiting, authentication middleware. Technical requirements: Use containerization (Docker), implement Redis for caching and message queuing, utilize a relational database for persistence, include load balancer configuration, implement comprehensive logging with structured formats, create automated deployment scripts, and establish monitoring dashboards. Deliverables include: complete source code with clear README, system architecture documentation with diagrams, API documentation, test suite with coverage reports, performance benchmarking results, deployment guide, and 10-minute video demonstration. Your implementation should handle 1000+ concurrent users and demonstrate horizontal scaling capabilities. Include proper error handling, input validation, and security measures including SQL injection prevention and XSS protection. Submit all materials via Git repository with clear commit history showing development progression.
grading_notes: Evaluate system architecture first - look for proper service separation, clear API boundaries, and scalability design. Code quality should demonstrate advanced programming concepts including proper abstraction, error handling, and performance optimization. Test the real-time functionality under load and verify scaling capabilities. Common issues include: inadequate error handling in distributed scenarios, poor database design leading to performance bottlenecks, insufficient testing coverage especially for concurrent operations, and lack of proper monitoring/logging. Grade distribution expectation: 15% excellent (90-100), 25% proficient (80-89), 35% developing (70-79), 20% below expectations (60-69), 5% insufficient (below 60). Pay special attention to system resilience under failure conditions and the quality of documentation for system maintenance.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Basic Statistics Exam
description: A comprehensive written and practical exam assessing students' understanding of fundamental data science concepts, statistical measures, data visualization principles, and basic data cleaning techniques using a provided dataset.
learning_objectives_assessed: Calculate and interpret descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Identify and handle missing data and outliers appropriately
Create and interpret basic data visualizations (histograms, scatter plots, box plots)
Distinguish between different data types and measurement scales
Apply basic statistical concepts to real-world scenarios
rubric_criteria: Statistical Calculations (25 points): Correctly computes descriptive statistics, shows work clearly, interprets results in context with appropriate units and terminology

Data Quality Assessment (25 points): Accurately identifies missing values and outliers, proposes appropriate handling methods with clear justification, demonstrates understanding of data integrity principles
Data Visualization (25 points): Creates appropriate chart types for given data, includes proper labels and titles, demonstrates understanding of when to use different visualization types
Conceptual Understanding (25 points): Correctly identifies data types and measurement scales, explains statistical concepts clearly, applies knowledge to interpret real-world scenarios
instructions:
This exam consists of four sections using the provided 'Customer Sales Dataset' (CSV file available on course platform). You may use calculators and basic statistical software/Excel, but no internet access or collaboration is permitted. Show all work for calculations and provide brief explanations for your reasoning.

Section 1: Calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for the 'purchase_amount' column. Interpret what these values tell us about customer spending patterns.

Section 2: Examine the dataset for missing values and outliers. Document your findings and explain how you would handle each issue. Consider the 'age' and 'purchase_amount' columns specifically.

Section 3: Create three different visualizations: a histogram of purchase amounts, a scatter plot of age vs. purchase amount, and a box plot comparing purchase amounts by customer category. Explain why each chart type is appropriate for the data being displayed.

Section 4: Answer conceptual questions about data types (identify whether variables are nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio) and interpret correlation coefficients provided in a correlation matrix.

Submit your work as a single PDF document with clearly labeled sections. Include any charts/graphs created and ensure all text is legible. Late submissions will be penalized 10% per day.
grading_notes: Use partial credit generously - award points for correct methodology even if final answers contain minor computational errors. Look for evidence of statistical thinking rather than perfect calculations. Common issues include: confusing median/mean interpretations, incorrect outlier identification (watch for students using arbitrary cutoffs rather than statistical methods like IQR), and inappropriate chart selections. Expect grade distribution: 90-100 (20%), 80-89 (40%), 70-79 (30%), below 70 (10%). Deduct 2-3 points for missing labels on charts, unclear work presentation, or failure to provide context in interpretations.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategy Discussion: Optimization in Real-World Contexts
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing different approaches to solving optimization problems, comparing algebraic and calculus-based methods, and evaluating the effectiveness of various problem-solving strategies in real-world scenarios.
estimated_time: 90 minutes (60 minutes preparation + 30 minutes discussion participation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multiple mathematical approaches to solve optimization problems involving quadratic functions and basic calculus
Analyze and compare the efficiency and appropriateness of different problem-solving strategies
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using proper notation and terminology
Evaluate real-world applications of optimization and justify mathematical modeling decisions
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy and Method Application (25 points): Correctly applies at least two different mathematical approaches (algebraic and calculus-based) with accurate calculations, proper notation, and clear mathematical reasoning

Strategic Analysis and Comparison (25 points): Thoroughly compares different solution methods, identifies advantages/disadvantages of each approach, and demonstrates understanding of when to use specific strategies

Communication and Mathematical Language (25 points): Uses precise mathematical terminology, shows work clearly, explains reasoning step-by-step, and responds constructively to peers using appropriate mathematical language

Real-World Application and Critical Thinking (25 points): Effectively connects mathematical solutions to practical implications, identifies assumptions and limitations of models, and demonstrates insight into optimization applications
instructions: You will participate in a discussion forum analyzing optimization problems using multiple solution strategies. Begin by solving the provided scenario: 'A farmer has 240 feet of fencing to create a rectangular enclosure against an existing barn wall. What dimensions maximize the enclosed area?' Solve this problem using both algebraic methods (completing the square) and calculus (derivatives). Post your initial response (400-500 words) including: (1) Complete solutions using both methods with all work shown, (2) Comparison of the two approaches discussing efficiency, complexity, and when each might be preferred, (3) Analysis of real-world considerations the mathematical model might not capture, (4) One additional optimization scenario from your own experience or research. After posting, respond substantively to at least two classmates' solutions (150-200 words each), focusing on: verifying their mathematical work, discussing alternative approaches they might have used, and building on their real-world applications. Use proper mathematical notation, show all algebraic steps, and explain your reasoning clearly. Include units in your final answers and discuss the practical meaning of your mathematical results.
grading_notes: Look for students who show complete mathematical work for both solution methods - many may skip steps in familiar algebraic processes. Strong responses will explicitly compare method efficiency and discuss trade-offs. Watch for proper use of mathematical notation, especially in derivative notation and function representation. Peer responses should go beyond 'I agree' to offer mathematical insights or alternative perspectives. Common issues include forgetting to include units, not connecting mathematical results to real-world meaning, and incomplete justification of optimization claims. Expect grade distribution: 15-20% earn 90-100 points (exceptional mathematical communication), 50-60% earn 80-89 points (solid mathematical work with minor communication issues), 20-25% earn 70-79 points (correct mathematics but weak analysis or peer interaction), <10% below 70 points (significant mathematical errors or insufficient participation).

title: Advanced System Architecture Design and Defense
description: Students will design a comprehensive distributed system architecture for a real-world scenario, present their technical solution to a panel, and defend their design decisions under rigorous questioning. This assessment evaluates advanced system design principles, scalability considerations, and professional communication skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed systems using advanced architectural patterns and principles
Evaluate trade-offs between different system design approaches (CAP theorem, consistency models, performance vs. reliability)
Apply security, monitoring, and fault tolerance strategies in complex system architectures
Communicate complex technical concepts effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
Critically analyze and defend technical decisions under expert scrutiny
rubric_criteria: Technical Architecture Design (30 points): Comprehensive system design including microservices/monolith decisions, database choices, caching strategies, load balancing, API design, and scalability planning. Must demonstrate deep understanding of distributed systems principles.

Implementation Strategy & Technology Stack (25 points): Justified selection of technologies, deployment strategies, CI/CD pipeline design, monitoring and logging solutions. Clear implementation roadmap with realistic timelines and resource allocation.

Presentation Quality & Communication (25 points): Clear visual aids, logical flow, appropriate technical depth for audience, effective use of diagrams and architectural drawings, professional delivery within time constraints.

Defense & Critical Thinking (20 points): Quality of responses during Q&A session, ability to justify design decisions, acknowledgment of limitations and trade-offs, demonstration of deep technical understanding under pressure.
instructions: Select one of the provided real-world scenarios (e.g., designing Netflix's video streaming architecture, Uber's ride-matching system, or a global e-commerce platform). Your presentation must include: (1) Problem analysis and requirements gathering, identifying key constraints and success metrics; (2) High-level system architecture with clear component diagrams showing data flow, service interactions, and external dependencies; (3) Database design including schema decisions, partitioning strategies, and consistency models; (4) Scalability and performance considerations including load balancing, caching layers, and bottleneck identification; (5) Security implementation covering authentication, authorization, data encryption, and vulnerability mitigation; (6) Monitoring, logging, and disaster recovery strategies; (7) Technology stack justification with specific tools, frameworks, and infrastructure choices. Prepare for intensive Q&A covering alternative approaches, failure scenarios, cost optimization, and implementation challenges. Submit architectural diagrams and a 2-page technical summary 24 hours before presentation. Use professional presentation tools and ensure all diagrams are clearly readable. Time limit strictly enforced: 30 minutes presentation, 15 minutes Q&A.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical depth over breadth - students should demonstrate mastery of core distributed systems concepts rather than superficial coverage of many topics. Look for realistic trade-off discussions and acknowledgment of system limitations. During Q&A, assess ability to think on feet and adapt solutions based on new constraints. Common issues: oversimplified scaling solutions, ignoring data consistency challenges, unrealistic performance claims, poor visual presentation of complex architectures. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90+), 25% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 20% below C-level. Deduct points for exceeding time limits or failing to address required components. Bonus consideration for innovative solutions or demonstration of cutting-edge technologies.

title: Predictive Analytics Case Study: Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will conduct a complete data science project analyzing customer churn for a telecommunications company, presenting their methodology, findings, and business recommendations through a 15-minute presentation with supporting materials.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply machine learning algorithms to solve real-world business problems
Perform comprehensive exploratory data analysis and feature engineering
Communicate technical findings to non-technical stakeholders effectively
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Translate data insights into actionable business recommendations
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis & Methodology (25 points): Quality of EDA, appropriate preprocessing steps, feature engineering creativity, proper handling of missing data and outliers, justified algorithm selection

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of multiple algorithms, proper train/validation/test splits, appropriate performance metrics, cross-validation usage, model comparison and selection rationale

Business Impact & Recommendations (25 points): Clear connection between technical findings and business value, specific actionable recommendations, cost-benefit considerations, implementation feasibility, stakeholder-focused insights

Presentation & Communication (25 points): Clear visual storytelling, appropriate technical depth for audience, effective use of visualizations, professional delivery, handling of questions, time management
instructions: You will analyze a telecommunications customer churn dataset to build predictive models and present actionable insights. Your presentation must include: (1) Problem definition and business context (2 minutes), (2) Data exploration findings with key visualizations (4 minutes), (3) Model development process showing at least 2 different algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, or gradient boosting) (4 minutes), (4) Model evaluation with performance metrics, confusion matrix, and feature importance (3 minutes), (5) Business recommendations with specific retention strategies and expected impact (2 minutes). Submit a PowerPoint/PDF presentation file and a Jupyter notebook with complete code 48 hours before your presentation slot. Your audience includes both technical team members and business stakeholders, so balance technical rigor with business relevance. Include at least 5 meaningful visualizations and demonstrate proper statistical validation. Address potential model limitations and next steps. Be prepared to answer questions about your methodology choices, alternative approaches, and implementation challenges.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of iterative analysis rather than just final results. Strong submissions will show multiple modeling approaches with clear comparison criteria. Common issues: inadequate EDA leading to poor feature selection, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced datasets, overly technical presentations without business context, and lack of validation rigor. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90+), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below C-level. Deduct points for late submissions (5 points per day) and presentations exceeding time limits (2 points per minute over). Award bonus points (up to 5) for exceptional creativity in feature engineering or innovative business recommendations.

title: Distributed System Performance Analysis: Implementing and Evaluating a Load-Balanced Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design, implement, and comprehensively analyze a distributed microservices system with load balancing, measure performance under various conditions, and provide detailed technical analysis of system behavior, bottlenecks, and optimization strategies.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement scalable distributed systems using microservices architecture patterns
Apply load balancing algorithms and evaluate their effectiveness in real-world scenarios
Conduct systematic performance analysis using appropriate metrics and profiling tools
Analyze system bottlenecks and propose evidence-based optimization solutions
Demonstrate advanced understanding of distributed systems concepts including consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
rubric_criteria: System Implementation (25 points): Complete microservices architecture with at least 3 services, proper API design, containerization, and functional load balancer implementation with multiple algorithm options

Performance Testing & Data Collection (25 points): Comprehensive test suite covering multiple load scenarios, proper use of monitoring tools, systematic data collection with statistical validity, and appropriate baseline measurements

Technical Analysis & Insights (25 points): Deep analysis of performance characteristics, identification of bottlenecks with supporting evidence, comparison of load balancing strategies, and discussion of CAP theorem implications

Documentation & Presentation (25 points): Professional lab report with clear methodology, well-structured findings, proper technical diagrams, reproducible setup instructions, and evidence of critical thinking in conclusions
instructions: Implement a distributed system consisting of at least three microservices (e.g., user authentication, data processing, and notification services) with a load balancer frontend. Use containerization (Docker) and implement at least two different load balancing algorithms (round-robin, weighted, least connections). Your system must handle realistic workloads and include proper logging and monitoring. Conduct performance tests under various conditions: low load (10 concurrent users), medium load (100 concurrent users), high load (500+ concurrent users), and stress testing until failure. Measure response times, throughput, resource utilization, and system stability. Use appropriate tools such as Apache Bench, JMeter, or custom scripts for load generation, and monitoring tools like Prometheus, Grafana, or built-in container metrics. Document your architecture decisions, test methodology, and provide a detailed analysis of results. Your report must include: system architecture diagram, implementation details, test scenarios and methodology, performance data with statistical analysis, bottleneck identification, load balancer algorithm comparison, and optimization recommendations. Submit source code, configuration files, test scripts, raw performance data, and a comprehensive technical report (8-12 pages). Include clear instructions for reproducing your setup and tests. Ensure your analysis addresses distributed systems concepts such as consistency trade-offs, failure scenarios, and scalability limitations.
grading_notes: Instructors should verify that implementations are student's original work and actually functional - require live demonstrations or detailed setup videos. Look for sophisticated understanding beyond basic implementation: students should demonstrate knowledge of distributed systems theory, not just coding ability. Performance analysis should show statistical rigor - watch for cherry-picked data or insufficient sample sizes. Excellent submissions will identify non-obvious bottlenecks (e.g., database connection pooling, serialization overhead) and provide creative optimization solutions. Common issues include: oversimplified microservices that don't reflect real distributed challenges, inadequate load testing that doesn't stress the system, superficial analysis that doesn't connect observations to underlying system behavior, and missing discussion of distributed systems trade-offs. Grade distribution should reflect the expert level: expect 15% A grades, 35% B grades, as this assessment requires integration of multiple complex concepts and significant independent problem-solving.

title: Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Exploring Real-World Data
description: A comprehensive beginner-level quiz assessing foundational data science concepts including data types, basic statistics, visualization interpretation, and the data science process. Students will answer multiple-choice and short-answer questions based on a provided sample dataset scenario.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify different types of data (categorical, numerical, ordinal)
Calculate and interpret basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Read and interpret common data visualizations (bar charts, histograms, scatter plots)
Understand the steps of the data science lifecycle
Recognize common data quality issues and their potential impact
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Structure (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, understands structured vs unstructured data, recognizes appropriate data collection methods
Basic Statistical Analysis (25 points): Accurately calculates descriptive statistics, interprets measures of central tendency and variability, identifies outliers
Data Visualization Interpretation (25 points): Reads charts and graphs correctly, identifies trends and patterns, selects appropriate visualization types for different data scenarios
Data Science Process and Quality (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of CRISP-DM or similar methodology, identifies data cleaning needs, recognizes ethical considerations in data collection
instructions:
This quiz consists of 20 questions divided into four sections corresponding to fundamental data science concepts. You will be provided with a sample dataset about customer purchases from an online retailer, including variables such as customer age, purchase amount, product category, and satisfaction rating.

Section 1 (Questions 1-5): Data Types and Structure - Examine the provided dataset and answer questions about variable types, data collection methods, and data organization.

Section 2 (Questions 6-10): Basic Statistics - Calculate descriptive statistics using the provided data summary tables. You may use a calculator but must show your work for calculation problems.

Section 3 (Questions 11-15): Visualization Interpretation - Analyze provided charts and graphs created from the dataset. Answer questions about trends, relationships, and appropriate visualization choices.

Section 4 (Questions 16-20): Process and Ethics - Answer conceptual questions about the data science lifecycle, data quality assessment, and ethical considerations.

Submission Requirements: Complete all questions within the time limit. For calculation problems, show your work clearly. For multiple-choice questions, select only one answer unless otherwise specified. Submit your completed quiz through the learning management system before the deadline. Late submissions will incur a 10% penalty per day.
grading_notes: Use the 4-point scale for each criterion: Exemplary (90-100%), Proficient (80-89%), Developing (70-79%), Inadequate (below 70%). Common issues to watch: students confusing ordinal vs nominal data, incorrect calculation of standard deviation, misreading axis labels on charts, and oversimplifying the data science process. Partial credit available for calculation problems with correct methodology but minor errors. Expected grade distribution: 15% A's, 35% B's, 35% C's, 15% D's/F's for typical beginner cohorts.

title: Community Garden Design: Applied Geometry and Data Analysis Project
description: Students will design a community garden layout using geometric principles, calculate areas and perimeters, analyze cost data, and present their design with mathematical justifications. This project integrates geometry, algebra, data analysis, and real-world problem solving.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply geometric formulas to calculate area and perimeter of composite shapes
Use algebraic expressions to model real-world constraints and optimization problems
Analyze and interpret data using graphs, tables, and statistical measures
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations and visual representations
rubric_criteria: Geometric Calculations (25 points): Accurate use of area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, circles, and triangles; correct calculations for total garden area, pathway dimensions, and plot allocations; appropriate use of units throughout

Algebraic Modeling (25 points): Development of cost function expressions; solving inequalities for budget constraints; optimization of garden layout within given parameters; clear variable definitions and equation setup

Data Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Creation of appropriate graphs and tables; calculation of mean, median, and range for cost comparisons; accurate interpretation of data trends; logical conclusions drawn from numerical evidence

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Clear explanations of mathematical reasoning; proper mathematical vocabulary and notation; well-organized presentation with labeled diagrams; justification of design choices using mathematical evidence
instructions: You are tasked with designing a rectangular community garden measuring 40 feet by 60 feet with a $2,400 budget. Your design must include: (1) At least 8 rectangular vegetable plots of varying sizes, (2) One circular herb garden with radius between 4-8 feet, (3) Triangular flower beds in at least two corners, (4) A pathway system that is 3 feet wide connecting all areas. Research and use realistic costs for materials: soil ($3 per cubic foot, 6 inches deep), seeds/plants ($15-50 per plot depending on size), pathway gravel ($2 per square foot), and fencing ($8 per linear foot for the perimeter). Create a scale drawing (1 inch = 5 feet) showing your complete design with all measurements labeled. Calculate the total area used for each garden type and the remaining space. Develop algebraic expressions for your total costs and prove your design stays within budget. Create a data table comparing costs of at least 3 different plot size options and graph this information. Write a 2-page report explaining your design choices, showing all calculations, and justifying how your garden maximizes growing space while staying within budget. Include a reflection on how you used mathematics to solve this real-world problem. Submit your scale drawing, all calculations, data analysis, and written report in a organized portfolio format.
grading_notes: Look for accuracy in basic geometric calculations first - this is foundational. Students often struggle with composite area calculations, so check their breakdown of complex shapes. For algebraic modeling, ensure variables are clearly defined and expressions are properly set up before checking arithmetic. In data analysis, verify that students choose appropriate graph types and scales. Common errors include unit conversion mistakes and not accounting for pathway area when calculating remaining space. Expect some variation in material costs due to research differences, but calculations should be internally consistent. Award partial credit for correct methods even with minor computational errors. Strong projects will show optimization thinking (comparing multiple layout options) and clear connections between mathematical concepts and practical constraints. Grade distribution typically ranges from 75-95, with most students scoring 80-88. Projects scoring below 75 usually have significant calculation errors or incomplete requirements.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Analysis Quiz
description: Expert-level assessment evaluating students' ability to design, implement, and critically analyze end-to-end machine learning pipelines for complex real-world scenarios, including advanced feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and production deployment considerations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement sophisticated feature engineering pipelines for high-dimensional, multi-modal datasets
Apply advanced model selection techniques and ensemble methods for complex prediction tasks
Perform comprehensive hyperparameter optimization using advanced techniques like Bayesian optimization
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics for imbalanced and multi-class problems
Analyze model interpretability and fairness in machine learning systems
Design scalable ML pipelines suitable for production deployment
rubric_criteria: Feature Engineering & Data Preprocessing (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of advanced feature selection, dimensionality reduction, handling missing data, feature scaling, and creating domain-specific features. Shows understanding of data leakage prevention and temporal considerations.

Model Development & Selection (25 points): Implements appropriate advanced algorithms (ensemble methods, neural networks, gradient boosting), demonstrates proper cross-validation strategies, shows understanding of bias-variance tradeoffs, and justifies model selection decisions.

Hyperparameter Optimization & Evaluation (25 points): Applies sophisticated optimization techniques (Grid Search, Random Search, Bayesian optimization), uses appropriate evaluation metrics for the problem context, demonstrates understanding of statistical significance in model comparison.

Production Readiness & Critical Analysis (25 points): Addresses model interpretability, fairness considerations, scalability requirements, monitoring strategies, and provides thoughtful analysis of limitations, potential improvements, and business impact.
instructions: Complete this comprehensive machine learning challenge within 3 hours. You will work with a complex dataset involving customer churn prediction for a telecommunications company with 50+ features, temporal dependencies, and significant class imbalance (5% churn rate). Your submission must include: 1) A Jupyter notebook with complete implementation showing data exploration, feature engineering pipeline, model development, and evaluation. Code must be well-documented with clear explanations of design decisions. 2) A technical report (1000-1500 words) analyzing your approach, model performance, interpretability insights, and production deployment strategy. 3) A presentation slide deck (8-10 slides) summarizing key findings and recommendations for stakeholders. Requirements: Implement at least 3 different algorithm families (tree-based, linear, neural network), apply advanced feature engineering techniques, use appropriate evaluation metrics beyond accuracy, address class imbalance, perform hyperparameter optimization, analyze feature importance and model interpretability, discuss fairness and bias considerations, and propose a monitoring strategy for production deployment. Submit all files in a single ZIP folder named 'LastName_FirstName_MLAssessment.zip' including the Jupyter notebook, technical report (PDF), presentation slides (PDF), and any additional supporting files. Ensure all code runs without errors and reproduces your results.
grading_notes: Use the 4-tier grading scale: Excellent (90-100%), Proficient (80-89%), Developing (70-79%), Inadequate (<70%). Focus on depth of understanding rather than just technical execution. Excellent work should demonstrate innovative approaches, critical thinking about model limitations, and clear communication of complex concepts. Common issues to watch: data leakage in feature engineering, inappropriate evaluation metrics for imbalanced data, overfitting due to inadequate validation strategies, lack of business context in analysis, poor code documentation. Expect 20% Excellent, 40% Proficient, 30% Developing, 10% Inadequate distribution. Deduct points for: code that doesn't run (-10 points), missing required components (-15 points each), inadequate technical explanation (-5-10 points), poor presentation quality (-5 points). Provide detailed feedback on technical accuracy, analytical depth, and communication effectiveness.

title: My Daily Math Journal: Exploring Numbers in Real Life
description: Students will create a week-long math journal documenting how they encounter and use basic mathematical concepts (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, and measurement) in their daily activities. This project demonstrates the practical application of fundamental math skills in real-world contexts.
estimated_time: 7 days for data collection + 2 hours for final compilation and reflection
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) to solve real-world problems
Recognize and use fractions and basic measurement units in practical situations
Communicate mathematical thinking clearly through written explanations and visual representations
Make connections between mathematical concepts and everyday experiences
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): All calculations are correct, appropriate operations are selected for each situation, proper units and labels are used consistently

Real-World Connections (25 points): Identifies diverse, meaningful examples of math in daily life, clearly explains how math concepts apply to each situation, demonstrates understanding of practical applications

Documentation Quality (25 points): Includes at least one math example per day for 7 days, entries are detailed and well-organized, includes visual elements (drawings, photos, charts) to support explanations

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses appropriate math vocabulary, explanations are clear and easy to follow, reflection demonstrates thoughtful analysis of learning, proper grammar and presentation
instructions: For one week, you will become a math detective, finding and documenting mathematical concepts in your daily life. Each day, record at least one example of how you use math, following these requirements: 1) Daily Entries: Write a brief description of the situation, identify the math concept(s) involved, show any calculations with work clearly displayed, explain why math was important in this situation, and include a visual element (drawing, photo, or simple chart). 2) Math Concepts to Look For: Basic operations (adding prices while shopping, calculating change), fractions (cooking measurements, time), measurement (height, weight, distance, temperature), and geometry (shapes in buildings, organizing space). 3) Format Requirements: Use a notebook, folder, or digital document with clear daily sections, write in complete sentences, show all mathematical work step-by-step, and include at least one visual per entry. 4) Final Reflection: After seven days, write a one-page reflection answering: What surprised you about math in daily life? Which math concept did you use most often? How has this project changed how you think about math? 5) Submission: Submit your complete journal with all daily entries, visuals, calculations, and final reflection by the due date. Be creative and thorough – math is everywhere once you start looking for it!
grading_notes: Look for genuine real-world applications rather than contrived examples. Students should demonstrate computational accuracy appropriate for their grade level. Accept creative interpretations of 'daily math' including cooking, sports, shopping, time management, and games. Common issues include: missing work shown for calculations, vague connections between situations and math concepts, insufficient detail in daily entries. Expect grade distribution: 90-100 points (exceeds expectations with creative examples and clear explanations), 80-89 points (meets all requirements with good mathematical accuracy), 70-79 points (meets most requirements but may lack detail or have minor calculation errors), below 70 points (missing significant components or major mathematical errors). Provide feedback on mathematical reasoning and encourage students to see math as relevant and accessible.

title: Ethical AI Implementation: Critical Analysis of Bias Mitigation Strategies in Production Systems
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world case studies of algorithmic bias, evaluate existing mitigation strategies, and propose comprehensive solutions for implementing ethical AI in production environments. This assessment focuses on critical thinking, technical depth, and practical application of bias detection and mitigation techniques.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours over 1 week (initial post: 2 hours, peer responses: 1.5 hours, final reflection: 1 hour)
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate and critique bias detection methodologies and fairness metrics in machine learning systems
Analyze the sociotechnical implications of algorithmic decision-making in high-stakes domains
Design comprehensive bias mitigation strategies that balance technical constraints with ethical considerations
Synthesize interdisciplinary perspectives on AI ethics, incorporating technical, legal, and social viewpoints
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis and Methodology (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of bias detection techniques, fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, etc.), and mitigation strategies. Uses appropriate technical terminology and shows mastery of statistical concepts relevant to fairness assessment.

Critical Evaluation and Case Study Analysis (25 points): Provides thorough analysis of provided case studies, identifies multiple sources and types of bias, evaluates effectiveness of implemented solutions, and demonstrates understanding of real-world constraints and trade-offs.

Solution Design and Innovation (25 points): Proposes comprehensive, technically feasible bias mitigation strategies that address multiple stages of the ML pipeline. Solutions show creativity, consideration of stakeholder needs, and integration of monitoring and feedback mechanisms.

Peer Engagement and Synthesis (25 points): Provides substantive responses to peers that advance the discussion, challenges assumptions constructively, incorporates diverse perspectives, and demonstrates ability to synthesize different viewpoints into coherent arguments.
instructions: This discussion unfolds in three phases over one week. **Phase 1 (Initial Post - Due Day 3):** Select one case study from the provided list (hiring algorithms, criminal justice risk assessment, healthcare AI, or credit scoring systems). Write a 800-1000 word analysis addressing: (1) Identification and classification of bias types present, (2) Evaluation of current mitigation strategies using at least 3 different fairness metrics, (3) Technical assessment of data collection and preprocessing issues, (4) Stakeholder impact analysis. **Phase 2 (Peer Responses - Due Day 5):** Respond to two classmates who analyzed different case studies (minimum 300 words each). Your responses should: compare bias manifestations across domains, challenge or support their proposed solutions with technical evidence, suggest alternative approaches, and identify potential unintended consequences. **Phase 3 (Synthesis Reflection - Due Day 7):** Post a 400-500 word reflection synthesizing insights from all discussions. Address: emerging patterns across domains, most promising mitigation strategies, implementation challenges in production environments, and recommendations for organizational bias auditing processes. **Format Requirements:** Use APA citations for all sources, include relevant code snippets or pseudocode where appropriate, reference specific research papers or industry reports, and maintain professional academic tone throughout. All posts must be original work with proper attribution of ideas and sources.
grading_notes: Instructors should evaluate technical accuracy by checking understanding of fairness metrics and bias detection methods - watch for superficial treatment of complex statistical concepts. Look for evidence of engagement with current research literature (posts should reference recent papers, not just general concepts). Grade peer responses particularly carefully - they should advance discussion rather than simply agreeing; excellent responses will connect ideas across different case studies. Common issues include: oversimplification of technical trade-offs, failure to consider implementation constraints, inadequate consideration of stakeholder perspectives beyond technical teams. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (exceptional technical depth + innovation), 35% B-level (solid technical understanding + good analysis), 40% C-level (basic requirements met), 10% below C-level. Deduct points for late submissions (5 points per day) and inadequate peer engagement (failure to respond substantively to others).

title: Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Exploring Open Problems in Number Theory
description: Students will research, analyze, and present on a current open problem in number theory, demonstrating deep mathematical understanding, rigorous proof techniques, and clear communication of complex mathematical concepts to both expert and general audiences.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate mastery of advanced number theory concepts and their interconnections
Analyze and synthesize current mathematical research literature
Construct rigorous mathematical arguments and identify proof strategies
Communicate complex mathematical ideas effectively to diverse audiences
Evaluate the significance and implications of unsolved mathematical problems
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Content and Rigor (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of the chosen problem, its historical context, related theorems, and partial results. Uses precise mathematical language and notation. Shows clear grasp of proof techniques and approaches attempted.

Research Quality and Literature Review (25 points): Incorporates recent peer-reviewed sources, identifies key contributors to the field, synthesizes multiple perspectives on the problem, and demonstrates awareness of current research directions and methodologies.

Presentation Clarity and Organization (25 points): Structures presentation logically from motivation through technical details to implications. Uses appropriate visual aids, provides clear definitions, and maintains audience engagement while building complexity systematically.

Critical Analysis and Mathematical Reasoning (25 points): Evaluates different approaches to the problem, discusses why the problem remains unsolved, identifies potential breakthrough directions, and demonstrates sophisticated mathematical thinking and problem-solving insights.
instructions: Select an open problem in number theory from the provided list or propose your own with instructor approval. Your 20-minute presentation must include: (1) Historical context and motivation for why this problem matters, (2) Precise statement of the problem with necessary definitions, (3) Overview of major attempts at solution and why they failed, (4) Discussion of partial results and related solved problems, (5) Analysis of current research approaches and recent developments, (6) Your assessment of potential solution strategies or breakthrough directions. Prepare slides that balance rigor with accessibility - assume your audience includes graduate students and faculty from other mathematical areas. Include a 2-page handout with key definitions, theorem statements, and references. Submit slides and handout 24 hours before presentation. Be prepared for technical questions during the Q&A session.
