Recommended problems include: Twin Prime Conjecture, Goldbach Conjecture, Collatz Conjecture, ABC Conjecture, or Riemann Hypothesis aspects. Your presentation should demonstrate graduate-level mathematical sophistication while being pedagogically sound.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - any significant errors in basic concepts or theorem statements should result in substantial point deductions. Look for evidence of genuine understanding vs. surface-level research compilation. Strong presentations will show personal insights and demonstrate ability to think critically about mathematical approaches. Expect most students to score 18-23 points per criterion; reserve 24-25 points for exceptional work showing original thinking or particularly sophisticated analysis. Common issues include: insufficient technical depth, poor time management, unclear notation, failure to explain motivation, and inability to answer basic questions about their chosen problem. Grade distribution should reflect the expert-level nature: 10% A+, 25% A, 35% A-/B+, 25% B range, 5% below B-.

title: Beginner Programming Portfolio: Personal Website with Interactive Features
description: Students will create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating fundamental programming concepts through building a personal website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The portfolio will showcase their understanding of web development basics, problem-solving skills, and ability to implement interactive features.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate proficiency in HTML structure and semantic markup
Apply CSS styling principles including layout, typography, and responsive design
Implement basic JavaScript functionality for user interaction
Practice problem-solving and debugging techniques
Document code effectively with comments and README files
Follow web development best practices and standards
rubric_criteria: HTML Structure & Content (25 points): Proper semantic HTML tags, well-organized content hierarchy, valid markup, includes required sections (header, navigation, about, projects, contact). Must include at least 3 interconnected pages.

CSS Design & Layout (25 points): Effective visual design with consistent styling, proper use of CSS selectors and properties, responsive layout that works on mobile and desktop, creative use of colors and typography.

JavaScript Functionality (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 interactive features (form validation, image gallery, accordion menu, or similar), proper event handling, error-free code execution, demonstrates understanding of DOM manipulation.

Code Quality & Documentation (25 points): Clean, readable code with consistent indentation and naming conventions, meaningful comments explaining complex sections, complete README file with project description and setup instructions, proper file organization and structure.
instructions: Create a personal portfolio website that showcases your programming skills and serves as an introduction to who you are as a developer. Your portfolio must include: 1) A homepage with your name, photo, and brief introduction, 2) An 'About Me' page with your background and interests, 3) A 'Projects' page showcasing at least 2 coding projects (can be class assignments), 4) A contact page with a working contact form. Technical requirements: Use semantic HTML5 elements, implement CSS Grid or Flexbox for layout, ensure mobile responsiveness using media queries, and add JavaScript interactivity such as form validation, image carousel, or dynamic content loading. Your site should demonstrate creativity while maintaining professional appearance. Submit all files in a organized folder structure with an index.html file as the entry point. Include a README.md file explaining your design choices, technologies used, and instructions for viewing your site. Test your website in at least two different browsers before submission. All code must be your original work with any external resources properly credited.
grading_notes: Evaluate based on both technical execution and creativity. Look for proper implementation of fundamental concepts rather than advanced techniques. Common issues include: missing semantic HTML elements, non-responsive design, JavaScript errors in console, poor code organization. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Provide specific feedback on code quality and suggest improvements. Bonus points (up to 5) can be awarded for exceptional creativity or going beyond requirements with additional features like animations or accessibility improvements.

title: Distributed Database System with Consensus Protocol Implementation
description: Students will design and implement a distributed database system that handles concurrent transactions across multiple nodes using a consensus protocol (Raft or PBFT). The system must demonstrate ACID properties, fault tolerance, and consistent data replication while handling network partitions and node failures.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems with consensus mechanisms
Demonstrate understanding of database consistency, availability, and partition tolerance trade-offs
Apply fault-tolerant algorithms in real-world scenarios
Optimize system performance under concurrent load
Analyze and evaluate distributed system behavior through comprehensive testing
rubric_criteria: System Architecture and Design (25 points): Clear system design with proper node communication, well-defined APIs, appropriate data structures, and comprehensive documentation of architectural decisions
Consensus Protocol Implementation (25 points): Correct implementation of chosen consensus algorithm with proper leader election, log replication, safety properties, and handling of edge cases

Fault Tolerance and Recovery (25 points): System handles node failures gracefully, implements proper recovery mechanisms, maintains data consistency during network partitions, and demonstrates Byzantine fault tolerance if PBFT is chosen

Performance and Testing (25 points): Comprehensive test suite including unit tests, integration tests, and chaos engineering scenarios; performance benchmarks showing throughput and latency under various loads; clear documentation of system limitations
instructions: Implement a distributed database system supporting basic CRUD operations across at least 5 nodes. Choose either Raft or PBFT consensus protocol and justify your selection. Your implementation must include: (1) A key-value store with transaction support, (2) Network communication layer using TCP/gRPC, (3) Consensus protocol implementation with leader election, (4) Fault detection and recovery mechanisms, (5) Client library with retry logic and load balancing. Deliverables include: complete source code with build instructions, architectural documentation (10-15 pages), performance evaluation report with benchmarks, demonstration video (15-20 minutes) showing normal operation and failure scenarios, and comprehensive test suite with >80% code coverage. Use any programming language but provide clear setup instructions. Submit via Git repository with proper version control history showing iterative development. Include README with quick-start guide and API documentation. System should handle at least 1000 concurrent transactions and recover from up to 2 simultaneous node failures in a 5-node cluster.
grading_notes: Evaluate code quality, commenting, and adherence to software engineering best practices. Pay special attention to correctness of consensus implementation - common mistakes include improper handling of split votes, incorrect term management, and race conditions. Performance benchmarks should be realistic and well-documented. Architectural documentation should demonstrate deep understanding of distributed systems concepts. Partial credit available for incomplete implementations if core concepts are demonstrated. Expect 10-15% of students to achieve full marks, with most scoring 70-85%. Deduct points for security vulnerabilities, memory leaks, or systems that fail basic functionality tests. Bonus points (up to 5) for innovative optimizations or additional features like sharding or compression.

title: Fundamentals of Data Science: Practical Analysis Exam
description: Students will demonstrate their understanding of core data science concepts by analyzing a provided dataset using Python/pandas, creating basic visualizations, and interpreting results. This exam covers data manipulation, exploratory data analysis, basic statistics, and data visualization principles.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic data manipulation techniques using pandas to clean and transform datasets
Perform exploratory data analysis to identify patterns and insights in data
Create appropriate data visualizations to communicate findings effectively
Calculate and interpret basic statistical measures and correlations
Draw meaningful conclusions from data analysis results
rubric_criteria: Data Manipulation & Cleaning (25 points): Correctly loads dataset, handles missing values, filters data appropriately, performs basic transformations like grouping and sorting
Statistical Analysis (25 points): Accurately calculates descriptive statistics, identifies correlations, applies appropriate statistical measures, demonstrates understanding of data distributions
Data Visualization (25 points): Creates clear, appropriately labeled charts (histogram, scatter plot, bar chart), chooses suitable visualization types for data, includes proper titles and axis labels

Interpretation & Communication (25 points): Provides accurate insights based on analysis, explains findings clearly, identifies meaningful patterns or trends, draws logical conclusions supported by data
instructions:
You will receive a CSV dataset containing customer purchase data from an e-commerce platform. Complete the following tasks using Python and pandas in a Jupyter notebook:

1. DATA EXPLORATION (25 points): Load the dataset and examine its structure. Identify and handle any missing values or data quality issues. Display the first 10 rows, dataset shape, and column data types. Create summary statistics for numerical columns.

2. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS (25 points): Calculate mean, median, and standard deviation for purchase amounts. Identify the correlation between customer age and purchase amount. Determine which product category has the highest average sales.

3. VISUALIZATION (25 points): Create three visualizations: a) histogram of purchase amounts, b) scatter plot of age vs. purchase amount, c) bar chart showing total sales by product category. Each chart must include proper titles, axis labels, and legends where appropriate.

4. INSIGHTS & CONCLUSIONS (25 points): Write 3-4 paragraphs explaining your key findings. What patterns did you discover? What recommendations would you make based on your analysis? Support your conclusions with specific data points from your analysis.

Submit your completed Jupyter notebook (.ipynb file) with all code cells executed and outputs visible. Include markdown cells with explanations for each section. Ensure your code is commented and follows basic Python conventions.
grading_notes: Grade generously for correct approach even if minor syntax errors exist. Deduct points for: missing visualizations (5 points each), incorrect statistical calculations (10 points), poor data cleaning (10 points), unsupported conclusions (15 points). Award partial credit for incomplete but conceptually correct work. Expect 70% of students to score 75+ points with proper preparation. Watch for copied code - require students to explain their approach if suspicious. Common issues include: forgetting to handle missing values, mislabeled charts, and conclusions not supported by analysis.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategies: Analyzing and Comparing Approaches
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing different solution methods for multi-step word problems involving systems of equations, evaluating the efficiency and appropriateness of various approaches, and explaining their mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multiple problem-solving strategies to solve systems of linear equations in real-world contexts
Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of different mathematical approaches
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using appropriate terminology
Critique and provide constructive feedback on mathematical solutions presented by peers
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): Solutions are correct with proper algebraic manipulation, appropriate units, and accurate calculations. All work is clearly shown with logical progression.

Strategy Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of multiple solution methods (graphing, substitution, elimination), clearly explains when each method is most appropriate, and provides valid mathematical justification for strategy selection.

Communication Quality (25 points): Uses precise mathematical vocabulary, explains reasoning clearly and logically, responds constructively to peers with specific mathematical evidence, and asks relevant clarifying questions.

Problem-Solving Depth (25 points): Shows comprehensive understanding of the problem context, identifies key relationships between variables, makes connections to real-world applications, and demonstrates ability to verify solutions for reasonableness.
instructions: You will analyze the following scenario: 'A theater sells adult tickets for $12 and student tickets for $8. Last night they sold 150 tickets total and collected $1,640 in revenue. How many of each type of ticket were sold?' First, solve this problem using at least two different methods (graphing, substitution, or elimination). Document your complete solution process for each method, showing all algebraic steps and explaining your reasoning. Next, prepare to discuss which method you found most efficient and why, considering factors like time, accuracy, and ease of checking your answer. During the discussion, you will present one of your solution methods to the class, explain your strategy selection, and provide feedback on at least two classmates' approaches. Be prepared to identify the strengths and potential drawbacks of different methods, and suggest improvements or alternative approaches. Your discussion contributions should include specific mathematical evidence to support your points. Submit your written solutions before the discussion begins, and be ready to defend your mathematical reasoning and engage constructively with different perspectives on problem-solving approaches.
grading_notes: Look for students who show complete algebraic work with proper notation and logical flow. Award full points for mathematical accuracy only when solutions are correct AND methodology is sound. For strategy analysis, students should demonstrate genuine understanding of why different methods work, not just mechanical application. Strong communication includes using terms like 'system of equations,' 'substitution,' 'elimination,' and 'graphical intersection' appropriately. Watch for students who can explain their thinking process, not just final answers. In problem-solving depth, reward students who verify their solutions (e.g., checking that 70 adult tickets + 80 student tickets = 150 total and $12(70) + $8(80) = $1,640). Expect 15% of students to earn 90+ points, 60% to earn 75-89 points, and 25% to earn below 75 points. Common issues include arithmetic errors, incomplete algebraic steps, and difficulty explaining why one method might be preferred over another.

title: Distributed System Architecture Design Presentation
description: Students will design and present a comprehensive distributed system architecture for a real-world application, demonstrating advanced understanding of scalability, fault tolerance, consistency models, and performance optimization. The presentation must include system design diagrams, technology justifications, and detailed analysis of trade-offs.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed systems with appropriate architectural patterns
Analyze trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (CAP theorem)
Evaluate and select appropriate technologies for distributed system components
Communicate complex technical concepts effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences
rubric_criteria: System Architecture Design (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of distributed system patterns, appropriate component selection, clear system boundaries, and scalable design principles with proper consideration of microservices, load balancing, and data partitioning strategies

Technical Analysis and Trade-offs (25 points): Shows deep analysis of CAP theorem implications, performance bottlenecks, fault tolerance mechanisms, security considerations, and provides well-reasoned justifications for technology choices with quantitative analysis where applicable

Visual Design and Documentation (25 points): Presents clear, professional system diagrams using appropriate notation, includes comprehensive component interactions, data flow diagrams, deployment architecture, and provides detailed technical specifications with proper documentation standards

Presentation Delivery and Q&A Response (25 points): Demonstrates clear communication of complex concepts, maintains audience engagement, shows mastery through confident responses to technical questions, manages time effectively, and adapts explanations appropriately for audience technical level
instructions: Design a distributed system architecture for a high-traffic application (e.g., social media platform, e-commerce site, real-time gaming system, or streaming service) that serves 10+ million users. Your presentation must include: (1) Problem statement and requirements analysis including expected load, user patterns, and SLAs; (2) High-level architecture diagram showing all major components, services, and their interactions; (3) Technology stack justification with specific tools, databases, messaging systems, and cloud services; (4) Detailed analysis of at least three critical design decisions explaining trade-offs considered; (5) Scalability strategy including horizontal/vertical scaling approaches, caching layers, and CDN usage; (6) Fault tolerance and disaster recovery mechanisms; (7) Security architecture including authentication, authorization, and data protection; (8) Performance optimization strategies and monitoring approach. Prepare 15-20 slides for a 20-minute presentation followed by 10 minutes of Q&A. Submit slides 24 hours before presentation in PDF format via course portal. Include a 2-page technical appendix with detailed specifications and references.
grading_notes: Expect 20% A grades for presentations showing innovative solutions with thorough analysis. Common weaknesses include: oversimplified architecture diagrams, lack of quantitative analysis, poor technology justifications, and inability to defend design choices during Q&A. Deduct points for presentations exceeding time limits. Strong presentations typically demonstrate understanding of real-world constraints, show awareness of current industry practices, and provide specific implementation details. During Q&A, probe understanding of alternative approaches, failure scenarios, and cost implications. Grade presentation delivery separately from technical content to ensure fair assessment of students with varying presentation skills.

title: End-to-End Predictive Analytics Portfolio: Customer Churn Prevention System
description: Students will design and implement a complete data science solution to predict customer churn for a telecommunications company, demonstrating mastery of the entire data science pipeline from problem formulation through model deployment and business impact assessment.
learning_objectives_assessed: Execute comprehensive exploratory data analysis using advanced statistical and visualization techniques
Design and implement feature engineering pipelines for complex, multi-dimensional datasets
Compare and optimize multiple machine learning algorithms using appropriate evaluation metrics
Communicate technical findings through professional-grade visualizations and executive summaries
Demonstrate understanding of model deployment considerations and business impact measurement
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis & Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive EDA with statistical significance testing, handling of missing data/outliers, creation of meaningful derived features, proper data validation and preprocessing pipeline documentation

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (tree-based, linear, and neural network), proper cross-validation strategy, hyperparameter optimization, appropriate metrics for imbalanced classification, model interpretability analysis

Technical Implementation (25 points): Clean, well-documented code following best practices, reproducible analysis with version control, proper handling of data leakage, scalable preprocessing pipeline, evidence of testing and validation procedures

Business Communication & Impact (25 points): Executive summary with actionable insights, cost-benefit analysis of churn prevention strategies, clear visualization of model performance and business metrics, recommendations for implementation and monitoring
instructions: You are a senior data scientist tasked with building a customer churn prediction system. Using the provided telecommunications dataset (50,000+ customer records with 20+ features), develop a complete solution including: 1) Exploratory analysis identifying key churn drivers and data quality issues, 2) Feature engineering pipeline creating at least 5 new predictive features, 3) Model comparison testing minimum 3 algorithms with proper validation, 4) Final model achieving >0.75 AUC with detailed performance analysis across customer segments. Deliverables: Jupyter notebook with complete analysis, Python module with reusable functions, executive presentation (10-12 slides), and technical documentation. All code must be production-ready with error handling, logging, and configuration management. Include discussion of ethical considerations, model monitoring strategy, and A/B testing framework for deployment. Submit via GitHub repository with clear README, requirements.txt, and organized folder structure. Dataset and starter template available on course portal.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical depth over breadth - look for sophisticated feature engineering rather than trying many algorithms superficially. Strong submissions will show evidence of iterative improvement and statistical rigor. Common issues: data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data, lack of business context in recommendations. Expect grade distribution: 15% A (90-100), 35% B (80-89), 35% C (70-79), 15% below 70. Partial credit available for incomplete but methodologically sound work. Bonus points (up to 5) for exceptional creativity in feature engineering or novel evaluation approaches.

title: Data Collection and Basic Statistics Lab Report
description: Students will design and conduct a simple data collection experiment, organize their data using tables and graphs, calculate basic statistics (mean, median, mode), and present their findings in a structured lab report format.
learning_objectives_assessed: Collect, organize, and display data using appropriate tables and visual representations
Calculate and interpret basic measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode)
Communicate mathematical findings clearly using proper terminology and formatting
Apply mathematical reasoning to draw conclusions from collected data
rubric_criteria: Data Collection and Organization (25 points): Data collection method is clearly described, minimum 20 data points collected, data is accurately recorded in organized tables with proper labels and units
Mathematical Calculations (25 points): Mean, median, and mode are calculated correctly with work shown, appropriate rounding is used, calculations are clearly labeled and easy to follow

Data Visualization (25 points): Creates appropriate graph or chart (bar graph, histogram, or line plot), graph includes title, labeled axes, and proper scale, visual representation accurately reflects collected data

Analysis and Communication (25 points): Draws reasonable conclusions from data, uses proper mathematical vocabulary, report is well-organized with clear sections, spelling and grammar are appropriate for grade level
instructions: Choose a topic you can easily collect numerical data about (examples: heights of classmates, number of pets owned by friends, daily temperatures, or favorite pizza toppings). Your lab report must include: 1) HYPOTHESIS SECTION: Write one paragraph explaining what you plan to measure and what you think you might discover. 2) DATA COLLECTION: Gather at least 20 data points. Create a clear data table showing all your measurements with appropriate labels. Explain how you collected your data. 3) CALCULATIONS: Calculate the mean (average), median (middle value), and mode (most frequent value) of your data. Show all your work step-by-step. 4) VISUAL REPRESENTATION: Create one graph or chart that best displays your data. Include a title, label your axes, and use appropriate spacing. 5) CONCLUSION: Write 2-3 sentences explaining what your data shows. Did your results match your hypothesis? What was surprising or interesting? Format your report with clear section headings, write your name and date at the top, and double-check all calculations. Submit your completed report along with any worksheets showing your calculation work. Reports should be 2-3 pages total including your graph.
grading_notes: Expect most students to score between 70-85 points initially. Common issues include: incomplete data collection (fewer than 20 points), calculation errors especially with median when data sets have even numbers, graphs missing titles or labels, and weak conclusions that don't reference the actual data. Award partial credit for correct process even if final answers are wrong. Look for evidence of mathematical reasoning rather than just correct answers. Students should demonstrate understanding of when to use mean vs. median vs. mode. Exceptional work (90+ points) will show creativity in topic selection, thorough explanations, and insights beyond basic requirements.

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will design, implement, and deploy a complete machine learning solution to predict customer churn using a real-world telecommunications dataset. This assessment evaluates the entire data science workflow from exploratory data analysis through model deployment and business insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced feature engineering techniques to prepare complex datasets for machine learning
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms for classification problems
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and statistical validation techniques
Communicate data science findings through clear visualizations and business-focused recommendations
Deploy machine learning models using cloud platforms or containerization technologies
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing & Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive EDA with statistical insights, appropriate handling of missing values and outliers, creation of meaningful engineered features, proper data splitting and scaling techniques

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper hyperparameter tuning using cross-validation, comprehensive evaluation using precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices

Technical Implementation & Code Quality (25 points): Clean, well-documented code following PEP 8 standards, proper use of version control, reproducible results with set random seeds, efficient use of pandas/numpy/scikit-learn, error handling and data validation

Business Impact & Communication (25 points): Clear executive summary with actionable recommendations, professional visualizations using matplotlib/seaborn/plotly, cost-benefit analysis of churn prevention strategies, model interpretability analysis using SHAP or similar tools
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (containing demographics, service usage, and churn labels), develop a complete machine learning solution to predict customer churn. Your submission must include: (1) A Jupyter notebook containing your complete analysis, clearly structured with markdown explanations for each section; (2) A Python script (.py file) with your final model training and prediction functions; (3) A requirements.txt file listing all dependencies; (4) A 2-page executive summary (PDF) presenting your findings to business stakeholders. Your analysis should demonstrate advanced techniques such as feature selection, handling class imbalance, and model interpretation. Include at least one ensemble method and provide statistical significance testing for model comparisons. Deploy your final model using either Flask API, Docker container, or cloud service (AWS/GCP/Azure) and provide access instructions. Address the business question: 'Which customers are most likely to churn and what actions should the company take?' Submit all files via GitHub repository with clear README documentation. Ensure your solution is reproducible by including data preprocessing steps and model serialization.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor over perfect accuracy scores - focus on methodology and justification of choices. Look for evidence of statistical thinking (hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, validation strategies). Common issues include data leakage, inappropriate cross-validation, and overcomplicating feature engineering. Excellent projects (90-100) demonstrate creative insights, robust validation, and clear business value. Good projects (80-89) show solid technical execution with minor gaps. Satisfactory projects (70-79) meet basic requirements but lack depth or have methodological issues. Below 70 indicates fundamental technical or communication problems. Pay special attention to reproducibility - deduct points if code doesn't run or results can't be replicated. Business communication should be accessible to non-technical stakeholders while technical documentation should be thorough enough for peer review.

title: Advanced Multivariable Calculus and Real Analysis Comprehensive Exam
description: A comprehensive examination assessing mastery of advanced calculus concepts including multivariable optimization, vector calculus, series convergence, and rigorous proof techniques. Students will demonstrate theoretical understanding and computational proficiency through a combination of proof-based problems and complex calculations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using epsilon-delta definitions and convergence criteria
Apply advanced optimization techniques to solve constrained multivariable problems using Lagrange multipliers
Evaluate complex line and surface integrals using Green's, Stokes', and Divergence theorems
Analyze convergence properties of infinite series and power series including radius of convergence
Demonstrate deep conceptual understanding of continuity, differentiability, and integrability in multiple dimensions
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Proof Construction (25 points): Demonstrates logical reasoning, uses appropriate theorems and definitions, provides complete justifications, maintains mathematical precision throughout solutions

Computational Accuracy and Technique (25 points): Executes complex calculations correctly, applies appropriate methods efficiently, shows clear work organization, arrives at correct numerical and algebraic answers

Conceptual Understanding and Application (25 points): Selects appropriate solution strategies, recognizes underlying mathematical structures, connects different mathematical concepts, interprets results in context

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Uses proper mathematical notation consistently, presents solutions clearly and logically, explains reasoning comprehensively, demonstrates professional mathematical writing standards
instructions:
This examination consists of 6 problems covering advanced topics in multivariable calculus and real analysis. You have 4 hours to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and justify all steps thoroughly. Partial credit will be awarded based on the quality of your mathematical reasoning, even if final answers are incorrect.

Problem types include: (1) Epsilon-delta proofs of limits and continuity, (2) Constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers with inequality constraints, (3) Vector field analysis and application of fundamental theorems of vector calculus, (4) Series convergence analysis using multiple convergence tests, (5) Implicit function theorem applications, and (6) Multiple integral evaluation with coordinate transformations.

Requirements: Use blue or black ink only. Write legibly and organize your work clearly. Begin each problem on a new page. State all theorems and definitions you reference. For proof problems, clearly identify your approach and maintain logical flow. For computational problems, show intermediate steps and check reasonableness of answers. Calculators are not permitted except for basic arithmetic verification.

Submission: Submit all work in the provided blue book. Write your student ID on every page. Do not remove pages or use additional paper without permission. Ensure your name appears only on the cover page to maintain anonymity during grading.
grading_notes: Grade holistically considering both process and final answers. Award significant partial credit for correct methodology even with computational errors. Expect 15% of students to score 90+, 60% to score 70-89, 20% to score 50-69, and 5% below 50. Watch for: incomplete proofs missing crucial logical steps, correct setup with minor arithmetic errors (deduct minimally), failure to check constraint qualifications in optimization problems, confusion between pointwise and uniform convergence, and improper application of vector calculus theorems without verifying hypotheses. Deduct points for unclear notation and lack of mathematical communication. Provide specific feedback on proof structure and suggest improvements for resubmission if needed.

title: Predictive Analytics Case Study Presentation
description: Students will analyze a real-world dataset, build and evaluate predictive models, and present their findings including methodology, results, and business recommendations to demonstrate end-to-end data science workflow competency.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply appropriate data preprocessing and feature engineering techniques to real-world datasets
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms for predictive modeling
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Communicate technical findings effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences
Translate data science results into actionable business insights and recommendations
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis & Preprocessing (25 points): Demonstrates thorough exploratory data analysis, appropriate handling of missing values/outliers, effective feature engineering, and clear documentation of data quality issues and solutions

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implements at least 3 different algorithms, uses proper train/validation/test splits, applies appropriate evaluation metrics, demonstrates hyperparameter tuning, and provides justified model selection

Technical Communication (25 points): Presents methodology clearly, explains model assumptions and limitations, uses appropriate visualizations, demonstrates understanding of statistical concepts, and handles technical Q&A effectively

Business Impact & Recommendations (25 points): Translates technical results into business value, provides specific actionable recommendations, discusses implementation considerations, addresses potential risks, and demonstrates understanding of domain context
instructions: Select a dataset from the provided list (retail sales, customer churn, housing prices, or healthcare outcomes) containing at least 1000 observations. Your presentation must include: (1) Problem definition and business context (2-3 minutes), (2) Data exploration findings with key insights and visualizations (3-4 minutes), (3) Model development process including at least three algorithms (linear/logistic regression, tree-based method, and one advanced technique like SVM or neural networks) (4-5 minutes), (4) Results comparison using appropriate metrics (accuracy, precision/recall, RMSE, etc.) with cross-validation (2-3 minutes), and (5) Business recommendations and implementation roadmap (2-3 minutes). Submit your Jupyter notebook and dataset 48 hours before presentation. Be prepared for 5 minutes of Q&A focusing on technical decisions, model interpretation, and business implications. Use professional slides with clear visualizations—avoid excessive text or code on slides. Your notebook should be well-documented with markdown explanations, reproducible results, and clean code structure.
grading_notes: Look for depth over breadth in analysis—students should demonstrate mastery rather than surface-level application. Common issues include: inadequate EDA leading to poor feature selection, data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate metrics for problem type, and overly technical presentations lacking business context. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Deduct points for late notebook submission (5 points), going significantly over time (3 points), or inability to answer basic questions about their approach (up to 10 points). Give extra credit for creative feature engineering, addressing ethical considerations, or exceptional presentation skills.

title: Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio: Real-World Applications of Calculus and Statistics
description: Students develop a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating mastery of advanced mathematical concepts through three real-world modeling projects that integrate calculus, statistics, and mathematical reasoning. Each project requires mathematical analysis, computational work, and written explanations of methodology and results.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply differential and integral calculus to solve complex real-world optimization and rate problems
Utilize statistical methods including regression analysis, hypothesis testing, and probability distributions to analyze data sets
Construct and validate mathematical models using multiple approaches and justify methodology choices
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations, graphical representations, and numerical analysis
Demonstrate metacognitive reflection on problem-solving processes and model limitations
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy and Techniques (25 points): Correct application of calculus and statistical methods, accurate computations, appropriate use of mathematical notation and formulas, error-free algebraic manipulations

Model Development and Validation (25 points): Construction of appropriate mathematical models, testing model assumptions, comparing multiple approaches, addressing model limitations and assumptions explicitly

Real-World Application and Analysis (25 points): Selection of meaningful real-world contexts, accurate data collection/usage, practical interpretation of mathematical results, consideration of real-world constraints and variables

Communication and Documentation (25 points): Clear written explanations of methodology, well-organized portfolio structure, appropriate use of graphs/tables/visual aids, professional presentation, proper citation of data sources
instructions: Create a portfolio containing three distinct mathematical modeling projects, each addressing a different real-world scenario using advanced mathematical techniques. Project 1: Optimization Problem - Use calculus to solve a business, engineering, or scientific optimization problem involving multiple variables and constraints. Include derivative analysis, critical point identification, and practical recommendations. Project 2: Statistical Analysis - Collect or obtain a substantial dataset (minimum 100 data points) and perform comprehensive statistical analysis including regression modeling, hypothesis testing, and probability calculations. Justify your statistical methods and interpret results in context. Project 3: Mathematical Model Comparison - Select a phenomenon that can be modeled using multiple mathematical approaches (e.g., exponential vs. logistic growth, different probability distributions). Compare at least three different models, analyze their strengths and weaknesses, and recommend the most appropriate model with justification. Each project must include: detailed mathematical work showing all steps, computer-generated graphs and calculations using appropriate software, written analysis explaining your methodology and reasoning, reflection on limitations and potential improvements, and properly cited data sources. Submit as a single PDF document with clear section divisions, professional formatting, and a table of contents. Include an executive summary highlighting key findings from all three projects. Total portfolio should be 25-35 pages including graphs, calculations, and appendices.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical rigor first - students must demonstrate mastery of calculus techniques (derivatives, integrals, optimization) and statistical methods (regression, hypothesis testing, probability). Look for evidence of original thinking in model development rather than cookbook approaches. Common issues include: insufficient explanation of mathematical steps, inappropriate statistical tests for data types, unrealistic assumptions in models, and poor connection between mathematical results and real-world implications. Expect grade distribution of approximately 15% A-level work (90+ points), 35% B-level work (80-89 points), 40% C-level work (70-79 points), 10% below proficient (under 70 points). Deduct points for late submissions, plagiarism, or failure to meet minimum requirements. Provide detailed feedback on mathematical errors and suggest resources for improvement. Consider allowing one revision opportunity for portfolios scoring below 75 points.

title: Distributed System Design and Implementation: Building a Fault-Tolerant Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design, implement, and analyze a distributed microservices system with fault tolerance mechanisms, load balancing, and monitoring capabilities. This comprehensive lab report assesses advanced systems design principles, distributed computing concepts, and practical implementation skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems using microservices architecture patterns
Implement fault tolerance mechanisms including circuit breakers, retries, and graceful degradation
Apply load balancing strategies and horizontal scaling techniques
Demonstrate proficiency in containerization, orchestration, and service mesh technologies
Analyze system performance, reliability metrics, and conduct failure analysis
Document complex system architectures and justify design decisions
rubric_criteria: System Architecture and Design (25 points): Comprehensive system design with clear component separation, well-defined APIs, appropriate technology stack selection, scalability considerations, and proper documentation of architectural decisions using industry-standard diagrams (UML, C4 model)

Implementation Quality and Fault Tolerance (25 points): Clean, well-structured code with proper error handling, implemented circuit breakers, retry mechanisms, timeout configurations, health checks, and graceful degradation under failure conditions. Code must follow SOLID principles and include comprehensive unit/integration tests

Performance Analysis and Monitoring (25 points): Implementation of comprehensive monitoring stack (metrics, logging, tracing), load testing results with performance bottleneck identification, analysis of system behavior under various load conditions, and optimization recommendations with quantitative justification

Documentation and Technical Communication (25 points): Professional-grade technical report including system overview, implementation details, deployment instructions, API documentation, failure scenarios analysis, lessons learned, and clear recommendations for production deployment
instructions: Implement a distributed e-commerce microservices system with the following components: User Management Service, Product Catalog Service, Order Processing Service, Payment Service, and Notification Service. Your system must handle at least 1000 concurrent users and demonstrate fault tolerance when individual services fail. Use containerization (Docker) and orchestration (Kubernetes) for deployment. Implement a service mesh (Istio recommended) for traffic management and security. Include a comprehensive monitoring stack using Prometheus, Grafana, and distributed tracing with Jaeger. Your implementation should demonstrate: database per service pattern, event-driven communication using message queues, API gateway implementation, and comprehensive security measures including authentication/authorization. Submit a detailed lab report (15-20 pages) containing: executive summary, system architecture overview with diagrams, detailed implementation explanation with code snippets, deployment guide, performance analysis with load testing results, failure scenario testing and recovery analysis, monitoring dashboard screenshots with metric interpretations, and reflection on design decisions. Include all source code, configuration files, and deployment scripts in a GitHub repository with clear README documentation. Provide a 10-minute video demonstration showcasing system functionality, fault tolerance capabilities, and monitoring dashboards under load.
grading_notes: Expect most students to score 75-85 points, with exceptional work scoring 90+. Common deductions: incomplete fault tolerance implementation (-5 to -10 points), inadequate performance testing (-5 points), poor documentation structure (-3 to -7 points), missing monitoring components (-5 points), security vulnerabilities (-5 to -10 points). Award bonus points (up to 5) for innovative features like chaos engineering, advanced deployment strategies (blue-green, canary), or superior code quality. Verify all systems are actually deployable and functional - non-working submissions receive maximum 50% credit. Pay special attention to architectural decisions justification and performance analysis depth. Students should demonstrate understanding of CAP theorem implications and eventual consistency challenges.

title: Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Exploring Customer Purchase Patterns
description: A comprehensive beginner-level quiz assessing foundational data science concepts through a practical customer data analysis scenario. Students will demonstrate understanding of data types, basic statistics, data visualization principles, and introductory machine learning concepts using a realistic e-commerce dataset context.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify different data types (numerical, categorical, ordinal) in real-world datasets
Calculate and interpret basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Understand fundamental data visualization principles and chart selection criteria
Recognize basic machine learning concepts including supervised vs unsupervised learning
Apply data science terminology correctly in context
Interpret simple data analysis results and draw basic conclusions
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Structure (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, understands data quality issues, recognizes structured vs unstructured data formats

Descriptive Statistics (25 points): Accurately calculates basic statistics, interprets measures of central tendency and dispersion, identifies appropriate statistical measures for different data types
Data Visualization (25 points): Selects appropriate chart types for different data relationships, understands visualization best practices, interprets graphs and charts correctly
Machine Learning Basics (25 points): Distinguishes between supervised and unsupervised learning, identifies common algorithms and their applications, understands model evaluation concepts
instructions: This quiz consists of 25 multiple-choice and short-answer questions based on a customer purchase dataset scenario. You are a junior data scientist at an e-commerce company analyzing customer behavior data containing 10,000 customer records with variables including age, gender, purchase amount, product category, purchase date, customer satisfaction rating, and geographic location. Read each question carefully and select the best answer or provide concise written responses where indicated. For calculation questions, show your work in the space provided. You may use a basic calculator, but no advanced software or internet access is permitted. Questions are worth 4 points each and cover four main areas: data types and structure (questions 1-6), descriptive statistics (questions 7-12), data visualization (questions 13-19), and machine learning fundamentals (questions 20-25). Pay attention to the context provided in each question as answers should reflect real-world data science applications. For multiple-choice questions, select only one answer unless otherwise specified. For short-answer questions, responses should be 2-3 sentences maximum. Submit your completed quiz within the allocated time period. Partial credit may be awarded for calculation questions that show correct methodology even if the final answer contains minor errors.
grading_notes: Award full points for completely correct answers. For calculation questions, give partial credit (2-3 points) if methodology is correct but contains computational errors. Common student errors include: confusing discrete vs continuous variables, selecting inappropriate measures of central tendency for skewed data, choosing wrong chart types for data relationships, and mixing up supervised vs unsupervised learning examples. Expect grade distribution: 90-100 points (15% of students), 80-89 points (35%), 70-79 points (35%), 60-69 points (12%), below 60 points (3%). Flag for review any student scoring below 60 points - may need additional foundational support. Look for consistent patterns in wrong answers that might indicate concept confusion requiring class review.

title: Community Park Redesign: Linear Programming and Geometric Optimization Project
description: Students will design an optimal layout for a community park using linear programming techniques, geometric principles, and data analysis to maximize recreational space while meeting budget and environmental constraints.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply linear programming to solve real-world optimization problems with multiple constraints
Calculate areas and perimeters of complex geometric shapes and composite figures
Interpret and analyze data to make mathematical decisions and justify solutions
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations and visual representations
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Modeling and Linear Programming (25 points): Correctly identifies variables, formulates objective function, establishes all constraints, and solves optimization problem using appropriate methods

Geometric Calculations and Spatial Design (25 points): Accurately calculates areas, perimeters, and dimensions of park features; demonstrates understanding of scale, proportion, and geometric relationships

Data Analysis and Problem-Solving (25 points): Effectively analyzes given data about community needs, budget constraints, and environmental factors; makes logical decisions based on mathematical evidence

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Provides clear written explanations of mathematical processes, creates accurate visual representations of the park design, and justifies design choices with mathematical reasoning
instructions:
You are a consultant hired to redesign Riverside Community Park. The city has provided you with a rectangular plot of land (200m × 150m), a budget of $500,000, and community survey data showing desired amenities. Your task is to create an optimal park layout that maximizes recreational space while meeting all constraints.

Project Requirements:
1. Create a linear programming model to optimize space allocation among at least 5 different park features (playground, sports courts, walking paths, green space, parking, etc.)
2. Calculate exact areas and dimensions for each feature using geometric principles
3. Analyze the provided community survey data (will be distributed separately) to determine priority weightings for your objective function
4. Design a scaled diagram of your optimal park layout with accurate measurements
5. Prepare a written report (4-6 pages) explaining your mathematical approach, calculations, and final recommendations

Deliverables:
- Mathematical model with clearly defined variables, constraints, and objective function
- Complete solution showing optimization work (graphical or simplex method)
- Geometric calculations sheet showing all area, perimeter, and dimension computations
- Professional park layout diagram drawn to scale with labels and measurements
- Written report with executive summary, methodology, results, and recommendations

Submission: Upload all materials as a single PDF file by [due date]. Include your name and clearly label each section.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first, then assess application quality. Look for: proper constraint formulation (students often miss non-negativity constraints), correct geometric calculations (watch for unit conversion errors), logical use of survey data in objective function, and clear communication of mathematical reasoning. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below 70. Common issues include incomplete constraint sets, calculation errors in area formulas for composite shapes, and insufficient justification of design decisions. Partial credit should be awarded for correct methodology even with computational errors.

title: Advanced Algorithms Design and Analysis Comprehensive Exam
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of advanced algorithmic concepts by designing efficient algorithms, analyzing their complexity, proving correctness, and implementing solutions for complex computational problems involving graph theory, dynamic programming, and network flow optimization.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement advanced algorithms for complex computational problems with optimal time and space complexity
Perform rigorous mathematical analysis of algorithm correctness using formal proof techniques including loop invariants and induction
Apply advanced algorithmic paradigms including dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and network flow to solve real-world optimization problems
Evaluate and compare multiple algorithmic approaches using asymptotic analysis and empirical performance metrics
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Design and Implementation (25 points): Correctness of algorithm logic, efficiency of approach, proper handling of edge cases, clean and well-structured code with appropriate data structures

Complexity Analysis (25 points): Accurate time and space complexity calculations using Big-O notation, clear mathematical reasoning, consideration of best/average/worst cases, comparison with alternative approaches

Mathematical Proof of Correctness (25 points): Rigorous formal proof using appropriate techniques (induction, loop invariants, contradiction), logical flow and mathematical rigor, complete coverage of all cases including base cases and termination conditions

Problem-Solving Strategy and Optimization (25 points): Selection of appropriate algorithmic paradigm, identification of optimal substructure or greedy choice property, creative approaches to complex constraints, discussion of trade-offs and alternative solutions
instructions:
This comprehensive exam consists of three interconnected problems requiring both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. You must solve all problems completely, showing all work and reasoning.

PROBLEM 1 (Graph Algorithms): Design an algorithm to find the minimum cost to connect all vertices in a weighted graph where edge weights change dynamically. Implement your solution and prove its correctness using mathematical induction.

PROBLEM 2 (Dynamic Programming): Given a set of projects with deadlines, profits, and resource requirements, design an optimal scheduling algorithm that maximizes profit while respecting resource constraints. Analyze the time and space complexity, and provide a formal proof of optimality.

PROBLEM 3 (Network Flow): Model and solve a real-world logistics problem involving multiple warehouses, delivery trucks with varying capacities, and time-sensitive orders. Implement a maximum flow solution and discuss how to handle dynamic updates to the network.

Submission Requirements: Submit clean, commented code in Python or C++, detailed complexity analysis with mathematical justification, complete formal proofs for correctness, and a brief discussion comparing your approach to at least two alternative methods. All solutions must handle edge cases appropriately and include test cases demonstrating correctness. Code must be executable and well-documented with clear variable names and logical structure.
grading_notes: Award full points only for solutions that demonstrate deep understanding of algorithmic principles. Partial credit: 70% for correct approach with minor implementation errors, 50% for correct high-level strategy with significant gaps, 30% for demonstrating relevant knowledge without complete solutions. Common issues to watch: incorrect complexity analysis (especially hidden factors), incomplete proofs missing edge cases, inefficient algorithms when optimal solutions exist, code that doesn't handle boundary conditions. Expect grade distribution: 15% A grades (90-100), 25% B grades (80-89), 35% C grades (70-79), 25% below 70%. Look for creative optimization techniques and evidence of independent thinking beyond standard textbook approaches.

title: Ethical AI and Algorithmic Bias Mitigation Strategy Discussion
description: Students will analyze a real-world case study involving algorithmic bias, propose comprehensive mitigation strategies, and engage in peer discussions about the ethical implications of AI deployment in high-stakes decision-making scenarios.
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate ethical implications and societal impacts of data science applications
Identify and propose solutions for algorithmic bias and fairness issues
Communicate complex technical concepts to diverse stakeholders
Apply critical thinking to analyze trade-offs between model performance and ethical considerations
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of bias sources, statistical fairness metrics, and technical mitigation approaches with specific references to appropriate literature
Strategic Recommendations (25 points): Provides comprehensive, actionable mitigation strategy with clear implementation timeline, resource requirements, and stakeholder considerations
Ethical Reasoning (25 points): Shows sophisticated understanding of ethical frameworks, considers multiple perspectives, addresses potential unintended consequences of proposed solutions

Discussion Engagement (25 points): Makes substantive contributions to peer discussions, asks probing questions, synthesizes different viewpoints, and demonstrates active listening through thoughtful responses
instructions: You will analyze the case study 'COMPAS Recidivism Risk Assessment Tool' (provided materials include ProPublica investigation findings, academic papers, and company responses). Your analysis must include: (1) A 1500-word technical analysis identifying specific bias sources, affected populations, and quantitative evidence of disparate impact using appropriate fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, etc.). (2) A detailed mitigation strategy document (1000 words) proposing technical solutions (re-sampling, algorithmic modifications, ensemble approaches), procedural changes (human oversight, audit processes), and governance frameworks. Include implementation timeline, success metrics, and stakeholder communication plan. (3) Participate in at least three threaded discussions responding to peers' analyses with substantive feedback (minimum 200 words per response). Consider alternative approaches, challenge assumptions respectfully, and explore implementation challenges. All responses must cite relevant literature and demonstrate engagement with course concepts. Submit your analysis as a PDF with proper citations (APA format) and participate in discussions throughout the week.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of original thinking beyond surface-level analysis. Strong submissions will reference current research (fairness-aware ML, interpretable AI). Common issues: oversimplified solutions ignoring real-world constraints, failure to consider stakeholder perspectives, inadequate engagement with technical literature. Grade distribution expectation: 15% excellent (90-100), 60% proficient (80-89), 20% developing (70-79), 5% inadequate (<70). Deduct points for late discussion participation as real-time engagement is crucial for learning objectives.

title: Basic Math Concepts Presentation: Real-World Applications
description: Students will create and deliver a 5-minute presentation demonstrating how fundamental mathematical concepts (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and basic fractions) are used in everyday situations. Students must include visual aids and solve at least three practical problems during their presentation.
estimated_time: 45 minutes (5 minutes presentation + 5 minutes Q&A per student)
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate understanding of basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division)
Apply mathematical concepts to solve real-world problems
Explain mathematical reasoning clearly and accurately
Use visual representations to support mathematical explanations
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Content (25 points): Correctly demonstrates all four basic operations and shows accurate problem-solving with appropriate methods and correct answers
Real-World Application (25 points): Clearly connects mathematical concepts to practical, relevant situations with meaningful examples that show genuine understanding
Communication and Delivery (25 points): Speaks clearly and confidently, maintains appropriate pace, engages audience, and stays within time limit
Visual Aids and Organization (25 points): Uses effective visual supports (charts, diagrams, props), presents information in logical sequence, and demonstrates preparation
instructions: Create a 5-minute presentation showing how basic math is used in real life. Choose a theme such as cooking, shopping, sports, or planning a party. Your presentation must include: (1) Introduction of your chosen real-world scenario, (2) Three different math problems from your scenario that use addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, (3) Step-by-step solutions to each problem explained aloud, (4) At least one example using basic fractions (halves, quarters, thirds), and (5) Visual aids such as posters, props, or drawings. You may use a calculator for complex calculations, but must explain each step. Dress appropriately and speak loudly enough for everyone to hear. After your presentation, be prepared to answer 1-2 questions from classmates or the instructor. Practice your timing - presentations under 4 minutes or over 6 minutes will lose points. Submit your visual aids and a one-page outline of your key points 24 hours before presenting. Examples of good themes: planning a birthday party (calculating guests, food quantities, costs), cooking a recipe (measuring ingredients, adjusting serving sizes), or organizing a sports tournament (scheduling, scoring, statistics).
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - incorrect calculations should significantly impact the Mathematical Content score. Look for genuine understanding rather than memorized procedures. For Real-World Application, scenarios should feel authentic and age-appropriate, not forced. Common issues include: rushing through calculations without explanation, visual aids that are too small to see, and choosing overly complex scenarios. Excellent presentations (90-100) show clear mastery and engaging delivery. Good presentations (80-89) demonstrate competency with minor errors. Satisfactory presentations (70-79) meet basic requirements but lack depth or have some mathematical errors. Below 70 indicates significant gaps in understanding or preparation. Encourage students who struggle with public speaking by focusing feedback on mathematical content and preparation.

title: Advanced Predictive Analytics Lab: Customer Churn Prediction with Model Interpretability
description: Students will complete an end-to-end machine learning project to predict customer churn using real-world telecommunications data. This assessment evaluates advanced data science skills including feature engineering, model comparison, hyperparameter optimization, and model interpretability using SHAP values.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced feature engineering techniques to improve model performance
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms with proper validation
Perform hyperparameter tuning using systematic optimization methods
Interpret complex models using SHAP values and communicate findings effectively
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing & Feature Engineering (25 points): Thorough EDA with visualizations, appropriate handling of missing values, categorical encoding, feature scaling, creation of meaningful engineered features, and proper train/validation/test splits

Model Implementation & Comparison (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper cross-validation, appropriate evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), and statistical significance testing of model differences

Hyperparameter Optimization & Model Selection (25 points): Systematic hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV, analysis of parameter sensitivity, final model selection with clear justification, and assessment of overfitting/underfitting

Model Interpretability & Business Insights (25 points): Implementation of SHAP analysis, clear visualization of feature importance, actionable business recommendations based on model insights, and discussion of model limitations and ethical considerations
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset, develop a comprehensive churn prediction model following these requirements: 1) Conduct exploratory data analysis with at least 5 meaningful visualizations and statistical summaries. Handle missing values appropriately and justify your approach. 2) Engineer at least 3 new features based on domain knowledge (e.g., customer lifetime value, usage patterns, service combinations). 3) Implement logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting classifiers. Use stratified 5-fold cross-validation and report precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC for each model. 4) Perform hyperparameter tuning for your best-performing model using systematic search methods. Document the parameter space explored and optimal values found. 5) Apply SHAP analysis to interpret your final model. Generate summary plots, dependence plots for top 5 features, and individual prediction explanations for 3 sample customers. 6) Provide business recommendations based on your findings, discussing which customer segments are at highest risk and what interventions might reduce churn. Submit a Jupyter notebook with clear markdown sections, well-commented code, and professional visualizations. Include a 2-page executive summary targeting business stakeholders. All code must be reproducible with random seeds set.
grading_notes: Look for sophisticated feature engineering beyond basic transformations - students should demonstrate domain understanding. Model comparison should include statistical tests (McNemar's test or paired t-test). Deduct points for data leakage, improper validation, or overly complex models without justification. SHAP analysis should go beyond basic plots to provide actionable insights. Executive summary should be accessible to non-technical audience. Expect 15-20% of students to achieve 90+ points, 50-60% to score 75-89 points. Common issues: inadequate EDA, inappropriate metric selection for imbalanced data, hyperparameter tuning without validation set isolation, and superficial business recommendations.

title: Advanced Mathematical Reasoning Forum: Real-World Optimization Problems
description: Students engage in peer discussions analyzing complex multi-variable optimization problems from economics, engineering, and data science. Assessment focuses on mathematical reasoning, problem-solving strategies, and ability to communicate mathematical concepts effectively in collaborative environments.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced calculus techniques (Lagrange multipliers, constrained optimization) to solve real-world problems
Analyze and critique mathematical solutions presented by peers using rigorous mathematical reasoning
Communicate complex mathematical concepts clearly using appropriate notation and terminology
Evaluate the validity and efficiency of different solution approaches to optimization problems
rubric_criteria: Initial Problem Solution (25 points): Demonstrates correct application of optimization techniques with clear mathematical work, appropriate use of calculus methods, and accurate computational results

Peer Analysis and Feedback (25 points): Provides substantive mathematical critique of at least two peer solutions, identifies errors or alternative approaches, and offers constructive suggestions with mathematical justification

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise mathematical language, proper notation, clear logical flow, and effective explanations that would be comprehensible to advanced mathematics students

Problem Extension and Synthesis (25 points): Proposes meaningful variations or extensions to original problems, connects solutions to broader mathematical principles, and demonstrates deep understanding of underlying concepts
instructions: You will participate in a week-long discussion forum analyzing three complex optimization problems: (1) A manufacturing company maximizing profit subject to resource constraints, (2) A machine learning model minimizing error with regularization parameters, and (3) An urban planning scenario optimizing land use. Begin by selecting ONE problem and posting a complete solution including: mathematical setup, constraint identification, method selection justification, detailed solution steps, and interpretation of results. Your initial post must include all mathematical work, proper notation, and be 400-500 words. Next, analyze and respond to at least TWO classmates' solutions with substantive mathematical feedback, identifying strengths, potential errors, or alternative approaches. Each response should be 200-300 words with specific mathematical references. Finally, engage in follow-up discussions addressing questions or critiques of your work. Post your initial solution by Wednesday, peer responses by Friday, and continue discussions through Sunday. All mathematical expressions should use proper notation (LaTeX formatting encouraged). Include references to relevant theorems, methods, or principles. Focus on mathematical rigor while maintaining clarity for peer understanding.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - incorrect fundamental applications should not exceed 15/25 points per criterion. Look for evidence of genuine peer engagement rather than superficial comments. Strong responses will identify specific mathematical errors or suggest concrete improvements. Communication assessment should consider both technical precision and accessibility to advanced students. Problem extensions might include sensitivity analysis, different constraint scenarios, or connections to related optimization types. Common issues include: incomplete constraint analysis, computational errors in Lagrange multiplier setup, vague peer feedback lacking mathematical specificity, and poor notation usage. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70%. Partial credit available within each criterion based on mathematical reasoning quality even if final answers contain errors.

title: Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture: Design and Implementation Strategy Presentation
description: Students will present a comprehensive architectural design for a large-scale distributed system, demonstrating mastery of distributed computing principles, system design patterns, and implementation strategies. The presentation must include technical depth, performance analysis, and justification of design decisions for handling real-world scalability challenges.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and analyze complex distributed system architectures using appropriate patterns and protocols
Evaluate trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance in distributed systems
Apply advanced concepts including consensus algorithms, distributed caching, and fault tolerance mechanisms
Communicate complex technical concepts clearly to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of distributed system components, appropriate use of design patterns (microservices, event-driven, etc.), clear system boundaries, and scalable architecture decisions

Technical Implementation Strategy (25 points): Shows deep knowledge of distributed algorithms (consensus, replication), data consistency models, fault tolerance mechanisms, and performance optimization techniques with specific technology choices justified

Problem Analysis & Trade-offs (25 points): Clearly articulates CAP theorem implications, analyzes bottlenecks and failure modes, demonstrates understanding of scalability challenges, and provides quantitative performance estimates with realistic assumptions

Presentation Quality & Technical Communication (25 points): Delivers clear, well-structured presentation with appropriate technical depth, handles Q&A demonstrating deep understanding, uses effective visualizations, and adapts explanations for audience comprehension
instructions: Design and present a distributed system architecture for a high-traffic application (e.g., social media platform, e-commerce system, or real-time gaming platform). Your 30-minute presentation must include: (1) Problem statement with specific requirements (user scale, throughput, latency constraints), (2) High-level system architecture diagram with component interactions, (3) Detailed technical design covering data storage strategy, communication protocols, load balancing, and caching layers, (4) Implementation of at least two advanced concepts: consensus algorithms (Raft/Paxos), event sourcing, CQRS, or distributed caching, (5) Failure mode analysis and disaster recovery strategy, (6) Performance analysis with capacity planning and bottleneck identification, (7) Technology stack justification with alternatives considered. Submit your presentation slides 24 hours before presenting. Include detailed speaker notes and architectural diagrams. Be prepared for technical questions about scalability limits, alternative approaches, and implementation challenges. Your presentation should demonstrate graduate-level understanding suitable for senior engineers and technical architects.
grading_notes: Expect 15% A grades for presentations showing exceptional depth and innovation. Look for sophisticated architectural patterns beyond basic load balancing. Strong presentations will quantify performance claims and demonstrate understanding of real-world implementation challenges. Deduct points for superficial treatment of distributed systems concepts or inability to defend design decisions during Q&A. Common weaknesses include oversimplified fault tolerance strategies, unrealistic performance assumptions, and poor justification of technology choices. Award full points only when students demonstrate ability to handle complex follow-up questions and show awareness of cutting-edge distributed systems research.

title: Beginner Data Science Portfolio: Customer Behavior Analysis
description: Students will create a comprehensive data science portfolio by analyzing a provided customer dataset using Python. The portfolio will demonstrate fundamental data science skills including data cleaning, exploratory data analysis, visualization, and basic statistical insights presentation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply data cleaning techniques to prepare raw datasets for analysis
Conduct exploratory data analysis using pandas and descriptive statistics
Create meaningful data visualizations using matplotlib or seaborn
Interpret statistical findings and communicate insights to non-technical audiences
Document analysis process using Jupyter notebooks with clear markdown explanations
rubric_criteria: Data Cleaning & Preparation (25 points): Identifies and handles missing values, duplicates, and data type issues. Code is clean and well-commented. Documents cleaning decisions with clear rationale.

Exploratory Data Analysis (25 points): Calculates appropriate descriptive statistics, examines data distributions, identifies patterns and relationships. Asks relevant business questions and investigates them systematically.

Data Visualization (25 points): Creates 4-6 appropriate and well-labeled visualizations that effectively communicate insights. Uses proper chart types, color schemes, and includes interpretive captions for each visualization.

Communication & Documentation (25 points): Provides clear markdown explanations throughout notebook, summarizes key findings in executive summary, uses proper grammar and professional presentation. Code is organized and reproducible.
instructions: Using the provided customer transaction dataset (retail_customer_data.csv), create a complete data science portfolio in a Jupyter notebook.
