Your portfolio must include: (1) Executive Summary section with 3-5 key business insights, (2) Data Cleaning section documenting all preprocessing steps with before/after data quality checks, (3) Exploratory Data Analysis section with descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and customer segmentation by purchase behavior, (4) Visualizations section with at least 4 charts including histograms, scatter plots, and bar charts showing customer demographics and spending patterns, (5) Findings & Recommendations section with actionable business recommendations based on your analysis. Submit your completed .ipynb file via the course portal. Ensure all code cells run successfully and markdown cells are properly formatted. Include your name and date in the notebook header. Use appropriate variable names and comment complex code sections. The dataset contains customer demographics, transaction history, and product categories - focus on identifying high-value customer segments and purchasing trends. Your analysis should be suitable for presentation to business stakeholders who may not have technical backgrounds.
grading_notes: Evaluate notebooks for both technical competency and business insight quality. Common issues include: insufficient data cleaning documentation, generic visualizations without business context, poor markdown formatting, and failure to connect analysis to actionable recommendations. Excellent portfolios (90-100 points) will demonstrate clear analytical thinking and professional presentation standards. Satisfactory work (70-89 points) meets basic requirements but may lack depth in insights or have presentation issues. Below 70 points indicates incomplete analysis or significant technical errors. Provide specific feedback on code quality, visualization effectiveness, and communication clarity. Expect most students to score in the 75-85 range for this beginner-level assessment.

title: Statistical Analysis Lab Report: Investigating Correlation and Regression
description: Students will collect real-world data, perform statistical analysis using correlation and linear regression techniques, and present their findings in a comprehensive lab report format. This assessment evaluates statistical reasoning, mathematical computation, and scientific communication skills.
estimated_time: 4-6 hours (data collection: 1-2 hours, analysis: 2-3 hours, report writing: 1-2 hours)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply correlation coefficients to measure the strength and direction of linear relationships between variables
Construct and interpret linear regression models to make predictions and analyze trends
Evaluate the validity and limitations of statistical models using residual analysis
Communicate mathematical findings effectively using appropriate statistical terminology and visualizations
rubric_criteria: Data Collection and Organization (25 points): Collects appropriate bivariate data set (minimum 20 data points), presents data clearly in tables, identifies variables correctly, and demonstrates proper data handling techniques

Mathematical Analysis (25 points): Correctly calculates correlation coefficient, constructs accurate scatter plot, determines regression equation using proper methods, and shows all mathematical work with appropriate formulas

Statistical Interpretation (25 points): Provides meaningful interpretation of correlation strength and direction, explains regression slope and y-intercept in context, makes reasonable predictions using the model, and discusses limitations and validity of results

Report Quality and Communication (25 points): Follows scientific report format (introduction, methods, results, conclusion), uses proper mathematical notation and terminology, includes clear graphs and charts, and demonstrates logical organization and professional presentation
instructions: Choose a topic that interests you and collect bivariate data to investigate a potential linear relationship. Examples include: height vs. shoe size, study time vs. test scores, temperature vs. ice cream sales, or advertising spending vs. revenue. Your dataset must contain at least 20 paired observations from reliable sources or personal collection. Create a comprehensive lab report including: (1) Introduction stating your research question and hypothesis about the relationship; (2) Methods section describing your data collection process and sample characteristics; (3) Results section presenting your data in a table, creating a scatter plot with proper scaling and labels, calculating the correlation coefficient (r) showing all work, determining the least-squares regression line equation, and creating a residual plot; (4) Analysis and Discussion interpreting the correlation strength, explaining what the slope and y-intercept mean in context, making at least two predictions using your model, discussing the coefficient of determination (r²), and identifying any outliers or limitations; (5) Conclusion summarizing your findings and their significance. Format your report professionally with numbered sections, proper mathematical notation, and clear graphs created using graphing technology or careful hand-drawing. Include all raw data and calculations in an appendix. Submit both digital and printed copies of your complete report including all supporting materials.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - correlation and regression calculations should be precise with clear work shown. Look for proper use of statistical terminology and context-appropriate interpretations rather than just numerical answers. Common issues include: incorrect formula applications, misinterpretation of correlation vs. causation, poor graph scaling or labeling, and generic conclusions not tied to specific data. Award full points for minor computational errors if the method is correct. Expect correlation coefficients between -1 and 1, and check that regression predictions are reasonable. Strong reports will demonstrate understanding that correlation measures relationship strength while regression enables prediction. Grade distribution should approximate: 90-100 points (excellent mathematical work with clear communication), 80-89 points (solid analysis with minor errors or unclear explanations), 70-79 points (basic requirements met but significant mathematical or communication issues), below 70 points (major errors in calculations or incomplete analysis).

title: Advanced Algorithm Analysis and Design Quiz

Partial credit is available for correct intermediate steps even if final answers are incorrect. Submit your work digitally with clear section labels and legible formatting.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct reasoning processes even with minor implementation errors. Look for students demonstrating deep understanding of algorithmic paradigms rather than just memorized solutions. Common issues include: incorrect complexity analysis (especially with recursive algorithms), failure to identify dynamic programming subproblems, incomplete handling of graph edge cases, and poor justification of algorithmic choices. Grade distribution should follow: 90-100 points for exceptional work showing mastery and optimization insights; 80-89 for solid understanding with minor errors; 70-79 for adequate grasp with some conceptual gaps; below 70 for significant misunderstandings. title: End-to-End Predictive Analytics Project: Customer Churn Prediction with MLOps Implementation
description: Students will complete a comprehensive data science project involving customer churn prediction, from data acquisition and preprocessing through model deployment and monitoring. This capstone project requires implementing MLOps best practices, conducting thorough model evaluation, and presenting business-ready insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement complete machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model selection
Apply advanced statistical methods and evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Implement MLOps practices including version control, automated testing, model monitoring, and deployment strategies
Communicate complex analytical findings to both technical and non-technical stakeholders through comprehensive reporting and visualization
rubric_criteria: Data Pipeline & Feature Engineering (25 points): Quality of data acquisition, cleaning, EDA, feature engineering creativity, handling of missing values, outliers, and class imbalance. Code modularity and reproducibility.

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Appropriate algorithm selection and hyperparameter tuning, proper cross-validation implementation, comprehensive performance metrics, statistical significance testing, and model interpretability analysis.

MLOps Implementation (25 points): Version control usage, automated testing implementation, CI/CD pipeline setup, model monitoring dashboard, containerization, and deployment architecture documentation.

Business Communication & Documentation (25 points): Executive summary quality, technical documentation completeness, visualization effectiveness, business impact quantification, and presentation clarity for stakeholder audiences.
instructions: You will develop a complete customer churn prediction system using a telecommunications dataset. Begin by acquiring data from Kaggle's Telco Customer Churn dataset or a similar business dataset of your choice. Your project must include: (1) Comprehensive EDA with statistical tests and advanced visualizations using tools like Plotly or Seaborn; (2) Feature engineering including creation of derived features, encoding strategies, and dimensionality reduction where appropriate; (3) Implementation of at least three different algorithms (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) with proper hyperparameter optimization using techniques like Bayesian optimization; (4) MLOps pipeline using tools such as MLflow for experiment tracking, Docker for containerization, and either AWS SageMaker, Azure ML, or Google Cloud AI Platform for deployment; (5) Model monitoring dashboard showing key metrics, data drift detection, and performance degradation alerts; (6) A/B testing framework design for model comparison in production. Deliverables include: a Jupyter notebook with complete analysis, Python modules for production code, MLOps configuration files, a business presentation (10-12 slides), and technical documentation. Use Git for version control with meaningful commit messages. Submit via GitHub repository link with README containing setup instructions and project overview. All code must be PEP8 compliant and include unit tests for critical functions.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical depth alongside practical business application. Strong projects will demonstrate advanced feature engineering creativity and statistical rigor in model validation. For MLOps component, look for proper separation of concerns, automated testing coverage >80%, and realistic monitoring strategies. Common weaknesses include inadequate handling of class imbalance, overfitting without proper detection, and superficial business insights. Grade distribution typically: 90-100 points (exceptional projects with novel approaches), 80-89 points (solid technical execution meeting all requirements), 70-79 points (good effort with minor gaps in methodology or documentation), below 70 points (missing key components or significant technical errors). Deduct points for late submissions: 5% per day up to one week. Bonus points (up to 5) available for innovative approaches like advanced interpretability methods, real-time streaming implementation, or comprehensive bias analysis.

title: Basic Arithmetic and Problem-Solving Skills Assessment
description: A comprehensive exam evaluating students' understanding of fundamental arithmetic operations, basic algebraic concepts, and their ability to solve multi-step word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform accurate calculations using all four basic arithmetic operations with whole numbers and decimals
Solve multi-step word problems by identifying relevant information and selecting appropriate operations
Apply order of operations (PEMDAS) correctly in mathematical expressions
Demonstrate understanding of basic algebraic concepts including variables and simple equations
rubric_criteria: Computational Accuracy (25 points): Correctly performs arithmetic operations with whole numbers, decimals, and fractions. Shows proper calculation steps and arrives at accurate answers.

Problem-Solving Strategy (25 points): Demonstrates logical approach to word problems by identifying given information, determining what needs to be found, and selecting appropriate mathematical operations.
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Shows clear work with organized step-by-step solutions. Uses proper mathematical notation and labels answers with appropriate units when applicable.

Application of Mathematical Rules (25 points): Correctly applies order of operations, demonstrates understanding of basic algebraic concepts, and follows mathematical conventions consistently throughout the exam.
instructions: This exam consists of 20 questions divided into four sections: arithmetic calculations (5 questions), word problems (8 questions), order of operations (4 questions), and basic algebra (3 questions). You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully before beginning your work. Show all your work clearly in the space provided - partial credit will be given for correct methods even if the final answer is incorrect. For word problems, clearly identify what information is given and what you need to find before setting up your calculations. Circle or box your final answers. Use proper mathematical notation and include units in your answers when appropriate. Calculators are permitted for questions 11-20 only. If you finish early, review your work and check your calculations. Make sure all answers are clearly marked and legible. For multiple-choice questions, select only one answer per question. For word problems, write a complete sentence stating your final answer in context of the problem. If you need extra space for any problem, use the back of the page and clearly indicate which question you are continuing. Manage your time wisely - spend approximately 20 minutes on arithmetic calculations, 40 minutes on word problems, 15 minutes on order of operations, and 15 minutes on basic algebra problems.
grading_notes: Award full points when students show complete, accurate work with correct final answers. Give partial credit (50-75% of points) for correct methods with minor calculation errors. Award 25-50% of points for appropriate problem-solving approach with significant errors in execution. No credit for answers without supporting work shown. Common issues to watch: incorrect order of operations application, failure to include units in word problem answers, arithmetic errors with decimals and fractions, and incomplete algebraic solutions. Expect grade distribution: 25% A grades (90-100), 35% B grades (80-89), 30% C grades (70-79), 10% below 70. Provide specific feedback on recurring errors and highlight strong problem-solving approaches in student work.

title: Database Design Trade-offs: Relational vs NoSQL Architecture Discussion
description: Students will analyze a realistic business scenario and engage in structured discussions about database architecture choices, defending their recommendations for either relational or NoSQL solutions while critically evaluating peers' proposals.
estimated_time: 3-4 hours (initial research and post writing: 2 hours, peer responses: 1-2 hours)
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate trade-offs between different database management systems based on specific use case requirements
Apply database design principles to real-world business scenarios
Communicate technical concepts clearly to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
Critically analyze and provide constructive feedback on database architecture proposals
rubric_criteria: Initial Analysis and Recommendation (30 points): Demonstrates thorough understanding of both relational and NoSQL systems, provides well-reasoned recommendation with specific technical justifications, addresses scalability, consistency, and performance considerations

Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Uses correct database terminology, shows understanding of ACID properties, CAP theorem, data modeling concepts, and accurately describes chosen system's architecture and limitations

Business Context Integration (20 points): Clearly connects technical choices to business requirements, considers factors like budget, timeline, team expertise, maintenance costs, and future growth projections

Peer Engagement and Critical Thinking (25 points): Provides substantive responses to at least two peers, asks thoughtful questions, identifies potential issues in others' proposals, offers alternative perspectives or solutions
instructions:
You are a database consultant for TechFlow, a rapidly growing e-commerce startup. They currently have 50,000 users, process 1,000 orders daily, and plan to expand internationally within 18 months. Their current MySQL system is experiencing performance issues during peak traffic. The development team has mixed experience with different database technologies.

**Your Task:**
1. **Initial Post (400-600 words):** Write a technical recommendation memo addressing: (a) Your recommended database solution (stick with improved relational setup, migrate to NoSQL like MongoDB/DynamoDB, or hybrid approach), (b) Specific technical justifications including data consistency needs, scalability requirements, and query patterns, (c) Implementation timeline and migration strategy, (d) Cost-benefit analysis including development time and infrastructure costs, (e) Risk assessment and mitigation strategies.

2. **Peer Responses (150-200 words each):** Respond to two classmates' recommendations by: (a) Identifying one strength in their analysis, (b) Raising one concern or potential challenge they may have overlooked, (c) Asking a specific technical question about their implementation approach, (d) Suggesting one alternative consideration or modification.

**Format Requirements:**
- Use professional memo format for initial post
- Include specific database technologies, tools, or services
- Reference at least 2 credible sources (documentation, case studies, or technical articles)
- Use proper technical terminology
- Submit initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM, responses by Sunday 11:59 PM

**Submission:** Post directly in the designated discussion forum. Use clear headings and professional formatting.
grading_notes: Look for students who go beyond surface-level comparisons and demonstrate deep understanding of database internals. Strong responses will mention specific technologies (e.g., PostgreSQL vs MongoDB vs DynamoDB), address data modeling differences, and show awareness of operational concerns like backup, monitoring, and team training. Deduct points for generic responses that could apply to any scenario. Excellent peer responses should demonstrate active engagement with others' technical reasoning rather than just agreeable comments. Watch for students who consider non-technical factors like team capabilities and organizational constraints. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Common issues include: oversimplifying NoSQL as 'always faster,' ignoring migration complexities, or failing to connect technical features to specific business needs.

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Defense
description: Students will design, implement, and present a complete machine learning solution for a real-world business problem, including data preprocessing, model selection, evaluation, and deployment considerations. The presentation must demonstrate technical mastery while communicating findings to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement complete machine learning pipelines from data ingestion to model deployment
Apply appropriate statistical methods and machine learning algorithms for complex problem-solving
Evaluate model performance using multiple metrics and validation techniques
Communicate technical findings effectively to diverse audiences
Demonstrate critical thinking in model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and result interpretation
Address ethical considerations and potential biases in machine learning implementations
rubric_criteria: Technical Implementation (25 points): Code quality, pipeline completeness, appropriate use of libraries/frameworks, reproducibility, proper version control, and adherence to best practices in data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model training

Methodology and Analysis (25 points): Justification of algorithm selection, proper cross-validation techniques, comprehensive model evaluation using appropriate metrics, statistical significance testing, and thorough analysis of results including limitations

Presentation and Communication (25 points): Clear articulation of problem statement, logical flow of presentation, effective use of visualizations, ability to explain technical concepts to non-technical audience, professional delivery, and time management

Problem-Solving and Critical Thinking (25 points): Demonstration of iterative improvement process, handling of edge cases and data quality issues, consideration of ethical implications and bias, discussion of deployment challenges, and thoughtful responses to questions during defense
instructions: Select a real-world dataset from Kaggle, UCI Repository, or obtain approval for a proprietary dataset (minimum 10,000 samples, 10+ features). Your presentation must include: (1) Problem definition with business context and success metrics, (2) Exploratory data analysis with statistical insights and visualizations, (3) Data preprocessing pipeline including handling missing values, outliers, and feature engineering, (4) Model selection process comparing at least 3 different algorithms with justified hyperparameter tuning, (5) Comprehensive evaluation using appropriate metrics, cross-validation, and statistical tests, (6) Discussion of model interpretability and feature importance, (7) Deployment considerations including scalability, monitoring, and maintenance, (8) Ethical considerations including bias detection and fairness metrics. Submit a GitHub repository containing all code, documentation, and a README file 48 hours before presentation. Code must be well-commented, reproducible, and include unit tests for critical functions. Presentation slides should be designed for a mixed audience of technical team members and business stakeholders. Be prepared to defend your methodological choices and answer questions about alternative approaches, potential improvements, and real-world implementation challenges.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor over complexity - a well-executed simple solution scores higher than an poorly implemented complex one. Look for evidence of iterative development and learning from initial approaches. Common deductions: insufficient EDA (loses 5-8 points), poor code documentation (loses 3-5 points), inappropriate evaluation metrics (loses 5-10 points), inability to explain methodology during Q&A (loses 5-15 points). Exceptional work (90-100) demonstrates novel insights, sophisticated feature engineering, or creative problem-solving. Average work (70-85) meets all requirements competently. Below average (60-75) has technical errors or incomplete analysis. Failing work (<60) has fundamental flaws in methodology or implementation. Encourage students to focus on storytelling and practical implications rather than just technical details.

title: Python Variables and Data Types Lab Report
description: Students will write, execute, and document Python programs demonstrating understanding of variables, data types, type conversion, and basic input/output operations. The lab report will include code snippets, output screenshots, and reflective analysis of programming concepts.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate understanding of Python variable declaration and assignment
Identify and use different data types (integers, floats, strings, booleans)
Apply type conversion functions and understand when they are needed
Implement basic input/output operations using input() and print() functions
Debug simple syntax and runtime errors in Python code
rubric_criteria: Code Implementation (25 points): All required programs run correctly without syntax errors, demonstrate proper use of variables and data types, and follow Python naming conventions
Documentation and Output (25 points): Code includes clear comments, screenshots of program output are provided and legible, and all required programs are included in the report

Technical Analysis (25 points): Student accurately explains variable assignments, correctly identifies data types, demonstrates understanding of type conversion, and provides valid examples of when different data types are used

Problem Solving and Reflection (25 points): Student successfully completes the debugging exercise, explains errors encountered and solutions applied, and provides thoughtful reflection on learning experience and challenges faced
instructions:
Complete the following programming exercises and compile your work into a lab report document (Word or PDF format). For each exercise, include: (1) the complete Python code with comments, (2) a screenshot of the program running successfully, and (3) a brief explanation of what the code does.

Exercise 1: Create a program that declares variables of each data type (int, float, string, boolean) and prints their values and types using the type() function.

Exercise 2: Write a program that asks the user for their name, age, and favorite number, then displays a formatted message using all three inputs. Demonstrate both string concatenation and f-string formatting.

Exercise 3: Create a simple calculator program that takes two numbers as input and performs addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, displaying results with appropriate labels.

Exercise 4: Debug the provided broken code snippet (will be given in class) that contains 3-4 common beginner errors. Document what errors you found and how you fixed them.

Your report should include: a title page with your name and date, introduction paragraph explaining the lab's purpose, completed exercises with code and screenshots, a reflection section (150-200 words) discussing what you learned and any challenges encountered, and proper formatting throughout. Submit as a single PDF file named 'LastName_FirstName_Lab1.pdf' to the course management system by 11:59 PM on the due date.
grading_notes: Focus on correctness of code execution rather than advanced programming style for beginners. Common issues to watch for: missing screenshots, uncommented code, incorrect variable naming (using reserved words), confusion between input types (strings vs numbers), and inadequate reflection responses. Expect 70-80% of students to score in the B range (80-89 points). Award full points for code that runs correctly even if not optimally written. Deduct points for missing components rather than minor syntax preferences. Provide specific feedback on debugging exercise as this develops critical troubleshooting skills.

title: Customer Segmentation Analysis: From Data Exploration to Business Insights
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive data science analysis of an e-commerce customer dataset, performing exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, clustering analysis, and providing actionable business recommendations. This assessment evaluates practical application of data science methodologies including statistical analysis, unsupervised learning, and data visualization skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply exploratory data analysis techniques to understand dataset characteristics and identify data quality issues
Implement feature engineering and preprocessing techniques appropriate for clustering analysis
Execute and evaluate unsupervised learning algorithms (K-means, hierarchical clustering) with proper parameter selection
Create effective data visualizations to communicate analytical findings and support business recommendations
Translate statistical findings into actionable business insights and strategic recommendations
rubric_criteria: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Quality (25 points): Comprehensive statistical summary, identification of missing values/outliers, appropriate data cleaning decisions, clear documentation of data characteristics and distributions

Feature Engineering & Preprocessing (25 points): Logical feature selection and creation, proper handling of categorical variables, appropriate scaling/normalization techniques, justification of preprocessing choices

Clustering Implementation & Evaluation (25 points): Correct implementation of at least two clustering algorithms, proper use of evaluation metrics (silhouette score, elbow method), appropriate cluster number selection with clear justification

Visualization & Business Insights (25 points): Clear, well-labeled visualizations that effectively communicate findings, actionable business recommendations supported by data analysis, professional presentation of results with logical flow
instructions: You are provided with an e-commerce customer dataset containing purchase history, demographic information, and behavioral metrics. Complete the following analysis in a Jupyter notebook with clear markdown explanations for each step. **Data Exploration (25%)**: Load the dataset and perform comprehensive exploratory data analysis. Calculate descriptive statistics, identify missing values and outliers, and create visualizations showing key relationships between variables. Document any data quality issues and your approach to handling them. **Feature Engineering (25%)**: Create meaningful features for customer segmentation such as RFM metrics (Recency, Frequency, Monetary), customer lifetime value indicators, or behavioral scores. Handle categorical variables appropriately and apply necessary scaling or normalization. Clearly justify your feature selection decisions. **Clustering Analysis (25%)**: Implement K-means and hierarchical clustering algorithms. Use appropriate methods to determine optimal cluster numbers (elbow method, silhouette analysis). Compare clustering results and select the best approach with clear justification. Profile each customer segment with statistical summaries. **Business Recommendations (25%)**: Create professional visualizations displaying your customer segments and their characteristics. Provide specific, actionable business recommendations for each segment including marketing strategies, product recommendations, or retention tactics. Submit your completed Jupyter notebook (.ipynb file) with all code executed and outputs visible. Include a 2-page executive summary (PDF) highlighting key findings and business recommendations for non-technical stakeholders.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should typically follow: 90-100 (Excellent - comprehensive analysis with innovative insights), 80-89 (Good - solid analysis meeting all requirements), 70-79 (Satisfactory - basic requirements met with minor gaps), Below 70 (Needs improvement). Watch for common issues: incomplete data exploration, inappropriate clustering evaluation, weak business justifications, poor code documentation, or visualizations lacking proper labels/context. Deduct points for: code that doesn't run (-10 points), missing executive summary (-15 points), or failure to implement required algorithms (-20 points). Award bonus consideration for: creative feature engineering, additional clustering algorithms, particularly insightful business recommendations, or exceptional data storytelling. Expect most students to identify 3-5 meaningful customer segments with clear business applications.

title: Advanced Data Structures and Algorithm Design Comprehensive Exam
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of advanced data structures, algorithm design paradigms, and complexity analysis through theoretical problems, implementation challenges, and optimization scenarios. This exam covers graph algorithms, dynamic programming, advanced tree structures, and computational complexity theory.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze and implement advanced data structures including B-trees, AVL trees, and graph representations
Design and analyze algorithms using dynamic programming, greedy methods, and divide-and-conquer paradigms
Evaluate time and space complexity of algorithms using asymptotic notation and prove correctness
Optimize existing algorithms and data structures for specific use cases and constraints
Apply graph algorithms including shortest path, minimum spanning tree, and network flow problems
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Design and Implementation (25 points): Correctness of algorithm logic, appropriate data structure selection, handling of edge cases, and code quality. Full credit requires working solutions with optimal time complexity.

Complexity Analysis and Mathematical Reasoning (25 points): Accurate Big-O, Omega, and Theta analysis, formal proofs of correctness, recurrence relation solving, and mathematical justification of design choices.

Problem Solving and Optimization (25 points): Identification of optimal approaches, creative solutions to constraints, trade-off analysis between time and space complexity, and demonstration of multiple solution strategies.

Technical Communication and Documentation (25 points): Clear explanation of algorithms, well-commented code, logical flow of solutions, proper use of technical terminology, and comprehensive analysis of results.
instructions:
This exam consists of four sections, each worth 25 points. You have 3 hours to complete all sections. Show all work and provide clear explanations for full credit.

Section 1 - Graph Algorithms (25 points): Implement Dijkstra's algorithm for a weighted directed graph and analyze a network flow problem. Provide complete pseudocode and trace through your algorithm with a given example.

Section 2 - Dynamic Programming (25 points): Solve two optimization problems using dynamic programming. One involves sequence alignment, the other requires designing a solution for optimal resource allocation. Include recurrence relations and space optimization analysis.

Section 3 - Advanced Data Structures (25 points): Design and analyze a self-balancing tree structure for a specific application. Compare your solution with existing structures and justify design decisions. Include insertion and deletion algorithms.

Section 4 - Complexity Theory (25 points): Prove the correctness of a given algorithm, analyze worst-case and average-case complexity, and discuss NP-completeness concepts through reduction proofs.

Submission Requirements: Submit handwritten work clearly labeled by section, or typed solutions with proper formatting. Include all diagrams, mathematical proofs, and code implementations. Late submissions will be penalized 10% per hour.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should target: 20% A-level (90-100), 30% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 20% below C-level. Common issues to watch: incomplete complexity analysis (often missing space complexity), incorrect handling of graph edge cases, inadequate mathematical rigor in proofs, and unclear algorithm explanations. Award partial credit for correct reasoning even with implementation errors. Deduct points for inefficient solutions when optimal algorithms exist. Pay special attention to students' ability to explain trade-offs and justify design choices, as this demonstrates deep understanding beyond mere memorization.

title: Data Science Project Lifecycle Discussion
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing the complete data science project lifecycle, from problem identification to deployment and monitoring. They will demonstrate understanding of each phase, identify potential challenges, and propose solutions based on real-world scenarios.
estimated_time: 2 hours (1 hour preparation + 1 hour discussion participation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and explain the key phases of the data science project lifecycle
Analyze potential challenges and bottlenecks in data science projects
Evaluate the importance of stakeholder communication in data science work
Apply data science concepts to real-world business scenarios
rubric_criteria: Phase Understanding (25 points): Accurately identifies and explains all major phases of the data science lifecycle (problem definition, data collection, exploration, modeling, validation, deployment, monitoring) with clear examples

Challenge Analysis (25 points): Identifies realistic challenges for each phase and demonstrates understanding of their impact on project success, showing awareness of technical, business, and ethical considerations

Solution Proposing (25 points): Provides practical, well-reasoned solutions to identified challenges, demonstrating critical thinking and consideration of trade-offs, resource constraints, and stakeholder needs

Discussion Participation (25 points): Actively engages with peers through thoughtful responses, asks relevant questions, builds on others' ideas constructively, and maintains professional communication throughout the discussion
instructions: You will participate in a structured online discussion about the data science project lifecycle using a provided business scenario. **Scenario**: A mid-sized e-commerce company wants to implement a recommendation system to increase sales. **Your Task**: 1) **Initial Post (due by Wednesday, 11:59 PM)**: Write a 400-500 word analysis covering: a) Identify the 6-7 key phases this project would go through, b) Describe 2-3 specific challenges the team might face in each phase, c) Propose practical solutions for the most critical challenges, d) Explain how you would measure project success. 2) **Peer Responses (due by Friday, 11:59 PM)**: Respond to at least 3 classmates' posts with substantive comments (100-150 words each). Ask clarifying questions, share alternative perspectives, or build upon their ideas. 3) **Format Requirements**: Use clear headings for each phase, support your points with specific examples, cite any external sources using APA format. Maintain professional tone throughout. 4) **Submission**: Post directly to the discussion forum. Late submissions will lose 10 points per day. Your contributions should demonstrate understanding of data science concepts while showing practical business awareness.
grading_notes: Look for evidence that students understand data science is not just technical work but involves significant business strategy, stakeholder management, and iterative problem-solving. Award full points for Phase Understanding when students go beyond listing phases to explain why each matters. For Challenge Analysis, prioritize realistic over theoretical challenges - students should show awareness that data quality, stakeholder buy-in, and resource constraints are often bigger issues than algorithm selection. Solution Proposing should be evaluated based on practicality rather than technical sophistication. Discussion Participation should reward quality over quantity - look for students who engage meaningfully rather than just meeting minimum requirements. Common issues to watch: students focusing too heavily on technical details while ignoring business context, unrealistic timelines or resource assumptions, and superficial peer responses. Expect grade distribution: 15% A+ (exceptional business insight), 35% A/A- (solid understanding), 40% B range (adequate with minor gaps), 10% C or below (significant conceptual issues).

title: Real-World Linear Functions: Analysis and Application Presentation
description: Students will research, analyze, and present a real-world scenario that can be modeled using linear functions, demonstrating their understanding of slope, y-intercept, domain, range, and practical applications of linear relationships.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and analyze linear relationships in real-world contexts
Calculate and interpret slope and y-intercept in practical situations
Determine appropriate domain and range for linear models
Create accurate graphs of linear functions with proper scaling and labeling
Communicate mathematical concepts clearly using appropriate terminology
Make predictions using linear models and evaluate their reasonableness
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): Correct identification of linear relationship, accurate calculations of slope and y-intercept, proper determination of domain and range, mathematically sound predictions

Real-World Application (25 points): Appropriate choice of scenario, clear connection between mathematical model and real situation, realistic data collection or research, meaningful interpretation of results
Visual Presentation (25 points): Clear and accurate graph with proper scaling, axis labels, and units; organized slide layout; effective use of visual aids; professional appearance

Communication and Understanding (25 points): Clear explanation of mathematical concepts, appropriate use of mathematical vocabulary, confident delivery, ability to answer questions, demonstration of conceptual understanding
instructions: Choose a real-world scenario that can be modeled with a linear function (examples: cell phone plans, car depreciation, population growth, temperature conversion, or subscription services). Your presentation must include: (1) Introduction of your chosen scenario with background information and data sources, (2) Mathematical analysis showing how to write the linear function, including identification of variables, calculation of slope with units and interpretation, determination of y-intercept and its meaning, and establishment of realistic domain and range, (3) Visual representation through a properly scaled graph with labeled axes, appropriate scale markings, clear title, and at least 5 plotted points, (4) Application component making two predictions using your model, explaining whether results are reasonable, and discussing limitations of the linear model. Format requirements: 6-8 slides total, 8-10 minute presentation, submit slides 24 hours before presentation, include a reference slide citing at least 2 credible sources. Avoid overly simple examples like distance-time with constant speed. Choose scenarios where the linear relationship provides meaningful insights.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - look for correct slope calculations, proper units, and realistic domain/range. Common errors include incorrect slope formula application and unrealistic domains. For real-world application, assess whether the linear model genuinely fits the scenario - some students may force non-linear relationships into linear models. Visual presentation should demonstrate understanding of graphing conventions; watch for unlabeled axes, inappropriate scaling, or missing units. Communication assessment should focus on mathematical vocabulary usage and conceptual understanding rather than presentation polish. Grade distribution expectation: 15% exemplary (90-100), 60% proficient (75-89), 20% developing (60-74), 5% beginning (below 60). Provide specific feedback on mathematical errors and suggest improvements for real-world connections.

title: Basic Arithmetic Operations and Problem-Solving Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' understanding of fundamental arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and their ability to apply these skills to solve real-world word problems involving whole numbers up to 1000.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform accurate addition and subtraction with whole numbers up to 1000, including regrouping
Execute multiplication and division operations with single and double-digit numbers
Interpret and solve multi-step word problems using appropriate arithmetic operations
Demonstrate understanding of mathematical vocabulary and show work clearly
rubric_criteria: Computation Accuracy (25 points): Correct execution of arithmetic operations with proper algorithms and minimal calculation errors
Problem-Solving Strategy (25 points): Identification of correct operations needed, logical sequence of steps, and appropriate mathematical reasoning
Work Organization (25 points): Clear presentation of calculations, proper use of mathematical symbols, and systematic approach to problem-solving
Word Problem Interpretation (25 points): Accurate identification of given information, understanding of what is being asked, and correct translation into mathematical expressions
instructions: This quiz consists of 20 questions divided into four sections. You have 45 minutes to complete all sections. Show all your work clearly in the space provided, as partial credit will be awarded for correct methods even if the final answer is incorrect. Use pencil and have an eraser ready. Calculators are not permitted. Section A (Questions 1-5): Basic addition and subtraction problems with numbers up to 1000. Some problems require regrouping. Write your calculations vertically and show each step. Section B (Questions 6-10): Multiplication and division problems involving single and double-digit numbers. Show your multiplication tables work and division steps including remainders where applicable. Section C (Questions 11-15): Single-step word problems. Read each problem carefully, identify the operation needed, write a number sentence, and solve. Circle your final answer and include appropriate units. Section D (Questions 16-20): Multi-step word problems requiring two operations. Identify all given information, determine what you need to find, show both calculation steps clearly, and write your answer in a complete sentence. If you finish early, review your work and check your calculations. Make sure all answers are reasonable and that you've answered what each question is asking.
grading_notes: Use partial credit generously - award points for correct setup and method even with computational errors. For word problems, give credit separately for interpretation (identifying correct operations) and execution (accurate calculations). Common issues to watch: regrouping errors in subtraction, multiplication table mistakes, misreading word problems, and forgetting units in final answers. Grade distribution expectation: 90-100 (excellent computational skills and problem-solving), 80-89 (good understanding with minor errors), 70-79 (basic competency with some conceptual gaps), below 70 (needs additional instruction). Provide specific feedback on recurring error patterns and note students who may benefit from additional practice with particular operations.

title: Personal Task Management System with REST API
description: Students will design and implement a complete task management system featuring a RESTful API backend, database integration, and a simple web interface. This assessment evaluates software architecture, API design, database modeling, and full-stack development skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement RESTful APIs following industry best practices
Apply object-oriented programming principles and design patterns
Integrate relational databases with application logic using appropriate data modeling
Demonstrate version control proficiency and code documentation standards
Implement error handling, input validation, and basic security measures
rubric_criteria: API Design & Implementation (25 points): RESTful endpoints follow HTTP conventions, proper status codes, JSON responses, CRUD operations for tasks/users, authentication middleware, comprehensive error handling

Database Design & Integration (25 points): Normalized database schema, appropriate data types and constraints, efficient queries, proper connection handling, data validation, migration scripts included

Code Quality & Architecture (25 points): Clean, readable code with consistent formatting, appropriate use of OOP principles, separation of concerns, proper project structure, meaningful variable/function names, code reusability

Documentation & Testing (25 points): Complete README with setup instructions, API documentation with endpoints and examples, unit tests covering core functionality, version control with meaningful commit messages, code comments where necessary
instructions: Develop a personal task management system with the following components: 1) Backend API supporting user registration/login, task CRUD operations (create, read, update, delete), task categorization, and due date management. 2) Database schema supporting users, tasks, and categories with appropriate relationships. 3) Frontend interface (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) allowing users to interact with all API features. 4) Authentication system using JWT tokens or sessions. Technical requirements: Use any modern programming language (Python/Flask, Node.js/Express, Java/Spring, etc.), implement at least 8 API endpoints, include input validation and error handling, use a relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, or SQLite), implement proper HTTP status codes, and ensure data persistence. Deliverables: Complete source code in a Git repository, database setup/migration scripts, comprehensive README with installation and usage instructions, API documentation (can use tools like Postman collection or Swagger), and a brief reflection document (500 words) discussing design decisions, challenges encountered, and potential improvements. Submit via GitHub repository link or zip file containing all materials. The system should handle at least 20 concurrent tasks per user and demonstrate professional-level code organization.
grading_notes: Evaluate functionality first - the system must work as specified. For API Design: Check HTTP methods align with operations (GET for retrieval, POST for creation), status codes are appropriate (200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500), and endpoints follow REST conventions. For Database: Look for normalized tables, foreign key relationships, appropriate indexing, and no SQL injection vulnerabilities. For Code Quality: Assess maintainability, readability, and adherence to language conventions. Partial credit available for incomplete features if architecture is sound. Common issues to watch: hardcoded values, missing error handling, poor variable naming, lack of input validation, and inadequate documentation. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Provide specific feedback on areas for improvement and acknowledge creative solutions or additional features beyond requirements.

title: Comprehensive Data Science Case Study: Customer Churn Prediction and Business Intelligence
description: A comprehensive practical examination where students analyze a real-world customer dataset to build predictive models for churn prediction, perform advanced statistical analysis, and create actionable business recommendations. Students must demonstrate proficiency in data preprocessing, feature engineering, multiple machine learning algorithms, model evaluation, and business interpretation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced data preprocessing techniques including handling missing data, outlier detection, and feature engineering
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms for classification problems
Perform comprehensive model evaluation using appropriate metrics and statistical tests
Translate technical findings into actionable business insights and recommendations
Demonstrate proficiency in data visualization and statistical interpretation
Apply proper experimental design and cross-validation techniques
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and Exploratory Analysis (25 points): Quality of data cleaning, missing value handling, outlier detection, feature engineering creativity, and depth of exploratory data analysis with appropriate visualizations

Machine Learning Implementation (25 points): Correct implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper hyperparameter tuning, appropriate train/validation/test splits, and code quality

Model Evaluation and Statistical Analysis (25 points): Use of appropriate evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), statistical significance testing, feature importance analysis, model interpretability techniques, and comparison methodology

Business Intelligence and Communication (25 points): Quality of business insights, actionable recommendations, clarity of visualizations, professional presentation of findings, and demonstrated understanding of business context
instructions:
You are provided with a telecommunications customer dataset containing 20 features and 5,000 customer records. Your task is to develop a comprehensive churn prediction solution and present business recommendations.

Deliverables:
1. Jupyter notebook with complete analysis (well-documented code, markdown explanations)
2. Executive summary (2-page PDF) with key findings and recommendations
3. Presentation slides (10 slides maximum) for stakeholder presentation

Specific Requirements:
- Perform thorough EDA with at least 5 meaningful visualizations
- Handle missing values and outliers with justification for methods chosen
- Create at least 2 new engineered features
- Implement minimum 3 different ML algorithms with hyperparameter optimization
- Use appropriate cross-validation and evaluation metrics
- Conduct feature importance analysis
- Provide confidence intervals for model performance
- Include business cost-benefit analysis of implementing your model
- Identify top 3 actionable strategies to reduce churn

Submission: Upload all files to the course portal as a compressed folder named 'LastName_FirstName_ChurnAnalysis'. Ensure all code runs without errors and produces consistent results. Include a requirements.txt file with all necessary libraries.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor and business acumen equally. Look for proper statistical methodology, not just high accuracy scores. Award partial credit for well-reasoned approaches even if execution has minor errors. Expect 10-15% of students to achieve 90+ points, 60-70% to score 75-89 points. Common issues to watch: overfitting, data leakage, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced classes, lack of business context in recommendations. Deduct points for non-reproducible code, missing documentation, or unrealistic business assumptions. Bonus consideration for creative feature engineering or advanced techniques like SHAP analysis.

title: Advanced Mathematical Modeling: Discussion on Optimization Techniques in Real-World Applications
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing the application of advanced optimization techniques (linear programming, nonlinear optimization, and stochastic optimization) to solve complex real-world problems. The assessment evaluates students' ability to synthesize theoretical knowledge, critically evaluate different approaches, and communicate mathematical reasoning effectively in a collaborative academic environment.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate mastery of advanced optimization theory and its mathematical foundations
Analyze and compare the effectiveness of different optimization methods for complex problems
Apply mathematical modeling techniques to real-world scenarios with multiple constraints
Communicate sophisticated mathematical concepts clearly and engage in scholarly discourse
Evaluate the limitations and assumptions of mathematical models in practical applications
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of optimization theory, uses precise mathematical terminology, provides accurate analysis of algorithms and their complexity, shows mastery of underlying mathematical principles

Critical Analysis and Problem-Solving (25 points): Effectively compares different optimization approaches, identifies appropriate methods for specific problem types, demonstrates insight into model limitations, proposes innovative solutions or modifications to existing methods

Real-World Application and Context (25 points): Successfully connects theoretical concepts to practical applications, demonstrates understanding of how mathematical constraints translate to real-world limitations, provides relevant examples from industry or research

Communication and Engagement (25 points): Articulates complex mathematical ideas clearly, responds thoughtfully to peers' contributions, asks probing questions that advance the discussion, maintains professional academic discourse throughout
instructions:
This discussion will unfold over one week with specific posting requirements. You will analyze three optimization scenarios: a supply chain logistics problem requiring linear programming, a machine learning parameter tuning challenge using nonlinear optimization, and a financial portfolio optimization under uncertainty using stochastic methods. 

Initial Post (due by Wednesday): Write a 800-1000 word analysis comparing these three optimization approaches. Address: (1) the mathematical foundations of each method, (2) why each method is most suitable for its respective scenario, (3) potential limitations and assumptions, and (4) how you would validate the solutions. Include at least one mathematical expression or algorithm description for each method. Cite a minimum of three recent academic sources.

Peer Responses (due by Friday): Respond substantively to at least two classmates' posts (minimum 300 words each). Challenge their assumptions, propose alternative approaches, or extend their analysis with additional insights. Focus on mathematical accuracy and theoretical depth rather than simple agreement.

Final Reflection (due by Sunday): Post a 400-500 word synthesis addressing: How has the discussion enhanced your understanding of optimization theory? What new perspectives emerged from peer interactions? Identify one area where further mathematical research would be valuable.

Format all mathematical expressions using proper notation. Submit through the course discussion board with clear subject lines indicating post type.
grading_notes: Evaluate posts for mathematical sophistication beyond basic textbook regurgitation. Look for evidence of independent thinking and advanced synthesis. Common issues include: oversimplified analysis of algorithm complexity, failure to address convergence criteria, insufficient consideration of computational constraints, and superficial peer engagement. Excellent work (90-100) demonstrates graduate-level mathematical insight and original thinking. Good work (80-89) shows solid understanding with minor gaps. Satisfactory work (70-79) meets requirements but lacks depth. Below 70 indicates fundamental misunderstandings or incomplete submissions. Deduct points for late submissions: 10% per day. Mathematical notation errors should be noted but not heavily penalized unless they indicate conceptual confusion.

title: Statistical Analysis and Modeling Lab Report: Population Growth Dynamics
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis of real-world population data, develop mathematical models to predict future trends, and critically evaluate their findings. This assessment combines data analysis, regression modeling, hypothesis testing, and mathematical interpretation skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced statistical methods including regression analysis, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing to real-world datasets
Construct and validate mathematical models using exponential, logistic, and polynomial functions to describe population dynamics
Critically analyze model assumptions, limitations, and accuracy through residual analysis and goodness-of-fit measures
Communicate complex mathematical findings through precise technical writing and professional data visualization
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis and Statistical Methods (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of descriptive statistics, performs appropriate regression analyses, correctly calculates confidence intervals, and conducts valid hypothesis tests with proper interpretation of p-values and statistical significance

Mathematical Modeling (25 points): Develops multiple population models (exponential, logistic, polynomial), uses appropriate mathematical notation, shows all derivations clearly, and demonstrates understanding of model parameters and their real-world meaning

Model Validation and Critical Analysis (25 points): Conducts thorough residual analysis, calculates R-squared and other goodness-of-fit measures, identifies model limitations and assumptions, compares competing models using appropriate criteria (AIC, BIC), and discusses prediction accuracy

Technical Communication and Professional Presentation (25 points): Uses proper mathematical notation throughout, creates clear and informative visualizations with appropriate labels and legends, writes coherent explanations of methodology and results, and follows scientific report format with logical organization
instructions: You will analyze population data from three different countries/regions over a 50-year period to develop predictive mathematical models. Begin by downloading datasets from the provided World Bank database links. Conduct exploratory data analysis including summary statistics, trend identification, and initial visualizations. Develop three different mathematical models: exponential growth (P(t) = P₀e^(rt)), logistic growth (P(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(-rt))), and polynomial regression of your chosen degree. For each model, show complete mathematical derivations, parameter estimation methods, and confidence intervals. Validate models using the last 10 years of data as a test set. Create professional-quality graphs showing original data, fitted models, confidence bands, and residual plots. Your report must include: (1) Executive summary (150 words), (2) Data description and methodology, (3) Mathematical model development with full derivations, (4) Results section with statistical analysis, (5) Model comparison and validation, (6) Discussion of limitations and real-world implications, (7) Conclusion with policy recommendations. Submit as a single PDF with embedded graphs and equations properly formatted. Include an appendix with your calculation code or detailed hand calculations. Length: 8-12 pages excluding appendices.
grading_notes: Look for mathematical rigor in model derivations - students should show parameter estimation methods, not just final results. Statistical analysis should include proper interpretation of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, not just calculation. Common issues include: incorrect residual analysis interpretation, failure to validate models on holdout data, poor graph formatting without proper labels/units, and superficial discussion of model limitations. Expect grade distribution: A (20-25%), B (40-45%), C (25-30%), D/F (10-15%). Deduct points for: missing mathematical notation (-3 pts), graphs without proper labels (-2 pts each), incorrect statistical interpretations (-5 pts each), and failure to discuss model assumptions (-5 pts). Excellence indicators include: creative model modifications, discussion of alternative approaches, connection to current demographic research, and sophisticated interpretation of results.

title: Customer Purchase Behavior Analysis Project
description: Students will analyze a retail customer dataset to identify purchasing patterns, create visualizations, and develop actionable business insights using Python and data science fundamentals. This project assesses core data manipulation, analysis, and communication skills essential for entry-level data science work.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) using Python pandas and descriptive statistics
Create effective data visualizations using matplotlib/seaborn to communicate findings
Apply data cleaning techniques to handle missing values and outliers
Draw meaningful business insights from data analysis and present recommendations
Document analysis process with clear, reproducible code and explanations
rubric_criteria: Data Cleaning & Preparation (25 points): Properly identifies and handles missing values, outliers, and data quality issues. Code is clean and well-commented. Dataset is appropriately prepared for analysis.

Exploratory Data Analysis (25 points): Conducts thorough statistical analysis including summary statistics, distributions, and correlations. Uses appropriate statistical measures and demonstrates understanding of the data structure.

Data Visualization (25 points): Creates 4-6 clear, well-labeled visualizations that effectively communicate key findings. Charts are appropriate for data types and include proper titles, axis labels, and legends.

Business Insights & Recommendations (25 points): Provides 3-5 actionable business recommendations based on analysis findings. Insights are clearly explained, logically derived from data, and relevant to retail customer behavior.
instructions: You will analyze the provided retail customer dataset (customers_data.csv) containing purchase history, demographics, and transaction details for 1,000 customers over 12 months. Your deliverable is a Jupyter notebook with your complete analysis. Requirements: (1) Data Cleaning: Load the dataset, identify and document data quality issues, handle missing values and outliers with justification for your approach. (2) Exploratory Analysis: Calculate key statistics, analyze customer demographics, purchase patterns by season/product category, and customer lifetime value. (3) Visualizations: Create at minimum - customer age distribution histogram, monthly sales trend line chart, product category sales bar chart, customer spending vs. frequency scatter plot, and two additional charts of your choice. (4) Business Insights: Conclude with a summary section containing specific, data-driven recommendations for marketing strategy, inventory management, or customer retention. Format: Submit a single .ipynb file with markdown cells explaining your methodology and findings. Include a brief executive summary at the top. Code should be clean, commented, and reproducible. All visualizations must have appropriate titles and labels. File naming: LastName_FirstName_CustomerAnalysis.ipynb. Due date: Submit via course portal by 11:59 PM on the specified deadline.
grading_notes: Grade holistically within each criterion - look for demonstration of understanding rather than perfect technique. For data cleaning, accept various valid approaches (dropping vs. imputing missing values) as long as decisions are justified. In EDA, prioritize correct interpretation over advanced techniques. For visualizations, focus on clarity and appropriateness rather than aesthetic perfection - students should demonstrate they can choose the right chart type for their data. Common issues to watch: failure to explain methodology, unlabeled charts, insights not supported by analysis, and code that doesn't run. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level work (90-100), 60% B-level work (80-89), 20% C-level work (70-79), 5% below 70. Provide specific feedback on code quality and suggest improvements for future projects.

title: Scalability Architecture Discussion: From Startup to Enterprise Scale
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing the architectural evolution of a web application from handling 1,000 users to 10 million users, defending their design decisions and critiquing peers' approaches using real-world case studies and distributed systems principles.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze and design scalable distributed system architectures for varying load requirements
Evaluate trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance in distributed systems
Apply caching strategies, load balancing, and database scaling techniques to real-world scenarios
Communicate complex technical decisions and justify architectural choices using industry best practices
rubric_criteria: Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of distributed systems concepts, correctly applies CAP theorem, identifies appropriate scaling patterns (horizontal/vertical), and shows mastery of caching strategies, database partitioning, and microservices architecture

Critical Analysis and Problem-Solving (25 points): Identifies key bottlenecks at each scale, proposes realistic solutions with specific technologies, considers cost implications, addresses security and monitoring concerns, and demonstrates systems thinking

Peer Engagement and Discussion Quality (25 points): Provides substantive responses to at least 3 peers, asks probing questions, challenges assumptions constructively, builds upon others' ideas, and facilitates meaningful technical discourse

Real-World Application and Case Study Integration (25 points): References specific companies/platforms (Netflix, Instagram, etc.), cites concrete examples of scaling challenges, connects theoretical concepts to practical implementations, and demonstrates awareness of industry trends
instructions: You are the lead architect for a social media startup that has experienced explosive growth. Your initial architecture handled 1,000 concurrent users, but you now need to scale to 10 million users globally. Create an initial post (800-1000 words) that: 1) Describes your original architecture and identifies the first major bottlenecks you encountered at 10,000 users, 2) Proposes a mid-scale architecture for 100,000 users, justifying your technology choices (database strategy, caching layer, load balancing), 3) Designs the final architecture for 10 million users, addressing data consistency, geographic distribution, and fault tolerance, 4) References at least two real-world case studies (e.g., Twitter's scaling journey, Instagram's acquisition-time architecture). Then engage with peers by responding to at least three classmates' architectures. In your responses, identify potential weaknesses, suggest alternatives, or ask clarifying questions about their design decisions. Each response should be 200-300 words and demonstrate deep technical understanding. All posts must include specific technologies, protocols, and quantitative reasoning (QPS estimates, storage calculations, etc.). Use proper technical terminology and cite sources for case studies. Submit your initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM, and complete peer responses by Sunday 11:59 PM.
grading_notes: Look for students who move beyond basic solutions to demonstrate nuanced understanding of distributed systems trade-offs. Excellent responses will mention specific technologies (Redis vs Memcached, PostgreSQL vs MongoDB vs Cassandra) with justification. Watch for students who consider non-functional requirements like monitoring, security, and cost optimization. In peer interactions, reward students who identify subtle issues others missed or propose creative alternatives. Common weaknesses include: oversimplifying database scaling, ignoring geographic latency, underestimating operational complexity, or making technology choices without justification. Grade distribution should typically be: 90-100 (20%), 80-89 (40%), 70-79 (30%), below 70 (10%). Deduct points for late submissions: 10% per day for initial post, 5% per day for responses.

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline: From Business Problem to Production Deployment
description: Students will present a comprehensive machine learning solution addressing a real-world business problem, demonstrating the complete data science workflow from problem formulation through model deployment and monitoring. The presentation must showcase technical depth, business acumen, and practical implementation skills expected of senior data scientists.
learning_objectives_assessed: Translate complex business requirements into well-defined machine learning problems with appropriate success metrics
Design and implement robust data preprocessing pipelines handling real-world data quality issues
Apply advanced machine learning techniques with proper model selection, validation, and interpretation
Develop production-ready solutions with consideration for scalability, monitoring, and maintenance
Communicate technical findings effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Problem Formulation & Business Understanding (25 points): Clear articulation of business problem, stakeholder analysis, success metrics definition, risk assessment, and ethical considerations. Demonstrates deep understanding of domain constraints and requirements.

Technical Implementation & Methodology (25 points): Sophisticated data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection with proper cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and performance evaluation. Code quality, reproducibility, and handling of edge cases.

Model Interpretation & Validation (25 points): Comprehensive model explainability using appropriate techniques (SHAP, LIME, etc.), robust validation strategy, bias detection, statistical significance testing, and uncertainty quantification.

Production Deployment & Monitoring (25 points): Complete deployment architecture, API design, monitoring dashboards, A/B testing framework, model versioning, rollback strategies, and maintenance protocols. Consideration of computational costs and scalability.
instructions: Develop and present a complete machine learning solution for a real business problem of your choice. Your presentation must include: (1) Business context with stakeholder analysis and success metrics, (2) Exploratory data analysis with at least 10,000 records from multiple sources, (3) Feature engineering pipeline with automated data quality checks, (4) Model development comparing at least 3 algorithms with proper validation, (5) Model interpretation using explainability tools, (6) Production deployment architecture with monitoring, and (7) Post-deployment evaluation plan. Submit a GitHub repository with complete code, documentation, and README 48 hours before presentation. Include a deployed model with API endpoints and monitoring dashboard. Your presentation should be structured for a mixed audience of technical team members and business stakeholders. Prepare to defend your methodological choices, discuss alternative approaches, and explain how your solution handles production challenges like data drift, model degradation, and scaling requirements. Visual aids must include architecture diagrams, performance metrics, and business impact projections.
grading_notes: Evaluate presentations using the 4-level scale: Exemplary (90-100%), Proficient (80-89%), Developing (70-79%), Inadequate (<70%). Focus on depth of technical understanding during Q&A - probe model assumptions, validation strategies, and production considerations. Common issues include: oversimplified problem formulation, inadequate validation methodologies, lack of production readiness, and poor stakeholder communication. Expect exemplary presentations to demonstrate novel approaches, handle complex data scenarios, and show sophisticated understanding of business-technical tradeoffs. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations with approximately 20% exemplary, 40% proficient, 30% developing, 10% inadequate.

title: Basic Math Skills Portfolio: Numbers in My Daily Life
description: Students will create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating their understanding of fundamental math concepts (counting, basic operations, measurement, shapes, and patterns) through real-world applications and problem-solving activities collected over 4 weeks.
estimated_time: 4 weeks (30 minutes per week + 2 hours compilation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate proficiency in basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) with numbers 1-100
Apply measurement concepts using standard units (length, weight, time, money)
Identify and describe 2D shapes and their properties in real-world contexts
Recognize and create simple patterns using numbers, shapes, and objects
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): All calculations are correct, proper use of mathematical symbols and units, accurate measurements and shape identification
Real-World Applications (25 points): Clear connections between math concepts and daily life, relevant examples, demonstrates understanding of when to use different operations
Problem-Solving Process (25 points): Shows clear work steps, uses appropriate strategies, explains reasoning, attempts multiple approaches when needed
Portfolio Organization and Presentation (25 points): Complete all required sections, neat and organized presentation, includes required reflections, submitted on time
instructions: Create a personal math portfolio by collecting examples of how you use math in your daily life. Your portfolio must include: (1) NUMBER OPERATIONS SECTION: Complete 5 real-world word problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (provided worksheet). Show all work and explain your thinking. Include one photo of yourself using math at home (cooking, shopping, etc.) with a written explanation. (2) MEASUREMENT SECTION: Measure 5 objects in your home using rulers, scales, or measuring cups. Record measurements and compare sizes. Include a time-tracking activity where you record how long daily activities take. (3) SHAPES AND PATTERNS SECTION: Take photos of 8 different 2D shapes found in your environment (signs, windows, tiles, etc.). Label each shape and describe its properties. Create and photograph an original pattern using household objects, then extend it 3 more steps. (4) REFLECTION SECTION: Write a one-page reflection answering: 'How do I use math every day?' and 'What was the most surprising math discovery in this project?' Organize all materials in a folder or binder with a decorated cover page including your name and title. Include a table of contents. All written work should be in pencil or blue/black pen with neat handwriting or typed. Submit your complete portfolio by [due date] during math class.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - basic arithmetic errors should result in point deductions from Mathematical Accuracy criterion. Look for genuine effort in connecting math to students' lives rather than perfect execution. Award full points for Real-World Applications if connections are logical, even if simple. Problem-solving processes should show work steps; partial credit available if method is correct but calculation errors occur. Organization points should be generous for beginner level - focus on completeness rather than perfection. Expect 80% of students to score in 70-85 range. Students scoring below 60 likely need additional basic skills support. Provide specific feedback on calculation errors and suggest resources for improvement.

title: Data Structures Implementation and Analysis Lab Report
