description: Students will implement and analyze the performance of different data structures (Array, Linked List, Binary Search Tree) by conducting empirical testing and comparing theoretical vs. actual time complexities for common operations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Implement fundamental data structures using object-oriented programming principles
Analyze and compare time complexity of data structure operations through empirical testing
Apply scientific methodology to computer science experimentation
Communicate technical findings through structured written reports
rubric_criteria: Implementation Quality (25 points): Code correctness, proper OOP design, error handling, code documentation and readability
Experimental Design (25 points): Appropriate test cases, varied data sizes, multiple trials, valid timing methodology
Data Analysis (25 points): Accurate performance measurements, correct complexity analysis, meaningful comparisons between structures
Report Quality (25 points): Clear writing, proper formatting, complete sections, supported conclusions, professional presentation
instructions: Implement three data structures in your chosen programming language: Dynamic Array, Singly Linked List, and Binary Search Tree. Each implementation must include insert, search, and delete operations with proper error handling and documentation. Design experiments to measure the actual runtime of these operations using datasets of varying sizes (100, 1000, 10000, 50000 elements). For each data structure and operation combination, conduct at least 5 trials and calculate average execution times. Your lab report must include: (1) Introduction explaining the purpose and methodology, (2) Implementation section with code snippets and design decisions, (3) Experimental setup describing test environment and procedures, (4) Results section with tables and graphs showing performance data, (5) Analysis comparing theoretical O-notation with empirical results, (6) Conclusion summarizing findings and limitations. Submit your complete source code, compiled executable, raw data files, and a PDF report (8-12 pages, double-spaced, 12pt font). Code must compile and run without errors. Include a README file with compilation and execution instructions. All graphs must be clearly labeled with appropriate scales and legends.
grading_notes: Verify code compiles and runs correctly before grading report content. Deduct 10 points for non-functional code. Look for proper object-oriented design patterns and adequate commenting. In experimental design, ensure students use appropriate timing mechanisms (not wall clock time) and account for system variations through multiple trials. Common issues include insufficient sample sizes, improper data randomization, and failure to warm up the system before timing. For analysis, students should demonstrate understanding that real-world performance may deviate from theoretical due to factors like cache effects and system overhead. Excellent reports (90-100) will show creative insights about when to use each data structure. Average reports (70-85) meet basic requirements but lack depth in analysis. Below average (60-75) typically have implementation errors or insufficient experimental rigor.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Model Evaluation and Optimization Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' ability to critically analyze machine learning models, interpret performance metrics, design experiments, and optimize model performance across different scenarios including imbalanced datasets, feature selection, and cross-validation strategies.
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate and compare machine learning models using appropriate metrics for different problem types
Design and implement robust cross-validation strategies for model selection and hyperparameter tuning
Analyze and address challenges in imbalanced datasets and feature selection
Interpret model performance results and make data-driven recommendations for model improvement
rubric_criteria: Model Evaluation Metrics (25 points): Correctly selects and interprets appropriate evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, RMSE) for different problem types, demonstrates understanding of when to use each metric, and accurately calculates metrics from confusion matrices

Cross-Validation and Experimental Design (25 points): Designs appropriate cross-validation strategies, identifies potential data leakage issues, explains stratification needs, and demonstrates understanding of nested CV for hyperparameter tuning

Imbalanced Data and Feature Engineering (25 points): Identifies class imbalance issues, proposes appropriate sampling techniques (SMOTE, undersampling, cost-sensitive learning), evaluates feature selection methods, and addresses curse of dimensionality

Model Optimization and Business Impact (25 points): Analyzes hyperparameter tuning results, compares multiple algorithms systematically, interprets feature importance, and translates technical findings into actionable business recommendations
instructions: This quiz consists of 4 sections with a mix of multiple-choice, short-answer, and analytical questions. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully and show your work for calculation problems. For scenario-based questions, justify your reasoning with specific examples and technical concepts. Section 1 (Questions 1-8): Model evaluation metrics - includes interpreting confusion matrices, calculating performance metrics, and selecting appropriate metrics for given scenarios. Section 2 (Questions 9-16): Cross-validation design - covers CV strategy selection, identifying data leakage, and experimental design principles. Section 3 (Questions 17-24): Handling imbalanced datasets and feature selection - includes sampling techniques, feature engineering approaches, and dimensionality reduction methods. Section 4 (Questions 25-30): Model optimization case study - analyze provided model performance data, compare algorithms, and make recommendations. Submit your answers in the designated format with clear explanations for open-ended responses. Partial credit will be awarded for showing relevant work and reasoning, even if final answers are incorrect. Use standard notation and terminology as covered in course materials.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for demonstrated understanding of concepts, even with minor calculation errors. Look for evidence of systematic thinking and appropriate methodology selection. Common issues to watch: confusing precision/recall definitions (deduct 2-3 points per instance), recommending inappropriate CV strategies without justification (deduct 5 points), failing to address class imbalance when clearly present (deduct 3-5 points), making business recommendations without supporting technical analysis (deduct 5 points). Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-range (90-100), 40% B-range (80-89), 30% C-range (70-79), 10% below 70. Students scoring below 60 should be offered remediation. Pay special attention to Section 4 case study responses - look for integration of concepts across all areas rather than isolated technical knowledge.

title: Fundamentals of Programming Logic and Basic Algorithms Exam
description: A comprehensive written and practical exam assessing students' understanding of basic programming concepts, problem-solving skills, algorithm design, and code comprehension. Students will demonstrate their ability to trace through code, write pseudocode, identify programming constructs, and solve fundamental computational problems.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply fundamental programming constructs including variables, loops, conditionals, and functions
Trace through simple algorithms and predict program output
Design basic algorithms using pseudocode to solve computational problems
Identify and correct common programming errors in simple code segments
rubric_criteria: Code Tracing and Output Prediction (25 points): Accurately traces through provided code segments and correctly predicts outputs for loops, conditionals, and function calls
Pseudocode Algorithm Design (25 points): Creates clear, logical pseudocode solutions that correctly implement required algorithms with proper sequence, selection, and iteration structures
Programming Concept Identification (25 points): Correctly identifies programming constructs, data types, operators, and explains the purpose of code segments in plain language
Problem-Solving and Error Detection (25 points): Identifies logical errors in provided code, suggests appropriate corrections, and demonstrates systematic approach to debugging
instructions:
This exam consists of four sections testing your understanding of basic programming concepts. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully and show your work where applicable.

Section 1 - Code Tracing (25 points): You will be given 5 code segments. Trace through each one step-by-step and write the exact output. Show your variable values at each step.

Section 2 - Pseudocode Writing (25 points): Write pseudocode algorithms for 3 given problems. Use proper pseudocode conventions including START/END, clear variable names, and structured logic flow. Focus on correctness and clarity rather than specific programming language syntax.

Section 3 - Concept Recognition (25 points): Answer multiple-choice and short-answer questions about programming fundamentals including data types, operators, control structures, and basic syntax rules.

Section 4 - Debugging (25 points): Find and fix errors in provided code snippets. Explain what each error was and why your correction resolves the issue.

Submission Requirements: Write all answers clearly in the provided answer booklet. For code tracing, use tables to show variable values. For pseudocode, use proper indentation. Circle or clearly mark your final answers. No electronic devices permitted except basic calculators if needed for mathematical computations within algorithms.
grading_notes: Grade each section independently using the 25-point rubric per section. For code tracing, award partial credit for correct methodology even if final answer is wrong due to early calculation errors. In pseudocode section, prioritize logical flow over perfect syntax - deduct points only for logic errors that would prevent algorithm from working. For debugging section, students must both identify the error AND provide correct fix to receive full credit. Expect score distribution: 90-100 (A): ~20%, 80-89 (B): ~35%, 70-79 (C): ~30%, below 70: ~15%. Common issues to watch: students confusing assignment vs. equality operators, off-by-one errors in loop tracing, incomplete pseudocode missing edge cases.

title: Advanced Calculus Applications: Optimization in Real-World Engineering Problems
description: Students will present a comprehensive analysis of a complex optimization problem from engineering or physics, demonstrating mastery of multivariable calculus, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization while communicating mathematical concepts to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multivariable calculus techniques to solve complex real-world optimization problems
Demonstrate proficiency with constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions
Analyze and interpret mathematical solutions within practical contexts and limitations
Communicate advanced mathematical concepts clearly to diverse audiences using multiple representations
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of optimization techniques, proper use of calculus methods, accurate calculations, appropriate handling of constraints, and valid mathematical reasoning throughout the solution process

Problem Selection and Real-World Application (25 points): Choice of sufficiently complex engineering/physics problem, clear articulation of practical significance, realistic constraints and variables, and meaningful interpretation of results within the application context

Presentation Quality and Communication (25 points): Clear organization and flow, effective use of visual aids, appropriate mathematical notation and terminology, engagement with audience, and ability to explain concepts at multiple technical levels

Critical Analysis and Extensions (25 points): Discussion of solution limitations, sensitivity analysis of key parameters, consideration of alternative approaches, and thoughtful responses to questions demonstrating deep understanding of the underlying mathematics
instructions: Select a complex optimization problem from engineering, physics, or applied sciences that requires multivariable calculus techniques. Your problem must involve at least three variables and include both equality and inequality constraints. Begin by clearly defining the practical context and explaining why optimization is important for this application. Formulate the mathematical model, identifying all variables, objective function, and constraints. Solve the optimization problem using appropriate calculus techniques, including partial derivatives, critical point analysis, and Lagrange multipliers or KKT conditions as needed. Create professional-quality visual aids including graphs, diagrams, and mathematical notation. Your presentation should include: (1) Problem introduction and real-world significance (3-4 minutes), (2) Mathematical formulation and model development (4-5 minutes), (3) Solution methodology and calculations (6-7 minutes), (4) Results interpretation and practical implications (3-4 minutes), and (5) Limitations and potential extensions (2-3 minutes). Prepare to answer technical questions about your mathematical approach and practical questions about real-world implementation. Submit your presentation slides and a detailed mathematical appendix showing all calculations 24 hours before your presentation date. Include a brief reflection on the most challenging aspects of the problem and what you learned about the relationship between theoretical mathematics and practical applications.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - incorrect fundamental calculus will significantly impact the Mathematical Rigor score regardless of presentation quality. Look for proper use of the chain rule, gradient calculations, and constraint handling. For Problem Selection, ensure the chosen problem genuinely requires advanced techniques and isn't artificially complicated. Strong presentations will seamlessly integrate mathematical formalism with intuitive explanations. Watch for students who memorize procedures without understanding - probe with follow-up questions about 'what if' scenarios. Grade distribution typically shows: 15% earning 90-100 points (exceptional mathematical insight and communication), 40% earning 80-89 points (solid technical work with good presentation), 35% earning 70-79 points (adequate mathematics but weaker communication or minor technical errors), and 10% below 70 points (significant mathematical errors or poor preparation). Common issues include: oversimplified problems, computational errors in partial derivatives, inadequate constraint analysis, and inability to explain the practical meaning of mathematical results.

title: Advanced Software Engineering Portfolio: Full-Stack Application Development
description: Students design, implement, and deploy a complete full-stack web application demonstrating advanced software engineering principles, including system architecture, database design, API development, testing strategies, and deployment practices. The portfolio must showcase professional-level code quality, documentation, and project management skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement scalable software architectures using industry-standard patterns and practices
Develop comprehensive testing strategies including unit, integration, and end-to-end testing
Apply advanced database design principles and optimize query performance
Implement secure authentication, authorization, and data validation mechanisms
Demonstrate proficiency in modern development workflows including CI/CD pipelines
Create professional technical documentation and project presentations
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Implementation (25 points): Application demonstrates sophisticated architectural patterns (MVC, microservices, or layered architecture), proper separation of concerns, scalable design decisions, clean code principles, and effective use of design patterns. Code must be production-ready with consistent formatting and meaningful naming conventions.

Database Design & Performance (25 points): Database schema shows proper normalization, indexing strategies, and relationship modeling. Includes complex queries with optimization, transaction handling, and data integrity constraints. Must demonstrate understanding of ACID properties and implement appropriate backup/recovery considerations.

Testing & Quality Assurance (25 points): Comprehensive test suite with 80%+ code coverage including unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. Implements automated testing pipeline, error handling, logging, and monitoring. Code quality metrics demonstrate maintainability and follows security best practices including input validation and SQL injection prevention.

Documentation & Professional Presentation (25 points): Complete technical documentation including architecture diagrams, API documentation, deployment guides, and user manuals. Professional README with setup instructions, feature descriptions, and technology justifications. Includes reflection on design decisions, challenges overcome, and lessons learned with clear articulation of technical trade-offs.
instructions: Develop a full-stack web application that solves a real-world problem of your choosing. Your application must include: (1) Frontend interface using modern framework (React, Vue, Angular) with responsive design and accessibility features, (2) Backend API with RESTful endpoints and proper HTTP status codes, (3) Database integration with at least 5 related tables and complex queries, (4) User authentication and role-based authorization, (5) Input validation and error handling, (6) Automated testing suite with CI/CD pipeline setup. Submit via GitHub repository containing: source code with clear commit history, comprehensive README with setup instructions, technical documentation folder with architecture diagrams and API docs, deployed application URL (using services like Heroku, AWS, or Vercel), 10-minute video presentation demonstrating key features and explaining architectural decisions. Repository must be public with professional-level documentation. Include a reflection document (1000 words) analyzing your design decisions, challenges faced, performance considerations, and potential improvements. All code must be original work with proper attribution for any external libraries or resources used.
grading_notes: Evaluate code quality using industry standards - look for consistent indentation, meaningful variable names, appropriate comments, and modular structure. Check that database queries are optimized and relationships are properly modeled. Verify that tests actually run and provide meaningful coverage - automated testing pipeline should execute without errors. Security implementations should follow OWASP guidelines. Documentation should be professional enough for a new developer to understand and contribute to the project. Common issues to watch: inadequate error handling, missing input validation, poor database design, insufficient testing coverage, unclear documentation. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades (exceptional work exceeding requirements), 35% B grades (solid work meeting all requirements), 40% C grades (adequate work with minor deficiencies), 10% D/F grades (incomplete or significantly deficient work). Provide specific feedback on architectural decisions and suggest concrete improvements for future projects.

title: Algebraic Functions and Real-World Applications Quiz
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of quadratic and exponential functions through problem-solving, graphical analysis, and real-world application scenarios. This assessment evaluates computational skills, conceptual understanding, and the ability to model practical situations using algebraic functions.
learning_objectives_assessed: Solve quadratic equations using multiple methods (factoring, completing the square, quadratic formula)
Graph quadratic and exponential functions and identify key features (vertex, intercepts, domain, range)
Model real-world situations using quadratic and exponential functions
Interpret function behavior and make predictions based on mathematical models
rubric_criteria: Problem-Solving Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of algebraic methods, accurate calculations, and appropriate solution techniques for quadratic and exponential equations
Graphical Analysis (25 points): Accurate plotting of functions, correct identification of key features (vertex, intercepts, asymptotes), and proper labeling of axes and scales
Mathematical Reasoning (25 points): Clear explanation of solution strategies, logical progression of steps, and appropriate justification for chosen methods
Real-World Application (25 points): Successful translation of word problems into mathematical models, correct interpretation of results in context, and reasonable predictions or conclusions
instructions:
This quiz consists of 12 problems divided into four sections. You have 75 minutes to complete all sections. Show all work clearly and organize your solutions step-by-step. Use proper mathematical notation throughout.

Section A (Problems 1-3): Solve quadratic equations using the method specified in each problem. Verify your solutions by substitution.

Section B (Problems 4-6): Graph the given functions on the provided coordinate planes. Identify and clearly label the vertex, x-intercepts, y-intercept, and axis of symmetry for quadratic functions. For exponential functions, identify intercepts, asymptotes, and describe end behavior.

Section C (Problems 7-9): Analyze word problems involving projectile motion, area optimization, and profit maximization. Set up the appropriate quadratic function, solve for the required values, and interpret your answers in the context of the problem.

Section D (Problems 10-12): Work with exponential growth and decay models including population growth, radioactive decay, and compound interest. Create the exponential function from given information and use it to make predictions.

Submission Requirements: Submit all work on the provided answer sheets. Graphs must be drawn accurately with proper scales. Final answers should be clearly indicated and include appropriate units where applicable. Partial credit will be awarded for correct methods even if final answers contain minor computational errors.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct methods and logical reasoning, even with computational errors. Deduct 2-3 points for minor calculation mistakes, 5-7 points for significant method errors. In graphing sections, accuracy of key features is more important than artistic quality. For word problems, credit problem setup and interpretation equally with computational accuracy. Common issues to watch: sign errors in quadratic formula, incorrect vertex form conversions, misinterpreting context in applications, and scale errors in graphing. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 10% below C-level. Provide written feedback on problem-solving approaches and suggest review topics for scores below 75.

title: Distributed System Design and Implementation: Building a Scalable Chat Application
description: Students will design, implement, and deploy a distributed chat application that demonstrates understanding of system architecture, scalability, fault tolerance, and distributed computing principles. The project requires building both backend microservices and a client interface while addressing real-world distributed system challenges.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed system architectures using microservices patterns
Apply concurrency and synchronization techniques in multi-threaded environments
Implement fault tolerance and error handling mechanisms in distributed systems
Demonstrate proficiency in database design and distributed data management
Evaluate system performance and implement optimization strategies
Apply security principles in distributed application development
rubric_criteria: System Architecture and Design (25 points): Clear microservices architecture with proper separation of concerns, well-documented API design, appropriate technology stack selection, and comprehensive system diagrams showing component interactions and data flow

Implementation Quality and Functionality (25 points): Clean, maintainable code following best practices, proper error handling and logging, complete core functionality (user authentication, real-time messaging, room management), and appropriate use of design patterns

Scalability and Performance (25 points): Implementation of load balancing, database optimization techniques, efficient message queuing system, horizontal scaling capabilities, and performance testing with documented results showing system behavior under load

Documentation and Deployment (25 points): Comprehensive technical documentation including setup instructions, API documentation, architecture decisions, successful deployment to cloud platform, and demonstration video showing all features working in production environment
instructions: You will build a distributed chat application supporting multiple chat rooms and concurrent users. Your system must include: (1) User Authentication Service - implement JWT-based authentication with user registration/login; (2) Message Service - handle real-time message delivery using WebSockets or similar technology; (3) Room Management Service - create, join, leave chat rooms with permission controls; (4) Database Layer - design schema for users, messages, and rooms with appropriate indexing; (5) Load Balancer - distribute traffic across multiple service instances; (6) Message Queue - implement asynchronous message processing using Redis/RabbitMQ. Technical requirements: Use at least 3 different programming languages/frameworks, implement proper logging and monitoring, include unit and integration tests with >80% coverage, deploy on AWS/GCP/Azure with auto-scaling, handle at least 100 concurrent users, implement rate limiting and basic security measures. Deliverables: Complete source code with Git history, architectural documentation with diagrams, deployment scripts and configuration files, performance testing results and analysis, 10-minute demonstration video, individual reflection report (500 words) discussing challenges and solutions. Submit via GitHub repository link with README containing setup and deployment instructions.
grading_notes: Evaluate architecture diagrams for clarity and technical accuracy - look for proper microservices separation and realistic system boundaries. Code quality assessment should focus on modularity, error handling, and adherence to language-specific best practices rather than perfect syntax. For scalability criterion, accept theoretical implementations if actual load testing isn't feasible due to resource constraints, but require detailed explanation of scaling strategies. Documentation should be professional-grade - deduct points for missing setup instructions or unclear API documentation. Common issues to watch: over-engineered solutions (reward simplicity), incomplete deployment instructions, missing error handling for network failures, inadequate security measures, and poor database design. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades, 35% B grades, 40% C grades, 10% below C. Students struggling with deployment should be offered alternative demonstration methods. Partial credit available for each criterion - a non-functional system with excellent documentation and architecture can still earn 60-70% overall.

title: Advanced Predictive Analytics: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation
description: Students will design, implement, and evaluate a complete machine learning solution for a complex real-world business problem, demonstrating mastery of the full data science lifecycle from raw data processing through model deployment and business interpretation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and execute comprehensive data preprocessing pipelines for complex, messy datasets
Apply advanced feature engineering techniques and justify feature selection decisions
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms with proper hyperparameter optimization
Conduct rigorous model evaluation using appropriate metrics and validation strategies
Communicate technical findings effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
Demonstrate understanding of ethical considerations and potential biases in machine learning applications
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated handling of missing data, outliers, and categorical variables; implements creative and justified feature engineering; shows clear data quality assessment and documentation

Model Development and Optimization (25 points): Implements multiple appropriate algorithms; demonstrates proper cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning; shows understanding of algorithm assumptions and limitations; code is efficient and well-documented

Model Evaluation and Validation (25 points): Uses appropriate evaluation metrics for the problem type; implements proper train/validation/test splits; conducts bias-variance analysis; addresses overfitting/underfitting; provides statistical significance testing where appropriate

Business Impact and Communication (25 points): Clearly articulates business value and actionable insights; addresses ethical considerations and potential biases; provides clear visualizations and executive summary; demonstrates understanding of deployment considerations and monitoring needs
instructions:
You are provided with a complex dataset containing customer transaction data, demographics, and behavioral patterns for a financial services company seeking to improve customer retention. Your task is to build a complete predictive analytics solution that identifies customers at risk of churning within the next 90 days.

Deliverables:
1. Jupyter notebook with complete analysis (well-commented code, markdown explanations)
2. Executive summary presentation (max 10 slides) for business stakeholders
3. Technical documentation (2-3 pages) detailing methodology and recommendations

Specific Requirements:
- Conduct thorough exploratory data analysis with meaningful visualizations
- Handle missing data and outliers with justified approaches
- Engineer at least 5 new features based on domain knowledge
- Implement minimum 3 different algorithm families (e.g., linear, tree-based, ensemble)
- Use proper cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization
- Address class imbalance if present
- Provide feature importance analysis and model interpretability
- Discuss ethical implications and potential biases
- Include deployment strategy and monitoring recommendations

Submission Format: Submit via learning management system as ZIP file containing all deliverables. Code must run without errors on provided dataset. Include requirements.txt file with all dependencies.

Evaluation will focus on technical rigor, business relevance, code quality, and communication effectiveness. Partial credit available for each component.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should target: A-level (90-100): 20%, B-level (80-89): 40%, C-level (70-79): 30%, Below 70: 10%. Key evaluation focus areas: (1) Technical sophistication - look for advanced techniques beyond basic implementations, (2) Business acumen - assess whether recommendations are actionable and valuable, (3) Code quality - check for efficiency, documentation, and reproducibility, (4) Critical thinking - evaluate justification of methodological choices. Common issues to deduct points for: hardcoded parameters, data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate evaluation metrics, overly complex models without justification, poor communication of uncertainty and limitations. Provide specific feedback on each rubric criterion. Consider offering bonus points (max 5) for exceptional creativity or insights. Ensure consistency by using the same dataset across all students and providing clear examples of each grade level.

title: Real-World Problem Solving: Planning a School Garden
description: Students will engage in a collaborative discussion to solve a multi-step real-world problem involving area, perimeter, budgeting, and basic data analysis while planning a rectangular school garden project.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) to solve real-world problems
Calculate area and perimeter of rectangles using appropriate formulas
Interpret and organize data to make mathematical decisions
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using appropriate vocabulary
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): Correctly applies formulas for area and perimeter, performs accurate calculations, and arrives at reasonable numerical answers
Problem-Solving Process (25 points): Demonstrates clear step-by-step approach, shows all work, identifies what information is needed, and explains mathematical reasoning
Real-World Application (25 points): Makes logical connections between math concepts and practical decisions, considers multiple factors (budget, space, materials), and provides realistic solutions
Communication and Participation (25 points): Uses proper mathematical vocabulary, explains thinking clearly to peers, actively participates in discussion, and responds constructively to others' ideas
instructions:
You are part of a planning committee tasked with designing a rectangular garden for your school. Work in groups of 3-4 students to discuss and solve this problem together.

SCENARIO: Your school has allocated a rectangular space that is 24 feet long and 16 feet wide for a garden. The budget is $200. You need to determine: (1) How much fencing is needed to enclose the garden and its cost at $3 per foot, (2) The total area available for planting, (3) How to divide the space between vegetables (60%) and flowers (40%), and (4) Whether you can afford both fencing ($3/foot) and soil ($2 per square foot for the entire area).

DISCUSSION REQUIREMENTS: Each group member must contribute to solving different parts of the problem. Show all calculations clearly on your group worksheet. Discuss your reasoning aloud and help teammates understand each step. Consider alternative solutions if the budget is insufficient. Prepare to share one key insight or challenge your group discovered.

SUBMISSION: Submit one completed worksheet per group showing all calculations, decisions made, and brief explanations of your reasoning. Include each member's name and contribution. Be prepared for a 2-minute group presentation of your solution.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical process over perfect answers. Award partial credit for correct setup even with calculation errors. Look for evidence of collaboration - all group members should contribute to the worksheet. Common issues include forgetting to double dimensions for perimeter and misunderstanding percentage calculations for area division. Expect most groups to discover the budget is insufficient, leading to creative problem-solving discussions. Grade generously on communication if mathematical vocabulary is attempted, even if imperfect. Strong responses will show multiple solution strategies or budget alternatives.

title: End-to-End Data Science Portfolio: Customer Churn Prediction and Business Intelligence Dashboard
description: Students will complete a comprehensive data science project involving data acquisition, exploratory analysis, predictive modeling, and business intelligence dashboard creation. The portfolio must demonstrate the full data science workflow from raw data to actionable business insights, including model deployment considerations and stakeholder communication.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply complete data science methodology from problem definition to solution deployment
Implement advanced machine learning algorithms for classification problems with proper validation techniques
Create professional data visualizations and interactive dashboards for business stakeholders
Demonstrate statistical analysis skills including hypothesis testing and feature engineering
Communicate complex analytical findings to both technical and non-technical audiences
Show proficiency in data manipulation, cleaning, and preprocessing at scale
rubric_criteria: Data Engineering & Preprocessing (25 points): Quality of data cleaning, feature engineering, handling missing values, outlier detection, data validation, and documentation of preprocessing pipeline. Must demonstrate handling of at least 50,000 records with multiple data types.

Statistical Analysis & Modeling (25 points): Implementation of multiple ML algorithms (minimum 3), proper cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, model comparison with statistical significance testing, and appropriate evaluation metrics for imbalanced datasets.

Visualization & Dashboard Development (25 points): Creation of interactive dashboard using tools like Plotly Dash, Streamlit, or similar. Must include at least 5 different chart types, filters, and real-time model prediction interface with professional styling.

Business Communication & Documentation (25 points): Executive summary, technical documentation, code quality with proper version control, reproducible analysis, and 10-minute video presentation explaining findings to business stakeholders.
instructions: Your portfolio must include: (1) Jupyter notebook with complete analysis workflow, (2) Python scripts for model training and deployment, (3) Interactive dashboard deployed on cloud platform, (4) Executive summary (2-page PDF), (5) Technical documentation, and (6) 10-minute video presentation. Use any customer churn dataset with >50K records (telecom, SaaS, retail). Your analysis must address: data quality assessment, exploratory data analysis with statistical testing, feature engineering including creation of at least 3 derived features, implementation and comparison of logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting models, handling of class imbalance, model interpretability analysis using SHAP or LIME, and business impact quantification. Dashboard requirements: customer segmentation view, churn risk scoring interface, feature importance visualization, model performance metrics, and business KPI tracking. Deploy dashboard using Heroku, Streamlit Cloud, or similar platform. Code must be version-controlled on GitHub with clear README and requirements.txt. Executive summary should focus on business value, key findings, and recommended actions. Video presentation should be suitable for C-level executives, avoiding technical jargon while demonstrating business impact. All work must be original and properly cited.
grading_notes: Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 10% below C-level. Key evaluation points: Code must run without errors when following provided instructions. Look for sophisticated feature engineering beyond basic transformations. Model comparison should include statistical significance testing, not just metric comparison. Dashboard interactivity and professional appearance are crucial - check all filters and features work properly. Business communication quality separates good from excellent submissions. Common issues to deduct points for: hardcoded file paths, missing error handling, poor code documentation, dashboard crashes or broken features, vague business recommendations, and insufficient model validation. Bonus consideration (up to 5 points) for: advanced techniques like ensemble methods, A/B testing framework integration, or MLOps pipeline implementation. Verify dashboard deployment actually works by testing provided URL. Technical documentation should enable another data scientist to reproduce results completely.

title: Statistical Analysis of Real-World Data: Mathematical Modeling Laboratory Report
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis of a real-world dataset, applying advanced mathematical concepts including hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and probability distributions. This lab report assesses students' ability to translate mathematical theory into practical applications, interpret results, and communicate findings effectively.
estimated_time: 6-8 hours (3-4 hours data analysis, 2-3 hours report writing, 1 hour peer review)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced statistical methods including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis to real-world datasets
Construct and validate mathematical models using appropriate probability distributions and statistical assumptions
Interpret statistical results in context and communicate mathematical findings to both technical and non-technical audiences
Evaluate the limitations and validity of statistical methods when applied to real-world scenarios
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Methods (25 points): Correct application of statistical tests, appropriate selection of methods, accurate calculations, proper use of mathematical notation and formulas
Data Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Thorough exploratory data analysis, identification of patterns and outliers, appropriate visualization techniques, valid conclusions drawn from results
Model Construction and Validation (25 points): Appropriate model selection, testing of assumptions, validation techniques employed, discussion of model limitations and confidence intervals
Communication and Presentation (25 points): Clear mathematical exposition, professional formatting, effective use of tables and figures, executive summary accessible to non-experts
instructions: Select a dataset from the provided repository (minimum 500 observations, 5+ variables) or obtain instructor approval for an alternative dataset. Your lab report must include: (1) Executive Summary (200 words): Summarize your research question, methods, and key findings for a general audience. (2) Data Description and Exploratory Analysis: Provide descriptive statistics, identify data quality issues, create appropriate visualizations, and discuss variable relationships. (3) Methodology Section: Justify your choice of statistical methods, state all assumptions clearly, and explain your modeling approach with mathematical notation. (4) Results and Analysis: Present hypothesis test results with p-values and confidence intervals, display regression output with interpretation of coefficients, include diagnostic plots and assumption checks. (5) Discussion and Limitations: Interpret results in practical context, discuss statistical significance versus practical significance, acknowledge limitations and suggest improvements. (6) Appendix: Include relevant R/Python code, additional tables, and detailed calculations. Format: 8-10 pages (excluding appendix), 12-point font, double-spaced, APA style citations. Submit as PDF with accompanying code file. Include a brief peer review of one classmate's draft (500 words) focusing on mathematical accuracy and clarity of interpretation.
grading_notes: Emphasis should be placed on mathematical accuracy (40% of grade) and practical interpretation (35% of grade), with communication quality accounting for remaining 25%. Common issues to watch: failure to check statistical assumptions, inappropriate test selection, overstating conclusions beyond data limitations, poor integration of mathematical theory with practical application. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades (90+), 35% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 10% below 70. Deduct 5 points for late submission, 10 points for missing peer review component. Partial credit should be awarded for methodology sections even with calculation errors if approach is sound. Look for evidence of original thinking in discussion sections rather than textbook regurgitation.

title: Fundamentals of Programming Logic and Data Types Quiz
description: This quiz assesses students' understanding of basic programming concepts including variables, data types, control structures, and simple problem-solving using pseudocode. Students will demonstrate their ability to trace through code, identify errors, and write basic algorithms.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify primitive data types (integers, strings, booleans, floats)
Trace through sequential and conditional program execution
Write pseudocode for simple algorithms using loops and conditionals
Debug basic logical errors in code snippets
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Variables (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, understands variable declaration and assignment, demonstrates knowledge of type compatibility
Control Flow Understanding (25 points): Accurately traces through if-else statements, loops, and sequential execution; predicts correct program output
Pseudocode Writing (25 points): Creates clear, logically correct pseudocode using proper syntax and structure; algorithms solve given problems effectively
Error Identification and Debugging (25 points): Identifies syntax and logic errors in code; provides appropriate corrections with clear explanations
instructions:
This quiz contains 20 questions divided into four sections. You have 45 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully and show your work where applicable.

Section A (Questions 1-5): Multiple choice questions about data types and variable declarations. Select the best answer for each question.

Section B (Questions 6-10): Code tracing exercises. You will be given short code snippets and asked to predict the output or trace through the execution step by step. Show your work by writing the value of variables at each step.

Section C (Questions 11-15): Pseudocode writing. Write pseudocode solutions for given problems using proper indentation and clear logic flow. Use standard pseudocode conventions (IF/THEN/ELSE, WHILE, FOR loops).

Section D (Questions 16-20): Debugging exercises. Identify errors in provided code snippets and explain how to fix them. Consider both syntax errors and logical errors.

Submission Requirements: Write your answers clearly in the provided answer booklet. For code tracing, show step-by-step work. For pseudocode, use proper indentation. For debugging questions, circle or highlight errors and write corrections below each snippet. Submit your completed answer booklet before time expires. No electronic devices or reference materials are permitted during this assessment.
grading_notes: Grade each section separately using the 25-point rubric per section. For Section A, award 5 points per correct answer. For Section B, award full points only when step-by-step tracing is shown, partial credit for correct final answers without work. Section C requires logical correctness and proper pseudocode syntax - deduct points for unclear logic or poor structure. Section D should show both error identification and appropriate corrections. Common issues to watch: students confusing assignment vs. equality operators, off-by-one errors in loops, incorrect variable scope understanding. Grade distribution expectation: 90-100 (A), 80-89 (B), 70-79 (C), 60-69 (D), below 60 (F). Provide specific feedback on incorrect answers to guide future learning.

title: Distributed Systems Architecture Design and Trade-off Analysis
description: Students will engage in a comprehensive discussion analyzing the architectural decisions, trade-offs, and implementation challenges of a large-scale distributed system, demonstrating expert-level understanding of distributed systems principles, scalability patterns, and real-world engineering constraints.
estimated_time: 4-6 hours preparation, 2 hours active discussion participation
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze complex distributed system architectures and evaluate design trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Synthesize advanced distributed systems concepts including consensus algorithms, data partitioning strategies, and fault tolerance mechanisms
Critically evaluate scalability bottlenecks and propose evidence-based solutions for high-throughput distributed applications
Demonstrate expert-level understanding of distributed systems challenges through technical discourse and peer engagement
rubric_criteria: Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of distributed systems concepts, correctly applies CAP theorem, consistency models, consensus algorithms, and accurately describes implementation details

Critical Analysis and Trade-off Evaluation (25 points): Provides sophisticated analysis of architectural decisions, identifies non-obvious trade-offs, considers multiple stakeholder perspectives, and evaluates solutions within realistic constraints

Evidence-Based Reasoning and Research Integration (25 points): Incorporates recent academic research, industry case studies, benchmarking data, and real-world examples to support arguments with proper citations and technical evidence

Discussion Leadership and Peer Engagement (25 points): Facilitates meaningful technical discourse, asks probing questions that advance understanding, provides constructive feedback, and synthesizes diverse viewpoints into coherent insights
instructions: You will participate in an expert-level discussion analyzing the Netflix microservices architecture transition. Prepare a 1000-word technical analysis addressing: (1) The specific distributed systems challenges Netflix faced during their monolith-to-microservices migration, (2) Critical evaluation of their service mesh implementation, data consistency strategies, and fault tolerance mechanisms, (3) Alternative architectural approaches they could have adopted, with detailed trade-off analysis considering their scale (200M+ users, global CDN), and (4) Lessons applicable to other large-scale distributed systems. Your analysis must reference at least 5 academic papers or technical reports from the last 3 years, include specific metrics/benchmarks where available, and demonstrate understanding of advanced concepts like eventual consistency, distributed consensus, circuit breakers, and chaos engineering. During the live discussion, actively engage with peers by asking technical questions, challenging assumptions constructively, and building upon others' insights. Be prepared to defend your architectural recommendations and discuss implementation complexities. Submit your written analysis 24 hours before the discussion session via the course platform. Bring printed copies of key diagrams or system models to reference during discussion.
grading_notes: Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (exceptional synthesis of theory and practice), 35% B-level (solid technical understanding with good analysis), 40% C-level (adequate grasp of concepts but limited critical evaluation), 10% below C-level. Look for: accurate use of distributed systems terminology, evidence of engaging with primary sources beyond textbooks, realistic consideration of engineering constraints, ability to connect theoretical concepts to practical implementations. Common issues: oversimplifying CAP theorem implications, ignoring operational complexity, making architectural recommendations without considering organizational constraints, failing to engage substantively with peer contributions. Deduct points for factual errors about consensus algorithms, misrepresenting consistency models, or superficial analysis lacking technical depth. Reward students who demonstrate understanding of subtle trade-offs, reference cutting-edge research, and facilitate productive technical discussions.

title: Real-World Mathematics Problem-Solving Portfolio
description: Students create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating their ability to apply mathematical concepts to solve authentic, real-world problems across multiple domains including statistics, algebra, geometry, and financial mathematics.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply algebraic, geometric, and statistical concepts to solve real-world problems
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations and visual representations
Analyze data patterns and make evidence-based conclusions using appropriate mathematical tools
Connect mathematical concepts across different domains and contexts
rubric_criteria: Problem Selection and Mathematical Content (25 points): Four problems demonstrate appropriate intermediate-level mathematics (linear/quadratic equations, statistical analysis, geometric applications, financial calculations). Problems show increasing complexity and connect to real-world contexts.

Mathematical Accuracy and Process (25 points): Calculations are correct with appropriate formulas, units, and mathematical notation. Work is shown clearly with logical step-by-step solutions. Any technology use is documented and appropriate.

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Solutions include clear written explanations of mathematical reasoning, appropriate use of mathematical vocabulary, well-organized layout with proper headings, and effective use of graphs, charts, or diagrams where applicable.

Reflection and Analysis (25 points): Each problem includes reflection on problem-solving approach, discussion of alternative methods considered, analysis of solution reasonableness, and connection to broader mathematical concepts or other problems in portfolio.
instructions: Create a portfolio containing four real-world mathematics problems that you solve using intermediate-level mathematical concepts. Choose problems from different contexts (business/economics, science/engineering, social issues, personal finance) that require different mathematical approaches. For each problem: (1) Clearly state the problem and explain why you selected it, (2) Show all mathematical work with proper notation and units, (3) Provide a complete solution with verification, (4) Write a one-paragraph reflection discussing your approach, any challenges encountered, and how this connects to other mathematical concepts. Format your portfolio professionally with a title page, table of contents, and consistent formatting. Include at least two visual representations (graphs, charts, diagrams) across your four problems. Problems should demonstrate progression in complexity. Submit as a single PDF document, 10-15 pages total. Due dates: Problem selection approval (Week 2), draft problems 1-2 (Week 3), draft problems 3-4 (Week 5), final portfolio (Week 6). You may use technology tools (graphing calculators, spreadsheets, statistical software) but must document their use and show understanding of underlying concepts.
grading_notes: Expect most students to score 75-85 points with proper effort. Deduct points for basic computational errors (5 points per problem), unclear explanations (reduce communication score), or problems that are too simple/complex for intermediate level. Look for evidence of genuine problem-solving rather than textbook exercises. Strong portfolios will show mathematical connections between problems and demonstrate metacognitive awareness in reflections. Common issues include insufficient explanation of reasoning, failure to verify solutions, and poor organization. Consider partial credit for problems with correct approach but minor errors. Portfolio should demonstrate growth in mathematical thinking across the four problems.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Optimization and Model Interpretability Assessment
description: Students will demonstrate expert-level proficiency in designing, implementing, and optimizing end-to-end machine learning pipelines while providing comprehensive model interpretability analysis. This assessment evaluates advanced techniques including hyperparameter optimization, feature engineering, model selection, and explainable AI methods.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement sophisticated machine learning pipelines with advanced preprocessing and feature engineering techniques
Apply and compare multiple optimization strategies for hyperparameter tuning and model selection
Implement comprehensive model interpretability and explainability methods for complex ML models
Critically evaluate model performance using appropriate statistical tests and cross-validation strategies
Communicate technical findings effectively through visualization and written analysis
rubric_criteria: Pipeline Architecture & Implementation (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of ML pipeline design including advanced preprocessing, feature engineering, data leakage prevention, and scalable implementation. Code is well-structured, documented, and follows best practices.

Optimization & Model Selection (25 points): Implements multiple hyperparameter optimization techniques (Bayesian optimization, grid search, random search), uses appropriate cross-validation strategies, compares multiple algorithms systematically, and demonstrates statistical significance testing.

Model Interpretability & Explainability (25 points): Applies diverse interpretability methods (SHAP, LIME, permutation importance, partial dependence plots), provides meaningful insights into model behavior, identifies potential biases or limitations, and validates explanations appropriately.

Analysis Quality & Communication (25 points): Presents clear, data-driven conclusions with appropriate visualizations, discusses practical implications and limitations, provides actionable recommendations, and demonstrates critical thinking about model deployment considerations.
instructions:
You are provided with a complex, real-world dataset containing both structured and unstructured features. Your task is to develop a comprehensive machine learning solution that not only achieves high predictive performance but also provides deep insights into model behavior and decision-making processes.

Deliverables:
1. Complete Jupyter notebook with well-documented code implementing your ML pipeline
2. Comparative analysis of at least 3 different algorithms with statistical significance testing
3. Implementation of at least 3 different hyperparameter optimization approaches
4. Comprehensive interpretability analysis using minimum 4 different explainability techniques
5. Executive summary (2-3 pages) presenting key findings, limitations, and deployment recommendations

Technical Requirements:
- Implement proper train/validation/test splits with time-series considerations if applicable
- Address class imbalance, missing data, and outliers systematically
- Use appropriate evaluation metrics with confidence intervals
- Validate interpretability results through perturbation testing or ground truth comparison
- Include computational efficiency analysis and scalability considerations

Submission Format: Submit a ZIP file containing: (1) Jupyter notebook (.ipynb), (2) Executive summary (PDF), (3) All supporting code files, (4) Requirements.txt file listing dependencies. Ensure all code runs without errors and produces consistent results through random seed setting.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical depth over breadth - sophisticated implementation of fewer techniques scores higher than superficial application of many. Look for evidence of deep understanding through thoughtful parameter choices, appropriate method selection for the specific dataset characteristics, and meaningful interpretation of results. Common issues to watch: data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate cross-validation strategies, overfitting in hyperparameter optimization, and misinterpretation of explainability results. Grade distribution expectation: 10% excellent (90-100), 25% proficient (80-89), 40% developing (70-79), 20% needs improvement (60-69), 5% unsatisfactory (<60). Partial credit available within each criterion - award points for correct methodology even if implementation has minor errors.

title: Ethics and Bias in Machine Learning Systems: A Critical Analysis Discussion
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world case studies of algorithmic bias and ethical failures in machine learning systems, proposing comprehensive mitigation strategies and evaluating the societal implications of data science decisions.
estimated_time: 3-4 hours (including research, initial post, and peer responses)
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate ethical implications and potential biases in machine learning algorithms and data collection processes
Analyze the societal impact of data science applications and propose responsible AI practices
Critically assess trade-offs between model performance and fairness in real-world scenarios
Synthesize multiple perspectives on data ethics and communicate complex technical concepts to diverse audiences
rubric_criteria: Case Study Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of the technical and ethical issues, identifies root causes of bias/failure, and connects to broader data science concepts with specific examples

Mitigation Strategy Development (25 points): Proposes comprehensive, technically feasible solutions addressing both technical and organizational aspects, considers implementation challenges and resource requirements

Critical Thinking and Evidence (25 points): Uses credible sources to support arguments, acknowledges multiple perspectives, identifies limitations of proposed solutions, and demonstrates nuanced understanding of complex trade-offs

Peer Engagement and Communication (25 points): Provides substantive responses that advance discussion, asks probing questions, synthesizes ideas across multiple posts, and communicates technical concepts clearly to non-technical audiences
instructions: This assessment consists of three phases over one week. **Phase 1 (Initial Post - Due Wednesday):** Select one case study from the provided list (facial recognition bias, predictive policing algorithms, hiring AI discrimination, or healthcare AI disparities) or propose your own with instructor approval. Write a 600-800 word analysis that: (1) Summarizes the technical and ethical issues involved, (2) Identifies specific sources of bias in data, algorithms, or deployment, (3) Analyzes stakeholder impacts, and (4) Proposes 3-4 concrete mitigation strategies with implementation timelines. Include at least 3 peer-reviewed sources and 2 industry reports. **Phase 2 (Peer Responses - Due Friday):** Respond substantively to at least 3 classmates' posts (200-300 words each). Challenge assumptions, suggest alternative approaches, or build upon their strategies. Focus on technical feasibility, ethical implications, and real-world constraints. **Phase 3 (Synthesis Post - Due Sunday):** Write a 300-400 word reflection synthesizing insights from the discussion, identifying common themes across cases, and proposing one overarching principle for ethical AI development. Format all posts with clear headers, proper citations (APA style), and professional tone suitable for industry stakeholders.
grading_notes: Excellent work (90-100) demonstrates graduate-level analysis connecting technical details to broader ethical frameworks, with innovative solutions and sophisticated peer engagement. Good work (80-89) shows solid understanding with adequate solutions but may lack depth in some areas. Satisfactory work (70-79) meets basic requirements but shows superficial analysis or limited engagement. Watch for: posts that focus only on technical aspects without ethical consideration, generic solutions without implementation details, peer responses that merely agree without adding value, and failure to cite credible sources. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-range, 60% B-range, 15% C-range, 5% below C. Provide specific feedback on technical accuracy of bias identification and feasibility of proposed solutions.

title: Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Modern Applications of Differential Topology
description: Students will research, analyze, and present a comprehensive examination of a specific application of differential topology in contemporary mathematics or physics, demonstrating mastery of advanced topological concepts and their real-world implications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate deep understanding of differential topology concepts including manifolds, vector bundles, and characteristic classes
Apply advanced topological methods to solve complex mathematical problems in research contexts
Synthesize current research literature and identify open problems in differential topology
Communicate sophisticated mathematical concepts clearly to expert audiences using appropriate notation and visual aids
Critically analyze the connections between abstract topological theory and concrete applications in physics, economics, or data science
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates flawless understanding of differential topology concepts, uses precise mathematical language and notation, presents theorems with complete proofs or rigorous proof sketches, shows mastery of technical details

Research Quality and Depth (25 points): Incorporates current peer-reviewed sources (minimum 8 recent publications), identifies and articulates open research questions, demonstrates understanding of historical development and contemporary significance, shows original analytical insights

Application and Problem-Solving (25 points): Clearly connects abstract topological concepts to concrete applications, demonstrates how differential topology provides unique solutions to real-world problems, presents specific examples with detailed mathematical analysis, shows innovative thinking in problem approach

Presentation Excellence and Communication (25 points): Delivers clear, well-organized presentation with logical flow, uses appropriate mathematical notation and high-quality visual aids, responds expertly to technical questions, maintains audience engagement while handling complex material, demonstrates teaching ability
instructions: Select a specific application of differential topology from approved research areas: quantum field theory, general relativity, financial mathematics, machine learning theory, or robotics/control systems. Your presentation must include: (1) Introduction establishing the mathematical foundation - define key concepts including smooth manifolds, tangent bundles, and relevant characteristic classes with precise mathematical statements; (2) Literature review of minimum 8 current research papers (published within last 5 years), identifying the specific topological tools employed and their advantages over alternative approaches; (3) Detailed analysis of at least two concrete examples showing step-by-step mathematical application of differential topology methods to solve specific problems; (4) Discussion of current open problems and potential future research directions in your chosen application area. Format requirements: 20-minute presentation using professional slides with proper LaTeX mathematical notation, followed by 10-minute technical Q&A session. Submit presentation slides, annotated bibliography, and detailed outline 48 hours prior to presentation date. Include rigorous mathematical proofs or detailed proof sketches for key results. Visual aids must include clear diagrams illustrating topological concepts and their applications. Be prepared to solve related problems on the board during Q&A.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical precision - look for correct use of terminology, accurate theorem statements, and rigorous logical flow. Common issues: insufficient rigor in definitions, superficial treatment of applications, poor connection between theory and practice. Expect expert-level presentations comparable to graduate research seminars. Grade distribution should reflect: 90-100 points for presentations demonstrating original insights and research-level understanding; 80-89 for solid presentations with minor technical gaps; 70-79 for adequate presentations lacking depth or containing significant errors; below 70 for presentations with fundamental misunderstandings. During Q&A, assess ability to handle unexpected questions, extend concepts to new contexts, and demonstrate flexible understanding beyond prepared material. Pay particular attention to students' ability to explain complex concepts clearly and their depth of understanding when pressed for details.

title: Programming Fundamentals Portfolio: From Concepts to Code
description: Students will create a comprehensive portfolio showcasing their understanding of basic programming concepts through four small projects: a simple calculator, a text-based guessing game, a basic data organizer, and a personal coding reflection journal. This portfolio demonstrates practical application of variables, control structures, functions, and problem-solving skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Implement basic programming constructs including variables, conditionals, and loops
Design and write functions to solve simple computational problems
Debug and test code systematically to ensure correct functionality
Document code clearly and reflect on programming problem-solving processes
rubric_criteria: Code Functionality (25 points): All four projects work correctly, handle basic edge cases, and meet specified requirements. Programs run without errors and produce expected outputs.
Programming Concepts (25 points): Demonstrates proper use of variables, data types, control structures (if/else, loops), and functions. Code shows understanding of fundamental programming logic.

Code Quality & Documentation (25 points): Code is well-organized, uses meaningful variable names, includes appropriate comments, and follows basic style conventions. Each project includes brief explanation of approach.

Reflection & Growth (25 points): Coding journal shows thoughtful reflection on learning process, documents challenges encountered and solutions found, and demonstrates progression in programming thinking over time.
instructions: Create a portfolio containing four programming projects and a reflection journal. Project 1: Build a calculator that performs basic arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /) on two numbers with user input validation. Project 2: Create a number guessing game where the computer generates a random number (1-100) and gives 'higher/lower' hints until the user guesses correctly, tracking number of attempts. Project 3: Develop a simple contact organizer that stores names and phone numbers, allowing users to add, display, and search contacts using lists or dictionaries. Project 4: Maintain a weekly coding journal documenting your learning process, challenges faced, solutions discovered, and 'aha moments' throughout the portfolio development. Each project should be 30-50 lines of code, include comments explaining key sections, and have a brief written description (100-150 words) of your problem-solving approach. Submit all files in a single folder with clear naming conventions (project1_calculator.py, journal_week1.txt, etc.). Include a README file listing all components and how to run each program. Test all programs thoroughly and include sample input/output examples. Portfolio demonstrates progression from simple concepts to more complex problem-solving, showing your growth as a beginning programmer.
grading_notes: Evaluate portfolios holistically, looking for evidence of learning progression rather than perfect code. Common issues include: inadequate input validation, missing error handling, unclear variable names, and superficial reflection entries. Expect beginner-level syntax and logic - focus on whether concepts are correctly applied rather than code elegance. Strong portfolios will show clear improvement from early to later projects, thoughtful problem decomposition, and genuine reflection on learning. Average students typically score 70-85 points, with points lost mainly on documentation and reflection quality. Provide specific feedback on code improvements and encourage continued practice.

title: Advanced Calculus Problem Solving Quiz: Optimization and Related Rates
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' ability to solve complex optimization problems, related rates problems, and apply advanced calculus concepts including implicit differentiation, critical point analysis, and real-world mathematical modeling.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply optimization techniques to solve multi-variable real-world problems with constraints
Solve related rates problems involving multiple changing variables and complex geometric relationships
Demonstrate mastery of implicit differentiation and chain rule in advanced contexts
Analyze critical points using second derivative tests and justify optimization solutions
Construct and interpret mathematical models from verbal problem descriptions
rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Mathematical Modeling (25 points): Correctly identifies given information, defines variables, establishes relationships between variables, and translates word problems into mathematical equations. Shows clear understanding of the physical or geometric constraints involved.

Differentiation Techniques and Mathematical Procedures (25 points): Demonstrates accurate use of differentiation rules including chain rule, product rule, quotient rule, and implicit differentiation. Shows proper algebraic manipulation and equation solving techniques throughout the solution process.

Critical Analysis and Solution Validation (25 points): Correctly identifies critical points, applies appropriate tests (first/second derivative tests), verifies solutions make sense in context, and checks boundary conditions where applicable. Shows understanding of maximum/minimum concepts.

Communication and Mathematical Reasoning (25 points): Presents solutions with clear logical flow, uses appropriate mathematical notation, provides complete sentences for final answers with proper units, and explains reasoning for key steps. Work is organized and easy to follow.
instructions:
This quiz consists of 4 multi-part problems designed to assess your mastery of advanced calculus applications. You have 90 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly - partial credit will be awarded based on your mathematical reasoning and problem-solving approach, even if final answers are incorrect.

For each problem: (1) Begin by clearly defining all variables and stating what you need to find, (2) Set up the appropriate equations or functions based on the given constraints, (3) Show all differentiation steps explicitly, (4) Solve for critical points and verify your solutions, (5) State your final answer in complete sentences with appropriate units.

Problem 1 (25 pts): Optimization - A rectangular box with square base must have a volume of 500 cubic inches. The material for the base costs $2 per square inch, sides cost $1 per square inch, and the top costs $1.50 per square inch. Find the dimensions that minimize the total cost.

Problem 2 (25 pts): Related Rates - A spherical balloon is being inflated at a rate of 10 cubic feet per minute. When the radius is 6 feet, how fast is the surface area increasing? Additionally, if the balloon material can only stretch until the surface area reaches 400π square feet, how much time remains before the balloon reaches its limit?

Problem 3 (25 pts): Implicit Differentiation - For the curve defined by x³ + y³ - 3xy = 0, find dy/dx and determine the equations of all horizontal and vertical tangent lines.

Problem 4 (25 pts): Applied Optimization - A Norman window consists of a rectangle topped by a semicircle. If the perimeter is fixed at 20 feet, find the dimensions that maximize the window's area.

Calculators are permitted. Express final numerical answers as exact values when possible, or round to three decimal places. Good luck!
grading_notes: Grade each problem out of 25 points using the four criteria equally weighted. Award 18-25 points for problems with correct setup, methodology, and answers; 12-17 points for problems with minor computational errors but sound approach; 6-11 points for problems showing partial understanding with significant errors; 0-5 points for minimal work or major conceptual misunderstandings. Common issues to watch: students forgetting to define variables clearly, setting up incorrect constraint equations, algebraic errors when solving for critical points, failing to verify solutions in context, and not including proper units. Expect class average around 75-80. Problems 1 and 4 typically score highest; Problem 3 often causes difficulty with implicit differentiation complexity.

title: Distributed Web Crawler System with Real-Time Analytics
description: Students will design and implement a scalable, distributed web crawler system capable of crawling websites while providing real-time analytics through a web dashboard. The system must handle concurrent crawling, data storage, error handling, and provide meaningful insights about crawled content.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems using appropriate architectural patterns
Apply advanced data structures and algorithms for large-scale data processing
Implement concurrent and parallel programming techniques for performance optimization
Integrate multiple technologies including databases, message queues, and web frameworks
Demonstrate understanding of system scalability, reliability, and fault tolerance principles
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Clear architectural diagram, appropriate design patterns, proper component separation, scalability considerations, and documentation of design decisions

Technical Implementation (25 points): Code quality, proper use of data structures/algorithms, concurrent programming implementation, error handling, and adherence to software engineering best practices
Functionality & Features (25 points): Working crawler with configurable parameters, real-time dashboard, data persistence, rate limiting, duplicate detection, and crawl statistics

Performance & Scalability (25 points): System handles concurrent crawling efficiently, demonstrates horizontal scalability, includes performance metrics, load testing results, and optimization strategies
instructions: Develop a distributed web crawler system with the following requirements: 1) Core Crawler: Implement a multi-threaded crawler that can simultaneously crawl multiple websites, respect robots.txt files, implement rate limiting, detect and handle duplicate URLs, and support configurable crawl depth and breadth limits. 2) Data Management: Use a distributed database (e.g., MongoDB, Cassandra) for storing crawled content, implement a message queue system (Redis/RabbitMQ) for task distribution, and create efficient indexing for fast retrieval. 3) Real-time Dashboard: Build a web interface displaying live crawling statistics, recently crawled pages, error rates, and system performance metrics.
