Include data visualization charts and the ability to start/stop/configure crawl jobs. 4) System Components: Implement at least 3 distributed worker nodes, a central coordinator service, a web API for system interaction, and comprehensive logging and monitoring. 5) Deliverables: Complete source code with clear documentation, architectural diagram and system design document, demo video (10-15 minutes) showing system operation, performance analysis report with benchmarks, and deployment instructions with Docker configuration. Submit all materials via GitHub repository with proper README, commit history showing development progression, and include unit tests with >80% code coverage.
grading_notes: Evaluate architectural soundness by checking if students chose appropriate technologies and patterns for distributed systems. Look for proper separation of concerns and clear component interfaces. For technical implementation, prioritize code readability, proper error handling, and evidence of testing. Common issues include inadequate error handling during network failures, poor rate limiting implementation, and insufficient consideration of edge cases. Functionality should be demonstrated through the working system and video demo - partial credit available if core features work despite missing advanced features. Performance evaluation should include actual metrics and testing results, not just theoretical analysis. Grade distribution expectation: 15% will achieve 90-100 points with exceptional systems showing advanced features like auto-scaling or machine learning integration, 60% will score 75-89 points with solid implementations meeting core requirements, 20% will score 60-74 points with basic functionality but missing key features, and 5% below 60 points for incomplete or non-functional submissions.

title: Fundamentals of Data Science Concepts and Basic Analysis
description: A comprehensive beginner-level exam testing foundational knowledge of data science concepts, basic statistical understanding, data visualization principles, and interpretation of simple analytical results. Students will demonstrate understanding through multiple choice questions, short answers, and basic data interpretation tasks.
learning_objectives_assessed: Define key data science terminology and explain the data science workflow
Identify appropriate data types and measurement scales for different variables
Interpret basic descriptive statistics and simple data visualizations
Recognize common data quality issues and basic data cleaning concepts
Understand fundamental concepts of correlation, causation, and statistical significance
rubric_criteria: Data Science Fundamentals (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of core data science concepts, workflow stages, and terminology. Correctly identifies roles and applications of data science across industries.

Data Types and Statistical Concepts (25 points): Accurately classifies variables by data type (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) and correctly interprets basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles).

Data Visualization and Interpretation (25 points): Properly reads and interprets common chart types (bar charts, histograms, scatter plots, box plots). Identifies appropriate visualization choices for different data types and research questions.

Data Quality and Ethics (25 points): Recognizes common data quality issues (missing values, outliers, inconsistencies) and understands basic ethical considerations in data collection and analysis, including privacy and bias concerns.
instructions:
This exam consists of 50 questions divided into four sections, each worth 25 points. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully and select the best answer for multiple choice questions. For short answer questions, provide clear, concise responses using proper terminology.

Section A (Questions 1-15): Multiple choice questions covering data science fundamentals, including definitions, workflow stages, and applications. Each question is worth 1.67 points.

Section B (Questions 16-30): Mixed format questions on data types, statistical measures, and basic probability concepts. Includes both multiple choice and fill-in-the-blank questions. Each question is worth 1.67 points.

Section C (Questions 31-40): Data interpretation questions featuring charts, graphs, and basic statistical outputs. You will analyze provided visualizations and answer related questions. Each question is worth 2.5 points.

Section D (Questions 41-50): Scenario-based questions addressing data quality issues and ethical considerations. Short answer format requiring 2-3 sentence responses. Each question is worth 2.5 points.

Submission Requirements: Complete all sections in order. Mark your answers clearly on the provided answer sheet. Show any calculations for partial credit consideration. Submit both the question booklet and answer sheet before the time limit expires.
grading_notes: Grade distribution expectation: A (90-100), B (80-89), C (70-79), D (60-69), F (below 60). Award partial credit for short answer questions showing correct reasoning even if the final answer is incomplete. Common issues to watch: students confusing correlation with causation, misidentifying data types (especially ordinal vs interval), and inadequate explanations in ethics questions. For Section C visualization questions, accept reasonable interpretations if students show proper analytical thinking. Deduct points for failure to use appropriate terminology. Flag answers suggesting fundamental misunderstanding of basic concepts for additional review.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategies Discussion: Real-World Applications of Linear Functions
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing and comparing different approaches to solving real-world problems involving linear functions, demonstrating their understanding of mathematical modeling, interpretation of results, and communication of mathematical reasoning.
estimated_time: 90 minutes (45 minutes preparation + 45 minutes discussion participation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply linear function concepts to model and solve real-world problems
Analyze and compare multiple problem-solving strategies for mathematical situations
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using appropriate terminology and notation
Evaluate the validity and efficiency of different mathematical approaches
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy and Application (25 points): Correctly applies linear function concepts, accurately sets up equations, performs calculations without errors, and appropriately interprets mathematical results in context

Problem-Solving Strategy Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates clear understanding of different solution approaches, compares methods effectively, identifies advantages and limitations of each strategy, and shows insight into when different methods are most appropriate

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise mathematical language and notation, explains reasoning clearly and logically, provides complete justifications for solutions, and presents ideas in an organized manner that others can follow

Discussion Participation and Peer Interaction (25 points): Actively contributes to discussion with meaningful posts, responds constructively to peers' solutions, asks thoughtful questions, builds on others' ideas, and demonstrates respectful engagement with alternative approaches
instructions: You will participate in an online discussion analyzing different approaches to solving this scenario: 'A small business owner needs to determine the break-even point for a new product. Fixed costs are $2,400 monthly, variable costs are $15 per unit, and the selling price is $35 per unit.' Your participation requires three components: First, solve the break-even problem using at least two different methods (algebraic, graphical, or table-based approaches). Show all work and explain each step clearly. Second, create one original real-world scenario involving linear functions and provide a complete solution with explanation. Third, respond to at least two classmates' posts by analyzing their solution methods, suggesting alternative approaches, or asking clarifying questions about their reasoning. All mathematical work must include proper notation, units where applicable, and interpretation of results in context. Initial posts are due by Wednesday at 11:59 PM, and response posts are due by Friday at 11:59 PM. Format your mathematical expressions clearly using proper notation or equation editor tools. Each post should be substantive (150-250 words) and demonstrate your mathematical thinking process, not just final answers.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for mathematical correctness and completeness of explanations before assessing discussion quality. Look for evidence that students understand the relationship between algebraic and graphical representations. Common issues include: incomplete justification of steps, confusion between break-even point as units vs. dollars, and superficial peer responses. Expect 15-20% of students to earn full points in each criterion, with most students scoring in the 70-85% range. Deduct points for late submissions according to course policy. Students who only provide final answers without showing reasoning should not exceed 60% on Mathematical Communication criterion. Exceptional responses that extend beyond requirements (such as discussing real-world limitations of mathematical models) may earn full points even with minor calculation errors.

title: Distributed System Architecture Design and Implementation Presentation
description: Students will design, implement a prototype of, and present a comprehensive distributed system solution addressing a real-world scalability challenge. The presentation must demonstrate deep understanding of distributed systems principles, architectural trade-offs, and practical implementation considerations.
estimated_time: 4-6 weeks preparation, 25-30 minute presentation + 10 minutes Q&A
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed system architectures considering CAP theorem constraints and consistency models
Evaluate and justify architectural trade-offs in distributed systems including performance, reliability, and maintainability
Implement and demonstrate distributed system components using appropriate technologies and patterns
Analyze fault tolerance mechanisms and recovery strategies in distributed environments
Communicate complex technical concepts effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
rubric_criteria: System Architecture and Design (25 points): Comprehensive system design with clear component interactions, appropriate technology choices, well-justified architectural decisions, consideration of scalability patterns, and thorough analysis of CAP theorem implications

Technical Implementation and Demonstration (25 points): Working prototype demonstrating key system components, effective use of distributed systems technologies, proper error handling and fault tolerance mechanisms, and clear evidence of distributed computing principles in action

Problem Analysis and Solution Justification (25 points): Clear articulation of the problem scope and requirements, thorough evaluation of alternative approaches, well-reasoned justification of design choices, identification of potential bottlenecks and failure points, and realistic assessment of system limitations

Presentation Quality and Technical Communication (25 points): Clear and logical presentation structure, effective use of visual aids and system diagrams, confident handling of technical questions, appropriate level of technical detail for audience, and professional delivery within time constraints
instructions: Select a real-world distributed system challenge (e.g., designing a global content delivery network, implementing a distributed database for financial transactions, or creating a fault-tolerant microservices architecture for e-commerce). Your presentation must include: (1) Problem statement with specific requirements including expected scale, performance metrics, and availability targets; (2) Comprehensive system architecture diagram showing all major components, data flow, and communication patterns; (3) Technology stack justification explaining your choice of databases, messaging systems, load balancers, and programming frameworks; (4) Live demonstration of a working prototype showcasing at least three core distributed system features (e.g., load balancing, data replication, service discovery); (5) Failure analysis discussing potential points of failure and your mitigation strategies; (6) Performance analysis with projected metrics and scaling considerations. Submit your slides, source code repository link, and a 2-page technical summary 48 hours before presentation. Code must be runnable with provided setup instructions. Presentation should be 25-30 minutes followed by 10 minutes of Q&A. Visual aids should include architecture diagrams, sequence diagrams, and live system demonstrations.
grading_notes: Look for depth of understanding in distributed systems concepts rather than just surface-level implementation. Students should demonstrate grasp of consistency models, partition tolerance, and distributed consensus algorithms. Code quality and documentation matter - check if the prototype actually demonstrates distributed principles or is just a monolithic application split across containers. Strong presentations will show awareness of industry best practices and current research. Common issues include: oversimplified architectures that don't truly require distribution, lack of consideration for network partitions and failures, unrealistic performance claims without supporting evidence, and inability to answer probing questions about system behavior under stress. Excellent work (90-100) should demonstrate graduate-level understanding with novel insights or optimizations. Good work (80-89) shows solid understanding with competent implementation. Satisfactory work (70-79) covers requirements but may lack depth in analysis or have implementation issues.

title: Mathematical Patterns Lab Report: Exploring Number Sequences in Nature
description: Students will investigate mathematical patterns found in nature (such as Fibonacci sequences in pinecones, geometric patterns in leaves, or symmetry in flowers) through hands-on data collection, analysis, and mathematical modeling. Students will document their findings in a structured lab report format.
estimated_time: 3-4 hours (including data collection, analysis, and report writing)
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and describe mathematical patterns in real-world contexts
Collect, organize, and analyze numerical data systematically
Apply basic mathematical operations and formulas to solve problems
Communicate mathematical findings clearly using appropriate terminology and visual representations
rubric_criteria: Data Collection and Organization (25 points): Accurately collects at least 10 data points, organizes data in clear tables/charts, shows proper measurement techniques and records units consistently

Mathematical Analysis (25 points): Correctly identifies patterns, applies appropriate mathematical operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), calculates averages or ratios when relevant, shows all work clearly

Visual Representation (25 points): Creates at least one graph, chart, or diagram that accurately represents the data, includes proper labels, titles, and scales, uses visual aids to support conclusions

Communication and Conclusions (25 points): Writes clear explanations of findings, uses proper mathematical vocabulary, draws logical conclusions based on data, discusses real-world applications of discovered patterns
instructions: Choose one mathematical pattern from nature to investigate (examples: count spiral patterns in pinecones or sunflowers, measure leaf dimensions to find ratios, examine symmetry in flowers or butterflies). Collect data from at least 10 samples of your chosen object. Your lab report must include: (1) Introduction explaining what pattern you're investigating and why it's mathematically interesting, (2) Methods section describing how you collected your data and what tools you used, (3) Data section with organized tables showing your measurements and calculations, (4) Results section with at least one graph or visual representation of your findings, (5) Conclusion discussing the mathematical pattern you discovered and where else it might appear in nature. Format your report with clear headings, double-spaced text, and include photos of your samples if possible. Show all mathematical calculations step-by-step. Submit your completed report as a PDF with your name and date. Reports should be 2-3 pages long excluding data tables and visuals.
grading_notes: Look for accuracy in basic calculations rather than advanced mathematical concepts. Students should demonstrate understanding of fundamental operations and pattern recognition. Common issues include: incomplete data collection, missing units in measurements, unclear or missing calculations, and conclusions not supported by data. Expect most students to score in the 70-85 range, with higher scores for exceptional organization and insight. Allow partial credit for work shown even if final answers are incorrect. Encourage creativity in pattern selection while ensuring mathematical content is appropriate for beginner level.

title: Advanced Mathematical Analysis and Problem-Solving Comprehensive Examination
description: A comprehensive examination assessing mastery of advanced calculus, abstract algebra, real analysis, and complex problem-solving techniques. Students will demonstrate their ability to prove theorems, solve multi-step analytical problems, and apply advanced mathematical concepts across multiple domains.
learning_objectives_assessed: Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using direct proof, contradiction, and induction techniques
Apply advanced calculus concepts including multivariable integration, series convergence, and differential equations
Demonstrate understanding of abstract algebraic structures including groups, rings, and fields
Analyze real-valued functions for continuity, differentiability, and convergence properties
Synthesize multiple mathematical concepts to solve complex, multi-domain problems
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Proof Construction (25 points): Demonstrates logical structure, uses appropriate mathematical notation, provides complete justifications for all steps, and employs valid proof techniques with precision

Computational Accuracy and Technique (25 points): Executes calculations correctly, applies formulas and theorems appropriately, shows all intermediate steps clearly, and arrives at correct numerical or analytical results

Conceptual Understanding and Application (25 points): Shows deep understanding of underlying mathematical principles, correctly identifies which theorems and methods apply to given problems, and makes appropriate connections between different mathematical domains

Problem-Solving Strategy and Communication (25 points): Develops coherent solution strategies, explains reasoning clearly, organizes work logically, and demonstrates ability to break down complex problems into manageable components
instructions: This examination consists of 6 problems spanning advanced calculus, real analysis, abstract algebra, and applied mathematics. You have 4 hours to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and provide complete justifications for your answers. Partial credit will be awarded based on the quality of your mathematical reasoning and the correctness of your approach, even if final answers are incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation throughout. For proof problems, state your approach clearly (direct proof, contradiction, induction, etc.) and ensure each logical step follows from the previous. For computational problems, show all intermediate steps and clearly identify your final answer. You may use standard mathematical reference materials and calculators, but all work must be your own. Problems are weighted equally, but allocate your time wisely as some may require more extensive work than others. If you cannot complete a problem fully, show as much progress as possible and explain your intended approach. Write legibly and organize your solutions clearly, numbering each problem and starting each on a new page. Submit all work, including scratch paper if it contains relevant solution attempts.
grading_notes: Grade holistically using the four criteria, awarding partial credit generously for correct mathematical reasoning even with computational errors. Look for evidence of mathematical maturity in proof construction and problem interpretation. Common issues include: insufficient justification of steps, computational errors that don't reflect conceptual misunderstanding, and incomplete proofs that nonetheless show correct reasoning. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 25% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 20% D-level (60-69), 5% below 60. Award full credit for alternative correct solution methods. Deduct points for unclear notation or organization only if it significantly impedes understanding of the solution.

title: Programming Paradigms Discussion: Comparing Object-Oriented vs. Procedural Programming
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion comparing object-oriented and procedural programming paradigms, analyzing their strengths, weaknesses, and appropriate use cases through examples and peer interaction.
estimated_time: 2 hours initial post + 1 hour peer responses
learning_objectives_assessed: Explain the fundamental differences between programming paradigms
Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of object-oriented vs. procedural programming
Evaluate appropriate use cases for different programming approaches
Communicate technical concepts clearly to peers
rubric_criteria: Technical Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates correct understanding of OOP and procedural programming concepts, including accurate definitions, proper use of terminology, and factually correct examples

Analysis and Critical Thinking (25 points): Provides thoughtful comparison of paradigms, identifies specific strengths/weaknesses, presents well-reasoned arguments for use cases, and shows depth of understanding beyond surface-level descriptions

Use of Examples (25 points): Includes relevant, clear code examples or real-world scenarios that effectively illustrate points, demonstrates practical application of concepts, and enhances understanding of abstract ideas

Peer Engagement (25 points): Responds meaningfully to at least two classmates' posts, asks thoughtful follow-up questions, builds upon others' ideas constructively, and contributes to collaborative learning environment
instructions: Create an initial discussion post (300-500 words) addressing the following: 1) Define object-oriented and procedural programming paradigms in your own words. 2) Compare and contrast these approaches, identifying at least three key differences. 3) Provide a specific example of a programming scenario where you would choose OOP over procedural programming, and explain why. Include a brief code snippet or pseudocode to illustrate your point. 4) Discuss one potential drawback of your chosen paradigm and how you might mitigate it. After posting your initial response, read and respond to at least two classmates' posts (100-150 words each). In your responses, either ask a clarifying question, provide an alternative perspective, or build upon their example with additional insights. Focus on fostering meaningful dialogue rather than simple agreement. Format your post with clear headings for each section. Use proper coding syntax if including code examples. Cite any external resources used. Submit your initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM and peer responses by Friday 11:59 PM. Posts submitted after the deadline will receive reduced credit.
grading_notes: Look for evidence that students understand core concepts rather than memorized definitions. High-quality responses will show original thinking and practical application. Common issues include: confusing syntax with paradigm concepts, providing generic examples without clear connection to paradigms, and superficial peer responses. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Deduct 10% for late initial posts, 5% for late peer responses. Award bonus points for exceptional peer engagement or innovative examples.

title: Data Science Project Analysis and Communication Presentation
description: Students will present a comprehensive analysis of a real-world dataset, demonstrating their ability to apply the complete data science pipeline from data exploration through model implementation and business insights communication.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply exploratory data analysis techniques to understand dataset characteristics and identify patterns
Implement appropriate machine learning models for predictive or classification tasks
Evaluate model performance using relevant metrics and validation techniques
Communicate technical findings and business insights effectively to diverse audiences
Demonstrate critical thinking in data interpretation and methodology selection
rubric_criteria: Data Exploration & Preprocessing (25 points): Thorough EDA with appropriate visualizations, proper handling of missing data/outliers, feature engineering decisions clearly justified, data quality assessment demonstrated

Model Implementation & Methodology (25 points): Appropriate algorithm selection with justification, proper train/validation/test splits, hyperparameter tuning evidence, comparison of multiple approaches where relevant

Results Analysis & Interpretation (25 points): Correct application of evaluation metrics, model performance assessment, identification of limitations, discussion of potential improvements, business impact quantified
Presentation Quality & Communication (25 points): Clear structure and flow, effective visualizations, appropriate technical depth for audience, confident delivery, thoughtful responses to questions
instructions: Select a dataset from the approved list (healthcare, finance, marketing, or e-commerce domains) or propose your own with instructor approval by Week 1. Your presentation must include: (1) Problem statement and business context (2-3 minutes), (2) Data exploration findings with key insights visualized (4-5 minutes), (3) Methodology explanation including algorithm choice rationale (3-4 minutes), (4) Results presentation with performance metrics and model interpretation (4-5 minutes), (5) Business recommendations and next steps (2-3 minutes). Technical requirements: minimum 1000 observations, at least 5 features, implement 2+ algorithms for comparison, include cross-validation, create minimum 4 visualizations. Deliverables: 15-minute presentation (PDF slides required), brief technical appendix with code snippets, and dataset description. Submit slides 24 hours before presentation date. Be prepared for 5-minute Q&A session covering methodology choices, alternative approaches, and practical implementation challenges. Presentations will be evaluated by instructor and peer feedback forms.
grading_notes: Focus on depth of analysis rather than complexity of algorithms - students often over-complicate models. Watch for: proper data splitting (common error: data leakage), realistic business context (avoid generic insights), appropriate visualization choices (not just correlation matrices). Expect score distribution: 90-100 (exceptional insight/communication), 80-89 (solid analysis with minor gaps), 70-79 (meets requirements but limited depth), below 70 (significant methodological issues). Encourage questions during Q&A - responsiveness shows understanding. Deduct points for: exceeding time limits, missing technical requirements, unclear visualizations, or inability to justify methodology choices. Consider bonus points for creative feature engineering or addressing ethical implications of model deployment.

title: Distributed System Performance Analysis and Optimization Lab Report
description: Students will design, implement, and analyze a distributed caching system using consistent hashing, evaluate its performance under various load conditions, identify bottlenecks, and propose optimizations. This comprehensive lab report assesses advanced distributed systems concepts, performance analysis methodologies, and system optimization strategies.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems using consistent hashing algorithms
Conduct rigorous performance analysis using appropriate metrics and benchmarking tools
Identify system bottlenecks through profiling and monitoring techniques
Propose and validate optimization strategies for distributed systems
Communicate complex technical findings through professional documentation
rubric_criteria: System Design and Implementation (25 points): Correct implementation of consistent hashing, proper handling of node failures, code quality, architecture documentation, and adherence to distributed systems principles

Performance Analysis and Metrics (25 points): Comprehensive benchmarking methodology, appropriate metric selection (latency, throughput, consistency), statistical validity of results, proper use of profiling tools, and analysis of system behavior under various loads

Problem Identification and Optimization (25 points): Accurate identification of performance bottlenecks, well-reasoned optimization proposals, implementation of at least two optimization strategies, quantitative validation of improvements, and discussion of trade-offs

Technical Communication and Documentation (25 points): Clear problem statement, logical report structure, professional writing quality, effective use of graphs/tables, reproducible methodology, proper citations, and actionable conclusions
instructions: Implement a distributed caching system with 3-5 cache nodes using consistent hashing for key distribution. Your system must handle node additions/removals and simulate realistic failure scenarios. Develop a comprehensive benchmarking suite testing various workloads (read-heavy, write-heavy, mixed) with different key distributions and request rates. Use profiling tools (e.g., perf, JProfiler, or language-specific profilers) to identify bottlenecks in CPU usage, memory allocation, and network I/O. Your lab report must include: (1) System architecture diagram and implementation details, (2) Detailed methodology for performance testing, (3) Results with statistical analysis and visualization, (4) Identification of at least three performance bottlenecks with supporting evidence, (5) Implementation and evaluation of minimum two optimization strategies, (6) Discussion of scalability limitations and trade-offs. Submit source code with clear documentation, raw performance data, analysis scripts, and a 15-20 page technical report in IEEE format. Include a README with setup/execution instructions and ensure all results are reproducible. Code should follow industry best practices with proper error handling, logging, and configuration management.
grading_notes: Expect 15-20% of students to struggle with distributed systems concepts - provide scaffolding on consistent hashing implementation. Common issues include inadequate statistical analysis (look for confidence intervals, multiple trial runs), superficial bottleneck identification, and optimization strategies that aren't properly validated. Grade implementation by running provided test cases and checking code quality metrics. For performance analysis, verify methodology rigor and statistical significance of results. Strong reports will demonstrate deep understanding of distributed systems trade-offs and provide insights beyond basic requirements. Grade distribution typically: 10% (90-100), 25% (80-89), 45% (70-79), 15% (60-69), 5% (<60). Deduct points for non-reproducible results, inadequate documentation, or systems that don't handle failure scenarios correctly.

title: Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Concepts, Tools, and Basic Analysis
description: A comprehensive beginner-level quiz assessing foundational knowledge of data science concepts, common tools and libraries, basic statistical measures, and data visualization principles. Students will demonstrate understanding through multiple-choice, short-answer, and scenario-based questions.
learning_objectives_assessed: Define key data science terminology and explain the data science lifecycle
Identify appropriate Python libraries and tools for different data science tasks
Calculate and interpret basic statistical measures (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Evaluate data visualization choices and identify best practices for different data types
rubric_criteria: Data Science Concepts (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of fundamental terminology, data types, and the data science process including problem formulation, data collection, analysis, and interpretation

Tools and Libraries Knowledge (25 points): Shows familiarity with essential Python libraries (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scikit-learn) and can identify appropriate tools for specific data science tasks
Statistical Foundations (25 points): Accurately calculates basic descriptive statistics, understands measures of central tendency and variability, and can interpret statistical results in context

Data Visualization Principles (25 points): Recognizes appropriate chart types for different data scenarios, understands visualization best practices, and can critique or improve basic data visualizations
instructions: This quiz contains 25 questions divided into four sections corresponding to core data science fundamentals. You have 60 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully and select the best answer for multiple-choice questions. For short-answer questions, provide concise but complete responses (2-3 sentences maximum). For calculation problems, show your work and round to two decimal places where applicable. The quiz is open-book, meaning you may reference course materials, but collaboration with other students is not permitted. Section 1 covers data science concepts and terminology (6 questions). Section 2 focuses on tools and libraries commonly used in data science (7 questions). Section 3 tests your understanding of basic statistics including measures of central tendency and variability (6 questions). Section 4 evaluates your knowledge of data visualization principles and best practices (6 questions). Make sure to attempt all questions as partial credit may be awarded for incomplete but thoughtful responses. Save your work frequently if taking the quiz online. Submit your completed quiz through the learning management system by the specified deadline. Late submissions will incur a 10% penalty per day unless prior arrangements have been made.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should follow: 90-100 (A): Demonstrates strong foundational understanding across all areas; 80-89 (B): Shows good grasp of most concepts with minor gaps; 70-79 (C): Adequate understanding but may struggle with application or show inconsistency; Below 70: Significant knowledge gaps requiring additional study. Common issues to watch: confusing correlation with causation, incorrect library selection for tasks, calculation errors in basic statistics, poor visualization choices for data types. Award partial credit for short answers that demonstrate understanding even if incomplete. For statistical calculations, give credit for correct methodology even with minor computational errors. Pay attention to explanations in visualization questions - students should demonstrate understanding of why certain charts are appropriate, not just identify correct answers. Flag students scoring below 60% for additional support. Most students should score between 75-85% on this beginner assessment.

title: Community Statistics Analysis Project
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive statistical investigation of a real-world community issue by collecting data, performing statistical analysis, and presenting findings with recommendations. This project integrates data collection, descriptive and inferential statistics, probability concepts, and mathematical communication skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement appropriate data collection methods for statistical investigations
Calculate and interpret measures of central tendency, variability, and distribution shape
Apply probability concepts to analyze and predict outcomes from sample data
Perform hypothesis testing and confidence interval estimation using appropriate statistical methods
Create effective visual representations of data using graphs, charts, and statistical plots
Communicate statistical findings clearly through written reports and oral presentations
Evaluate the reliability and validity of statistical conclusions and identify potential sources of bias
rubric_criteria: Data Collection and Methodology (25 points): Quality of research question formulation, appropriateness of sampling method, sample size justification, data collection procedures, identification of variables (quantitative vs. qualitative), and ethical considerations in data gathering

Statistical Analysis and Calculations (25 points): Accuracy of descriptive statistics calculations, proper application of probability concepts, correct execution of inferential statistics (hypothesis tests, confidence intervals), appropriate use of statistical formulas, and demonstration of mathematical reasoning

Data Visualization and Presentation (25 points): Effectiveness of graphs and charts in representing data patterns, proper labeling and scaling of visual elements, variety of visualization techniques used, professional appearance of materials, and clarity of statistical displays

Communication and Conclusions (25 points): Clear articulation of findings in written report, logical organization of ideas, appropriate use of statistical terminology, valid interpretation of results, practical recommendations based on analysis, acknowledgment of limitations, and overall presentation quality
instructions: Select a community issue that interests you (examples: traffic patterns, environmental concerns, local business trends, school performance, housing costs, or public health topics). Your project must include: 1) A clear research question with operational definitions of key variables. 2) Collection of at least 50 data points using surveys, observations, or reliable secondary sources. Document your methodology and ensure ethical data collection. 3) Comprehensive statistical analysis including: descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles), at least three different types of graphs/charts, probability calculations relevant to your topic, one hypothesis test with proper interpretation, and one confidence interval with practical meaning. 4) A formal written report (1,500-2,000 words) containing: executive summary, introduction with research question, methodology section, results with statistical analysis, discussion of findings, limitations and potential sources of bias, and practical recommendations. 5) A 10-minute presentation to the class with visual aids summarizing your key findings and recommendations. Submit all raw data, calculations (showing work), statistical software outputs if used, the written report, and presentation slides. Cite all sources using proper academic format. Projects must demonstrate original work and statistical thinking beyond simple calculation. Focus on connecting mathematical concepts to real-world applications and drawing meaningful conclusions from your analysis.
grading_notes: Evaluate projects holistically while ensuring mathematical accuracy. Look for evidence of statistical thinking beyond mechanical calculation. Common issues include: inadequate sample sizes, biased sampling methods, misinterpretation of correlation vs. causation, inappropriate statistical tests for data types, and conclusions that overstate findings. Excellent projects (90-100) demonstrate sophisticated statistical reasoning and clear real-world connections. Proficient projects (80-89) show solid understanding with minor errors or limitations. Developing projects (70-79) display basic competency but lack depth or contain significant errors. Below 70 indicates fundamental misunderstandings requiring remediation. Encourage creativity in topic selection while maintaining statistical rigor. Weight mathematical accuracy heavily but also value clear communication and practical applications. Provide feedback on both statistical methodology and presentation skills.

title: Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Exam
description: Comprehensive examination testing students' ability to design efficient algorithms, analyze computational complexity, prove correctness, and optimize solutions for complex computational problems across multiple paradigms including dynamic programming, graph algorithms, and advanced data structures.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement advanced algorithms using dynamic programming, greedy methods, and divide-and-conquer strategies
Perform rigorous time and space complexity analysis using Big-O, Big-Theta, and Big-Omega notations
Construct formal correctness proofs for algorithms using mathematical induction and loop invariants
Optimize algorithm performance through advanced data structure selection and algorithmic paradigm application
Solve complex computational problems by reducing them to known algorithmic patterns and frameworks
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Design and Implementation (25 points): Correctness of algorithmic logic, appropriate choice of algorithmic paradigm, proper handling of edge cases, and clean pseudocode or implementation
Complexity Analysis (25 points): Accurate time and space complexity calculations, proper use of asymptotic notation, detailed step-by-step analysis, and identification of dominant operations
Mathematical Rigor and Proofs (25 points): Valid correctness proofs using induction or loop invariants, clear logical reasoning, proper mathematical notation, and complete proof structure

Problem-Solving and Optimization (25 points): Identification of optimal solutions, comparison of alternative approaches, justification of design choices, and demonstration of advanced algorithmic thinking
instructions: This exam consists of four comprehensive problems requiring algorithm design, complexity analysis, and mathematical proofs. You have 3 hours to complete all sections. Write all solutions clearly in the provided answer booklet, showing all work and intermediate steps. For algorithm problems, provide detailed pseudocode or clear implementation steps, not just high-level descriptions. For complexity analysis, show the mathematical derivation of your complexity bounds, identifying the dominant operations and worst-case scenarios. All correctness proofs must be rigorous and complete, using proper mathematical induction or loop invariant techniques. You may use standard algorithmic paradigms (DP, greedy, divide-and-conquer) and assume access to basic data structures (arrays, linked lists, hash tables, heaps, balanced trees) with their standard complexity guarantees. Partial credit will be awarded for incomplete solutions that demonstrate correct reasoning and approach. Clearly label each part of your solution and box final answers. No external materials, calculators, or electronic devices are permitted. If you need additional space, raise your hand for extra paper. Begin each problem on a new page and manage your time carefully across all four problems.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct approaches even with minor implementation errors. For complexity analysis, accept equivalent correct forms (O(n log n) vs O(n lg n)). Proof requirements should be strict - incomplete proofs receive significant deduction. Look for common errors: off-by-one mistakes in DP, incorrect base cases in recursion, and missing edge case handling. Expected grade distribution: 15% A-range (90-100), 30% B-range (80-89), 35% C-range (70-79), 20% below 70. Deduct 5 points for poor notation or illegible work. Solutions showing multiple valid approaches should receive bonus consideration. Flag papers showing identical error patterns for academic integrity review.

title: Critical Analysis of ML Model Bias and Fairness in High-Stakes Applications
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world cases of algorithmic bias in high-stakes domains (healthcare, criminal justice, hiring), evaluating mitigation strategies, and proposing comprehensive solutions that balance technical feasibility with ethical considerations.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (including research, initial post, and peer responses)
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate ethical implications and societal impacts of machine learning models in real-world applications
Analyze bias detection methods and fairness metrics across different algorithmic contexts
Synthesize technical solutions with regulatory frameworks and business constraints
Critically assess trade-offs between model performance, fairness, and interpretability
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of bias types, detection methods, and fairness metrics with accurate technical explanations and appropriate mathematical concepts
Case Study Integration (25 points): Provides comprehensive analysis of assigned real-world case with specific details, stakeholder impact assessment, and clear connection to broader systemic issues

Solution Framework (25 points): Proposes well-reasoned, multi-faceted mitigation strategies that address technical, regulatory, and implementation challenges with realistic timelines and resource considerations

Peer Engagement (25 points): Contributes substantive responses that challenge assumptions, extend discussions with additional insights, and demonstrate synthesis of multiple perspectives with evidence-based reasoning
instructions: You will analyze a high-stakes ML application case study focusing on bias and fairness concerns. Choose one case from the provided list (COMPAS recidivism prediction, medical diagnosis algorithms, or automated resume screening). Your analysis must include: (1) Technical Assessment - Identify specific bias types present, evaluate detection methods used/proposed, and analyze relevant fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, etc.) with mathematical justification. (2) Stakeholder Impact - Examine affected communities, quantify potential harms, and assess current mitigation efforts. (3) Solution Framework - Propose a comprehensive remediation strategy addressing data collection, model architecture, evaluation metrics, and monitoring systems. Include regulatory compliance considerations and implementation timeline. (4) Trade-off Analysis - Discuss tensions between accuracy, fairness, and interpretability, providing quantitative examples where possible. Your initial post should be 800-1000 words with at least 8 peer-reviewed sources. Respond substantively to 3 classmates' posts (200-300 words each), focusing on alternative approaches, implementation challenges, or additional ethical considerations. Use proper APA citations and include relevant code snippets or algorithmic pseudocode where appropriate. Submit initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM, responses by Sunday 11:59 PM.
grading_notes: Look for sophisticated understanding of fairness-accuracy trade-offs rather than simplistic solutions. Expect students to cite recent research (2020-2024) and demonstrate awareness of evolving regulatory landscape (EU AI Act, proposed US frameworks). Common weaknesses include oversimplified bias definitions, lack of quantitative analysis, and failure to address implementation constraints. Excellent responses will connect technical solutions to broader sociotechnical systems thinking. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations: 20% A-level work showing original insights and synthesis, 60% B-level work meeting all requirements with solid analysis, 20% requiring revision for incomplete technical understanding or insufficient peer engagement.

title: Basic Shapes and Measurements: Visual Math Presentation
description: Students will create and deliver a 5-minute presentation demonstrating their understanding of 2D shapes, perimeter, and area through real-world examples and visual aids.
estimated_time: 45 minutes for presentation preparation + 5 minutes presentation time
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify basic 2D shapes (squares, rectangles, triangles, circles)
Calculate perimeter and area of rectangles and squares using appropriate formulas
Apply mathematical concepts to solve real-world measurement problems
Communicate mathematical thinking clearly using proper terminology
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): Correct identification of shapes, accurate calculations of perimeter and area, proper use of measurement units
Real-World Application (25 points): Meaningful examples from daily life, clear connection between math concepts and practical situations, appropriate problem-solving approach
Visual Presentation (25 points): Clear, organized visual aids (poster, slides, or drawings), neat and readable displays, effective use of diagrams and labels
Communication Skills (25 points): Clear speaking voice, proper math vocabulary, logical organization of ideas, engagement with audience, stays within time limit
instructions: Create a 5-minute presentation about shapes and measurements that you encounter in everyday life. Your presentation must include: (1) At least 3 different 2D shapes found in your home, school, or community - identify each shape by name and explain its properties, (2) Two calculation examples showing how to find the perimeter of a rectangle or square with specific measurements, (3) Two calculation examples showing how to find the area of a rectangle or square with specific measurements, (4) Visual aids such as drawings, photos, or a poster to support your presentation. Use proper mathematical vocabulary including: perimeter, area, length, width, square units, and shape names. Practice your presentation beforehand and be prepared to answer one question from the audience. You may use a poster board, simple slides, or hand-drawn materials - no advanced technology required. Submit your visual aids to the teacher immediately after your presentation. Remember to speak clearly, make eye contact with your audience, and show your work for all calculations step-by-step.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - deduct points for calculation errors or misidentified shapes. Look for genuine real-world connections rather than forced examples. Visual aids should enhance understanding, not distract. For communication, focus on clarity and use of math vocabulary over presentation polish. Expect most students to score 20-23 points per criterion. Award full points (25) for exceptional work that exceeds basic requirements. Common issues: rushed calculations, mixing up perimeter/area formulas, unclear visual aids, not using proper units. Provide immediate feedback on mathematical errors and positive reinforcement for creative real-world applications.

title: Predictive Analytics Pipeline Lab Report: Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will develop and evaluate a complete machine learning pipeline to predict customer churn using real-world telecommunications data. The assessment requires data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and comprehensive performance analysis with business insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines for business problems
Apply advanced feature engineering techniques and handle missing data appropriately
Compare multiple algorithms and justify model selection using appropriate metrics
Interpret model results and provide actionable business recommendations
Communicate technical findings effectively through clear documentation and visualization
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and EDA (25 points): Thorough exploratory analysis with meaningful visualizations, proper handling of missing values and outliers, appropriate feature scaling/encoding, clear documentation of preprocessing decisions

Feature Engineering and Model Implementation (25 points): Creative and justified feature creation, implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper cross-validation setup, appropriate handling of class imbalance

Model Evaluation and Selection (25 points): Comprehensive evaluation using multiple metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), statistical significance testing, hyperparameter tuning with grid/random search, feature importance analysis, model interpretability techniques (SHAP/LIME)

Business Analysis and Communication (25 points): Clear executive summary, actionable business recommendations, cost-benefit analysis of churn prevention strategies, professional report formatting, reproducible code with proper documentation
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (telecom_churn.csv), develop a machine learning pipeline to predict customer churn. Your submission must include: (1) Jupyter notebook with complete analysis workflow, (2) Executive summary report (2-3 pages), (3) All code files and requirements.txt. Begin with comprehensive EDA including correlation analysis, distribution plots, and churn rate by customer segments. Implement data preprocessing pipeline handling missing values, categorical encoding, and feature scaling. Engineer at least 3 new features based on domain knowledge (e.g., tenure categories, usage ratios). Train and compare minimum 3 algorithms using stratified k-fold cross-validation. Perform hyperparameter tuning and evaluate using appropriate metrics for imbalanced classification. Analyze feature importance and model interpretability. Calculate business impact: if prevention campaign costs $50 per customer with 30% success rate, and average customer lifetime value is $1200, what's the optimal probability threshold? Provide specific recommendations for customer retention strategies. Code must be well-documented, reproducible, and follow PEP-8 standards. Include model persistence (pickle/joblib) and brief deployment considerations. Submit via GitHub repository link with clear README.md file.
grading_notes: Expect 15% A grades (90-100), 25% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 20% below 70. Common issues: inadequate EDA depth, improper cross-validation (data leakage), ignoring class imbalance, weak business analysis, poor code documentation. Award full credit only for comprehensive feature importance analysis and clear business impact calculations. Deduct 5 points for non-reproducible code, 10 points for missing executive summary. Look for creative feature engineering and thoughtful model selection justification. Bonus consideration for advanced techniques like ensemble methods or deep learning approaches with proper justification.

title: Advanced Multivariable Calculus and Real Analysis Comprehensive Quiz
description: This expert-level assessment evaluates students' mastery of advanced calculus concepts including multivariable optimization, vector field analysis, surface integrals, and convergence theory. Students will demonstrate rigorous mathematical reasoning, proof techniques, and applications of theoretical concepts to complex problems.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced optimization techniques including Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization in multiple dimensions
Analyze convergence and divergence of complex series and sequences using sophisticated tests
Evaluate surface integrals and apply divergence and Stokes' theorems to vector fields
Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using epsilon-delta definitions and advanced proof techniques
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Proof Construction (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of formal proof techniques, uses precise mathematical language, applies epsilon-delta definitions correctly, and constructs logically sound arguments with clear justification for each step

Problem-Solving Strategy and Method Selection (25 points): Selects appropriate techniques for complex problems, demonstrates understanding of when to apply specific theorems or methods, shows efficient problem-solving approaches, and adapts strategies when initial approaches prove inadequate

Computational Accuracy and Technical Execution (25 points): Performs complex calculations correctly including partial derivatives, multiple integrals, series computations, and vector operations; shows proper use of mathematical notation and maintains accuracy throughout multi-step solutions

Conceptual Understanding and Application (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of theoretical foundations, correctly interprets results in context, makes connections between different areas of analysis, and applies abstract concepts to concrete problems with appropriate justification
instructions: This assessment consists of 6 problems covering advanced topics in multivariable calculus and real analysis. You have 3 hours to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and provide complete justifications for your answers. Partial credit will be awarded based on the quality of your reasoning and methodology, even if final answers are incorrect. Problem 1 (15 points): Prove convergence or divergence of a given series using appropriate convergence tests. Problem 2 (20 points): Find and classify all critical points of a multivariable function, including analysis of the Hessian matrix. Problem 3 (15 points): Evaluate a surface integral over a parametrically defined surface. Problem 4 (20 points): Apply optimization techniques with constraints using Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world problem. Problem 5 (15 points): Verify and apply either the divergence theorem or Stokes' theorem to evaluate a vector field integral. Problem 6 (15 points): Construct an epsilon-delta proof for a limit involving multiple variables. Use proper mathematical notation throughout. Clearly state any theorems or definitions you invoke. If you make assumptions, state them explicitly. Submit your work on separate sheets with your name and problem numbers clearly marked. Late submissions will be penalized 10% per hour. Calculators are permitted for arithmetic verification only; symbolic computation tools are prohibited.
grading_notes: Evaluate proofs for logical completeness and mathematical rigor - partial credit should focus on correct reasoning rather than computational errors. Watch for common issues: incomplete justification in optimization problems, incorrect application of convergence tests, and imprecise use of theoretical results. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 25% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 20% D-level (60-69), 5% F-level (below 60). Award full credit for alternative valid solution methods. Deduct points for unjustified assertions and unclear mathematical exposition. Students struggling with proof construction may benefit from scaffolded feedback on logical structure.

title: Mathematical Proof Techniques and Applications Discussion Forum
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing different proof techniques, critiquing mathematical arguments, and collaboratively solving advanced problems involving real analysis, abstract algebra, or topology. This assessment evaluates students' ability to communicate complex mathematical concepts, construct rigorous arguments, and provide meaningful peer feedback.
learning_objectives_assessed: Construct and analyze rigorous mathematical proofs using various techniques (direct, contradiction, induction, contrapositive)
Communicate complex mathematical ideas clearly and precisely using appropriate notation and terminology
Evaluate and critique mathematical arguments for logical validity and completeness
Collaborate effectively to solve advanced mathematical problems and build upon others' mathematical reasoning
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of proof techniques, uses correct mathematical notation, presents logically sound arguments with appropriate level of detail and precision

Communication and Clarity (25 points): Explains mathematical concepts clearly, uses precise mathematical language, organizes ideas coherently, makes arguments accessible to peers while maintaining rigor

Critical Analysis and Peer Engagement (25 points): Provides substantive feedback on others' proofs, identifies gaps or errors constructively, asks meaningful questions, builds upon peers' ideas to advance mathematical understanding

Problem-Solving and Innovation (25 points): Demonstrates creative approaches to complex problems, makes connections between different mathematical concepts, proposes alternative methods or extensions, shows deep conceptual understanding
instructions: This discussion forum consists of three phases over two weeks. **Phase 1 (Days 1-4):** Choose one advanced problem from the provided set (covering real analysis, abstract algebra, or topology). Post your complete solution with detailed proof, explaining your reasoning at each step. Your initial post must be 500-800 words, include proper mathematical notation using LaTeX formatting, and clearly state all assumptions and definitions used. **Phase 2 (Days 5-10):** Review and respond to at least three peers' solutions. For each response: (1) Verify the mathematical accuracy of their proof, (2) Identify any gaps or suggest improvements, (3) Discuss alternative approaches or extensions, and (4) Ask clarifying questions that promote deeper understanding. Each response should be 200-300 words. **Phase 3 (Days 11-14):** Based on peer feedback, revise your original solution if necessary and post a reflection (300-400 words) discussing what you learned from the collaborative process, how peer feedback influenced your understanding, and connections you discovered between different mathematical concepts. All mathematical notation must use proper LaTeX syntax. Citations are required when referencing theorems or results not covered in class. Late submissions will be penalized 10% per day. Maintain respectful, professional discourse focused on mathematical content.
grading_notes: Grade initial posts primarily on mathematical correctness and proof structure - look for complete logical arguments with appropriate rigor for the course level. Common issues include: insufficient justification of steps, unclear notation, or missing edge cases. For peer responses, prioritize quality over quantity - substantive mathematical feedback should receive full credit even if slightly under word count. Watch for responses that merely summarize rather than analyze. Reflection posts should demonstrate genuine learning and mathematical growth. Grade distribution typically follows: 20% earn 90-100 points (exceptional mathematical insight and communication), 60% earn 75-89 points (solid mathematical work with minor gaps), 15% earn 60-74 points (adequate but lacking depth), 5% earn below 60 points (significant mathematical errors or insufficient engagement). Provide specific feedback on mathematical errors and suggest resources for improvement.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Architecture Design and Implementation Showcase
description: Students will design, implement, and present a comprehensive machine learning solution for a complex real-world problem, demonstrating mastery of advanced ML concepts, system architecture, and professional communication skills through a formal presentation to industry professionals and peers.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and architect scalable machine learning systems for complex, multi-faceted problems
Implement advanced ML algorithms and evaluate their performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Analyze and justify architectural decisions considering scalability, maintainability, and ethical implications
Communicate complex technical concepts effectively to diverse audiences including technical and non-technical stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Technical Implementation and Architecture (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of ML algorithms, implements robust and scalable system architecture, shows evidence of proper version control, testing, and documentation practices

title: Beginner Data Science Portfolio: Customer Shopping Analysis

Create effective data visualizations to communicate patterns and trends in data
Perform basic statistical analysis and interpret results in business context
Document and present data science work in a professional, reproducible format
rubric_criteria: Data Cleaning & Preprocessing (25 points): Properly identifies and handles missing values, duplicates, and data type issues. Documents all preprocessing steps with clear rationale. Dataset is analysis-ready.

Data Visualization & Exploration (25 points): Creates 4-6 appropriate visualizations that reveal meaningful patterns. Uses proper chart types, clear labels, and professional formatting. Includes both univariate and bivariate analysis.

Statistical Analysis & Insights (25 points): Calculates relevant descriptive statistics, identifies key trends and patterns, and draws valid conclusions. Connects findings to business context with actionable recommendations.

title: Statistical Analysis Lab Report: Population Growth Modeling

Interpret mathematical models in context and make data-driven predictions

Statistical Analysis (25 points): Calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients, analysis of residual plots, comparison of model fits using R-squared values, and identification of outliers or trends

Scientific Communication (25 points): Professional lab report format with abstract, methodology, results, and conclusions; clear graphs with proper labels and scales; logical flow of ideas; and evidence-based recommendations
instructions: Select a real population dataset (city, country, species, etc.) covering at least 10 time periods from reliable sources like census data, wildlife databases, or demographic studies. Create both exponential and logistic growth models using graphing technology or statistical software. Your lab report must include: (1) Abstract summarizing your findings in 100 words, (2) Data section with source citations and organized tables, (3) Methodology explaining your modeling approach and technology used, (4) Results section featuring fitted models, statistical measures, residual analysis, and professional graphs comparing actual vs. predicted values, (5) Discussion analyzing which model better fits your data, limitations of each approach, and factors affecting population growth, (6) Conclusion with specific predictions for future population values and confidence levels. title: Fundamentals of Arithmetic and Basic Problem Solving Exam
description: A comprehensive assessment covering essential arithmetic operations, word problems, basic geometry, and fundamental algebraic concepts. Students will demonstrate their understanding of whole numbers, fractions, decimals, measurement, and introductory equation solving through a mix of computational problems and real-world applications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform accurate calculations with whole numbers, fractions, and decimals using all four operations
Solve multi-step word problems involving money, time, and measurement
Calculate perimeter, area, and volume of basic geometric shapes
Solve simple one-variable linear equations and evaluate basic algebraic expressions
rubric_criteria: Arithmetic Operations (25 points): Demonstrates accuracy in addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of whole numbers, fractions, and decimals with proper computational methods and correct final answers

Word Problem Analysis (25 points): Shows clear problem-solving strategy, correctly identifies given information and what needs to be found, sets up appropriate equations or calculations, and provides reasonable answers with proper units

Geometric Calculations (25 points): Accurately applies formulas for perimeter, area, and volume, shows all work clearly, uses correct units in measurements, and demonstrates understanding of geometric properties

Basic Algebra (25 points): Correctly solves simple linear equations using appropriate algebraic steps, evaluates expressions by substituting values, and shows understanding of variables and algebraic notation
instructions: This exam consists of 40 questions divided into four sections. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Show all your work clearly, as partial credit will be awarded for correct methods even if the final answer is incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation and include units where appropriate. Section A (Questions 1-10): Arithmetic Operations - Solve computational problems involving whole numbers, fractions, and decimals. No calculator permitted for this section. Section B (Questions 11-20): Word Problems - Read each problem carefully, identify what information is given and what you need to find, show your problem-solving process, and write your final answer in a complete sentence. Section C (Questions 21-30): Geometry - Calculate perimeter, area, and volume using the provided formulas. Draw diagrams where helpful and label your measurements. Section D (Questions 31-40): Basic Algebra - Solve equations for the unknown variable and evaluate expressions. Show each algebraic step clearly. Write your final answers clearly in the designated spaces. If you need to change an answer, cross out the incorrect work neatly. Manage your time wisely, spending approximately 20-25 minutes per section. If you finish early, review your work and check your calculations. Submit your completed exam with your name and date clearly written on the first page.
grading_notes: Award full credit only when both method and answer are correct. Give partial credit (50-75%) for correct method with minor computational errors. Award 25% credit for appropriate problem setup with significant errors in execution. Common issues to watch: incorrect order of operations, failure to reduce fractions, missing units in measurement problems, and incomplete algebraic steps. Grade distribution expectation: 90-100% (A) for students showing mastery across all areas, 80-89% (B) for solid understanding with minor errors, 70-79% (C) for basic competency with some conceptual gaps, below 70% indicates need for additional support. Pay special attention to work shown - students who arrive at correct answers without showing work should receive reduced credit. Look for evidence of mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies rather than just computational accuracy.

title: Database Design Trade-offs: Relational vs. NoSQL Implementation Discussion
description: Students will analyze and discuss the architectural trade-offs between relational and NoSQL database systems through a structured forum discussion, evaluating real-world scenarios and defending design decisions with technical justification.
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different database paradigms
Apply systems thinking to analyze trade-offs in software architecture decisions
Communicate technical concepts clearly and defend design choices with evidence
Critically analyze peer solutions and provide constructive technical feedback
rubric_criteria: Initial Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates thorough understanding of both database paradigms, correctly identifies 3+ specific trade-offs (performance, consistency, scalability, complexity), provides concrete examples with technical details

Scenario Application (25 points): Correctly applies database concepts to given scenarios, justifies recommendations with specific technical reasoning, addresses data modeling implications and system requirements

Peer Engagement (25 points): Responds meaningfully to 2+ classmates with substantive technical questions or alternative perspectives, builds upon others' ideas constructively, demonstrates active listening through referenced responses

Technical Communication (25 points): Uses precise technical terminology correctly, explanations are clear and logical, writing is professional and well-organized, includes relevant code snippets or diagrams where appropriate
instructions: You will participate in a week-long structured discussion analyzing database design decisions. **Initial Post (due Wednesday):** Choose one scenario from the provided list (e-commerce platform, real-time chat application, or analytics dashboard). Write a 400-500 word analysis comparing how you would implement the data layer using: 1) A relational database (MySQL/PostgreSQL), and 2) A NoSQL solution (MongoDB/Cassandra/Redis). Address specific trade-offs including: data consistency requirements, scalability needs, query complexity, development speed, and operational overhead. Include a simple data model sketch for each approach. **Peer Responses (due Friday):** Respond to at least two classmates' posts with 150-200 word replies. Ask probing questions, suggest alternative approaches, or challenge assumptions with technical reasoning. Focus on aspects they may have overlooked. **Final Reflection (due Sunday):** Post a 200-word reflection on insights gained from peer discussions. Did any responses change your perspective? What new considerations emerged? **Submission Format:** Use discussion forum with clear subject lines. Include code snippets in markdown format. Cite any external sources. Late posts receive 10% deduction per day. All responses must demonstrate original thinking - no generic agreement posts.
grading_notes: Look for depth over breadth - students should demonstrate genuine understanding rather than surface-level comparisons. Strong responses will mention specific database features (ACID properties, eventual consistency, partitioning strategies). Watch for common misconceptions: assuming NoSQL always scales better, or that relational databases can't handle large datasets. Excellent posts will discuss CAP theorem implications or mention specific tools/frameworks. For peer engagement, quality matters more than quantity - meaningful technical dialogue should be rewarded over multiple shallow responses. Deduct points for factual errors about database capabilities. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level work (comprehensive analysis with nuanced understanding), 60% B-level (solid understanding with minor gaps), 20% C-level (basic understanding but missing key concepts), 5% below C-level.

title: Customer Churn Analysis and Prediction Quiz

learning_objectives_assessed: Apply exploratory data analysis techniques to identify patterns and insights in customer datasets

Section 4: Interpret your best-performing model results, identify the top 5 factors contributing to churn, and provide three specific business recommendations for reducing customer churn. Peer Responses (25 points): Provides meaningful responses to at least two classmates, asks thoughtful questions, builds on others' ideas, demonstrates active listening and respectful dialogue (150+ words each)

Provide a real-world example. (2) Research and describe two specific data science career paths that interest you (e.g., data analyst, machine learning engineer, data scientist, business intelligence analyst). Compare their typical responsibilities, required skills, educational requirements, and salary ranges. Explain which path aligns better with your current interests and skills, and identify areas where you need development. Your initial post should be 300-400 words total. Your responses should be substantive (150+ words each) and can include asking clarifying questions, sharing additional resources, offering different perspectives, or relating their experiences to your own career goals. Peer responses should go beyond simple agreement; award full points only for responses that advance the conversation meaningfully. Deduct points for posts submitted late (5 points per day) or those that don't meet minimum word counts. Expect grade distribution of 20% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 15% C-level (70-79), and 5% below C-level. title: Real-World Linear Functions: Mathematical Modeling Presentation
