Mathematical Communication (25 points): Explains reasoning clearly in word problems and uses appropriate mathematical vocabulary. Full credit: Clear, complete explanations, Partial credit: Mostly clear with minor gaps, Minimal credit: Partial explanations, No credit: Unclear or missing explanations
instructions:
This quiz consists of 20 questions divided into four sections. You have 45 minutes to complete all sections. Read each question carefully before answering.

Section A (Questions 1-8): Basic arithmetic problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Calculate each problem and write your answer in the space provided. Show your work for full credit.

Section B (Questions 9-14): Word problems involving money, time, and measurement. Read each problem carefully, identify what operation(s) you need to use, and solve step-by-step. Write your final answer with appropriate units (dollars, minutes, inches, etc.).

Section C (Questions 15-18): Multi-step problems that require more than one operation. Break down each problem into smaller steps, show all your work, and clearly indicate your final answer.

Section D (Questions 19-20): Explanation problems where you must not only solve the problem but also explain your thinking in 2-3 complete sentences.

Requirements: Use pencil only, show all work in the space provided, circle or box your final answers, include proper units where applicable, and write explanations in complete sentences. If you need extra space, use the back of the page and clearly indicate which problem you're continuing. No calculators permitted. Check your work before submitting.
grading_notes: Grade each section separately using the rubric criteria. Pay special attention to students who get correct answers but show no work - deduct points from 'Work Shown' criterion. Common issues include: forgetting units in measurement problems, arithmetic errors in multi-step problems, and incomplete explanations in Section D. Expect grade distribution: 15% A's (90-100), 35% B's (80-89), 35% C's (70-79), 15% D's or below (60-69). Provide specific feedback on calculation errors and problem-solving approaches. Students scoring below 70% should receive additional practice recommendations.

title: Library Management System Design and Implementation
description: Students will design and implement a console-based library management system using object-oriented programming principles. The system must handle book inventory, user management, and checkout/return operations with data persistence and error handling.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply object-oriented programming concepts including inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism
Implement data structures and algorithms for efficient data management
Design and implement file I/O operations for data persistence
Demonstrate proper error handling and input validation techniques
Create clean, documented, and maintainable code following best practices
rubric_criteria: System Design & Architecture (25 points): Proper use of OOP principles, class hierarchy design, appropriate data structures, UML class diagram accuracy and completeness
Core Functionality Implementation (25 points): All required features working correctly (add/remove books, user registration, checkout/return, search functionality), proper algorithm implementation
Code Quality & Documentation (25 points): Clean, readable code with consistent formatting, comprehensive comments and documentation, meaningful variable/method names, adherence to coding standards
Error Handling & Testing (25 points): Robust input validation, appropriate exception handling, comprehensive test cases with documented results, edge case consideration
instructions: Develop a console-based Library Management System in Java, Python, or C++. Your system must include: (1) Book class with ISBN, title, author, availability status; (2) User class supporting both Student and Faculty user types with different borrowing privileges; (3) Library class managing inventory and operations. Required functionality: add/remove books, register users, checkout/return books with due date tracking, search books by title/author/ISBN, display overdue books, and generate simple reports. Implement file-based data persistence to save/load all data between sessions. Create a UML class diagram showing relationships between classes. Provide a test plan document with at least 10 test cases covering normal operations and edge cases. Submit source code files, UML diagram (PDF), test plan document, and a brief user manual explaining how to run and use your system. Code must compile and run without errors. Include sample data files demonstrating your system's capabilities.
grading_notes: Evaluate UML diagrams for proper notation and logical class relationships. Test all core functionality personally - deduct points for any non-working features. Look for proper inheritance usage (Student/Faculty extending User class) and encapsulation (private fields with public methods). Code should handle invalid inputs gracefully without crashing. Common issues: inadequate file I/O error handling, missing input validation, poor class design with everything in main method, hardcoded values instead of user input. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades, 25% B grades, 40% C grades, 20% D/F grades. Provide specific feedback on code structure and suggest improvements for future projects.

title: Comprehensive Machine Learning Pipeline Implementation and Analysis Exam
description: Students will design, implement, and evaluate a complete machine learning solution for a real-world predictive analytics problem, demonstrating mastery of data preprocessing, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and statistical interpretation of results.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing and feature engineering
Apply advanced model selection techniques and hyperparameter optimization strategies
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and statistical tests
Interpret and communicate results with proper statistical reasoning and business context
Implement cross-validation and handle data leakage prevention in complex scenarios
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering (25 points): Proper handling of missing values, outliers, categorical encoding, feature scaling, and creation of meaningful derived features with clear justification

Model Implementation and Optimization (25 points): Correct implementation of multiple algorithms, systematic hyperparameter tuning using grid search or Bayesian optimization, and proper use of pipeline structures

Model Evaluation and Validation (25 points): Appropriate train/validation/test splits, correct application of cross-validation, use of relevant metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), statistical significance testing, and bias-variance analysis

Code Quality and Documentation (25 points): Clean, efficient, well-documented code following best practices, proper version control usage, reproducible results with random seeds, and comprehensive markdown explanations
instructions:
You are provided with a customer churn dataset from a telecommunications company containing 50,000 records with demographic, service usage, and billing features. Your task is to build a production-ready machine learning pipeline that predicts customer churn probability.

Deliverables:
1. Jupyter notebook with complete analysis including EDA, preprocessing pipeline, model comparison (minimum 3 algorithms), hyperparameter optimization, and final model evaluation
2. Python script (.py file) containing clean, modular functions for the final pipeline
3. Written report (1000 words) discussing methodology, results interpretation, business implications, and limitations
4. Requirements.txt file with all dependencies

Specific Requirements:
- Handle class imbalance appropriately
- Implement proper cross-validation strategy
- Compare at least 3 different algorithm families (e.g., tree-based, linear, ensemble)
- Perform feature importance analysis
- Include calibration analysis for probability predictions
- Address potential data leakage issues
- Provide confidence intervals for performance metrics
- Create at least 2 meaningful visualizations of results

Submission: Upload all files in a ZIP archive named 'LastName_FirstName_MLExam.zip' to the course portal. Ensure all code runs successfully with provided requirements.txt. Late submissions lose 10 points per hour.
grading_notes: Grade holistically within each criterion. Excellence (23-25 pts) requires going beyond basic requirements with innovative approaches or deeper insights. Proficiency (20-22 pts) meets all requirements correctly. Developing (15-19 pts) has minor errors or missing elements. Inadequate (<15 pts) has major flaws or missing components. Common issues to watch: data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data, overfitting due to improper validation, lack of statistical interpretation of results. Expect grade distribution: 10% A+ (95-100), 20% A (90-94), 30% B+ (85-89), 25% B (80-84), 15% below 80. Provide specific feedback on code efficiency, statistical reasoning quality, and business insight depth.

title: Mathematical Proof Techniques and Applications in Abstract Algebra
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing various proof techniques through complex problems in group theory and ring theory, demonstrating mastery of advanced mathematical reasoning and communication skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Construct and critique rigorous mathematical proofs using multiple techniques (direct, contradiction, induction, contrapositive)
Analyze complex algebraic structures and identify appropriate proof strategies
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly and respond constructively to peer arguments
Synthesize connections between different areas of abstract algebra through proof analysis
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates flawless logical reasoning, correct application of theorems, precise mathematical language, and error-free calculations in all posts and responses
Proof Strategy and Innovation (25 points): Selects optimal proof techniques, presents creative alternative approaches, shows deep understanding of when and why specific methods are most effective

Peer Engagement and Critique (25 points): Provides substantive, constructive feedback on others' proofs, asks insightful questions, identifies logical gaps or errors diplomatically, builds meaningfully on peer contributions

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise notation and terminology, explains complex concepts clearly, structures arguments logically, makes ideas accessible while maintaining mathematical sophistication
instructions:
This assessment occurs over five days in your course discussion forum. You will analyze three challenging problems in abstract algebra, each requiring different proof techniques.

DAY 1-2: Initial Analysis (40 points total)
Post your complete solutions to Problems A (group homomorphism properties), B (ideal generation in polynomial rings), and C (finite field characteristics). Each solution must include: (1) clear problem restatement, (2) identification of your chosen proof technique with justification, (3) complete formal proof with all steps explained, (4) reflection on alternative approaches considered.

DAY 3-4: Peer Review and Discussion (35 points total)
Respond substantively to at least three classmates' solutions. Focus on: proof validity, clarity of exposition, efficiency of chosen methods, and potential improvements. If you identify errors, explain them constructively and suggest corrections. Propose alternative proof approaches where applicable.

DAY 5: Synthesis and Reflection (25 points total)
Create a final post synthesizing the discussion. Compare different proof techniques used across all problems, identify patterns in when certain methods are most effective, and reflect on insights gained from peer feedback. Include one revised proof incorporating improvements suggested by classmates.

Formatting Requirements: Use LaTeX notation for all mathematical expressions. Posts must be 300-500 words each. Cite any external sources beyond course materials. Maintain professional, collaborative tone throughout.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for mathematical correctness first, then assess proof elegance and explanation quality. Look for students who go beyond minimum requirements by exploring multiple approaches. In peer interactions, reward those who provide specific, actionable feedback rather than generic praise. Watch for students who struggle with formal proof structure versus those with communication issues. Deduct points for late submissions (10% per day) but allow resubmission of mathematically incorrect proofs once within 48 hours. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Students scoring below 70 typically have fundamental proof construction issues requiring individual consultation.

title: Mathematical Modeling Lab Report: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Calculus and Differential Equations
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive mathematical analysis of traffic flow optimization at a multi-intersection urban network, applying calculus, differential equations, and optimization theory to develop and validate a mathematical model. The lab report must include theoretical development, computational implementation, data analysis, and practical recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve complex real-world problems
Formulate and solve systems of differential equations modeling dynamic systems
Implement computational methods for numerical analysis and data visualization
Communicate mathematical findings through rigorous written analysis and interpretation
Evaluate the validity and limitations of mathematical models in practical applications
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Formulation and Theory (25 points): Correct derivation of traffic flow differential equations, proper application of optimization constraints, accurate use of calculus concepts including partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers, clear mathematical notation and logical progression

Computational Implementation and Analysis (25 points): Successful numerical solution of differential equations using appropriate methods (Euler's method, Runge-Kutta), accurate optimization calculations, proper use of mathematical software, clear data visualization with appropriate graphs and charts

Data Interpretation and Model Validation (25 points): Thorough analysis of results including sensitivity analysis, comparison with real traffic data, identification of model limitations, discussion of parameter effects, assessment of model accuracy and practical feasibility

Professional Communication and Documentation (25 points): Clear executive summary, well-organized methodology section, proper mathematical formatting, appropriate use of technical vocabulary, complete bibliography, adherence to scientific writing standards, actionable recommendations for city planners
instructions: Your task is to develop a comprehensive mathematical model for optimizing traffic light timing at a 4-intersection urban network to minimize average vehicle wait time. Your lab report must include: (1) Executive Summary (1 page): Non-technical overview of your approach, key findings, and recommendations. (2) Mathematical Model Development (2-3 pages): Derive differential equations governing traffic flow using conservation principles, formulate the optimization problem with appropriate constraints, and establish boundary conditions. Include all mathematical derivations with clear explanations. (3) Computational Implementation (2-3 pages): Implement numerical solutions using software of your choice (MATLAB, Python, Mathematica, etc.). Include code snippets, parameter values, and convergence analysis. Create visualizations showing traffic density over time and optimal timing sequences. (4) Results and Analysis (2-3 pages): Present your optimal traffic light timing solution, conduct sensitivity analysis varying traffic volume parameters by ±20%, compare your model predictions with provided real traffic data, and discuss discrepancies and model limitations. (5) Conclusions and Recommendations (1 page): Summarize key findings, propose practical implementation strategies for city traffic engineers, and suggest model improvements. Submit as a single PDF with all code and datasets included as appendices. Use proper mathematical notation, cite at least 5 peer-reviewed sources, and include figure captions and numbered equations. Due date allows for one round of instructor feedback before final submission.
grading_notes: Look for mathematical rigor in derivations - students often skip steps in optimization constraint formulation. Pay attention to boundary condition justification and units consistency throughout. Common computational errors include improper discretization step sizes and failure to check solution convergence. Strong submissions will include discussion of multiple solution methods and their trade-offs. Watch for oversimplified assumptions without acknowledgment of limitations. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Deduct 5 points for late submission within 24 hours, 10 points thereafter. Partial credit available for each rubric section - mathematical formulation errors should receive 50% credit if approach is sound but execution flawed.

title: Software Architecture Trade-offs in Large-Scale Systems
description: Students analyze and debate critical architectural decisions in distributed systems by examining real-world case studies, evaluating trade-offs between different design patterns, and defending their recommendations for scalability, reliability, and performance optimization.
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate architectural patterns and their trade-offs in distributed systems design
Analyze scalability, consistency, and availability challenges using CAP theorem principles
Synthesize technical arguments and defend architectural decisions with evidence
Apply systems thinking to complex software engineering problems
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of architectural patterns, correctly identifies system constraints, and accurately applies distributed systems principles (CAP theorem, consistency models, fault tolerance)

Critical Evaluation (25 points): Provides comprehensive analysis of trade-offs, considers multiple perspectives, weighs costs and benefits effectively, and identifies potential failure modes and mitigation strategies

Evidence-Based Arguments (25 points): Supports claims with concrete examples, references industry best practices, cites relevant research or case studies, and uses quantitative reasoning where appropriate
Discussion Participation (25 points): Actively engages with peers' arguments, asks insightful questions, builds upon others' ideas constructively, and facilitates productive technical discourse
instructions: You will participate in a structured discussion analyzing architectural decisions for three case studies: Netflix's microservices migration, Discord's database scaling challenges, and Uber's real-time dispatch system. Prior to the discussion session, prepare by: (1) Reading the provided case study materials and supplementary articles on distributed systems patterns; (2) Preparing a 3-minute position statement for each case study that identifies the core architectural challenge, evaluates 2-3 alternative solutions, and recommends an approach with clear justification; (3) Developing 2-3 probing questions for each case study to challenge peers' assumptions. During the 90-minute discussion session, you'll present your position statements, engage in moderated debates about optimal solutions, and participate in cross-case analysis to identify common patterns and anti-patterns. Come prepared to discuss specific technologies (databases, message queues, load balancers), quantitative metrics (latency, throughput, consistency guarantees), and real-world constraints (team size, budget, timeline). Submit your preparation notes and post-discussion reflection (500 words) analyzing how the discussion changed or reinforced your initial positions within 24 hours of the session.
grading_notes: Look for students who move beyond surface-level observations to demonstrate systems thinking and principled reasoning. Strong responses will reference specific technical concepts (eventual consistency, circuit breakers, data partitioning) rather than generic statements. Watch for students who can articulate nuanced trade-offs rather than claiming one solution is universally superior. Deduct points for factually incorrect statements about distributed systems principles. Participation should be evaluated on quality over quantity - thoughtful questions and building on others' ideas should score higher than frequent but shallow contributions. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-range (90-100), 50% B-range (80-89), 25% C-range (70-79), 5% below 70. Students struggling typically lack preparation or make fundamental conceptual errors about distributed systems.

title: Database Design and Implementation Lab Report
description: Students will design, implement, and analyze a relational database system for a small business scenario, documenting their process, challenges, and optimization decisions in a comprehensive lab report.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design normalized relational database schemas using entity-relationship modeling
Implement databases using SQL DDL and DML statements
Analyze query performance and apply basic optimization techniques
Document technical processes and justify design decisions
rubric_criteria: Database Design (25 points): ER diagram completeness, normalization to 3NF, appropriate relationships and constraints, clear entity/attribute identification
SQL Implementation (25 points): Correct table creation with proper data types, constraints, and indexes; functional sample queries; error-free syntax
Performance Analysis (25 points): Query execution plan analysis, identification of bottlenecks, appropriate optimization strategies, before/after performance metrics
Documentation Quality (25 points): Clear problem statement, logical flow, proper technical terminology, code commenting, professional formatting, conclusion with lessons learned
instructions: You will create a database system for 'TechBooks Online' - a small bookstore that sells technical books online. title: Mathematical Modeling and Optimization of Urban Transportation Networks

grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical rigor by checking derivations step-by-step and verifying computational accuracy. title: Ethical Considerations in Machine Learning Model Deployment
description: Students will participate in a structured discussion analyzing real-world ethical dilemmas in machine learning deployment, demonstrating understanding of bias, fairness, privacy, and stakeholder impact considerations through case study analysis and peer engagement.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and analyze ethical issues in data science projects including algorithmic bias, privacy violations, and fairness concerns
Evaluate the societal impact of machine learning models on different stakeholder groups
Propose mitigation strategies for ethical challenges in model deployment
Communicate complex ethical considerations clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences
rubric_criteria: Case Analysis Depth (25 points): Demonstrates thorough understanding of ethical issues, identifies multiple stakeholders, analyzes root causes of problems, and shows awareness of broader societal implications
Critical Thinking & Evidence (25 points): Uses relevant examples, cites credible sources, makes logical connections between concepts, challenges assumptions, and considers multiple perspectives
Solution Quality (25 points): Proposes practical and feasible mitigation strategies, addresses implementation challenges, considers trade-offs, and demonstrates understanding of technical constraints
Discussion Engagement (25 points): Makes substantive contributions to peer discussions, asks thoughtful questions, builds on others' ideas constructively, and facilitates productive dialogue
instructions:
You will analyze one of three provided case studies involving ethical challenges in ML deployment: (1) facial recognition in hiring, (2) predictive policing algorithms, or (3) healthcare diagnostic AI. Prepare a 500-word initial analysis addressing: What ethical issues are present? Who are the affected stakeholders and how? What are the potential harms and benefits? What mitigation strategies would you recommend?

Post your analysis to the discussion forum by the deadline. Then, engage with at least three peers' posts by asking clarifying questions, offering alternative perspectives, or building on their proposed solutions. Your responses should be substantive (100-150 words each) and demonstrate critical thinking.

Include at least two credible sources (academic papers, industry reports, or reputable news articles) to support your analysis. Use APA format for citations. Consider technical feasibility, cost implications, and regulatory requirements in your recommendations.

Evaluation focuses on depth of ethical reasoning, quality of proposed solutions, use of evidence, and constructive peer engagement. Avoid superficial responses or simply agreeing/disagreeing without justification.
grading_notes: Look for students who move beyond obvious ethical concerns to identify subtle biases and systemic issues. High-scoring responses should demonstrate understanding of both technical and social dimensions. Common issues include: oversimplified solutions ignoring implementation complexity, failure to consider multiple stakeholder perspectives, weak peer engagement that doesn't advance discussion. Grade distribution should roughly follow: 20% excellent (90-100), 50% proficient (75-89), 25% developing (60-74), 5% inadequate (below 60). Provide specific feedback on reasoning quality and suggest resources for improvement.

title: Advanced Software Engineering Portfolio: Full-Stack Application with Microservices Architecture
description: Students design, implement, and deploy a complete full-stack application using microservices architecture, demonstrating advanced software engineering principles, system design skills, and professional development practices. The portfolio includes system architecture documentation, source code, deployment configurations, testing suites, and reflective analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement scalable microservices architectures with appropriate technology stacks
Apply advanced software engineering principles including SOLID principles, design patterns, and clean architecture
Demonstrate proficiency in DevOps practices including CI/CD, containerization, and cloud deployment
Implement comprehensive testing strategies including unit, integration, and end-to-end testing
Evaluate system performance, security, and scalability through monitoring and analysis
Communicate complex technical decisions and trade-offs through professional documentation
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of microservices patterns, appropriate service decomposition, well-designed APIs, database design with proper normalization, and clear architectural diagrams with justified technology choices

Code Quality & Implementation (25 points): Exhibits expert-level programming with clean, maintainable code following SOLID principles, appropriate design patterns, comprehensive error handling, security best practices, and proper version control with meaningful commit history

Testing & DevOps (25 points): Implements robust testing pyramid with >80% code coverage, automated CI/CD pipeline, containerized deployment, infrastructure as code, monitoring/logging, and documented deployment procedures

Documentation & Professional Presentation (25 points): Provides comprehensive technical documentation including API specifications, architecture decisions, setup instructions, performance analysis, and reflective essay demonstrating critical thinking about design trade-offs
instructions: Create a portfolio showcasing a complete full-stack application built with microservices architecture. Your application must solve a real-world problem and demonstrate advanced software engineering practices. Portfolio components: 1) System Architecture Document (15-20 pages) including problem statement, requirements analysis, service decomposition rationale, technology stack justification, database schema design, API specifications, security considerations, and scalability analysis. 2) Source Code Repository with minimum 3 microservices, frontend application, database migrations, Docker configurations, CI/CD pipeline configurations, comprehensive test suites, and infrastructure as code. 3) Deployment Package including live deployed application, monitoring dashboard access, performance benchmarks, and deployment documentation. 4) Technical Reflection Essay (2000-2500 words) analyzing design decisions, challenges encountered, lessons learned, performance optimization strategies, and future enhancement recommendations. Submit via Git repository with README containing live application URLs, demo credentials, and portfolio navigation guide. Code must be original with any third-party libraries properly attributed. Application should handle realistic data volumes and demonstrate professional-grade error handling and user experience.
grading_notes: Evaluate portfolios holistically, looking for evidence of expert-level thinking rather than just technical completion. Grade distribution should reflect: 90-100% for portfolios demonstrating innovation, exceptional code quality, and deep architectural understanding; 80-89% for solid implementations meeting all requirements with good practices; 70-79% for functional applications with some architectural or implementation weaknesses; below 70% for incomplete or poorly executed work. Common issues to assess: over-engineering vs. appropriate complexity, security vulnerabilities, inadequate error handling, poor API design, insufficient testing coverage, unclear documentation, and unrealistic performance claims. Verify all applications are actually deployed and functional. Look for evidence of iterative development and problem-solving in commit history. Exceptional portfolios may demonstrate advanced patterns like event sourcing, CQRS, or sophisticated monitoring/observability implementations.

title: Algebraic Functions and Real-World Modeling Quiz
description: Students will demonstrate proficiency in working with quadratic and linear functions, including graphing, solving systems of equations, and applying these concepts to real-world scenarios involving optimization and break-even analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Solve quadratic equations using multiple methods (factoring, quadratic formula, completing the square)
Graph quadratic and linear functions and identify key features (vertex, intercepts, domain, range)
Solve systems of linear equations algebraically and graphically
Apply function concepts to model and solve real-world optimization problems
Interpret mathematical results in context and communicate solutions clearly
rubric_criteria: Algebraic Manipulation and Equation Solving (25 points): Correctly applies appropriate methods to solve quadratic equations and systems. Shows all work with proper algebraic steps. Minor computational errors acceptable if method is correct.

Graphing and Function Analysis (25 points): Accurately graphs functions, correctly identifies and labels key features (vertex, intercepts, axis of symmetry). Demonstrates understanding of function behavior and transformations.

Real-World Problem Solving (25 points): Successfully translates word problems into mathematical models, sets up appropriate equations/functions, and solves systematically. Shows clear understanding of the problem context.

Mathematical Communication and Reasoning (25 points): Provides clear explanations of solution processes, interprets answers in context, shows logical reasoning throughout. Work is organized and easy to follow with appropriate mathematical notation.
instructions:
This quiz consists of 8 problems covering quadratic functions, linear systems, and real-world applications. You have 75 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly - partial credit will be awarded based on your problem-solving process even if final answers are incorrect.

Section A (Problems 1-3): Solve the given quadratic equations using the specified method for each problem. Graph the corresponding quadratic function and identify the vertex, x-intercepts, y-intercept, and axis of symmetry.

Section B (Problems 4-5): Solve the systems of linear equations both algebraically and graphically. Verify your solutions and classify each system as consistent independent, consistent dependent, or inconsistent.

Section C (Problems 6-8): Real-world application problems involving a business profit optimization scenario, a projectile motion problem, and a break-even analysis. For each problem: (a) Define variables clearly, (b) Set up the appropriate mathematical model, (c) Solve the problem completely, (d) Interpret your answer in the context of the original situation, (e) State any assumptions or limitations of your model.

Submission Requirements: Submit your work on the provided answer sheets. Use pencil for graphs and pen for calculations. Circle or box final answers. If you need additional space, use the back of sheets and clearly indicate continuation. Calculators are permitted for arithmetic but show algebraic steps. No collaboration allowed - this is an individual assessment.
grading_notes: Grade holistically within each rubric criterion rather than point-by-point. Award full points (23-25) for mastery with minor errors, good points (18-22) for solid understanding with some mistakes, developing points (13-17) for partial understanding with significant gaps, and beginning points (0-12) for minimal understanding. Common issues to watch: sign errors in algebraic manipulation, incorrect vertex form conversions, failure to check solutions in original equations, unrealistic interpretations in word problems, and incomplete labeling of graphs. Expect grade distribution of approximately 15% A's, 35% B's, 35% C's, 15% D/F. Provide specific feedback on error patterns and suggest remediation strategies for students scoring below 70%.

title: Distributed Chat Application with Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design and implement a real-time distributed chat application using microservices architecture, including user authentication, message persistence, real-time communication, and containerized deployment with comprehensive documentation and testing.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems using microservices architecture patterns
Implement real-time communication protocols and message queuing systems
Apply containerization and orchestration technologies for scalable deployment
Demonstrate proficiency in database design, API development, and system integration
Conduct comprehensive testing including unit, integration, and load testing
Document system architecture and provide deployment instructions for production environments
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Microservices decomposition, API design, database schema, message queue implementation, scalability considerations, and architectural documentation with clear service boundaries and communication patterns

Implementation Quality (25 points): Code organization, design patterns usage, error handling, security implementation (authentication/authorization), real-time messaging functionality, data persistence, and adherence to coding standards with proper version control practices

Testing & Quality Assurance (25 points): Comprehensive unit tests (>80% coverage), integration tests for service communication, load testing results, API testing, error scenario handling, and automated testing pipeline setup

Deployment & Documentation (25 points): Docker containerization, orchestration setup (Kubernetes/Docker Compose), deployment automation, comprehensive README with setup instructions, API documentation, architecture diagrams, and production deployment guide
instructions: Develop a distributed chat application supporting multiple chat rooms with real-time messaging. Your system must include: (1) User Service - handle registration, authentication, and user profiles using JWT tokens; (2) Chat Service - manage chat rooms, message routing, and real-time communication via WebSockets; (3) Message Service - persist messages with MongoDB/PostgreSQL and handle message history; (4) Notification Service - send push notifications and email alerts; (5) API Gateway - route requests and handle load balancing. Technical requirements: Use at least 3 different programming languages/frameworks (e.g., Node.js for real-time, Python for ML-based features, Go for high-performance services). Implement Redis for caching and message queuing. Include rate limiting, input validation, and SQL injection prevention. Support minimum 100 concurrent users with <200ms message latency. Deliverables: Complete source code in Git repository with proper branching strategy, Docker files for all services, Kubernetes/Docker Compose deployment configuration, comprehensive test suite with CI/CD pipeline, detailed documentation including API specs, architecture diagrams, and setup instructions. Submit via Git repository link with live deployment URL and demonstration video (10-15 minutes) showcasing key features, load testing results, and system monitoring dashboard.
grading_notes: Evaluate based on system complexity and real-world applicability. Look for proper microservices patterns (not just multiple repositories), actual distributed communication, and production-ready deployment. Common issues: monolithic code split into multiple services without true microservices benefits, missing error handling between services, inadequate testing of distributed scenarios, poor documentation of service dependencies. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (exceptional architecture with advanced features like service mesh, comprehensive monitoring), 35% B-level (solid implementation meeting all requirements), 40% C-level (functional system with minor architectural issues), 10% below C (missing core requirements or non-functional deployment). Deduct points for: non-working deployment (-10), missing tests (-15), poor documentation (-10), security vulnerabilities (-15). Bonus points available for: advanced monitoring/logging (+5), ML-powered features (+5), mobile client (+10).

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Design and Implementation Exam
description: Comprehensive practical examination requiring students to design, implement, and evaluate a complete machine learning pipeline for a complex real-world dataset, including advanced feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and production deployment considerations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing and feature engineering techniques
Apply advanced model selection strategies including ensemble methods and hyperparameter optimization
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and statistical validation techniques
Demonstrate understanding of production deployment considerations including model monitoring and scalability
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive handling of missing values, outliers, categorical encoding, feature scaling, dimensionality reduction, and creation of meaningful derived features with proper justification

Model Development and Selection (25 points): Implementation of multiple algorithms, proper train/validation/test splits, cross-validation, ensemble methods, and systematic hyperparameter optimization with documented rationale

Model Evaluation and Validation (25 points): Use of appropriate evaluation metrics, statistical significance testing, bias-variance analysis, learning curves, and interpretation of results with business context

Production Readiness and Documentation (25 points): Code quality, reproducibility, scalability considerations, model monitoring strategies, comprehensive documentation, and clear presentation of findings
instructions: You are provided with a complex multi-modal dataset containing customer transaction data, demographic information, and behavioral metrics for an e-commerce platform. Your task is to build a complete machine learning pipeline to predict customer lifetime value (CLV) over the next 12 months. Your submission must include: 1) A Jupyter notebook with complete, well-documented code implementing your entire pipeline from data exploration through model deployment preparation. 2) A technical report (maximum 2000 words) documenting your methodology, key findings, model selection rationale, and production deployment recommendations. 3) A Python script containing your final production-ready model with proper error handling and logging. Your solution must handle the inherent challenges in this dataset including missing values, class imbalance, temporal dependencies, and mixed data types. Implement at least three different modeling approaches and compare their performance using appropriate cross-validation techniques. Include feature importance analysis and model interpretability components. Address scalability concerns for deployment on datasets 100x larger. Submit all files in a compressed folder named 'LastName_FirstName_MLPipeline.zip' with clear file organization and a README file explaining the structure.
grading_notes: Evaluate code functionality by running notebooks end-to-end - deduct points for execution errors. Look for sophisticated feature engineering beyond basic preprocessing (polynomial features, interaction terms, domain-specific metrics). Assess model selection rigor - students should demonstrate understanding of when to use different algorithms. Strong submissions will include ensemble methods and proper hyperparameter optimization. For evaluation criteria, expect multiple metrics appropriate for regression (MAE, RMSE, R²) and business metrics. Production readiness assessment should include error handling, input validation, and monitoring considerations. Grade distribution expectation: A-level (90-100): Complete pipeline with advanced techniques and excellent documentation; B-level (80-89): Solid implementation with minor gaps in methodology or documentation; C-level (70-79): Basic requirements met but limited sophistication in approach. Common issues: inadequate validation strategies, poor feature engineering justification, missing business context interpretation.

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Portfolio: Predicting Customer Churn with Business Impact Analysis
description: Students will develop a comprehensive data science portfolio project that demonstrates the complete machine learning lifecycle, from business problem formulation through model deployment and impact measurement. The portfolio must include data exploration, feature engineering, multiple modeling approaches, model interpretation, and a business presentation with actionable recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply the complete data science methodology to solve a real-world business problem
Demonstrate proficiency in data preprocessing, feature engineering, and exploratory data analysis
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms with proper validation techniques
Interpret model results and translate technical findings into business insights
Communicate data science findings effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders
Apply ethical considerations and bias detection in machine learning workflows
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis & Feature Engineering (25 points): Thorough exploratory data analysis with meaningful visualizations, appropriate handling of missing data and outliers, creative and justified feature engineering, proper data preprocessing pipeline

Model Development & Validation (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms, proper cross-validation methodology, hyperparameter tuning, appropriate evaluation metrics for business context, model comparison with statistical significance testing

Model Interpretation & Ethics (25 points): Feature importance analysis, model explainability using SHAP or LIME, bias detection and fairness assessment, discussion of model limitations and potential risks, ethical considerations in deployment

Business Communication & Impact (25 points): Executive summary with clear business recommendations, cost-benefit analysis of model implementation, deployment strategy with monitoring plan, professional presentation suitable for stakeholders, code documentation and reproducibility
instructions: Create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating the complete data science workflow using a customer churn prediction problem. Your submission must include: 1) A Jupyter notebook with complete analysis (well-documented code, clear markdown explanations, professional visualizations), 2) A business presentation (10-15 slides) suitable for executive stakeholders, 3) A technical report (8-12 pages) detailing methodology and findings, 4) All code in a GitHub repository with proper documentation. Use the provided telecommunications customer dataset or obtain approval for an alternative dataset with similar complexity. Your analysis must include: comprehensive EDA with at least 10 meaningful visualizations, feature engineering creating at least 5 new variables, implementation of logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting models, proper train/validation/test splits with cross-validation, hyperparameter optimization, model interpretation using explainability tools, bias analysis across customer segments, and a deployment plan with monitoring strategy. The business presentation should focus on ROI calculation, implementation timeline, and specific recommendations. All code must be reproducible with clear requirements.txt file. Submit via GitHub link plus uploaded presentation and report files.
grading_notes: Grade holistically considering both technical rigor and business application. Look for: statistical soundness in methodology, creativity in feature engineering, appropriate model selection justification, depth of business understanding, and communication clarity. Common issues include: inadequate cross-validation, overfitting without detection, missing bias analysis, weak business connection, and poor code documentation. Expect grade distribution: 15% A+ (exceptional insight/creativity), 25% A (meets all criteria excellently), 35% B (solid work with minor gaps), 20% C (adequate but missing key components), 5% below C (major deficiencies). Deduct points for late submission, broken code, or failure to use version control. Bonus consideration for novel approaches, external data integration, or particularly insightful business recommendations.

title: Advanced Numerical Analysis Lab: Comparative Study of Root-Finding Algorithms
description: Students will implement, analyze, and compare the performance of four numerical root-finding algorithms (Bisection, Newton-Raphson, Secant, and Brent's method) on a set of challenging functions, documenting convergence behavior, computational efficiency, and numerical stability through rigorous mathematical analysis and computational experimentation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Implement and analyze convergence properties of iterative numerical algorithms
Evaluate computational complexity and numerical stability of mathematical methods
Apply error analysis techniques to assess algorithm performance and accuracy
Communicate mathematical findings through formal scientific writing and data visualization
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Implementation & Correctness (25 points): All four algorithms correctly implemented with proper error handling, termination criteria, and edge case management. Code is well-documented with clear variable naming and logical structure.

Mathematical Analysis & Theory (25 points): Thorough theoretical analysis including convergence order derivation, stability analysis, and error bound calculations. Proper use of mathematical notation and rigorous proof techniques where applicable.

Experimental Design & Results (25 points): Comprehensive testing on at least 6 diverse functions (polynomial, transcendental, pathological cases). Clear presentation of convergence plots, performance tables, and statistical analysis of results with appropriate metrics.

Scientific Communication & Interpretation (25 points): Professional lab report format with clear methodology, well-organized results section, insightful discussion of findings, and appropriate conclusions. Proper citation of numerical analysis literature and mathematical references.
instructions: Your task is to conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of numerical root-finding algorithms. You must implement four algorithms: Bisection Method, Newton-Raphson Method, Secant Method, and Brent's Method. Test each algorithm on the following function set: f₁(x) = x³ - 2x - 5, f₂(x) = e^x - 3x, f₃(x) = x·sin(x) - 1, f₄(x) = x² - 2 (near x=√2), f₅(x) = (x-1)¹⁰, and f₆(x) = tan(x) - x (near x=4.5). For each algorithm-function pair, record: number of iterations to convergence, final error estimate, computational time, and any convergence failures. Set tolerance ε = 10⁻¹² and maximum iterations = 1000. Your report must include: (1) Introduction with theoretical background, (2) Methodology section describing implementation details, (3) Results section with convergence plots and performance tables, (4) Discussion analyzing convergence behavior, computational efficiency, and when each method is preferred, (5) Conclusions summarizing key findings. Include your source code as an appendix. Submit as a PDF with embedded plots and properly formatted mathematical expressions. All numerical results must be presented with appropriate significant figures and uncertainty analysis.
grading_notes: Evaluate code functionality by testing with provided functions - deduct heavily for non-working implementations. Look for proper implementation of stopping criteria (both tolerance and maximum iterations). In mathematical analysis, expect students to demonstrate understanding of linear vs quadratic convergence, and to identify why certain algorithms fail on specific functions (e.g., Newton-Raphson near inflection points). Strong submissions will include discussion of computational complexity (function evaluations vs derivative evaluations) and practical considerations like initial guess sensitivity. Common issues include: inadequate error handling, poor choice of initial intervals/guesses, insufficient discussion of algorithm limitations, and missing theoretical analysis. Expect grade distribution: A-level (>90): comprehensive analysis with novel insights; B-level (80-89): solid implementation and analysis with minor gaps; C-level (70-79): basic requirements met but lacking depth; Below 70: significant implementation errors or missing components.

title: Data Science Process Presentation: From Question to Insight
description: Students will create and deliver a 10-minute presentation demonstrating their understanding of the complete data science workflow by walking through a real-world scenario from problem definition to actionable insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Articulate the key stages of the data science process and their interconnections
Identify appropriate data types and collection methods for specific business problems
Explain basic data analysis techniques and when to apply them
Communicate data-driven insights to non-technical audiences effectively
rubric_criteria: Problem Definition & Data Identification (25 points): Clearly defines a realistic business problem, identifies what data would be needed, explains data sources and types, demonstrates understanding of data collection challenges

Data Science Process Knowledge (25 points): Accurately describes all major steps (problem definition, data collection, cleaning, analysis, interpretation, communication), shows understanding of how steps connect, identifies potential challenges at each stage

Analysis Approach & Tools (25 points): Selects appropriate analysis methods for the problem type, explains chosen techniques in simple terms, demonstrates awareness of tool options (Excel, Python, R, etc.), shows understanding of limitations

Communication & Presentation Skills (25 points): Uses clear, jargon-free language appropriate for business audience, includes effective visuals or examples, stays within time limit, demonstrates confidence and preparedness, provides actionable recommendations
instructions: Choose a business problem from the provided list (customer churn, sales forecasting, inventory optimization, or marketing effectiveness) or propose your own with instructor approval. Create a 10-minute presentation that walks through how you would apply the data science process to solve this problem. Your presentation must include: (1) Clear problem statement with business context, (2) Description of what data you would collect and from where, (3) Step-by-step walkthrough of your analysis approach, (4) Mock insights or findings you might discover, (5) Specific recommendations for stakeholders. Use 8-12 slides maximum. Focus on demonstrating your understanding of the process rather than technical implementation details. Your audience is business managers with no data science background. Include at least one visual aid (chart, diagram, or infographic). Submit your slides 24 hours before presentation day. During presentation, you'll have 10 minutes to present plus 3 minutes for questions. Dress professionally and be prepared to explain any terminology you use.
grading_notes: Focus on conceptual understanding over technical depth - students should demonstrate they grasp the big picture of data science workflow. Common issues include: too much technical jargon, unrealistic problem scoping, missing steps in the process, poor time management. Excellent presentations (90-100) show creativity and real-world awareness. Good presentations (80-89) cover all requirements with minor gaps. Satisfactory (70-79) meet basic requirements but lack depth. Below 70 indicates missing major components or poor understanding. Encourage students who struggle with public speaking but show strong content knowledge. Provide immediate verbal feedback after each presentation focusing on one strength and one improvement area.

title: Distributed Systems Performance Analysis: Load Balancing Algorithm Implementation and Evaluation
description: Students will implement and evaluate multiple load balancing algorithms in a distributed web server environment, analyze their performance under various load conditions, and present findings in a comprehensive lab report with empirical data analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems components with consideration for scalability and fault tolerance
Apply performance analysis techniques to evaluate system efficiency under varying load conditions
Analyze trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches in distributed computing contexts
Communicate technical findings through structured scientific reporting with data visualization
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Implementation (25 points): Correct implementation of at least 3 load balancing algorithms (Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connections) with proper error handling, clean code structure, and appropriate use of data structures

Experimental Design & Data Collection (25 points): Systematic performance testing with varying load conditions (100, 500, 1000, 2000 concurrent requests), consistent methodology across algorithms, comprehensive metrics collection (response time, throughput, CPU utilization, memory usage)

Analysis & Interpretation (25 points): Statistical analysis of performance data, identification of performance bottlenecks, comparison of algorithm efficiency under different scenarios, discussion of scalability implications and trade-offs between algorithms

Report Quality & Technical Communication (25 points): Clear problem statement, well-structured methodology section, effective data visualization (graphs, charts), professional formatting, proper citations, conclusions supported by empirical evidence
instructions: Implement three load balancing algorithms in your chosen programming language (Python, Java, or C++) for a simulated web server cluster with 5 backend servers. Create a test harness that can generate concurrent HTTP requests with configurable load patterns. Test each algorithm under four load conditions: 100, 500, 1000, and 2000 concurrent requests. Measure and record response times, throughput (requests/second), server CPU utilization, and memory usage. Run each test scenario 5 times and calculate statistical averages. Your lab report must include: (1) Introduction with problem statement and algorithm descriptions, (2) Implementation details with code architecture explanation, (3) Experimental methodology and test environment specifications, (4) Results section with data tables and visualizations comparing algorithm performance, (5) Analysis discussing trade-offs, scalability patterns, and performance bottlenecks, (6) Conclusions with recommendations for real-world deployment scenarios. Submit your report as a PDF with source code in a separate ZIP file. Include a README with compilation/execution instructions. All graphs must be properly labeled with axes, legends, and captions. Code must be commented and follow consistent style guidelines.
grading_notes: Grade implementation by testing functionality with provided test cases - algorithms should distribute load correctly and handle edge cases. Verify experimental data is realistic and consistent across runs. Look for statistical rigor in analysis (means, standard deviations, confidence intervals). Common issues: insufficient testing scenarios, poorly labeled graphs, missing error handling in code, superficial analysis without deeper insights. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (sophisticated analysis with insights beyond requirements), 60% B-level (meets all requirements competently), 20% C-level (basic implementation with minimal analysis), 5% below C (incomplete or non-functional). Deduct points for late submissions (5% per day), missing components, or academic integrity violations.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Assessment: End-to-End Predictive Analytics

learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement production-ready machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing and feature engineering
Apply advanced model selection techniques and hyperparameter optimization strategies for complex datasets
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and statistical validation methods
Communicate technical findings and business recommendations through comprehensive analysis and visualization
Demonstrate understanding of ML deployment considerations including scalability, interpretability, and ethical implications
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing & Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive EDA with statistical insights, appropriate handling of missing values/outliers, creative and justified feature engineering, proper data splitting and preprocessing pipeline implementation

Model Development & Optimization (25 points): Systematic comparison of multiple algorithms, sophisticated hyperparameter tuning using grid/random/Bayesian search, proper cross-validation implementation, evidence of avoiding overfitting

Model Evaluation & Validation (25 points): Use of appropriate evaluation metrics for problem type, statistical significance testing, learning curves analysis, bias-variance tradeoff discussion, robust validation methodology

Technical Communication & Business Impact (25 points): Clear code documentation and reproducibility, insightful visualizations, actionable business recommendations, discussion of model limitations and deployment considerations, professional presentation quality
instructions: You are provided with a complex tabular dataset containing customer transaction data for a financial services company. Your task is to build a complete machine learning pipeline to predict customer churn probability. Submit a Jupyter notebook containing: (1) Comprehensive exploratory data analysis with at least 5 statistical insights and professional visualizations, (2) Feature engineering pipeline including at least 3 derived features with justification, (3) Implementation and comparison of minimum 4 different algorithms (must include tree-based, linear, and ensemble methods), (4) Hyperparameter optimization using at least 2 different search strategies, (5) Model evaluation using multiple metrics appropriate for imbalanced classification, including precision-recall analysis and ROC curves, (6) Statistical validation of results including confidence intervals and significance testing, (7) Business recommendations section discussing model interpretability, deployment strategy, and potential risks. Code must be well-documented with markdown explanations. Include a 2-page executive summary discussing business impact, model limitations, and next steps. Common issues: inadequate EDA depth, poor feature engineering justification, overfitting due to improper validation, weak business contextualization. Deduct points for: non-reproducible code (-10), missing statistical validation (-15), inadequate business discussion (-10), poor code documentation (-5). Bonus points available (+5) for exceptional insights or innovative approaches.

title: My Dream Bedroom Budget Project
description: Students will create a budget plan for redesigning their dream bedroom by researching furniture prices, calculating costs, and determining if they can afford their choices within a given budget. This project integrates real-world application of basic arithmetic, budgeting skills, and data organization.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply addition and subtraction skills to solve real-world problems involving money
Compare and order decimal numbers in the context of pricing
Create and interpret basic data tables and charts
Demonstrate understanding of budgeting concepts and financial decision-making
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): All calculations are correct, decimal operations performed accurately, final budget totals match itemized costs
Research and Data Organization (25 points): At least 8 furniture/decor items researched with accurate prices, information clearly organized in provided template

Budget Analysis (25 points): Correctly identifies whether dream bedroom fits in budget, shows mathematical reasoning for staying within or going over budget, provides realistic alternatives if over budget
Presentation and Completeness (25 points): All project components included, work is neat and organized, includes required visual element (drawing/collage), follows submission guidelines
instructions: You have received $1,500 to redesign your bedroom! Your task is to research and plan your dream bedroom while staying within budget. Step 1: Research at least 8 items you want for your bedroom (bed, desk, chair, decorations, etc.) using online stores, catalogs, or by visiting stores with family. Record the name, price, and where you found each item. Step 2: Use the provided budget template to list all items and their costs. Calculate subtotals for different categories (furniture, decorations, etc.) and determine your final total. Step 3: Compare your total to your $1,500 budget. If you're over budget, identify which items you could remove or replace with less expensive options to stay within budget. Show all your mathematical work. Step 4: Create a visual representation of your bedroom plan through a drawing, magazine collage, or digital design. Label your items with their costs. Step 5: Write a one-paragraph reflection explaining your favorite purchases and any difficult budget decisions you had to make. Submit your completed budget template, calculations worksheet, visual bedroom plan, and written reflection. All mathematical work must be shown clearly. Project is due in two weeks and will be presented briefly to the class.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical accuracy first - ensure students show their work for all calculations and properly handle decimal addition/subtraction. Look for realistic price research (items should reflect actual market prices, not artificially low/high). Students going over budget should demonstrate clear mathematical reasoning about what to cut or substitute. Common issues include: forgetting to show work, unrealistic pricing, missing calculation steps, and incomplete budget analysis. Expect most students to initially go over budget - this is intentional and valuable for learning. Grade generously on creativity and effort for visual components while maintaining high standards for mathematical accuracy. Students should demonstrate genuine engagement with budgeting concepts beyond just arithmetic.

title: Bias Detection and Mitigation in Machine Learning Systems: A Critical Analysis Discussion
description: Students will conduct an in-depth analysis of bias in machine learning systems by examining a real-world case study, identifying multiple types of bias, proposing mitigation strategies, and engaging in peer discussion about the ethical implications and technical solutions.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (3 hours preparation, 1-2 hours discussion participation)
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and analyze various types of bias in machine learning models and datasets
Evaluate the societal and business impact of biased ML systems
Design and justify technical and procedural strategies for bias detection and mitigation
Critically assess trade-offs between model performance, fairness, and interpretability
Communicate complex technical concepts to diverse stakeholders effectively
rubric_criteria: Case Study Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of bias types present, identifies root causes in data collection/model development, and analyzes downstream impacts with specific evidence

Technical Mitigation Strategies (25 points): Proposes appropriate pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing techniques with clear justification, addresses implementation challenges, and considers computational trade-offs
Ethical and Business Impact Assessment (25 points): Evaluates societal consequences, discusses stakeholder perspectives, addresses legal/regulatory considerations, and proposes governance frameworks

Discussion Engagement and Communication (25 points): Provides substantive responses to peers, asks insightful follow-up questions, synthesizes multiple viewpoints, and explains technical concepts clearly to non-technical audiences
instructions: You will analyze a provided case study of a biased ML system (options include hiring algorithms, facial recognition systems, or credit scoring models). Submit a 1000-word initial analysis covering: (1) Identification of at least three types of bias with specific evidence, (2) Root cause analysis examining data sources, feature selection, and model assumptions, (3) Technical mitigation strategies including specific algorithms/techniques and implementation considerations, (4) Assessment of ethical implications and stakeholder impacts, (5) Proposed monitoring and governance framework. Your analysis must reference at least 5 peer-reviewed sources and industry best practices. After submission, participate in the discussion forum by responding substantively to at least 3 peer analyses, focusing on alternative mitigation approaches, implementation challenges, or ethical considerations they may have missed. Your responses should be 150-200 words each and demonstrate critical thinking. Include questions that probe deeper into technical assumptions or ethical frameworks. Format: PDF submission for initial analysis, discussion forum posts for peer engagement. Cite all sources using APA format.
grading_notes: Look for depth of technical understanding beyond surface-level bias identification. Strong submissions will connect specific bias types to concrete examples in the case study and demonstrate understanding of the bias-variance-fairness trade-off space. In mitigation strategies, assess feasibility and appropriateness of proposed techniques - students should show awareness that different fairness metrics can conflict. For ethical analysis, expect consideration of multiple stakeholder perspectives and awareness of systemic vs. individual impacts. Discussion participation should show genuine engagement rather than superficial agreement - reward students who challenge assumptions constructively or offer alternative frameworks. Common weaknesses include: conflating correlation with causation in bias identification, proposing mitigation strategies without considering implementation constraints, and failing to address the inherent tensions between different fairness definitions. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Exceptional work will demonstrate original thinking about novel bias detection methods or creative governance solutions.

title: Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Real-World Applications of Differential Equations
description: Students will research, analyze, and present a comprehensive examination of how differential equations are applied to solve complex real-world problems in their chosen field (physics, engineering, biology, economics, etc.). The presentation must demonstrate deep mathematical understanding, rigorous analytical skills, and the ability to communicate advanced mathematical concepts to both technical and non-technical audiences.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate mastery of differential equation theory and solution methods
Apply advanced mathematical modeling techniques to real-world scenarios
Analyze the validity and limitations of mathematical models
Communicate complex mathematical concepts clearly and effectively
Evaluate the accuracy and appropriateness of mathematical solutions in practical contexts
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates correct application of differential equation theory, shows all mathematical work clearly, uses appropriate notation, and provides accurate solutions with proper justification of methods chosen

Model Development and Analysis (25 points): Develops a sophisticated mathematical model from real-world constraints, identifies key variables and parameters, justifies assumptions made, and critically evaluates model limitations and validity

Presentation Quality and Communication (25 points): Delivers clear, well-organized presentation with effective visual aids, explains complex concepts accessibly, maintains audience engagement, and demonstrates confidence in subject matter

Problem-Solving Depth and Innovation (25 points): Selects appropriately challenging real-world application, demonstrates creative problem-solving approaches, connects mathematical theory to practical implications, and shows evidence of independent research and analysis
instructions: Select a real-world application where differential equations play a crucial role in modeling and solving complex problems. Your presentation must include: (1) Clear problem statement with background context and significance, (2) Mathematical model development showing the derivation of relevant differential equations from first principles, (3) Detailed solution process using appropriate analytical or numerical methods, (4) Critical analysis of results including sensitivity analysis and model validation, (5) Discussion of practical implications and limitations. Prepare a 30-minute presentation using professional-quality slides, including mathematical derivations, graphs, and visual representations. Be prepared for a 15-minute technical Q&A session. Submit presentation slides and a 2-page mathematical appendix showing detailed calculations 24 hours before your scheduled presentation time. Examples of suitable topics include: population dynamics modeling, heat transfer in engineering systems, financial derivatives pricing, epidemiological modeling, or circuit analysis. Your mathematical work must demonstrate graduate-level understanding of differential equations, including existence and uniqueness theorems, stability analysis, and appropriate solution techniques. Presentations will be evaluated on mathematical correctness, depth of analysis, clarity of communication, and ability to defend your approach during questioning.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical work for both correctness and sophistication - look for proper use of advanced techniques rather than elementary approaches. Pay attention to how well students handle the transition between mathematical theory and real-world application. During Q&A, assess depth of understanding by asking about alternative solution methods, model assumptions, and extensions. Common issues include: oversimplified models that don't require advanced mathematics, computational errors in complex calculations, poor explanation of mathematical concepts to mixed audiences, and inability to defend modeling choices. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations: 90-100 points for exceptional work showing mastery and innovation, 80-89 for solid competent work with minor issues, 70-79 for adequate work with notable gaps, below 70 for work not meeting graduate standards. Document specific mathematical errors and communication issues for feedback.

title: Customer Churn Prediction and Analysis Lab Report
description: Students will conduct a complete data science analysis on a customer churn dataset, implementing data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, model building, and business recommendation formulation. This assessment evaluates practical application of machine learning workflows and communication of technical findings.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply data preprocessing techniques including handling missing values, outliers, and categorical encoding
Conduct comprehensive exploratory data analysis using statistical and visualization methods
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms for classification problems
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Communicate technical findings and business recommendations effectively
rubric_criteria: Data Preprocessing and EDA (25 points): Proper handling of missing values, outlier detection, appropriate visualizations, statistical summaries, and data quality assessment with clear documentation of decisions made

Feature Engineering and Model Implementation (25 points): Meaningful feature creation/selection, correct implementation of at least 2 classification algorithms (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper train/validation/test splits

Model Evaluation and Comparison (25 points): Use of multiple evaluation metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC), cross-validation implementation, model comparison with statistical significance testing, hyperparameter tuning evidence

Technical Communication and Business Insights (25 points): Clear code documentation, well-structured report narrative, actionable business recommendations based on findings, discussion of model limitations and potential improvements
instructions: Using the provided customer churn dataset (or acquire a publicly available one from Kaggle/UCI), complete a full data science analysis following these requirements: 1) Data Exploration: Load and examine the dataset structure, identify data types, missing values, and basic statistics. Create at least 5 meaningful visualizations exploring relationships between features and churn. 2) Data Preprocessing: Handle missing values with justified methods, encode categorical variables appropriately, detect and address outliers, and perform feature scaling if needed. 3) Feature Engineering: Create at least 3 new features that could improve model performance, perform feature selection using statistical or model-based methods. 4) Model Building: Implement at least two different classification algorithms, use proper train/validation/test splits (60/20/20), and tune hyperparameters using grid search or random search. 5) Model Evaluation: Calculate and compare multiple performance metrics, create confusion matrices and ROC curves, perform cross-validation, and conduct statistical tests for model comparison. 6) Business Recommendations: Provide specific, actionable recommendations for reducing customer churn based on your analysis, discuss the potential business impact of implementing your model, and identify key factors driving churn. Submit your work as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) with clear markdown explanations, all code properly commented, and outputs visible. Include a 2-page executive summary PDF highlighting key findings and recommendations for non-technical stakeholders.
grading_notes: Evaluate code functionality by running notebooks - deduct points if code doesn't execute properly. Look for statistical rigor in approach (proper validation, significance testing, avoiding data leakage). Assess creativity in feature engineering and depth of analysis beyond basic requirements. Common issues to watch: data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate train/test splits, overfitting without proper validation, weak business recommendations disconnected from technical findings. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades (90-100), 35% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 10% below 70. Bonus points (up to 5) can be awarded for exceptional insights, advanced techniques (ensemble methods, deep learning), or outstanding visualization quality.

title: Advanced Calculus Applications: Optimization and Related Rates Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' ability to solve complex optimization problems, related rates scenarios, and applications of derivatives in real-world contexts. Students will demonstrate mastery of calculus techniques, mathematical modeling, and analytical problem-solving skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply derivative concepts to solve multi-step optimization problems with constraints
Analyze and solve related rates problems involving multiple variables and geometric relationships
Construct mathematical models from real-world scenarios using calculus principles
Demonstrate proficiency in implicit differentiation and chain rule applications
Interpret calculus solutions within practical contexts and validate reasonableness of results
