rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Mathematical Modeling (25 points): Correctly identifies variables, establishes relationships, sets up equations, and defines constraints. Shows clear understanding of the problem context and translates real-world scenarios into mathematical expressions.

Calculus Techniques and Computation (25 points): Accurately applies differentiation rules, implicit differentiation, and chain rule. Performs algebraic manipulations correctly and shows proper mathematical notation and symbolic reasoning throughout the solution process.

Solution Strategy and Logic (25 points): Demonstrates systematic approach to problem-solving, identifies appropriate calculus methods, shows logical progression from setup to final answer, and handles multi-step processes efficiently with clear mathematical reasoning.

Interpretation and Validation (25 points): Interprets mathematical results in context of original problem, checks solutions for reasonableness, includes appropriate units, addresses domain restrictions, and provides clear final answers with proper justification.
instructions: This quiz consists of four comprehensive problems requiring advanced calculus applications. You have 90 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and systematically - partial credit will be awarded based on your problem-solving process, mathematical reasoning, and correct application of calculus concepts. For each problem: (1) Clearly define your variables and state what you're solving for, (2) Set up all necessary equations and relationships, (3) Show all differentiation steps with proper notation, (4) Solve algebraically with clear work shown, (5) Interpret your final answer in the context of the original problem, including units where appropriate. Problem 1 involves optimization of a manufacturing scenario with cost constraints. Problem 2 requires solving a related rates problem involving changing geometric relationships. Problem 3 presents a business application requiring revenue optimization with market constraints. Problem 4 combines multiple calculus concepts in a physics-based scenario. You may use a scientific calculator, but all calculus work must be shown by hand. Graphing calculators or symbolic computation devices are not permitted. Clearly box or circle your final answers. If you make an error early in a problem but continue with correct mathematical reasoning, you can still earn substantial partial credit.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct mathematical processes even with computational errors. Key grading focus areas: correct variable identification (5 pts per problem), proper equation setup (5 pts), accurate differentiation (10 pts), correct algebraic manipulation (5 pts). Common issues to watch: students often forget to check domain restrictions in optimization problems, may incorrectly apply chain rule in related rates, and frequently omit units in final answers. Grade distribution expectation: 15-20% A-level (90+), 25-30% B-level (80-89), 30-35% C-level (70-79), remaining below 70. Look for evidence of conceptual understanding over perfect computation. Students showing strong setup and methodology with minor errors should score in B range minimum.

title: Distributed Database System with ACID Compliance and Performance Optimization
description: Design and implement a distributed database system that ensures ACID properties across multiple nodes, incorporates advanced indexing strategies, and demonstrates horizontal scaling capabilities with comprehensive performance analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems architecture with fault tolerance mechanisms
Apply database theory including ACID properties, concurrency control, and transaction management
Analyze system performance through benchmarking and optimization techniques
Demonstrate advanced software engineering practices including testing, documentation, and version control
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Implementation (25 points): Correct implementation of distributed consensus algorithm (Raft/PBFT), proper network communication protocols, effective data partitioning strategy, and robust error handling mechanisms

ACID Compliance & Transaction Management (25 points): Proper implementation of atomicity through two-phase commit or similar protocol, consistency maintenance across nodes, isolation levels implementation, and durability through write-ahead logging or equivalent

Performance Analysis & Optimization (25 points): Comprehensive benchmarking suite measuring throughput/latency under various loads, implementation of at least two indexing strategies (B+ trees, hash indexes, etc.), demonstration of horizontal scaling benefits, and identification of bottlenecks with optimization solutions

Code Quality & Documentation (25 points): Clean, modular, and well-commented code following industry standards, comprehensive technical documentation including system design diagrams, complete unit and integration test coverage (>80%), and proper use of version control with meaningful commit messages
instructions: Develop a distributed database system supporting basic SQL operations (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) across at least 3 nodes. Your system must handle node failures gracefully and maintain data consistency. Required deliverables: (1) Complete source code with build instructions, (2) Technical design document (10-15 pages) including architecture diagrams, consensus algorithm choice justification, and data model specification, (3) Performance analysis report comparing your system against a baseline single-node implementation, measuring queries/second, average latency, and scaling characteristics with 1-5 nodes, (4) Demonstration video (10-15 minutes) showing system functionality, failure recovery, and performance benchmarks. Use any programming language, but justify your choice. Implement proper logging and monitoring. Your system should handle concurrent transactions and demonstrate snapshot isolation or higher. Include at least 1000 test records across multiple tables with foreign key relationships. Submit via GitHub repository with detailed README, ensure all code compiles and runs on standard Linux environment. Include docker-compose configuration for easy deployment.
grading_notes: Evaluate system correctness first - non-functional systems receive maximum 60% regardless of documentation quality. Pay special attention to edge cases in distributed consensus and transaction handling. Common issues include: improper handling of network partitions, race conditions in concurrent operations, insufficient error recovery mechanisms. Expect 15% of projects to achieve full marks, 70% to score 70-85 points, remainder below 70. Deduct 5 points per day for late submissions. Bonus points (up to 10) for exceptional innovations like advanced query optimization, additional consistency models, or sophisticated monitoring dashboards.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategies Discussion Forum
description: Students will engage in collaborative discussions analyzing different problem-solving approaches for multi-step algebraic word problems, evaluate peer solutions, and reflect on the effectiveness of various mathematical strategies.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multiple problem-solving strategies to solve complex algebraic word problems
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using appropriate terminology and notation
Analyze and critique mathematical solutions presented by peers
Reflect on the effectiveness of different problem-solving approaches
rubric_criteria: Initial Problem Solution (25 points): Demonstrates correct mathematical approach, shows all work clearly, arrives at accurate solution with proper units/context
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise mathematical language, proper notation, logical sequence of steps, and clear explanations of reasoning
Peer Analysis and Feedback (25 points): Provides constructive critique of at least two peer solutions, identifies strengths/weaknesses, suggests improvements or alternative approaches
Reflection and Strategy Comparison (25 points): Thoughtfully compares different problem-solving methods, discusses when each approach is most effective, demonstrates metacognitive awareness
instructions:
This week you will participate in a collaborative problem-solving discussion focusing on algebraic word problems. You have been assigned to Discussion Group [X] and will work with the following problem: 'A rectangular garden has a perimeter of 84 feet. If the length is 6 feet more than twice the width, find the dimensions and calculate the area.' 

Your participation must include four components: 

1) INITIAL SOLUTION POST (due by Wednesday): Solve the assigned problem showing all mathematical work. Include your variable definitions, equation setup, algebraic steps, and final answer with units. Explain your problem-solving strategy and why you chose this approach. 

2) PEER RESPONSES (due by Friday): Analyze at least two classmates' solutions. Compare their methods to yours, identify any errors or alternative approaches, and provide constructive feedback. If you find a different correct method, explain how it connects to your solution. 

3) STRATEGY REFLECTION (due by Sunday): After reviewing multiple approaches, write a 150-word reflection comparing at least three different problem-solving strategies observed in your group. Discuss the advantages and limitations of each method. 

4) FOLLOW-UP ENGAGEMENT: Respond thoughtfully to any questions or feedback about your original solution. 

All posts must use proper mathematical notation and terminology. Show respect for diverse approaches while maintaining mathematical accuracy. Posts should be substantial and demonstrate mathematical thinking beyond simple agreement or disagreement.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first, then communication quality. Look for evidence of mathematical reasoning process, not just correct answers. Credit partial solutions that show logical thinking. In peer feedback, reward specific mathematical observations over general comments. For reflections, assess depth of analysis and metacognitive awareness about problem-solving strategies. Common issues include: incomplete algebraic steps, missing units, vague peer feedback, and superficial reflections. Expect 15% excellent (90-100), 60% proficient (80-89), 20% developing (70-79), 5% inadequate (below 70). Deduct points for late submissions according to course policy.

title: Advanced System Architecture Design Presentation: Scalable Distributed Application
description: Students will design and present a comprehensive distributed system architecture for a high-traffic application, demonstrating advanced understanding of scalability, fault tolerance, data consistency, and modern system design principles. The presentation must include architectural diagrams, technology justification, and performance analysis.
estimated_time: 6-8 weeks for preparation, 20 minutes presentation + 10 minutes Q&A
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed systems using appropriate architectural patterns and technologies
Analyze trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance in distributed systems
Evaluate and justify technology choices for specific system requirements and constraints
Communicate complex technical concepts effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences
rubric_criteria: Architecture Design & Technical Depth (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of distributed systems concepts, appropriate use of design patterns (microservices, event-driven, etc.), comprehensive consideration of scalability, fault tolerance, and data management strategies

Technology Selection & Justification (25 points): Shows deep knowledge of modern technologies, databases, frameworks, and tools; provides well-reasoned justifications for choices based on requirements; addresses trade-offs and alternatives with technical merit

System Analysis & Performance Considerations (25 points): Includes thorough analysis of system bottlenecks, performance metrics, capacity planning, monitoring strategies, and disaster recovery; demonstrates understanding of CAP theorem implications and consistency models

Presentation Quality & Communication (25 points): Delivers clear, well-structured presentation with professional visual aids; effectively explains complex concepts; handles questions confidently; maintains appropriate technical depth for audience
instructions: Design a distributed system architecture for a specified high-traffic application (e.g., social media platform, e-commerce site, or streaming service handling 10M+ daily active users). Your presentation must include: (1) System overview with clear architectural diagrams showing all major components, services, and data flows; (2) Detailed technology stack with specific databases, frameworks, cloud services, and justification for each choice; (3) Scalability strategy including horizontal/vertical scaling approaches, load balancing, caching layers, and CDN implementation; (4) Data management design covering database selection, sharding strategies, replication, and consistency models; (5) Fault tolerance and reliability measures including circuit breakers, bulkheads, monitoring, and disaster recovery; (6) Performance analysis with capacity planning, expected throughput, latency considerations, and key metrics; (7) Security considerations and deployment strategy. Prepare 15-20 slides focusing on architectural decisions rather than implementation details. Include at least one detailed sequence diagram and one system architecture diagram. Submit slides 24 hours before presentation. Be prepared for technical questions about scalability limits, failure scenarios, and alternative approaches.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of advanced systems thinking beyond basic CRUD applications. Strong presentations will demonstrate understanding of real-world constraints and trade-offs. Deduct points for unrealistic assumptions about scale or oversimplified solutions. Excellent work (90-100) should show innovation and deep technical insight. Good work (80-89) covers all requirements competently. Satisfactory work (70-79) shows basic understanding but lacks depth or has minor technical errors. Below 70 indicates significant gaps in understanding or incomplete work. Pay special attention to how students handle Q&A - this reveals true depth of understanding. Common issues to watch: oversimplified database designs, ignoring network latency, unrealistic performance assumptions, lack of monitoring strategy.

title: End-to-End Predictive Analytics Project: Customer Churn Prediction and Business Intelligence Dashboard
description: Students will complete a comprehensive data science project involving customer churn prediction for a telecommunications company. The project requires data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, model development, evaluation, and creation of an interactive business intelligence dashboard with actionable recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced data preprocessing and feature engineering techniques to real-world datasets
Implement and compare multiple machine learning algorithms for classification problems
Conduct comprehensive model evaluation using appropriate metrics and validation techniques
Create data visualizations and interactive dashboards for business stakeholders
Translate technical findings into actionable business recommendations
Document and communicate data science workflows effectively
rubric_criteria: Data Processing & Feature Engineering (25 points): Quality of data cleaning, handling missing values, outlier treatment, feature creation, and data transformation. Code efficiency and documentation of preprocessing steps.

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms, proper cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, appropriate evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), and model comparison with statistical significance testing.

Dashboard & Visualization (25 points): Interactive dashboard functionality, appropriate chart types, visual design principles, user experience, and integration of model predictions with business metrics.

Business Impact & Communication (25 points): Quality of executive summary, actionable recommendations, ROI analysis, presentation clarity, and demonstration of business understanding of churn prevention strategies.
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (available on course portal), develop a complete churn prediction solution. Your submission must include: 1) Jupyter notebook with complete analysis workflow including data exploration, preprocessing, feature engineering, and model development with clear markdown explanations; 2) Interactive dashboard built using Streamlit, Dash, or Tableau showing key metrics, model performance, and customer segments at risk; 3) Executive summary (2-3 pages) presenting findings, model performance, and specific business recommendations with estimated financial impact; 4) GitHub repository with organized code, requirements.txt, and README with setup instructions. Technical requirements: Handle class imbalance appropriately, implement at least three algorithms (must include ensemble method), use proper train/validation/test splits, perform feature importance analysis, and include model interpretability components (SHAP values or similar). Dashboard must be functional with sample predictions and allow filtering by customer segments. All code must be well-documented with docstrings and comments. Submit GitHub repository link and executive summary PDF through course portal by 11:59 PM on due date.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor and business applicability equally. Look for proper handling of imbalanced datasets (SMOTE, class weights, or stratified sampling). Expect F1-scores above 0.75 and AUC-ROC above 0.85 for full model performance credit. Dashboard should load without errors and demonstrate interactive features. Common issues: inadequate cross-validation, data leakage in feature engineering, overfitting without proper validation, weak business recommendations, and non-functional dashboards. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A grades (90-100), 35% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 10% below 70. Deduct 10 points for late submissions within 48 hours, 20 points thereafter. Bonus points (up to 5) for exceptional creativity in feature engineering or advanced techniques like deep learning implementation.

title: Advanced Mathematical Analysis and Proof Construction Examination
description: A comprehensive examination assessing mastery of advanced mathematical concepts including real analysis, abstract algebra, and proof techniques. Students will demonstrate their ability to construct rigorous proofs, analyze complex mathematical structures, and solve challenging problems across multiple mathematical domains.
learning_objectives_assessed: Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using direct, indirect, and induction methods
Analyze properties of metric spaces, topological spaces, and continuous functions
Apply advanced techniques in group theory and ring theory to solve abstract problems
Synthesize knowledge across mathematical domains to solve multi-step complex problems
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Proof Construction (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of proof techniques with logically sound arguments, proper mathematical notation, and complete justification of all steps
Problem-Solving and Analytical Thinking (25 points): Shows sophisticated problem-solving strategies, identifies key insights, and applies appropriate theorems and methods effectively
Technical Accuracy and Computation (25 points): Performs complex calculations correctly, manipulates abstract mathematical objects accurately, and arrives at correct conclusions
Communication and Mathematical Writing (25 points): Presents solutions clearly and coherently, uses precise mathematical language, and organizes work in a logical sequence
instructions: This examination consists of 8 problems across four mathematical areas: Real Analysis (2 problems), Abstract Algebra (2 problems), Topology (2 problems), and Integrated Applications (2 problems). You have 4 hours to complete all problems. Show all work and provide complete justifications for your answers. Partial credit will be awarded for correct methods even if final answers are incorrect. Use only the provided formula sheet and approved calculator. No collaboration or external resources are permitted. Begin each problem on a new page and clearly label your solutions. For proof problems, state what you are proving, outline your approach, and write complete arguments. For computational problems, show intermediate steps and verify your answers when possible. If you cannot complete a problem, write down your approach and any relevant observations for partial credit. Manage your time effectively - spend approximately 30 minutes per problem. Read all problems before beginning and start with those you find most straightforward. Remember that clarity of presentation is as important as correctness of content. Use standard mathematical notation and define any non-standard symbols you introduce.
grading_notes: Grade holistically within each rubric criterion rather than assigning points per problem. Look for evidence of deep mathematical understanding beyond mere computation. Award full credit for alternative correct solution methods. Common deductions: incomplete proofs (-3 to -5 points), computational errors that don't reflect conceptual misunderstanding (-2 points), unclear mathematical writing (-2 to -4 points). Expect grade distribution: A-level (85-100): 15-20%, B-level (70-84): 30-35%, C-level (55-69): 30-35%, D/F level (below 55): 15-20%. Pay special attention to proof structure and logical flow. Students should demonstrate university-level mathematical maturity. Provide specific feedback on proof technique and suggest areas for improvement.

title: Introduction to Programming Languages Discussion
description: Students will participate in a structured discussion comparing programming paradigms and their real-world applications, demonstrating understanding of different programming approaches and their appropriate use cases.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and explain key characteristics of different programming paradigms (procedural, object-oriented, functional)
Analyze and compare the strengths and weaknesses of various programming languages
Demonstrate understanding of how programming language choice affects software development
rubric_criteria: Initial Post Quality (25 points): Demonstrates clear understanding of programming paradigms with specific examples, uses proper terminology, and provides thoughtful analysis of at least two different paradigms

Response Posts Quality (25 points): Provides meaningful responses to at least two classmates with constructive feedback, asks clarifying questions, or adds relevant insights that advance the discussion

Use of Examples and Evidence (25 points): Incorporates specific programming language examples, references course materials or external sources appropriately, and connects theoretical concepts to practical applications

Communication and Engagement (25 points): Uses clear, professional writing with proper grammar and formatting, responds in a timely manner throughout the discussion period, and maintains respectful academic discourse
instructions:
This week's discussion focuses on programming paradigms and language selection. Your task is to compare different programming approaches and explain when each might be most appropriate.

Initial Post Requirements (due by Wednesday 11:59 PM):
1. Choose two programming paradigms from our course materials (procedural, object-oriented, functional, or declarative)
2. Explain the key characteristics of each paradigm in your own words
3. Provide a specific programming language example for each paradigm
4. Discuss one real-world scenario where each paradigm would be the best choice
5. Your post should be 300-400 words

Response Posts Requirements (due by Sunday 11:59 PM):
1. Respond meaningfully to at least two classmates' posts
2. Each response should be 100-150 words
3. Consider asking questions like: 'Have you considered how [paradigm] handles [specific problem]?' or 'What challenges might arise when using [language] for [scenario]?'
4. Share additional examples or alternative perspectives

Submission Format:
- Post directly in the course discussion forum
- Use clear paragraph structure
- Include a descriptive subject line for your initial post
- Cite any external sources using APA format

Remember to check spelling and grammar before posting, and maintain a professional, respectful tone throughout all interactions.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for technical accuracy - students should correctly identify paradigm characteristics without major misconceptions. Look for specific, appropriate examples rather than vague generalizations. Quality responses should go beyond simple agreement; reward posts that introduce new perspectives or ask thoughtful questions. Deduct points for late submissions (5 points per day late). Common issues include confusing programming languages with paradigms, overly general examples, and superficial responses. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level work (90-100), 60% B-level work (80-89), 20% C-level or below. Provide specific feedback on technical content and suggest resources for students showing misconceptions about programming concepts.

title: Predictive Analytics Business Solution Presentation
description: Students will develop and present a complete data science solution to a real-world business problem, demonstrating their ability to communicate technical findings to non-technical stakeholders. The presentation must include problem definition, data analysis methodology, model development, results interpretation, and actionable business recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply statistical modeling and machine learning techniques to solve business problems
Communicate complex data science concepts effectively to diverse audiences
Demonstrate proficiency in data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model evaluation
Translate analytical findings into actionable business insights and recommendations
Critically evaluate model performance and limitations in real-world contexts
rubric_criteria: Problem Definition & Data Understanding (25 points): Clear articulation of business problem, appropriate dataset selection, thorough exploratory data analysis with meaningful insights, proper identification of target variables and success metrics

Technical Implementation & Methodology (25 points): Appropriate preprocessing techniques, justified model selection, proper feature engineering, correct implementation of algorithms, adequate model validation and performance evaluation using relevant metrics

Results Interpretation & Business Impact (25 points): Accurate interpretation of model outputs, clear explanation of feature importance, quantified business impact, realistic implementation timeline, identification of potential risks and limitations

Presentation Quality & Communication (25 points): Clear slide design appropriate for business audience, effective use of visualizations, confident delivery within time limits, professional responses to questions, minimal technical jargon with clear explanations when necessary
instructions: Select a publicly available dataset relevant to a business domain (e.g., customer churn, sales forecasting, fraud detection, marketing optimization). Your 15-minute presentation should follow this structure: (1) Business Problem (3 minutes): Define the problem, explain why it matters, and identify key stakeholders. (2) Data & Methodology (4 minutes): Describe your dataset, preprocessing steps, and chosen analytical approach. Use visualizations to highlight key data insights. (3) Technical Solution (4 minutes): Explain your model selection rationale, key features, and validation approach. Present performance metrics clearly. (4) Business Recommendations (4 minutes): Translate technical findings into specific, actionable recommendations with estimated impact and implementation steps. Submit your presentation slides (PDF) and a technical appendix (max 3 pages) containing code snippets, detailed model metrics, and assumptions 24 hours before your presentation date. Be prepared for questions about methodology choices, alternative approaches, and practical implementation challenges. Your audience consists of business managers with limited technical background, so focus on insights and recommendations rather than technical details.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor while prioritizing communication effectiveness. Excellent presentations (90-100) demonstrate sophisticated analysis with clear business value. Good presentations (80-89) show solid technical work but may lack depth in business application. Satisfactory presentations (70-79) meet basic requirements but have gaps in analysis or communication. Pay attention to: appropriate complexity for intermediate level, realistic business scenarios, proper statistical interpretation, and professional presentation skills. Common issues include: over-technical explanations, unrealistic business recommendations, insufficient model validation, poor time management, and inadequate preparation for Q&A. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level, 35% B-level, 40% C-level, 10% below C-level.

title: Advanced Mathematical Modeling and Analysis Portfolio
description: Students create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating mastery of advanced mathematical concepts through real-world problem solving, including calculus applications, statistical analysis, linear algebra, and mathematical proof techniques. The portfolio showcases mathematical reasoning, computational skills, and communication abilities across multiple mathematical domains.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced calculus concepts (derivatives, integrals, differential equations) to solve complex real-world problems
Demonstrate proficiency in statistical analysis and probability theory with practical applications
Utilize linear algebra techniques for multidimensional problem solving
Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using various proof techniques
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations and visual representations
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy and Rigor (25 points): Correct application of mathematical concepts, accurate calculations, proper use of mathematical notation, and logical consistency throughout all portfolio components

Problem-Solving and Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated problem-solving strategies, makes appropriate mathematical connections, shows deep understanding of underlying concepts, and provides insightful analysis of results

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Clear mathematical writing, effective use of graphs/diagrams, proper organization of ideas, appropriate mathematical vocabulary, and professional portfolio formatting

Real-World Applications and Connections (25 points): Selects meaningful real-world problems, demonstrates relevance of mathematical concepts, makes connections between different mathematical domains, and shows understanding of limitations and assumptions
instructions: Create a portfolio containing four distinct components: (1) Calculus Application Project - Select a real-world optimization or rate-of-change problem, solve using calculus techniques, and analyze results with graphs and interpretations (3-4 pages); (2) Statistical Analysis Report - Collect or use existing data to perform hypothesis testing, regression analysis, or probability modeling with detailed methodology and conclusions (4-5 pages); (3) Linear Algebra Case Study - Apply matrix operations, eigenvalues, or systems of equations to solve a multidimensional problem from engineering, economics, or computer science (3-4 pages); (4) Mathematical Proof Section - Construct two formal proofs using different techniques (direct, contradiction, induction, etc.) with complete justifications and explanations (2-3 pages). Each component must include: problem statement, mathematical methodology, detailed solutions with work shown, analysis of results, and reflection on mathematical concepts learned. Use proper mathematical notation, include relevant graphs/tables, and maintain professional formatting throughout. Submit as a single PDF with table of contents, page numbers, and bibliography of sources used. Portfolio should total 12-16 pages excluding appendices.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first, then assess depth of understanding through explanations and connections made. Look for evidence of independent thinking rather than textbook mimicry. Deduct points for computational errors, but focus primarily on conceptual understanding and reasoning processes. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level work (90-100 points), 35% B-level work (80-89 points), 35% C-level work (70-79 points), 15% below C-level. Common issues include: insufficient real-world context, lack of mathematical rigor in explanations, poor organization, and failure to connect different mathematical concepts. Provide specific feedback on mathematical reasoning and suggest areas for deeper exploration.

title: Distributed Systems Consensus Algorithm Implementation and Analysis
description: Students will implement a Raft consensus algorithm for a distributed key-value store, conduct performance analysis under various failure scenarios, and provide comprehensive documentation of their system's behavior and theoretical foundations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement fault-tolerant distributed systems using consensus algorithms
Analyze system performance under network partitions and node failures
Apply theoretical knowledge of distributed systems to practical implementation challenges
Evaluate trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance in distributed systems
rubric_criteria: Implementation Quality (25 points): Correct Raft algorithm implementation with leader election, log replication, and safety guarantees. Code demonstrates proper handling of edge cases, clean architecture, and efficient data structures.

Experimental Design and Analysis (25 points): Comprehensive testing framework with systematic evaluation of failure scenarios, network partitions, and performance metrics. Statistical analysis of results with appropriate visualization and interpretation.

Technical Documentation (25 points): Clear system architecture documentation, algorithm explanation with state diagrams, API specification, and thorough analysis of experimental results with theoretical justification.

System Robustness and Performance (25 points): Demonstration of fault tolerance under various failure modes, performance optimization, scalability analysis, and proper resource management with memory/CPU profiling.
instructions:
Implement a distributed key-value store using the Raft consensus algorithm with at least 5 nodes. Your implementation must handle leader election, log replication, and maintain strong consistency guarantees. The system should support basic operations (GET, PUT, DELETE) through a REST API.

Technical Requirements: Use any programming language (Python, Java, Go, or C++ recommended). Implement network communication using TCP sockets or HTTP. Include configuration files for cluster setup and provide Docker containerization. Your code must be version-controlled with clear commit history.

Experimental Component: Design and execute experiments testing: (1) Leader election under various failure scenarios, (2) Log replication with network delays and partitions, (3) Performance analysis measuring throughput and latency, (4) Recovery behavior after node failures. Collect quantitative data and provide statistical analysis.

Deliverables: Submit source code with build instructions, comprehensive README with architecture overview, experimental report (8-10 pages) including methodology, results, and analysis, and a 10-minute video demonstration showing system operation under failure scenarios.

Submission Format: Create a GitHub repository with organized directory structure. Include all source code, documentation, experimental data, and video link. Provide clear instructions for system setup and experiment reproduction. Submit repository link and ensure all team members have contribution history visible.
grading_notes: Evaluate code functionality through automated testing and manual review. Check for proper Raft implementation by testing leader election, log consistency, and safety properties. Assessment should verify experimental reproducibility - students must provide scripts and data for experiment replication. Common issues include incomplete failure handling, inefficient network communication, and insufficient experimental rigor. Grade distribution typically: 15% excellent implementations with novel optimizations, 60% solid implementations meeting all requirements, 20% adequate implementations with minor issues, 5% incomplete or significantly flawed work. Deduct points for late submissions (10% per day) and non-functional code. Bonus points (up to 10) for exceptional performance optimizations or additional features like dynamic membership changes.

title: Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Data Types, Visualization, and Basic Statistics
description: A comprehensive quiz assessing fundamental data science concepts including data types and structures, basic statistical measures, data visualization principles, and the data science process. Students will demonstrate understanding through multiple choice, short answer, and practical application questions.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify different data types (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) and data structures
Calculate and interpret basic statistical measures (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Select appropriate visualization types for different data scenarios
Describe the steps of the data science process and methodology
Interpret basic data visualizations and draw conclusions from datasets
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Structures Knowledge (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, understands structured vs unstructured data, and recognizes appropriate data formats for different scenarios
Statistical Concepts Understanding (25 points): Accurately calculates basic statistics, interprets measures of central tendency and variability, and understands their practical applications
Data Visualization Principles (25 points): Selects appropriate chart types for different data types, understands visualization best practices, and can interpret common graphs and charts
Data Science Process and Application (25 points): Demonstrates understanding of the data science lifecycle, problem-solving approach, and can apply concepts to real-world scenarios
instructions: This quiz consists of 25 questions across four main areas of data science fundamentals. You will have 60 minutes to complete all sections. The quiz includes: 15 multiple-choice questions (2 points each), 5 short-answer questions (4 points each), and 5 practical application questions (10 points each). Read each question carefully and select the best answer for multiple-choice items. For short-answer questions, provide concise but complete responses in 1-2 sentences. For practical application questions, show your work where calculations are involved and explain your reasoning clearly. You may use a calculator but no other external resources. Questions cover: identification of data types in given scenarios, calculation of basic statistical measures from small datasets, selection of appropriate visualization types for specific data analysis goals, sequencing steps in the data science process, and interpretation of simple charts and graphs. Partial credit will be awarded for practical application questions that show correct methodology even if the final answer contains minor errors. Submit your completed quiz through the learning management system. Ensure all questions are answered before submission as you cannot return to modify responses once submitted.
grading_notes: Award full credit for multiple-choice questions only when the correct answer is selected. For short-answer questions, accept alternative wording that demonstrates understanding of core concepts. Common mistakes to watch for: confusing ordinal vs interval data types, incorrectly calculating standard deviation, choosing inappropriate chart types for categorical data, and missing key steps in the data science process. For practical application questions, award partial credit using this breakdown: 40% for correct approach/methodology, 40% for accurate calculations/analysis, 20% for clear explanation. Expect score distribution: 90-100 points (A-level, 20-25% of students), 80-89 points (B-level, 40-45% of students), 70-79 points (C-level, 25-30% of students), below 70 points (5-10% of students). Flag scores below 60% for additional review and potential remediation. Pay particular attention to consistent errors across statistical calculations as this may indicate need for additional instruction in mathematical concepts.

title: Mathematical Modeling Project: Optimizing City Transportation
description: Students will create a comprehensive mathematical model to analyze and optimize a city's public transportation system, incorporating linear programming, statistical analysis, and cost-benefit calculations to propose evidence-based improvements.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply linear programming techniques to solve real-world optimization problems
Collect, analyze, and interpret data using statistical methods and graphical representations
Construct mathematical models that incorporate multiple variables and constraints
Communicate mathematical reasoning and solutions clearly through written and visual presentations
Evaluate the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of proposed solutions using mathematical analysis
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Model Development (25 points): Creates accurate linear programming model with clearly defined variables, objective function, and realistic constraints; demonstrates understanding of optimization principles

Data Analysis and Statistical Methods (25 points): Collects relevant data from credible sources, applies appropriate statistical techniques, creates meaningful graphs and charts, interprets results accurately

Problem-Solving and Calculations (25 points): Shows complete work for all calculations, uses correct mathematical procedures, arrives at reasonable solutions, addresses optimization questions thoroughly

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Provides clear written explanations, uses proper mathematical notation, creates professional visual aids, presents feasible recommendations with supporting evidence
instructions: You will analyze a city's public transportation system and develop mathematical solutions to improve efficiency and reduce costs. Choose a real city with available transportation data (population 100,000-500,000 recommended). Your project must include: (1) Problem Statement: Identify specific transportation challenges using data on ridership, routes, costs, and service gaps. (2) Mathematical Model: Develop a linear programming model to optimize either route planning, resource allocation, or scheduling. Define variables (minimum 4), create an objective function, and establish at least 6 realistic constraints. (3) Data Collection: Gather actual data from city websites, transportation authorities, or census data. Include ridership statistics, operational costs, demographic information, and current service metrics. (4) Analysis: Solve your optimization problem using graphical or algebraic methods. Create visual representations of your data and solutions using graphs, charts, or maps. Calculate cost-benefit ratios for your proposed changes. (5) Recommendations: Present 3-5 specific, implementable recommendations supported by your mathematical analysis. Include estimated costs, expected benefits, and potential challenges. Deliverables: 8-10 page written report, Excel spreadsheet with calculations and data, 10-minute presentation with visual aids. Submit all components as a single PDF plus Excel file. Due date allows for peer review session in week 3. Citations required for all data sources using APA format.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy before conceptual understanding. Award partial credit for correct setup even if calculations contain minor errors. Strong projects will show creativity in constraint development and demonstrate clear understanding of optimization trade-offs. Watch for unrealistic constraints or oversimplified models. Data should be current (within 5 years) and from credible sources. Deduct points for insufficient citations or questionable data sources. Presentation component should demonstrate student understanding beyond reading from slides. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90+), 30% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 15% below C-level. Common issues include: overly complex models that students cannot solve, insufficient constraints leading to unrealistic solutions, poor data visualization, and recommendations not supported by mathematical analysis. Provide feedback on mathematical notation and professional presentation standards.

title: Advanced Algorithms and Data Structures Comprehensive Exam
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of advanced algorithmic concepts through problem-solving, complexity analysis, and implementation design. The exam covers dynamic programming, graph algorithms, advanced data structures, and algorithmic optimization techniques.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze and design efficient algorithms for complex computational problems
Apply advanced data structures to optimize algorithm performance
Evaluate time and space complexity using asymptotic notation
Implement and optimize dynamic programming solutions
Design and analyze graph algorithms for real-world applications
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Design and Correctness (25 points): Demonstrates ability to design correct algorithms that solve given problems completely, with proper handling of edge cases and clear logical flow
Complexity Analysis (25 points): Provides accurate time and space complexity analysis using Big-O notation, with detailed justification and consideration of best/average/worst cases
Implementation Strategy (25 points): Shows detailed pseudocode or implementation plans that are efficient, readable, and demonstrate understanding of data structure operations and algorithm mechanics
Problem-Solving and Optimization (25 points): Exhibits advanced problem-solving skills, identifies optimization opportunities, compares alternative approaches, and justifies design decisions
instructions: This exam consists of four major problems requiring comprehensive solutions. For each problem, you must: (1) Provide a complete algorithm design with clear explanation of your approach, (2) Write detailed pseudocode or implementation outline, (3) Perform thorough complexity analysis including time and space requirements, and (4) Discuss any optimization considerations or alternative approaches. Show all work and reasoning. Problem 1: Design a dynamic programming solution for the optimal binary search tree problem, given key frequencies. Problem 2: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm modification to find the k-shortest paths between two vertices in a weighted graph. Problem 3: Design a data structure supporting range minimum queries with updates in logarithmic time, explaining your choice of underlying structure. Problem 4: Solve the maximum flow problem using Ford-Fulkerson method, then modify to handle minimum cost maximum flow. Each solution should include algorithm description, pseudocode, complexity analysis, and example walkthrough. Submit handwritten work clearly or typed solutions with proper formatting. Partial credit available for incomplete but correct reasoning.
grading_notes: Grade each criterion independently using the 25-point scale. Award full points (22-25) for exceptional work exceeding expectations, good points (18-21) for solid understanding with minor gaps, acceptable points (14-17) for basic competency with some errors, and needs improvement (0-13) for significant deficiencies. Common issues: students often struggle with space complexity analysis, forget edge cases in algorithm design, or provide incomplete pseudocode. Look for creative optimizations and clear communication of ideas. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90+), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below C-level. Provide specific feedback on algorithmic thinking process and suggest resources for improvement areas.

title: Ethical AI and Bias Mitigation in Production Systems: A Critical Analysis Discussion
description: Students will conduct an in-depth analysis of a real-world case study involving algorithmic bias, evaluate the ethical implications, and propose comprehensive mitigation strategies for production deployment. This assessment requires synthesis of technical knowledge, ethical reasoning, and practical implementation considerations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Evaluate and identify sources of bias in machine learning models and datasets
Apply ethical frameworks to assess the societal impact of AI systems
Design comprehensive bias detection and mitigation strategies for production environments
Communicate complex technical and ethical concepts to diverse stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Technical Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of bias types, statistical measures for bias detection, and technical root causes. Correctly identifies at least 3 different bias sources with specific examples and quantitative analysis where applicable.

Ethical Framework Application (25 points): Applies established ethical frameworks (utilitarian, deontological, virtue ethics, or fairness principles) to evaluate harm and benefits. Shows nuanced understanding of competing values and stakeholder perspectives.

Mitigation Strategy Design (25 points): Proposes comprehensive, technically feasible solutions including pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing approaches. Addresses monitoring, governance, and continuous improvement in production systems.

Critical Reasoning and Communication (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated argumentation, acknowledges limitations and trade-offs, uses appropriate technical terminology, and presents ideas clearly for both technical and non-technical audiences.
instructions: Select one of the provided case studies (or propose your own with instructor approval): hiring algorithms, criminal justice risk assessment, healthcare diagnostic systems, or financial lending models. Your analysis must include: (1) A technical examination identifying specific types of bias present (sampling, representation, measurement, algorithmic, evaluation bias), supported by evidence from the case or similar real-world examples. Include relevant metrics such as demographic parity, equalized odds, or calibration measures. (2) An ethical analysis using at least two established frameworks to evaluate the system's impact on affected communities, considering both intended and unintended consequences. Address questions of fairness, autonomy, transparency, and accountability. (3) A detailed mitigation strategy covering the entire ML pipeline: data collection and preprocessing techniques, algorithmic modifications during training, post-processing adjustments, ongoing monitoring systems, and governance structures. Your recommendations must be technically implementable and include specific tools, methodologies, or frameworks. (4) A reflection on trade-offs between different fairness metrics, performance implications of your proposed solutions, and potential limitations or risks of your mitigation approach. Format your response as a structured analysis (2000-2500 words) with clear sections, citations to relevant literature, and executive summary. Include visualizations, pseudocode, or technical diagrams where appropriate. Submit as PDF with properly formatted references.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of expert-level thinking including: nuanced understanding that perfect fairness is often impossible and requires trade-offs; recognition that bias mitigation is an ongoing process, not a one-time fix; awareness of intersectionality and multiple protected attributes; understanding of regulatory and legal contexts (GDPR, fair lending laws, etc.). Common issues to deduct points for: oversimplified solutions that ignore technical constraints; failure to consider stakeholder perspectives beyond the technical team; proposing mitigation strategies without addressing implementation challenges; inadequate discussion of monitoring and maintenance. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 30% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 15% below C-level. A-level responses should demonstrate original thinking and synthesis across technical, ethical, and practical domains.

title: Basic Shapes and Their Properties - Interactive Presentation
description: Students will create and deliver a 5-minute presentation explaining the properties of basic geometric shapes (triangle, square, rectangle, circle) using visual aids and real-world examples to demonstrate understanding of fundamental geometry concepts.
estimated_time: 45 minutes (30 min preparation + 5 min presentation + 10 min Q&A)
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and name basic geometric shapes (triangle, square, rectangle, circle)
Describe key properties of each shape (number of sides, angles, symmetry)
Recognize geometric shapes in real-world objects and environments
Communicate mathematical concepts clearly using appropriate vocabulary
rubric_criteria: Content Accuracy (25 points): Correctly identifies all four shapes, states accurate number of sides/vertices, describes basic properties without mathematical errors
Real-World Connections (25 points): Provides at least 2 clear, relevant examples of each shape found in everyday life, explains why objects match the geometric shape
Visual Presentation (25 points): Uses clear, well-organized visual aids (drawings, props, or slides), shapes are drawn accurately, presentation is neat and easy to follow
Communication Skills (25 points): Speaks clearly and confidently, uses proper mathematical vocabulary, maintains eye contact, completes presentation within 4-6 minute timeframe
instructions: You will create and deliver a 5-minute presentation about four basic geometric shapes: triangle, square, rectangle, and circle. Your presentation must include: 1) A clear introduction stating which shapes you will discuss, 2) For each shape, explain how many sides it has, describe its key properties (such as equal sides, right angles, or curves), and show or describe at least 2 real-world examples where you can find this shape, 3) Visual aids such as hand-drawn pictures, cut-out shapes, household objects, or simple slides to help illustrate your points, 4) A brief conclusion summarizing what makes each shape unique. Practice your presentation beforehand and aim for 4-6 minutes total speaking time. You may use note cards with key points, but avoid reading directly from them. During your presentation, speak loudly and clearly so everyone can hear, make eye contact with your audience, and be prepared to answer 1-2 simple questions about shapes afterward. Submit any visual materials (drawings, slides) along with a brief outline of your presentation 10 minutes before your speaking slot.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical accuracy first - ensure students correctly identify basic properties without errors. Look for genuine understanding rather than memorized facts by observing how they explain real-world connections. Common issues include: confusing rectangles and squares (squares are special rectangles), forgetting that circles have no sides/vertices, using unclear or inaccurate drawings. Award full visual presentation points for effort and clarity even if artistic ability is limited. For communication, prioritize mathematical vocabulary usage and content delivery over presentation polish. Grade distribution expectation: 20% should earn 90-100 points, 60% should earn 75-89 points, 20% should earn 60-74 points. Provide specific feedback on one strength and one area for improvement for each student.

title: Software Development Portfolio: Multi-Feature Web Application
description: Students will design, implement, and document a complete web application demonstrating proficiency in full-stack development, database integration, user interface design, and software engineering best practices. The portfolio will showcase technical skills, problem-solving abilities, and professional development practices.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply software engineering principles to design and implement a complete application
Demonstrate proficiency in both front-end and back-end web technologies
Integrate databases effectively with proper data modeling and querying
Implement user authentication and security best practices
Document code and create professional technical documentation
Use version control systems and collaborative development workflows
rubric_criteria: Technical Implementation (25 points): Application functionality, code quality, proper use of frameworks/libraries, error handling, security implementation, and adherence to coding standards
Database Design and Integration (25 points): Appropriate data modeling, efficient queries, proper relationships, data validation, and successful CRUD operations with error handling
User Interface and Experience (25 points): Responsive design, intuitive navigation, accessibility considerations, visual appeal, and user feedback mechanisms
Documentation and Professionalism (25 points): Clear README file, code comments, API documentation, deployment instructions, version control usage, and overall project organization
instructions: Create a full-stack web application that solves a real-world problem of your choice. Your application must include: (1) A responsive front-end using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (framework optional), (2) A back-end API using your preferred server-side language/framework, (3) Database integration with at least 3 related tables, (4) User authentication and authorization system, (5) At least 5 distinct features/functionalities. Submit your portfolio as a GitHub repository containing: complete source code with clear folder structure, comprehensive README.md file explaining your project, setup/installation instructions, API documentation, database schema diagram, deployed application URL (use free hosting services like Heroku, Netlify, or Vercel), and a 3-5 minute video demonstration showcasing key features. Your code must be well-commented, follow consistent naming conventions, and include basic error handling. The application should be fully functional with no critical bugs. Document any known limitations or future enhancements in your README. Ensure your repository commit history shows consistent development progress over the project timeline.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical implementation by testing all features thoroughly - check for edge cases, security vulnerabilities, and code organization. Look for proper separation of concerns, DRY principles, and appropriate use of design patterns. For database assessment, examine the schema design logic, query efficiency, and data integrity measures. UI evaluation should consider both desktop and mobile experiences. Documentation quality significantly impacts grades - incomplete READMEs or poor code comments result in major point deductions. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 40% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 10% below C-level. Common issues include: inadequate error handling, poor security practices, missing responsive design, insufficient documentation, and last-minute rushed commits. Bonus consideration for creative problem-solving, advanced features, or exceptional code quality.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Lab Report: Customer Churn Prediction with MLOps Integration
description: Students will build, evaluate, and deploy a complete machine learning pipeline for customer churn prediction, documenting their methodology, results, and deployment strategy in a comprehensive lab report that demonstrates mastery of advanced data science practices.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model selection
Apply advanced evaluation techniques including cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and model interpretability methods
Demonstrate proficiency in MLOps practices including version control, automated testing, and model deployment
Communicate technical findings effectively through data visualization and written analysis
rubric_criteria: Data Engineering & Preprocessing (25 points): Quality of data cleaning, feature engineering techniques, handling of missing values/outliers, and data pipeline design with proper validation splits

Model Development & Evaluation (25 points): Implementation of multiple algorithms, systematic hyperparameter tuning, appropriate evaluation metrics, cross-validation methodology, and model comparison analysis
MLOps Implementation & Deployment (25 points): Code organization and documentation, version control usage, automated testing implementation, model deployment strategy, and monitoring/logging setup

Technical Communication & Analysis (25 points): Quality of written report, effectiveness of data visualizations, interpretation of results, business impact analysis, and identification of limitations/future improvements
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset, develop a comprehensive machine learning solution to predict customer churn. Your submission must include: (1) A Jupyter notebook with complete data analysis, preprocessing pipeline, and model development workflow, (2) Python scripts for production-ready model training and inference, (3) A detailed lab report (8-10 pages) documenting your methodology, results, and deployment strategy, and (4) All supporting files including requirements.txt, configuration files, and deployment scripts. Technical requirements: Implement at least 3 different algorithms (must include ensemble methods), perform comprehensive feature engineering with domain knowledge application, conduct proper statistical validation with appropriate metrics, implement automated testing for key functions, create reproducible results with version control, and deploy your final model using containerization. Your report should include executive summary, literature review of churn prediction techniques, detailed methodology section, results analysis with statistical significance testing, business impact assessment with actionable recommendations, and thorough discussion of model limitations and ethical considerations. All code must be well-documented with docstrings, include error handling, and follow PEP 8 standards. Submit via GitHub repository with clear README and organized file structure.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should follow: 90-100 (Exceptional work demonstrating mastery beyond course requirements), 80-89 (Proficient work meeting all advanced requirements), 70-79 (Satisfactory work with minor gaps in advanced concepts), Below 70 (Needs improvement in core areas). Key evaluation focus areas: assess code quality and reproducibility by running submitted notebooks, evaluate statistical rigor in model validation and hypothesis testing, check for proper implementation of MLOps practices including CI/CD concepts, verify business relevance and practical applicability of recommendations. Common issues to watch for: inadequate treatment of class imbalance in churn datasets, overfitting due to improper validation methodology, lack of feature importance analysis and model interpretability, insufficient discussion of ethical implications and bias considerations, poor code organization that hinders reproducibility. Deduct points for: missing automated tests (-5 points), inadequate documentation (-5 points), results that cannot be reproduced (-10 points), failure to address business context (-10 points). Provide detailed feedback on technical implementation choices and suggest improvements for production deployment scenarios.

title: Mathematical Modeling and Analysis Discussion: Real-World Optimization Problems
description: Students will engage in collaborative mathematical discourse by analyzing, modeling, and solving complex optimization problems from real-world scenarios. This assessment evaluates students' ability to translate practical problems into mathematical frameworks, justify solution approaches, and critically evaluate alternative methods through structured peer discussions.
estimated_time: 3-4 hours (initial analysis: 90 minutes, discussion participation: 120 minutes, reflection: 30 minutes)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced calculus and optimization techniques to solve complex real-world problems
Construct and analyze mathematical models using multiple variable functions, constraints, and boundary conditions
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through written explanations and peer discourse
Evaluate and critique alternative solution methods using mathematical justification
Synthesize connections between theoretical mathematical concepts and practical applications
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Modeling and Setup (25 points): Accurately identifies variables, constraints, and objective functions; correctly translates real-world problem into mathematical framework; demonstrates understanding of problem scope and limitations

Solution Method and Execution (25 points): Selects appropriate optimization techniques (Lagrange multipliers, linear programming, calculus-based methods); executes calculations correctly; shows complete mathematical work with proper notation

Discussion Participation and Mathematical Communication (25 points): Provides substantive responses to peers with mathematical evidence; asks probing questions that advance mathematical understanding; explains reasoning clearly using appropriate mathematical language and notation

Critical Analysis and Reflection (25 points): Evaluates strengths and weaknesses of different approaches; identifies assumptions and their impact on solutions; discusses practical implications and validates results in real-world context
instructions: You will work with a complex optimization scenario involving resource allocation for a renewable energy company planning solar panel installations across multiple locations with varying constraints. Begin by individually analyzing the provided case study, which includes cost functions, efficiency variables, geographical constraints, and regulatory requirements. Develop a mathematical model identifying all relevant variables, objective functions, and constraints. Choose and implement an appropriate optimization method, showing all mathematical work. Post your initial solution approach in the discussion forum within 48 hours, including your mathematical model, chosen solution method, complete calculations, and interpretation of results. Over the following week, engage with at least three classmates' solutions by providing mathematical feedback, suggesting alternative approaches, or identifying potential errors. Your responses must include specific mathematical references and, where applicable, worked examples of alternative methods. Address at least two responses from peers regarding your own solution, defending your approach or acknowledging improvements with mathematical justification. Conclude with a 300-word reflection comparing different solution methods encountered in the discussions, analyzing which approaches were most effective for this problem type, and discussing how the mathematical solutions translate to practical business decisions. All mathematical work must be clearly formatted using proper notation, and any graphs or visual aids should be appropriately labeled and referenced in your explanations.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first, then communication quality. Look for proper use of optimization techniques - common errors include incorrect constraint setup, misapplication of Lagrange multipliers, and failure to check boundary conditions. Strong responses will show multiple solution approaches or verify results using different methods. In discussion evaluation, prioritize mathematical substance over quantity - one detailed, mathematically rigorous response is better than multiple superficial posts. Watch for students who demonstrate understanding of when different optimization methods are appropriate. Expect 15-20% of students to achieve full points in mathematical execution, 60-70% to show solid understanding with minor errors, and 10-15% to struggle with model setup. Grade discussions holistically - students who ask insightful mathematical questions or identify subtle errors in peers' work should receive high marks even if their initial solution has minor flaws. Reflection quality varies significantly - look for evidence that students can compare methodological approaches and understand practical implications of mathematical assumptions.

title: Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture Design and Defense
description: Students will design and present a comprehensive distributed systems architecture for a real-world application, demonstrating mastery of scalability, fault tolerance, consistency models, and system trade-offs. This includes a 25-minute technical presentation followed by a 10-minute Q&A session with expert-level questioning.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed systems architectures using appropriate patterns and technologies
Analyze and justify trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (CAP theorem)
Implement fault tolerance and disaster recovery strategies in distributed environments
Evaluate performance characteristics and bottlenecks in complex distributed systems
Communicate complex technical designs effectively to expert audiences
rubric_criteria: Architecture Design & Technical Depth (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of distributed systems patterns, appropriate technology selection, comprehensive system design including data flow, service boundaries, and integration points

Trade-off Analysis & Justification (25 points): Provides thorough analysis of CAP theorem implications, performance vs. consistency trade-offs, cost-benefit analysis of architectural decisions, and alternative approach considerations

Fault Tolerance & Scalability (25 points): Designs robust error handling, implements appropriate redundancy and backup strategies, addresses horizontal and vertical scaling approaches, and includes monitoring and observability solutions

Presentation Quality & Expert Defense (25 points): Delivers clear, well-structured presentation with appropriate technical depth, effectively handles expert-level questions during Q&A, demonstrates confident mastery of subject matter
instructions: Select a real-world application domain (e.g., global financial trading platform, multiplayer gaming infrastructure, IoT sensor network, streaming media service) and design a complete distributed systems architecture. Your presentation must include: (1) System requirements and constraints analysis, (2) High-level architecture diagram with detailed component descriptions, (3) Data storage and management strategy including database selection and sharding approaches, (4) Communication protocols and message passing mechanisms, (5) Load balancing and auto-scaling implementations, (6) Security architecture and access control, (7) Monitoring, logging, and alerting systems, (8) Disaster recovery and business continuity plans, (9) Performance benchmarks and capacity planning, (10) Cost analysis and operational considerations. Prepare for expert-level questions covering implementation details, alternative approaches, failure scenarios, and emerging technologies. Submit architecture diagrams, technical specifications, and presentation slides 48 hours before presentation date. Use professional presentation software and include live system demonstrations or detailed mockups where applicable.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical accuracy and depth - expect graduate-level understanding of distributed systems concepts. Look for innovative solutions and creative problem-solving, not just textbook approaches. During Q&A, probe understanding of implementation details, scalability limits, and edge cases. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations: 90-100 points for exceptional work showing research-level insight, 80-89 for solid professional-grade designs, 70-79 for adequate but basic solutions, below 70 for insufficient technical depth. Pay special attention to how students handle unexpected questions and their ability to think through problems in real-time. Common issues include oversimplified fault tolerance, inadequate consideration of network partitions, unrealistic performance assumptions, and poor understanding of consistency models.

title: Data Science Foundations Portfolio: Exploratory Data Analysis Project
description: Students will complete a comprehensive exploratory data analysis (EDA) project demonstrating fundamental data science skills including data cleaning, visualization, statistical analysis, and insight communication using a real-world dataset.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply data cleaning and preprocessing techniques to handle missing values, outliers, and inconsistent data formats
Create meaningful data visualizations using appropriate chart types to reveal patterns and relationships
Perform basic statistical analysis including descriptive statistics and correlation analysis
Communicate data-driven insights effectively through written summaries and visual presentations
rubric_criteria: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing (25 points): Properly identifies and handles missing values, outliers, and data quality issues. Code is well-documented with clear explanations of cleaning decisions.

Data Visualization (25 points): Creates 5-7 appropriate and effective visualizations (histograms, scatter plots, bar charts, etc.) with proper labels, titles, and formatting. Visualizations clearly support analysis goals.

Statistical Analysis (25 points): Calculates and interprets descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles). Identifies correlations and patterns in the data with statistical backing.

Communication and Documentation (25 points): Provides clear written insights and conclusions. Code is well-commented and organized. Final report is professional and includes actionable recommendations based on findings.

instructions:

Create at least 2 engineered features that could improve model performance (e.g., tenure categories, total charges per service). Split data into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets.

Technical requirements: Use object-oriented programming with at least one main Task class. Implement command-line argument parsing (using argparse or similar). Store data persistently in files (JSON recommended). Include proper error handling for invalid inputs and file operations. Your submission should include: all source code files, a requirements.txt file if using external libraries, a comprehensive README.md with setup and usage instructions, and at least 5 sample tasks demonstrating different features. Code should be well-commented and follow consistent formatting. Include a brief reflection (200-300 words) discussing your design decisions, challenges faced, and potential improvements. Submit as a ZIP file or provide a GitHub repository link.
grading_notes: Focus on functionality first - the application should work as specified without crashes. Look for proper OOP implementation; students often struggle with appropriate class design and method organization. Common issues include: inadequate error handling (especially file operations), poor command-line interface design, and insufficient data validation. Expect 15% A grades (90-100), 25% B grades (80-89), 40% C grades (70-79), 15% D grades (60-69), 5% F grades (below 60). Partial credit should be given for incomplete functionality if code demonstrates understanding of concepts. Pay attention to code organization and documentation - this significantly impacts maintainability. Extra credit (up to 5 points) can be awarded for additional features like task categories, recurring tasks, or data export functionality.

title: Advanced Predictive Modeling and Analysis Comprehensive Exam
description: A comprehensive practical examination where students build, validate, and interpret a complete machine learning pipeline using real-world data, demonstrating advanced data science skills including feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and business interpretation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced machine learning algorithms to solve complex real-world problems with appropriate model selection and justification
Perform comprehensive feature engineering, data preprocessing, and exploratory data analysis on messy, real-world datasets
Implement proper model validation techniques including cross-validation, bias-variance analysis, and performance metric selection
Interpret and communicate model results to both technical and non-technical stakeholders with actionable business insights
Demonstrate proficiency in handling imbalanced datasets, missing data, and model deployment considerations
rubric_criteria: Data Exploration and Preprocessing (25 points): Thorough EDA with meaningful visualizations, appropriate handling of missing values, outliers, and categorical variables, feature scaling and transformation, identification of data quality issues and biases

Feature Engineering and Model Development (25 points): Creative and justified feature creation, appropriate algorithm selection with reasoning, proper train/validation/test splits, implementation of multiple modeling approaches, hyperparameter optimization using grid search or Bayesian methods

Model Evaluation and Validation (25 points): Selection of appropriate evaluation metrics for the problem type, comprehensive cross-validation strategy, analysis of model performance across different data segments, bias-variance tradeoff discussion, overfitting detection and mitigation

Business Interpretation and Communication (25 points): Clear executive summary with actionable insights, model interpretability analysis (feature importance, SHAP values, etc.), discussion of model limitations and assumptions, recommendations for model deployment and monitoring, risk assessment and ethical considerations
instructions: You will receive a real-world dataset with a specific business problem to solve. Your task is to build a complete machine learning solution and present your findings. DATASET: You'll work with a customer churn prediction dataset containing 50,000+ records with mixed data types, missing values, and class imbalance.
