DELIVERABLES: Submit a Jupyter notebook with your complete analysis and a 2-page executive summary PDF. Your notebook must include: (1) Comprehensive EDA with at least 8 meaningful visualizations explaining data patterns, (2) Data preprocessing pipeline with clear justification for each step, (3) Implementation of at least 3 different ML algorithms with hyperparameter tuning, (4) Detailed model comparison using multiple evaluation metrics, (5) Feature importance analysis and model interpretability section, (6) Discussion of production deployment considerations. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: Use Python with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib/seaborn. Include proper code documentation and markdown explanations. Handle the class imbalance problem using at least two different techniques. Implement proper cross-validation (minimum 5-fold). EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: Must include business impact quantification, model performance summary, key insights, implementation roadmap, and risk mitigation strategies. Submit both files via the course portal by the end of the exam period.
grading_notes: Grade distributions should target: A (90-100): Exceptional work demonstrating mastery of advanced concepts, creative solutions, and clear business acumen. B (80-89): Solid technical implementation with good insights and proper methodology. C (70-79): Adequate technical skills but lacking depth in analysis or business understanding. Deduct points for: incorrect train/test procedures (-10), poor handling of class imbalance (-5), missing cross-validation (-5), inadequate EDA (-5), unclear business recommendations (-10). Look for: creative feature engineering, proper statistical testing, discussion of model assumptions, consideration of fairness/bias issues, realistic deployment timeline. Common issues: data leakage in preprocessing, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data, overly complex models without justification, lack of confidence intervals, missing discussion of model limitations. Bonus consideration (+5) for: advanced techniques like ensemble methods, thorough bias analysis, innovative visualization approaches.

title: Mathematical Modeling and Analysis: Real-World Optimization Problems
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing complex optimization problems from multiple mathematical perspectives, comparing solution approaches, and evaluating the mathematical reasoning and assumptions underlying different modeling strategies.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze and compare multiple mathematical approaches to complex optimization problems
Evaluate the validity and limitations of mathematical models in real-world contexts
Construct rigorous mathematical arguments and critique peers' reasoning
Apply advanced calculus, linear algebra, and statistical concepts to interdisciplinary problems
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Analysis and Problem-Solving (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of optimization techniques, correctly applies calculus/linear algebra concepts, shows sophisticated understanding of constraints and objective functions

Critical Evaluation and Comparison (25 points): Provides insightful analysis of different solution approaches, identifies strengths/weaknesses of various methods, evaluates assumptions and their implications

Mathematical Communication and Reasoning (25 points): Presents clear, logically structured arguments using proper mathematical notation, explains complex concepts accessibly, supports claims with rigorous justification

Peer Engagement and Discussion Quality (25 points): Responds thoughtfully to peers with substantive mathematical feedback, asks probing questions that advance discussion, builds constructively on others' ideas
instructions: You will participate in a week-long discussion analyzing three optimization scenarios: resource allocation in supply chain management, portfolio optimization under uncertainty, and energy distribution network design. Your participation requires: (1) Initial Analysis Post (due Day 2): Choose one scenario and provide a comprehensive mathematical analysis including problem formulation, solution approach, and validation of results. Use proper mathematical notation and cite relevant theorems or principles. Include graphs, equations, or diagrams as needed. (2) Comparative Analysis Post (due Day 4): Compare your chosen scenario with a peer's analysis of a different scenario. Identify common mathematical principles, discuss why different approaches were selected, and evaluate which method might be more robust or generalizable. (3) Critical Review Posts (due Day 6): Respond to at least two peers with detailed mathematical feedback. Point out potential errors, suggest alternative approaches, or extend their analysis to related problems. Each response should demonstrate your own mathematical understanding. All posts must show original thinking beyond simple agreement or disagreement. Use mathematical evidence to support your arguments and maintain professional academic discourse throughout.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - incorrect fundamental concepts should significantly impact scores regardless of presentation quality. Look for evidence of deep understanding rather than memorized procedures. Award full points in Mathematical Analysis only when students demonstrate mastery of advanced techniques with minimal errors. For Critical Evaluation, expect students to go beyond surface-level comparisons to examine underlying mathematical structures. Communication scores should reflect clarity for mathematically sophisticated audiences, not general audiences. Peer Engagement should show genuine mathematical discourse - simple praise or basic corrections earn lower scores. Expect 15-20% of students to earn 90+ points, with most students in the 75-85 range. Students scoring below 70 likely show fundamental conceptual gaps requiring additional support.

title: Mathematical Modeling Lab Report: Optimization of Solar Panel Array Configuration
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive mathematical analysis to determine the optimal configuration of solar panels for maximum energy output, considering constraints such as available space, seasonal sun angles, and shadowing effects. This lab integrates calculus, linear algebra, and statistical analysis to solve a real-world optimization problem.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve complex real-world problems
Use linear algebra methods to model spatial relationships and geometric constraints
Implement statistical analysis to validate mathematical models against empirical data
Communicate mathematical findings through formal technical writing with appropriate notation and visualization
Demonstrate proficiency in mathematical software tools for computation and graphing
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of calculus optimization methods, proper use of Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization, accurate linear algebra calculations for spatial transformations, and error-free statistical computations with appropriate significance testing

Problem Formulation and Modeling (25 points): Clear identification of decision variables, objective function, and constraints; realistic assumptions with proper justification; comprehensive consideration of all relevant factors including seasonal variations, geographical location, and physical limitations

Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Thorough sensitivity analysis of optimal solution, meaningful comparison of different configuration scenarios, proper validation of results against provided empirical data, and insightful discussion of practical implications and limitations of the mathematical model

Technical Communication and Presentation (25 points): Professional lab report format with proper mathematical notation, clear and accurate graphs/visualizations created using mathematical software, logical organization of content, precise technical writing, and comprehensive documentation of all computational procedures and code
instructions: You will analyze the optimal placement and orientation of solar panels on a rectangular rooftop measuring 50m × 30m. Using provided meteorological data for your assigned geographical location, determine the configuration that maximizes annual energy output. Your analysis must include: (1) Mathematical model using multivariable calculus to optimize panel angles and spacing, incorporating seasonal sun path variations; (2) Linear algebra approach to handle spatial constraints and coordinate transformations; (3) Statistical validation comparing your theoretical model against provided empirical performance data from similar installations. Submit a formal lab report (8-12 pages) including executive summary, mathematical methodology, detailed calculations, graphical analysis using software like MATLAB/Python/Mathematica, results interpretation, and conclusions. Include all code as appendices. Address shadowing effects between panel rows, seasonal optimization trade-offs, and economic implications of your solution. Your report must demonstrate graduate-level mathematical sophistication while remaining accessible to engineering professionals. Submit as PDF with all supporting computational files.
grading_notes: Expect most students to earn 75-85 points, with exceptional work reaching 90-95 points. Common issues include: inadequate treatment of constraint optimization (deduct 5-10 points), missing or superficial sensitivity analysis (deduct 5-8 points), poor integration of statistical validation (deduct 8-12 points), and insufficient mathematical rigor in modeling assumptions (deduct 10-15 points). Award full credit only for work demonstrating mastery of multiple mathematical domains with seamless integration. Strong submissions will show creative approaches to handling complex constraints and provide meaningful insights beyond basic optimization. Partial credit available for each criterion: 90-100% (A), 80-89% (B), 70-79% (C), 60-69% (D), below 60% (F). Plagiarism of code or mathematical approaches results in automatic failure.

title: Algebraic Problem Solving and Function Analysis Exam
description: A comprehensive intermediate-level mathematics exam assessing students' ability to solve quadratic equations, analyze linear and quadratic functions, and apply algebraic concepts to real-world scenarios. Students will demonstrate proficiency in graphing, interpreting function behavior, and solving multi-step word problems.
learning_objectives_assessed: Solve quadratic equations using multiple methods (factoring, quadratic formula, completing the square)
Graph and analyze properties of linear and quadratic functions including domain, range, intercepts, and vertex
Apply algebraic problem-solving strategies to real-world contexts involving optimization and modeling
Interpret and manipulate algebraic expressions and equations with accuracy and mathematical reasoning
rubric_criteria: Problem-Solving Methods (25 points): Demonstrates correct application of algebraic techniques including factoring, quadratic formula, and systematic approaches. Shows all work clearly with proper mathematical notation.

Function Analysis and Graphing (25 points): Accurately identifies function properties, creates correct graphs, and interprets key features such as intercepts, vertex, axis of symmetry, and transformations.
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise mathematical language, shows logical reasoning steps, and provides clear explanations for solutions. Work is organized and easy to follow.

Application and Real-World Problem Solving (25 points): Successfully translates word problems into mathematical expressions, makes reasonable assumptions, and provides contextually appropriate answers with proper units and interpretations.
instructions: This exam consists of 8 problems covering quadratic equations, function analysis, and real-world applications. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Show all work clearly - partial credit will be awarded for correct methods even if final answers are incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation throughout. Calculators are permitted for arithmetic computations only; all algebraic work must be shown step-by-step. For graphing problems, use the provided coordinate grids and label all key points, axes, and scales clearly. Word problems require you to define variables, set up equations, solve systematically, and interpret your answers in context. Round decimal answers to three significant figures unless otherwise specified. If you cannot complete a problem, show your approach and explain your reasoning for partial credit. Budget your time wisely - spend approximately 10-12 minutes per problem. Review your work if time permits, checking for computational errors and ensuring all questions are answered completely. Write legibly and box or circle final answers. For multi-part questions, clearly label each section of your response.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct methods and logical reasoning, even with computational errors. Deduct 1-2 points for minor arithmetic mistakes, 3-5 points for conceptual errors. Zero credit only for completely incorrect approaches or blank responses. Common issues to watch: sign errors in quadratic formula, incorrect vertex form conversions, missing domain/range restrictions, unrealistic real-world interpretations. Expect grade distribution: 15% A's (90-100), 25% B's (80-89), 35% C's (70-79), 20% D's (60-69), 5% F's (below 60). Students scoring below 70% should be recommended for additional practice with algebraic manipulation and function concepts.

title: Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Discussion
description: Students engage in structured discussions analyzing the trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches for complex computational problems, evaluating time/space complexity, and proposing optimizations for real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze and compare algorithmic complexity using Big O notation for time and space requirements
Evaluate trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches for solving complex problems
Synthesize theoretical knowledge with practical implementation considerations
Communicate technical concepts clearly and engage constructively with peer analyses
rubric_criteria: Technical Accuracy (25 points): Correct complexity analysis, accurate algorithmic descriptions, proper use of Big O notation, and mathematically sound reasoning
Critical Analysis (25 points): Depth of comparison between approaches, identification of trade-offs, consideration of edge cases, and evaluation of real-world applicability
Original Contribution (25 points): Quality of proposed optimizations, novel insights, creative problem-solving approaches, and demonstration of advanced understanding
Discussion Engagement (25 points): Constructive responses to peers, asking thoughtful questions, building on others' ideas, and maintaining professional discourse throughout the discussion period
instructions: You will participate in a week-long discussion analyzing algorithmic approaches to the following problem: 'Design an efficient system for detecting plagiarism in a database of 10 million academic papers, each averaging 8,000 words.' Your participation must include: (1) Initial Post (due by Wednesday): Propose at least two distinct algorithmic approaches, provide detailed complexity analysis for each, compare their trade-offs, and justify your recommended solution. Include pseudocode for key components and discuss memory requirements, scalability limitations, and potential optimizations. Your post should be 800-1000 words with proper citations to relevant literature. (2) Peer Responses (minimum 3, due by Friday): Analyze classmates' proposed solutions, identify strengths and potential weaknesses, suggest improvements, or pose challenging questions about edge cases or implementation details. Each response should be 200-300 words and demonstrate deep engagement with their technical content. (3) Follow-up Contributions (due by Sunday): Respond to feedback on your initial post, refine your analysis based on class discussion, or explore additional optimizations suggested by peers. All posts must use proper computer science terminology, include relevant complexity analysis, and maintain academic integrity. Code snippets should be properly formatted and explained.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for mathematical rigor in complexity analysis - look for proper Big O notation and consideration of both average and worst-case scenarios. Strong responses will demonstrate understanding of advanced data structures (suffix trees, bloom filters, etc.) and their applications. For peer engagement, assess quality over quantity - meaningful technical critique scores higher than superficial agreement. Common issues include: oversimplified complexity analysis, ignoring practical constraints like memory limitations, and failing to consider real-world implementation challenges. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level work (demonstrates graduate-level algorithmic thinking), 60% B-level work (solid technical understanding with minor gaps), 25% C-level or below (significant technical errors or insufficient engagement). Deduct points for late submissions and inappropriate tone in discussions.

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline: Business Impact Analysis and Technical Implementation
description: Students will present a comprehensive analysis of a real-world machine learning project they've designed and implemented, demonstrating mastery of the complete data science lifecycle from problem formulation through deployment considerations. The presentation must address both technical rigor and business impact, showcasing advanced statistical modeling, feature engineering, model evaluation, and strategic recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Synthesize complex data science concepts to solve authentic business problems using advanced statistical and machine learning techniques
Critically evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation strategies while identifying limitations and potential biases
Communicate technical findings effectively to diverse stakeholders, translating complex analytical insights into actionable business recommendations
Demonstrate proficiency in the complete ML pipeline including data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and deployment considerations
rubric_criteria: Problem Formulation & Data Strategy (25 points): Clear business problem definition, appropriate dataset selection/collection, thorough exploratory data analysis with advanced statistical techniques, identification of data quality issues and biases, justification of analytical approach

Technical Implementation & Methodology (25 points): Advanced feature engineering with domain expertise, appropriate algorithm selection with theoretical justification, proper cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning, comparison of multiple modeling approaches, code quality and reproducibility

Model Evaluation & Validation (25 points): Comprehensive performance assessment using multiple appropriate metrics, statistical significance testing, bias-variance analysis, interpretation of model behavior and feature importance, honest discussion of limitations and failure modes

Business Impact & Communication (25 points): Clear articulation of business value and ROI, actionable recommendations with implementation roadmap, effective visual communication of complex concepts, confident handling of technical questions, consideration of ethical implications and deployment challenges
instructions: Select a substantial business problem that can be addressed through machine learning (minimum 10,000 samples, 15+ features). Your project must demonstrate the complete data science lifecycle: 1) Problem Definition: Clearly articulate the business problem, success metrics, and stakeholder requirements. Define your target variable and evaluation criteria. 2) Data Acquisition & EDA: Source or simulate realistic data, perform comprehensive exploratory analysis including statistical tests, correlation analysis, and bias detection. 3) Feature Engineering: Create meaningful features using domain knowledge, handle missing data appropriately, perform feature selection using statistical methods. 4) Model Development: Implement and compare at least three different algorithms (must include one ensemble method and one deep learning approach), perform hyperparameter optimization, use appropriate cross-validation strategies. 5) Evaluation: Assess performance using multiple metrics, conduct statistical significance tests, analyze model interpretability, discuss limitations honestly. 6) Business Application: Quantify business impact, provide implementation roadmap, address deployment considerations including monitoring and maintenance. Deliverables: 20-minute presentation (12-15 slides maximum), complete documented code repository with README, technical appendix with detailed methodology. Be prepared for rigorous questioning on statistical assumptions, algorithm choices, and business implications.
grading_notes: Expect sophisticated technical depth appropriate for expert-level practitioners. Look for evidence of advanced statistical thinking, not just tool usage. Strong presentations will demonstrate original insights, creative feature engineering, and nuanced understanding of model trade-offs. Common weaknesses include: insufficient statistical rigor in evaluation, over-reliance on default parameters, weak connection between technical work and business value, inability to defend methodological choices under questioning. Grade distribution should reflect expert-level expectations: 90-100 (exceptional insight and execution), 80-89 (solid technical work with good business application), 70-79 (adequate technical skills but limited depth or business connection), below 70 (significant gaps in technical execution or understanding). Pay special attention to how students handle challenging questions during Q&A, as this reveals true depth of understanding versus surface-level implementation.

title: My Math Journey Portfolio: Basic Number Operations and Problem Solving
description: Students create a comprehensive portfolio documenting their learning journey with whole number operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and basic problem-solving strategies through work samples, reflections, and real-world applications over a 4-week period.
estimated_time: 4 weeks with 30 minutes per week for portfolio work, plus 2 hours for final compilation
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate fluency in basic arithmetic operations with whole numbers up to 1000
Apply problem-solving strategies to solve multi-step word problems
Explain mathematical thinking and reasoning using appropriate vocabulary
Connect mathematical concepts to real-world situations and personal experiences
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points): Work samples show correct computation, appropriate strategies, and minimal calculation errors across all four operations
Problem-Solving Process (25 points): Clear evidence of systematic approach including identifying given information, planning solution steps, and checking reasonableness of answers
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses proper mathematical vocabulary, shows work clearly, and provides logical explanations of thinking processes in written reflections
Real-World Connections (25 points): Demonstrates understanding by creating original word problems, identifying math in daily life, and explaining how math concepts apply outside the classroom
instructions: Your Math Journey Portfolio will showcase your growth in understanding basic number operations over the next four weeks. Your portfolio must include: (1) Weekly Work Samples - Select your best 2-3 completed assignments each week, including worksheets, problem-solving activities, and corrected work that shows your learning progression. (2) Reflection Entries - Write a brief paragraph each week describing what you learned, what challenged you, and what strategies helped you succeed. Use math vocabulary words like 'sum,' 'difference,' 'product,' and 'quotient' in your explanations. (3) Real-World Math Journal - Document at least 8 examples of how you use math outside school (shopping, cooking, sports, games, etc.) with photos or drawings and explanations. (4) Problem Creator Section - Write and solve 4 original word problems (one for each operation) based on your interests or experiences. (5) Math Goal Setting - Include an initial goal sheet about what you want to learn and a final reflection on your progress. Organize materials in a folder or binder with clear section dividers and labels. Include a table of contents and decorate your cover creatively. All work should be neat, complete, and show your mathematical thinking clearly. Submit your completed portfolio at the end of week 4 along with a brief presentation (2-3 minutes) sharing your favorite learning moment.
grading_notes: Evaluate portfolios holistically, looking for evidence of mathematical growth rather than perfection. Mathematical Accuracy should show improvement over time - early work may have more errors than later samples. For Problem-Solving Process, look for evidence students can identify key information, choose appropriate operations, and verify answers make sense. Mathematical Communication should show increasing use of math vocabulary and clearer explanations of thinking. Real-World Connections should demonstrate genuine understanding of how math applies to student experiences. Expect 20% of students to earn 90-100 points (exceeds expectations with exceptional organization and insights), 60% to earn 75-89 points (meets expectations with solid evidence of learning), 15% to earn 60-74 points (approaching expectations with some gaps), and 5% to earn below 60 points (needs significant support). Common issues include: incomplete reflection entries, messy organization, copied rather than original word problems, and failure to show work clearly. Provide specific feedback on mathematical vocabulary usage and encourage students to explain their thinking more thoroughly.

title: Data Structures Performance Analysis Lab Report
description: Students will implement and analyze the performance characteristics of three fundamental data structures (ArrayList, LinkedList, and Binary Search Tree) through empirical testing, then document their findings in a comprehensive lab report comparing theoretical vs. actual performance.
estimated_time: 4-6 hours (2-3 hours implementation, 2-3 hours analysis and report writing)
learning_objectives_assessed: Implement fundamental data structures with proper time complexity considerations
Conduct empirical performance analysis using systematic testing methodologies
Compare theoretical Big O complexity with real-world performance measurements
Communicate technical findings through clear data visualization and written analysis
rubric_criteria: Implementation Quality (25 points): All three data structures correctly implemented with proper methods (insert, delete, search). Code follows best practices with appropriate comments and error handling.

Performance Testing Methodology (25 points): Systematic testing approach with multiple dataset sizes (minimum 5 different sizes from 1K to 100K elements). Proper timing measurements using appropriate tools. Multiple trial runs with average calculations.

Data Analysis and Visualization (25 points): Clear graphs/charts showing performance trends. Accurate comparison of theoretical vs. empirical results. Statistical analysis including average execution times and growth rate calculations.

Report Quality and Technical Communication (25 points): Well-structured report with clear methodology section, results presentation, and conclusions. Proper discussion of findings, limitations, and insights. Professional formatting with proper citations if external sources used.
instructions: Implement ArrayList, LinkedList, and Binary Search Tree classes in your chosen programming language (Java, C++, or Python). Each implementation must include insert(), delete(), search(), and size() methods. Create a testing framework that measures execution time for each operation across different dataset sizes: 1,000, 5,000, 10,000, 50,000, and 100,000 elements. Run each test 5 times and calculate average execution times. Your lab report must include: (1) Introduction explaining the purpose and scope, (2) Implementation section with code snippets and design decisions, (3) Methodology describing your testing approach, (4) Results section with tables and graphs showing performance data, (5) Analysis comparing your empirical results with theoretical Big O complexities, and (6) Conclusion discussing findings and real-world applications. Submit your complete source code, raw data files, and a PDF report (6-8 pages). Include all graphs as embedded images, not separate files. Use consistent formatting with 12pt font, 1-inch margins, and proper section headers. Code should compile and run without errors on standard development environments.
grading_notes: Focus on correctness of implementations first - non-functional code cannot receive full credit regardless of report quality. Look for proper time complexity understanding in the analysis section. Students should demonstrate clear grasp of why certain operations perform differently than expected (e.g., cache effects, JVM optimization). Common issues include: insufficient test iterations leading to unreliable timing data, failure to warm up JVM/compiler optimizations, incorrect Big O analysis, and poor graph scaling/labeling. Grade distribution expectation: 15% should receive 90+ points, 60% should receive 75-89 points, 20% should receive 60-74 points, 5% below 60 points. Partial credit available for each criterion - even incomplete implementations can earn points if approach is sound. Deduct 5 points for late submission within 24 hours, 10 points after 24 hours.

title: Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Optimization and Model Interpretability Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' ability to design, optimize, and interpret complex machine learning pipelines. Students will analyze real-world scenarios involving model selection, hyperparameter tuning, bias detection, and explainable AI techniques across different data types and business contexts.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper validation strategies
Apply advanced hyperparameter optimization techniques and evaluate model performance trade-offs
Identify and mitigate algorithmic bias in machine learning models
Implement and interpret model explainability techniques (SHAP, LIME, permutation importance)
Select appropriate evaluation metrics for different problem types and business objectives
Analyze model drift and implement monitoring strategies for production systems
rubric_criteria: Pipeline Design & Implementation (25 points): Demonstrates mastery of ML pipeline components including data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, and validation strategies. Shows understanding of cross-validation, data leakage prevention, and pipeline reproducibility.

Optimization & Performance Analysis (25 points): Effectively applies hyperparameter tuning methods (Grid Search, Random Search, Bayesian Optimization), analyzes bias-variance tradeoffs, selects appropriate evaluation metrics, and interprets performance across different model types and datasets.

Bias Detection & Fairness Assessment (25 points): Identifies potential sources of algorithmic bias, applies fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, disparate impact), implements bias mitigation techniques, and evaluates model fairness across protected attributes.

Model Interpretability & Explainability (25 points): Correctly implements and interprets explainability techniques, analyzes feature importance and model decisions, communicates model behavior to non-technical stakeholders, and identifies when interpretability is critical for business decisions.
instructions: This quiz consists of 20 multiple-choice and scenario-based questions testing advanced data science concepts. You will encounter four main sections: (1) ML Pipeline Design - analyze code snippets and identify best practices, potential issues, and optimization opportunities; (2) Model Optimization - solve hyperparameter tuning scenarios and interpret performance metrics across different validation strategies; (3) Bias & Fairness - evaluate fairness metrics, identify discriminatory patterns, and select appropriate mitigation strategies; (4) Model Explainability - interpret SHAP values, LIME explanations, and feature importance plots for various model types. Each question provides realistic business contexts requiring you to balance technical accuracy with practical constraints. Read scenarios carefully as they contain specific requirements about data types, business objectives, and regulatory constraints. For calculation-based questions, show your reasoning process. Multiple-choice questions may have more than one correct answer - select all that apply. You have 120 minutes to complete all questions. The quiz is open-book, allowing reference materials, but collaboration is prohibited. Submit your responses through the learning management system before the deadline. Late submissions will incur a 10% penalty per hour. Ensure stable internet connection as the quiz must be completed in one session without ability to save and return.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should approximate: 15% A-level (90-100), 25% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 20% D-level (60-69), 5% below 60. Watch for common issues: confusion between validation techniques, incorrect bias metric interpretation, misunderstanding of explainability tool outputs, and failure to consider business context in technical decisions. Partial credit available for scenario questions showing correct reasoning despite minor errors. Pay attention to students who excel in technical implementation but struggle with practical application or ethical considerations. Questions testing recent techniques (like SHAP) may show wider performance variance. Consider providing feedback on specific areas for improvement, especially for bias detection and interpretability concepts which are crucial for industry practice.

title: Advanced Calculus Applications in Real-World Optimization Problems
description: Students will create and deliver a comprehensive presentation analyzing a real-world optimization problem using advanced calculus techniques, including multivariable calculus, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization. The presentation must demonstrate deep understanding of mathematical theory and its practical applications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve complex real-world problems
Demonstrate proficiency in using Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization methods
Communicate mathematical concepts clearly and effectively to diverse audiences
Analyze and interpret mathematical results in practical contexts
Evaluate the limitations and assumptions of mathematical models
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Correct application of calculus concepts, accurate calculations, proper use of mathematical notation, and demonstration of deep theoretical understanding

Problem Analysis and Solution Strategy (25 points): Clear problem identification, appropriate method selection, logical solution approach, consideration of constraints and assumptions, and validation of results
Real-World Application and Context (25 points): Relevance of chosen problem, practical significance of solution, discussion of implementation challenges, and connection between theory and practice
Presentation Quality and Communication (25 points): Clear verbal explanation, effective visual aids, appropriate use of mathematical language, engagement with audience questions, and time management
instructions: Select a real-world optimization problem from engineering, economics, physics, or business that requires advanced calculus techniques. Your 20-minute presentation must include: (1) Clear problem statement with background context and significance, (2) Mathematical model development including variable identification, constraint formulation, and objective function setup, (3) Detailed solution process using appropriate calculus techniques (partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, second derivative tests, etc.), (4) Analysis of results including sensitivity analysis and interpretation of optimal values, (5) Discussion of practical implementation, limitations, and potential extensions. Prepare 8-12 slides with clear mathematical notation, graphs, and visualizations. Include a one-page handout summarizing key equations and results. Be prepared to answer questions about your methodology, alternative approaches, and real-world implications. Submit your slides and handout 24 hours before presentation. Examples of suitable problems: portfolio optimization with risk constraints, manufacturing cost minimization with production limits, optimal design of structures under material constraints, or resource allocation in logistics networks.
grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical accuracy first - incorrect fundamental calculus applications should result in significant point deductions. Look for evidence of genuine understanding versus memorized procedures through questioning. Strong presentations will demonstrate clear connections between mathematical theory and practical outcomes. Common issues include: oversimplified constraints, failure to verify critical points, inadequate discussion of boundary conditions, and poor explanation of why chosen methods are appropriate. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), 10% below 70. Partial credit available for presentations with strong analysis but minor computational errors.

title: Advanced Software Systems Portfolio: Full-Stack Application with Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design, develop, and deploy a complete software system demonstrating mastery of advanced computer science concepts including system architecture, algorithms, data structures, security, and software engineering practices. The portfolio must showcase a full-stack application with microservices architecture, comprehensive documentation, and deployment to cloud infrastructure.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement complex software systems using appropriate architectural patterns and design principles
Demonstrate proficiency in advanced algorithms, data structures, and computational complexity analysis
Apply software engineering best practices including version control, testing, CI/CD, and documentation
Implement secure coding practices and system security measures
Deploy and manage applications using cloud infrastructure and DevOps practices
Analyze system performance, scalability, and reliability through monitoring and optimization
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of microservices architecture, API design, database design, and system integration. Includes comprehensive system diagrams, architectural decisions documentation, and scalability considerations.

Technical Implementation & Code Quality (25 points): Code demonstrates advanced programming concepts, optimal algorithm selection, proper data structure usage, adherence to SOLID principles, comprehensive error handling, and industry-standard coding practices with 90%+ test coverage.

Security & Deployment (25 points): Implements robust security measures including authentication, authorization, input validation, and data encryption. Successfully deploys to cloud platform with proper configuration management, monitoring, and automated deployment pipeline.

Documentation & Professional Practice (25 points): Provides comprehensive technical documentation including API documentation, deployment guides, architecture decisions, performance analysis, and reflection on development process. Demonstrates professional git workflow and project management.
instructions: Create a portfolio containing: 1) A full-stack web application with at least 3 microservices (user management, data processing, and one domain-specific service) built using modern frameworks (React/Vue.js frontend, Node.js/Python/Java backend). 2) Implementation of at least two advanced algorithms or data structures with complexity analysis. 3) Comprehensive test suite with unit, integration, and end-to-end tests achieving minimum 90% code coverage. 4) Security implementation including JWT authentication, input validation, SQL injection prevention, and HTTPS configuration. 5) Deployment to cloud platform (AWS/Azure/GCP) with containerization using Docker, orchestration with Kubernetes or similar, and CI/CD pipeline setup. 6) Performance monitoring and optimization documentation showing load testing results and system metrics. 7) Complete technical documentation including README with setup instructions, API documentation (using Swagger/OpenAPI), architectural decision records, and code comments. 8) Git repository with professional commit history, branching strategy, and pull request workflow. Submit portfolio as GitHub repository link with live application URL and comprehensive README. Include 10-minute video demonstration showcasing key features and technical decisions.
grading_notes: Evaluate based on technical depth rather than application complexity - a well-architected simple application scores higher than a complex but poorly designed one. Key indicators of expert-level work: proper separation of concerns, scalable architecture, comprehensive error handling, security-first approach, and professional documentation. Common issues: inadequate security implementation (automatic 10-point deduction), missing tests (5-point deduction per missing test type), poor documentation (up to 15-point deduction), non-functional deployment (10-point deduction). Grade distribution expectation: 90-100 points (20% of students) - exceeds professional standards, 80-89 points (40% of students) - meets professional standards, 70-79 points (30% of students) - meets academic standards with minor gaps, below 70 points (10% of students) - significant technical deficiencies requiring revision.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis Lab Report: Customer Purchase Behavior Dataset
description: Students will perform a comprehensive exploratory data analysis (EDA) on a customer purchase dataset, demonstrating fundamental data science skills including data cleaning, visualization, statistical analysis, and insight generation. The lab report will document their methodology, findings, and business recommendations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply data cleaning techniques to handle missing values, outliers, and data quality issues
Create appropriate data visualizations to explore relationships and patterns in data
Perform basic descriptive statistical analysis and interpret results
Communicate data science findings clearly through written reports with actionable insights
rubric_criteria: Data Cleaning and Preparation (25 points): Properly identifies and handles missing values, outliers, and data inconsistencies. Documents all preprocessing steps with clear justification. Creates clean, analysis-ready dataset with appropriate data types.

Data Visualization and Exploration (25 points): Creates at least 5 meaningful visualizations (histograms, scatter plots, box plots, etc.) that effectively reveal data patterns. Uses appropriate chart types, includes proper labels/titles, and follows visualization best practices.

Statistical Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Calculates relevant descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, correlations). Correctly interprets statistical measures and identifies significant patterns or relationships in the data.

Report Quality and Business Insights (25 points): Presents findings in a well-structured report with clear sections, professional formatting, and proper grammar. Provides actionable business recommendations based on data analysis with clear reasoning.
instructions:
You will analyze a customer purchase behavior dataset containing information about customer demographics, purchase history, and product preferences. Your task is to conduct a thorough exploratory data analysis and present your findings in a professional lab report.

Dataset: Download the 'customer_purchases.csv' file from the course portal. It contains 1000+ records with variables including customer_id, age, gender, income, purchase_amount, product_category, and purchase_date.

Required Analysis Components:
1. Data Overview: Load the dataset, examine its structure, identify data types and missing values
2. Data Cleaning: Handle missing values, remove duplicates, treat outliers, and fix data inconsistencies
3. Univariate Analysis: Analyze individual variables using histograms, box plots, and summary statistics
4. Bivariate Analysis: Explore relationships between variables using scatter plots, correlation analysis, and cross-tabulations
5. Business Insights: Generate at least 3 actionable business recommendations based on your findings

Deliverables: Submit a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb file) containing your complete analysis with markdown cells explaining each step. Include a 1-page executive summary (separate PDF) highlighting key findings and recommendations for business stakeholders.

Submission Format: Upload both files to the course portal by 11:59 PM on the due date. Name files as 'LastName_FirstName_EDA_Lab.ipynb' and 'LastName_FirstName_Executive_Summary.pdf'.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should typically be: 90-100 (A): Exceptional analysis with creative insights; 80-89 (B): Good analysis meeting all requirements; 70-79 (C): Adequate analysis with minor issues; Below 70: Significant deficiencies. Common issues to watch for: insufficient data cleaning documentation, inappropriate visualization choices, misinterpretation of statistical results, weak or unsupported business recommendations, poor code organization, and missing executive summary. Deduct 5 points for late submission (up to 24 hours), 10 points for missing executive summary, and 15 points for incomplete analysis sections. Provide specific feedback on code quality, statistical interpretation accuracy, and business insight relevance.

title: Linear Functions and Systems: Problem-Solving Assessment
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of linear functions, graphing, and solving systems of equations through multi-step word problems and analytical questions covering slope-intercept form, parallel/perpendicular lines, and real-world applications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Convert between different forms of linear equations and interpret slope and y-intercept in context
Graph linear functions and identify key characteristics including domain, range, and intercepts
Solve systems of linear equations using substitution, elimination, and graphing methods
Apply linear functions to model and solve real-world problems involving rates of change
Determine relationships between lines (parallel, perpendicular, intersecting) using slope analysis
rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Equation Formation (25 points): Correctly identifies variables, translates word problems into mathematical expressions, and writes appropriate linear equations or systems. Shows clear understanding of problem context and mathematical modeling.

Mathematical Computation and Methods (25 points): Demonstrates accurate algebraic manipulation, uses appropriate solution methods (graphing, substitution, elimination), performs calculations correctly, and shows systematic problem-solving approaches.

Graphing and Visual Representation (25 points): Creates accurate coordinate graphs with proper scaling, labels axes and key points, correctly plots lines and intersection points, and interprets graphical information to support solutions.

Communication and Justification (25 points): Provides clear explanations of solution steps, justifies method choices, interprets results in context of original problems, and presents work in organized, logical sequence with appropriate mathematical vocabulary.
instructions:
This assessment consists of 8 problems covering linear functions and systems of equations. You have 90 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and provide explanations where requested. Use proper mathematical notation and label all graphs completely.

Problem Types:
- Problems 1-2: Converting between slope-intercept, point-slope, and standard forms
- Problems 3-4: Graphing linear functions and identifying key features
- Problems 5-6: Solving systems of equations using different methods
- Problems 7-8: Real-world applications requiring linear modeling

Requirements:
- Show all algebraic steps for full credit
- Graph problems must include properly labeled axes, scale, and key points
- Word problems require clear variable definitions and contextual interpretations
- Circle or box final answers
- For systems problems, verify solutions by substitution

Materials Allowed: Calculator, ruler, graph paper
Submission: Submit all work on provided answer sheets. Ensure your name and class period are clearly written. If you need additional space, clearly indicate continuation and attach extra sheets securely.
grading_notes: Use partial credit generously - award points for correct setup even if computational errors occur. Look for mathematical reasoning and appropriate method selection. Common issues: students forgetting to check solutions in original equations, mislabeling graph axes, and failing to interpret answers in context for word problems. Expect score distribution: 85-100 (advanced), 70-84 (proficient), 60-69 (developing), below 60 (beginning). Provide specific feedback on method errors and suggest review topics. Consider allowing corrections for partial credit recovery on major conceptual errors.

title: Distributed Hash Table Implementation with Fault Tolerance
description: Students will design and implement a distributed hash table (DHT) system that supports key-value operations across multiple nodes with automatic load balancing, data replication, and fault tolerance mechanisms. The system must handle node failures gracefully and maintain data consistency.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems with fault tolerance
Apply consistent hashing algorithms for load balancing
Implement network communication protocols and error handling
Demonstrate understanding of data replication and consistency models
Analyze system performance and scalability characteristics
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Well-documented system architecture with clear component separation, appropriate use of design patterns, and scalable design decisions. Includes comprehensive system diagrams and justified technology choices.

Core DHT Functionality (25 points): Correct implementation of consistent hashing, key-value operations (GET, PUT, DELETE), automatic node joining/leaving, and data migration. System maintains O(log N) lookup complexity and balanced load distribution.

Fault Tolerance & Replication (25 points): Robust implementation of data replication (minimum 3 replicas), failure detection mechanisms, automatic failover, and data recovery procedures. System continues operating with up to 33% node failures.

Testing & Performance Analysis (25 points): Comprehensive test suite covering unit tests, integration tests, and failure scenarios. Detailed performance benchmarks measuring throughput, latency, and scalability. Clear documentation of testing methodology and results interpretation.
instructions: Implement a distributed hash table supporting a minimum of 5 nodes with the following requirements: 1) Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes for load balancing, 2) Implement TCP-based communication protocol with custom message formats, 3) Support concurrent operations with thread-safe data structures, 4) Provide REST API endpoints for external clients, 5) Include configuration management for cluster setup. Your submission must include: source code with clear documentation and comments, README with setup/deployment instructions, architectural design document (5-10 pages) explaining system design decisions, comprehensive test suite with at least 80% code coverage, performance analysis report comparing your implementation against theoretical expectations. Code must be version-controlled using Git with meaningful commit messages. Provide Docker containerization for easy deployment. Include failure simulation scripts demonstrating system resilience. Document all external dependencies and provide clear build instructions. System should handle minimum 1000 operations/second under normal conditions and gracefully degrade during failures.
grading_notes: Evaluate code quality including readability, modularity, and adherence to best practices. Test the system with various failure scenarios including network partitions, gradual node failures, and sudden crashes. Verify that data consistency is maintained during failures and recoveries. Check that performance benchmarks are realistic and methodology is sound. Common issues to watch: insufficient error handling, poor thread synchronization, inadequate testing coverage, unrealistic performance claims, missing edge cases in failure scenarios. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (exceptional implementation with novel optimizations), 40% B-level (solid implementation meeting all requirements), 30% C-level (functional but with some limitations), 10% below C-level (significant missing functionality or poor implementation).

title: End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline Development and Deployment Exam
description: Students will design, implement, and evaluate a complete machine learning solution for a real-world business problem, demonstrating advanced skills in data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and model deployment with comprehensive documentation and business insights.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines with proper data preprocessing and feature engineering techniques
Apply advanced model selection, hyperparameter optimization, and cross-validation strategies for robust model development
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and interpret results in business context with actionable recommendations
Demonstrate proficiency in model deployment, monitoring, and documentation following industry best practices
rubric_criteria: Data Analysis and Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive exploratory data analysis with statistical insights, handling of missing values and outliers, creation of meaningful features, proper data transformations, and validation of data quality assumptions

Model Development and Optimization (25 points): Implementation of multiple appropriate algorithms, systematic hyperparameter tuning using grid/random search or Bayesian optimization, proper cross-validation strategy, handling of class imbalance if applicable, and comparison of model architectures

Model Evaluation and Interpretation (25 points): Selection and calculation of appropriate evaluation metrics, statistical significance testing, comprehensive error analysis, model interpretability techniques (SHAP, LIME, etc.), and identification of model limitations and potential biases

Business Impact and Technical Implementation (25 points): Clear articulation of business value and ROI, deployment-ready code with proper error handling, comprehensive documentation, consideration of scalability and maintenance, and actionable recommendations with implementation timeline
instructions: You are provided with a dataset containing customer transaction data for an e-commerce company experiencing declining retention rates. Your task is to develop a complete machine learning solution to predict customer churn and provide actionable business recommendations. Submit a Jupyter notebook containing: (1) Exploratory Data Analysis with at least 5 statistical insights and 3 visualizations explaining customer behavior patterns, (2) Feature engineering pipeline including handling of categorical variables, missing values, and creation of at least 3 domain-specific features, (3) Implementation and comparison of minimum 3 different algorithms (must include at least one ensemble method), with proper hyperparameter optimization and 5-fold cross-validation, (4) Model evaluation using precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and business-relevant metrics like customer lifetime value impact, (5) Model interpretation using SHAP or LIME with explanation of top 5 most important features, (6) Deployment code including API endpoint creation, input validation, and error handling, (7) Executive summary (500 words) translating technical findings into business recommendations with estimated financial impact and implementation roadmap. Include all preprocessing steps in a reusable pipeline, ensure reproducibility with random seeds, and provide clear markdown explanations for each section. Code must be production-ready with proper exception handling and logging.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor and business acumen equally. Look for sophisticated feature engineering beyond basic transformations, proper statistical validation of findings, and evidence of deep domain understanding. Deduct points for data leakage, improper cross-validation, or overfitting indicators. Award bonus consideration for creative feature engineering, advanced techniques like stacking/blending, or innovative business insights. Common issues include: inadequate EDA leading to missed insights, feature engineering without business justification, hyperparameter tuning without proper validation splits, evaluation metrics inappropriate for business context, and technical solutions without actionable business recommendations. Grade distribution expectation: 15% should score 90+, 30% score 80-89, 40% score 70-79, 15% below 70. Partial credit available for each criterion - award points for correct methodology even if implementation has minor issues.

title: End-to-End Data Science Portfolio: Predictive Analytics for Business Decision Making
description: Students will develop a comprehensive data science portfolio demonstrating the complete machine learning pipeline from data acquisition through model deployment and business insights. The portfolio must include multiple projects showcasing different ML techniques, proper documentation, and real-world business applications with measurable impact analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines for complex, real-world problems
Apply advanced statistical methods and ML algorithms with proper validation techniques
Communicate technical findings effectively to both technical and business stakeholders
Demonstrate ethical data science practices and address bias in ML systems
Deploy ML models in production environments with monitoring and maintenance protocols
rubric_criteria: Technical Implementation (25 points): Code quality, algorithm selection appropriateness, feature engineering sophistication, model validation rigor, and deployment architecture effectiveness
Data Quality & Ethics (25 points): Data collection methodology, preprocessing completeness, bias identification and mitigation strategies, privacy considerations, and ethical framework application
Business Impact & Insights (25 points): Problem definition clarity, stakeholder analysis depth, ROI quantification accuracy, actionable recommendations quality, and strategic alignment demonstration

Communication & Documentation (25 points): Technical documentation completeness, visualization effectiveness, presentation clarity for multiple audiences, reproducibility of results, and professional portfolio presentation
instructions: Create a professional data science portfolio containing three distinct projects: (1) A supervised learning project solving a classification or regression problem with business impact analysis, (2) An unsupervised learning project revealing hidden patterns or customer segmentation, and (3) A time series forecasting project for operational planning. Each project must include: complete Jupyter notebooks with documented code, comprehensive EDA with statistical tests, multiple ML algorithms comparison with hyperparameter tuning, model validation using appropriate metrics, bias analysis and ethical considerations, deployment strategy or prototype, and executive summary with business recommendations. Submit via GitHub repository with README, requirements.txt, and structured folders. Include a 10-minute video presentation highlighting key insights and business value. All data sources must be cited, and synthetic data generation is acceptable if real data is unavailable. Portfolio should demonstrate progression in complexity and showcase different aspects of the data science lifecycle including A/B testing, feature selection, ensemble methods, and model interpretation techniques.
grading_notes: Evaluate technical depth over breadth - advanced implementation of fewer techniques is preferred over superficial coverage of many. Expect 15-20% of students to achieve excellence (90-100 points) with exceptional business insight and technical innovation. Common weaknesses include inadequate validation techniques, poor business problem framing, and insufficient bias analysis. Strong portfolios demonstrate clear problem-solving progression, acknowledge limitations, and show iterative improvement. Deduct points for non-reproducible code, missing ethical considerations, or purely academic problems without business context. Bonus consideration for creative visualization, novel algorithm applications, or demonstrated real-world deployment with user feedback.

title: Numerical Analysis Lab Report: Comparative Study of Root-Finding Algorithms
description: Students will implement and analyze three numerical root-finding algorithms (Bisection, Newton-Raphson, and Secant methods) to solve a complex polynomial equation, comparing their convergence rates, accuracy, and computational efficiency through rigorous mathematical analysis and computational implementation.
learning_objectives_assessed: Implement and optimize advanced numerical algorithms for solving nonlinear equations
Analyze convergence behavior and error propagation in iterative mathematical methods
Evaluate computational complexity and efficiency trade-offs in numerical methods
Communicate mathematical findings through formal scientific reporting with rigorous mathematical notation
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Implementation and Code Quality (25 points): Correct implementation of all three algorithms with proper error handling, well-commented code, and efficient computational structure. Includes proper stopping criteria and convergence testing.

Mathematical Analysis and Theoretical Understanding (25 points): Accurate theoretical analysis of convergence rates, error bounds, and mathematical properties of each method. Includes proper derivations, mathematical notation, and theoretical comparisons.

Experimental Design and Data Analysis (25 points): Systematic testing with multiple test cases, comprehensive data collection, statistical analysis of results, graphical representations of convergence behavior, and quantitative performance comparisons.

Scientific Communication and Report Quality (25 points): Clear executive summary, well-structured methodology section, comprehensive results discussion, appropriate conclusions, proper mathematical formatting, and professional presentation standards.
instructions: You will conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of three numerical root-finding algorithms applied to the polynomial f(x) = x⁵ - 3x⁴ + 2x³ - x² + 4x - 2. Your lab report must include: (1) Implementation section with working code for Bisection, Newton-Raphson, and Secant methods in your chosen programming language, including proper documentation and error handling; (2) Theoretical analysis section deriving convergence conditions and error bounds for each method, with mathematical proofs where applicable; (3) Experimental methodology describing your testing protocol, including at least 5 different starting conditions and tolerance levels from 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹²; (4) Results section presenting convergence data, iteration counts, final accuracy, and computational time for each method, supported by appropriate graphs and tables; (5) Discussion analyzing the trade-offs between convergence speed, stability, and computational cost, including identification of optimal use cases for each algorithm; (6) Conclusions summarizing key findings and recommendations. Submit a PDF report (8-12 pages) with complete source code as appendix. Use IEEE format for mathematical notation and citations. Include all raw data, graphs, and computational outputs. Test your implementations thoroughly and verify results using commercial software like Mathematica or MATLAB for validation.
grading_notes: Evaluate code functionality by running implementations with provided test cases - deduct heavily for non-working code. Look for mathematical rigor in theoretical sections, particularly proper use of Big-O notation and convergence analysis. Assess experimental design completeness - students should test edge cases and provide statistical significance of timing measurements. Common issues: insufficient error analysis, poor choice of stopping criteria, inadequate discussion of numerical stability, and missing validation against analytical solutions where possible. Expect 20% A grades for exceptional mathematical insight and implementation efficiency, 40% B grades for solid work meeting all requirements, 30% C grades for adequate but incomplete analysis, 10% below C for significant mathematical errors or non-functional code.

title: Programming Fundamentals Quiz: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Operations
description: A comprehensive quiz assessing students' understanding of fundamental programming concepts including variable declaration, data types, basic arithmetic operations, and simple input/output operations using Python syntax.
learning_objectives_assessed: Demonstrate understanding of primitive data types (int, float, string, boolean) and their appropriate use cases
Create and manipulate variables following proper naming conventions and syntax rules
Perform basic arithmetic and string operations with correct operator precedence
Write simple input/output statements using print() and input() functions
Debug basic syntax errors in variable declarations and assignments
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Variable Declaration (25 points): Correctly identifies data types, demonstrates proper variable naming conventions, shows understanding of type conversion between int, float, and string
Basic Operations and Expressions (25 points): Accurately performs arithmetic operations, understands operator precedence, correctly concatenates strings and formats output
Input/Output Operations (25 points): Properly uses print() and input() functions, formats output with appropriate spacing and labels, handles user input conversion
Syntax and Code Reading (25 points): Identifies and corrects syntax errors, predicts output of given code snippets, demonstrates understanding of Python syntax rules
instructions: This quiz consists of 20 multiple-choice and short-answer questions covering basic programming concepts in Python. You have 45 minutes to complete all questions. Read each question carefully before selecting or writing your answer. For coding questions, write your answers using proper Python syntax. You may use basic arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /, //, %, **) and comparison operators. For multiple-choice questions, select the single best answer. For short-answer questions, provide complete code snippets or explanations as requested. When writing variable names, follow Python naming conventions (lowercase with underscores). For questions asking you to predict output, write exactly what would appear on screen, including quotation marks for strings where applicable. If a code snippet contains an error, clearly identify the error and provide the correction. You may use scratch paper for calculations, but all final answers must be clearly marked on the quiz. Questions cover: variable assignment and naming (Questions 1-5), data types and type conversion (Questions 6-10), arithmetic and string operations (Questions 11-15), and input/output operations with debugging (Questions 16-20). Show your work for calculation problems. Double-check your syntax for coding answers. Submit your completed quiz face-down when finished.
grading_notes: Use partial credit for coding questions - award points for correct logic even if syntax is slightly off. Common errors include: forgetting quotes around strings, incorrect variable naming (using spaces or starting with numbers), confusion between = and ==, forgetting parentheses in print statements. For output prediction questions, be strict about exact formatting including spaces and quotation marks. Expected grade distribution: 90-100 points (A) for students who demonstrate solid understanding with minor errors, 80-89 points (B) for good understanding with some conceptual gaps, 70-79 points (C) for basic understanding with multiple syntax or logic errors, below 70 points for students needing additional instruction. Pay special attention to recurring errors that indicate fundamental misunderstandings requiring remediation.

title: Advanced Calculus Integration Techniques and Applications Examination
description: Comprehensive assessment evaluating student mastery of advanced integration methods including integration by parts, partial fractions, trigonometric substitutions, and their applications to real-world problems involving area, volume, and differential equations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced integration techniques (by parts, partial fractions, trigonometric substitution) to solve complex integrals
Evaluate improper integrals and determine convergence or divergence
Use integration to solve real-world applications including area between curves, volumes of revolution, and center of mass
Set up and solve first-order differential equations using separation of variables and integrating factors
Analyze and interpret results in context of applied problems
rubric_criteria: Technique Selection and Setup (25 points): Correctly identifies appropriate integration method, properly sets up integrals with correct limits and substitutions, demonstrates clear mathematical reasoning for approach chosen

Mathematical Execution (25 points): Accurately performs algebraic manipulations, applies integration rules correctly, shows all intermediate steps clearly, arrives at correct antiderivatives and definite integral values

Application and Modeling (25 points): Translates word problems into mathematical expressions, correctly interprets geometric and physical contexts, sets up appropriate integral models for area, volume, and differential equation problems

Communication and Justification (25 points): Provides clear explanations for solution methods, shows complete work with logical progression, interprets final answers in context, demonstrates understanding of concepts beyond mechanical computation
instructions: This examination consists of 8 problems worth varying point values totaling 100 points. You have 3 hours to complete all problems. Show ALL work clearly - partial credit will be awarded based on correct methodology even if final answers are incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation throughout. Calculators are permitted for arithmetic verification only; all integration must be performed analytically. For application problems, clearly define variables, set up integrals with proper limits, and interpret your final answers in the context of the problem. When evaluating improper integrals, explicitly show limit processes and state whether integrals converge or diverge. For differential equations, verify your solutions by substitution when possible. If you cannot complete a problem, show your approach and explain where you encounter difficulty for partial credit. Write legibly and organize your work logically. Circle or box final answers. If you need additional space, clearly indicate continuation and number all pages. You may use the provided formula sheet but must show understanding of when and how to apply formulas. Begin each problem on a new page and manage your time carefully across all problems.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct methodology and setup, even with computational errors. Look for evidence of conceptual understanding beyond mechanical computation. Common issues to watch: incorrect bounds on definite integrals, sign errors in integration by parts, improper handling of absolute values in partial fractions, confusion between area and net area. Expect grade distribution: A (20%), B (30%), C (30%), D/F (20%). Deduct points for missing work even if answers are correct. Give full credit for alternative correct solution methods. For borderline cases, consider consistency of errors and overall mathematical maturity demonstrated.

title: Distributed Systems Architecture Design Discussion: Building a Global Content Delivery Network
description: Students will engage in a comprehensive discussion analyzing the architectural decisions, trade-offs, and implementation challenges involved in designing a global content delivery network (CDN) capable of serving 100 million+ users with sub-100ms latency requirements.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (including research, initial post, and peer responses)
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze complex distributed system architectures and evaluate trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Design scalable systems that handle high-throughput, low-latency requirements across geographically distributed environments
Critically evaluate peer solutions and provide constructive technical feedback on system design decisions
Communicate complex technical concepts clearly and defend architectural choices with evidence-based reasoning
rubric_criteria: Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of distributed systems concepts including caching strategies, load balancing, data replication, consensus algorithms, and fault tolerance mechanisms. Uses correct terminology and shows mastery of CAP theorem implications.

System Design Quality (25 points): Proposes a well-structured, scalable architecture with clear component interactions, appropriate technology choices, and realistic performance estimates. Addresses bottlenecks, failure scenarios, and monitoring strategies.

Critical Analysis and Trade-off Evaluation (25 points): Thoroughly analyzes design decisions, compares alternative approaches, quantifies trade-offs between performance/cost/complexity, and demonstrates understanding of real-world constraints and business requirements.

Peer Engagement and Communication (25 points): Provides substantive, technically accurate responses to at least 3 peers, asks thoughtful follow-up questions, challenges assumptions constructively, and communicates complex ideas clearly with appropriate technical depth.
instructions: You are tasked with designing a global CDN architecture capable of serving 100M+ users with <100ms latency worldwide. Your discussion should include: (1) Initial Post (300-500 words): Present your high-level architecture including edge server placement strategy, caching hierarchy, content routing algorithms, and data consistency approach. Specify technologies/protocols you would use and provide latency/throughput estimates. Address how your design handles cache invalidation, geographic load distribution, and failure recovery. Include a simple architectural diagram or detailed textual description. (2) Technical Deep-dive (200-300 words): Choose one critical component (e.g., cache eviction policy, routing algorithm, consensus mechanism) and explain your implementation approach, including algorithmic complexity, expected performance characteristics, and why you chose this approach over alternatives. (3) Peer Responses (150+ words each, minimum 3 responses): Analyze peers' designs, identify strengths/weaknesses, suggest improvements, or pose challenging scenarios their system might face. Focus on technical merit rather than general praise. Submit initial post by Wednesday 11:59 PM, peer responses by Sunday 11:59 PM. Use proper citations for any external sources and ensure all technical claims are justified.
grading_notes: Look for evidence of genuine understanding rather than superficial coverage of buzzwords. Strong responses will demonstrate knowledge of specific algorithms (consistent hashing, Paxos/Raft, LRU variants), realistic performance analysis, and awareness of real-world CDN challenges (China's Great Firewall, submarine cable failures, regulatory compliance). Deduct points for: vague architectural descriptions, unrealistic performance claims, shallow peer responses, or failure to address failure scenarios. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level or below. Students earning top marks should demonstrate graduate-level systems thinking with specific, implementable solutions and insightful peer critique.

title: Data Science Project Showcase: Analyzing a Real-World Dataset
description: Students will conduct a complete data science workflow on a provided dataset and present their findings through a 10-minute presentation. This assessment evaluates students' ability to perform exploratory data analysis, create meaningful visualizations, draw insights, and communicate findings effectively to a non-technical audience.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform exploratory data analysis using appropriate statistical methods and visualizations
Identify patterns, trends, and outliers in datasets using descriptive statistics
Create clear and appropriate data visualizations using tools like Python/R or Excel
Communicate data insights effectively to non-technical stakeholders
Apply the data science workflow from data exploration to actionable recommendations
rubric_criteria: Data Exploration and Analysis (25 points): Demonstrates thorough exploration of the dataset including summary statistics, data quality assessment, identification of missing values, and appropriate statistical analysis techniques

Visualization Quality (25 points): Creates 3-4 clear, appropriate, and well-labeled visualizations that effectively communicate key findings. Charts are properly formatted with titles, axis labels, and legends where needed

Insights and Interpretation (25 points): Identifies meaningful patterns, trends, or relationships in the data and provides accurate interpretations. Makes at least 2 specific, data-driven recommendations based on findings
