Presentation and Communication (25 points): Delivers a clear, organized 8-10 minute presentation using non-technical language. Maintains good eye contact, speaks clearly, and effectively explains visualizations to the audience
instructions: You will analyze one of the provided datasets (choose from: customer sales data, website traffic analytics, or employee satisfaction survey) and present your findings to the class. Your presentation must include: (1) A brief overview of the dataset and your analysis approach (2 minutes), (2) Three to four key visualizations showing your most important findings (5 minutes), (3) Two specific, actionable recommendations based on your analysis (2 minutes), and (4) A brief conclusion and time for questions (1 minute). Technical requirements: Use any tool you're comfortable with (Excel, Python, R, Tableau, etc.). Create a slide deck with 6-8 slides maximum. Include at least one bar/column chart, one line chart or scatter plot, and one additional chart type of your choice. Submit your slide deck as PDF and any analysis files 24 hours before your presentation date. Practice your timing - presentations going significantly over or under 8-10 minutes will lose points. Focus on telling a story with your data rather than just showing statistics. Assume your audience consists of business managers with no technical background.
grading_notes: Use the 4-point scale for each criterion: Excellent (23-25 pts), Good (20-22 pts), Satisfactory (17-19 pts), Needs Improvement (0-16 pts). Common issues to watch for: students focusing too much on technical details rather than insights, poor chart formatting or inappropriate chart types, going over time limits, and making recommendations not supported by their analysis. Expect grade distribution around 80-85 average for beginner level. Provide specific feedback on visualization improvements and communication clarity. Allow minor technical difficulties but deduct points if students are unprepared with backups.

title: Ethical AI and Algorithmic Bias: Case Study Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Discussion
description: Students will analyze real-world cases of algorithmic bias, evaluate their societal impact, and propose comprehensive mitigation strategies while engaging in peer discussion about the ethical implications of data science practices in high-stakes applications.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (2 hours preparation, 1 hour initial post, 2 hours peer engagement)
learning_objectives_assessed: Critically evaluate ethical implications and potential biases in machine learning algorithms and data science applications
Analyze the intersection of technical implementation choices and societal outcomes in data-driven systems
Synthesize technical knowledge with ethical frameworks to propose actionable solutions for bias mitigation
Communicate complex technical and ethical concepts effectively to diverse stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Case Analysis and Technical Understanding (25 points): Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of the technical causes of bias in the chosen case, accurately identifies specific algorithmic, data collection, or preprocessing issues, and explains the mechanism by which bias manifested in the system's outputs

Ethical Framework Application and Impact Assessment (25 points): Applies relevant ethical frameworks (fairness, accountability, transparency, etc.) to evaluate societal impact, considers multiple stakeholder perspectives, and demonstrates understanding of both immediate and long-term consequences

Mitigation Strategy Development (25 points): Proposes specific, technically feasible solutions addressing root causes, considers implementation challenges and trade-offs, includes both technical interventions and process improvements, and addresses monitoring and evaluation mechanisms

Discussion Engagement and Professional Communication (25 points): Provides substantive responses to at least 3 peers with constructive feedback or alternative perspectives, uses appropriate technical terminology while remaining accessible, demonstrates respectful engagement with differing viewpoints, and contributes meaningfully to collective understanding
instructions: Select one documented case of algorithmic bias from the provided list (COMPAS recidivism prediction, facial recognition accuracy disparities, resume screening algorithms, healthcare risk prediction, or mortgage lending algorithms) or propose an alternative case with instructor approval. Your analysis should include: (1) A detailed examination of the technical factors that contributed to bias, including data collection methods, feature selection, model architecture, and evaluation metrics used; (2) An assessment of the real-world impact on affected communities, supported by evidence from academic sources, news reports, or policy documents; (3) A comprehensive mitigation strategy that addresses technical, procedural, and organizational changes needed to prevent similar issues, including specific recommendations for data collection, model development, validation, and ongoing monitoring; (4) A reflection on the broader implications for data science practice and professional responsibility. Your initial post should be 1200-1500 words, properly cited using APA format. After posting, engage meaningfully with at least three classmates' analyses by Friday of the assessment week. Your responses should offer constructive feedback, alternative perspectives, or connections to additional cases or frameworks. Each response should be 200-300 words and demonstrate critical thinking beyond simple agreement or disagreement.
grading_notes: Look for depth over breadth - students should demonstrate sophisticated understanding of chosen case rather than surface-level coverage of multiple issues. Strong responses will connect technical details to ethical implications and show awareness of implementation complexity. Common issues include: oversimplifying technical causes, proposing unrealistic solutions without considering constraints, failing to consider multiple stakeholder perspectives, and superficial peer engagement. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level work (90-100 points), 50% B-level work (80-89 points), 25% C-level work (70-79 points), 5% below expectations (<70 points). Deduct points for late submissions: 5 points per day for initial post, 3 points per day for peer responses. Plagiarism or AI-generated content results in automatic zero with opportunity for resubmission at 80% maximum credit.

title: Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation: Novel Applications of Differential Equations
description: Students will conduct independent research on cutting-edge applications of differential equations in modern science or engineering, then present their findings in a 20-minute academic presentation that demonstrates mastery of advanced mathematical concepts, research methodology, and communication skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced differential equation theory to solve complex real-world problems
Synthesize mathematical research from primary academic sources
Demonstrate mastery of mathematical proof techniques and rigorous argumentation
Communicate sophisticated mathematical concepts clearly to expert audiences
Evaluate the significance and limitations of mathematical models in practical applications
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Rigor and Accuracy (25 points): Demonstrates flawless understanding of differential equation theory, presents mathematically sound derivations and proofs, uses precise mathematical notation and terminology, shows mastery of relevant theorems and techniques

Research Quality and Innovation (25 points): Selects cutting-edge, significant application area; synthesizes multiple high-quality academic sources; demonstrates original thinking in analysis or approach; identifies gaps in current research or proposes novel extensions

Presentation Delivery and Clarity (25 points): Delivers clear, well-organized presentation with logical flow; uses appropriate visual aids and mathematical notation; maintains audience engagement; demonstrates confidence with material; manages time effectively within 20-minute limit

Critical Analysis and Problem-Solving (25 points): Provides thorough analysis of mathematical model limitations; discusses assumptions and their validity; compares multiple solution approaches; addresses potential extensions or generalizations; demonstrates deep conceptual understanding
instructions: Select a cutting-edge application of differential equations from fields such as mathematical biology, climate modeling, financial mathematics, fluid dynamics, or quantum mechanics that has emerged or significantly evolved within the last 5 years. Your presentation must include: (1) Introduction to the real-world problem and its significance, (2) Mathematical formulation including the specific differential equation(s) involved, (3) Detailed solution methodology with complete mathematical derivations, (4) Analysis of results including graphical representations and interpretations, (5) Discussion of model limitations and assumptions, (6) Comparison with alternative approaches or previous models, (7) Implications for future research or applications. Prepare a 20-minute presentation using professional slides with proper mathematical notation (LaTeX recommended). Include at least 6 peer-reviewed sources published within the last 10 years, with at least 3 from the last 5 years. Submit presentation slides 24 hours before your scheduled presentation date. Be prepared for a 10-minute Q&A session where you will defend your mathematical reasoning and discuss extensions or modifications to your approach.
grading_notes: Expect expert-level mathematical sophistication - students should demonstrate graduate-level understanding of differential equations theory. Look for original insights beyond simple application of known methods. Common issues include: insufficient mathematical rigor in derivations, superficial treatment of assumptions and limitations, poor time management during presentation, inability to answer probing questions about mathematical foundations. Grade distribution should reflect expert difficulty: 90-100 (exceptional work showing research-level insight), 80-89 (solid expert-level understanding with minor gaps), 70-79 (competent but lacking depth or rigor), below 70 (fundamental misunderstandings or incomplete work). Pay special attention to students' ability to handle unexpected questions during Q&A, as this demonstrates true mastery versus memorization.

title: Advanced Calculus Problem-Solving Assessment: Optimization and Related Rates
description: Students will demonstrate mastery of advanced calculus concepts by solving complex optimization problems and related rates scenarios. This assessment evaluates analytical thinking, mathematical modeling, and the application of derivatives to real-world situations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply optimization techniques to solve complex multi-variable problems with constraints
Model and solve related rates problems involving multiple changing quantities
Demonstrate proficiency in setting up and solving differential equations from word problems
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly through detailed solution processes
rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Mathematical Modeling (25 points): Correctly identifies variables, establishes relationships, sets up equations, and defines constraints from problem descriptions
Mathematical Procedures and Calculations (25 points): Accurately applies calculus techniques including differentiation rules, chain rule, implicit differentiation, and algebraic manipulations
Solution Accuracy and Verification (25 points): Arrives at correct final answers, checks solutions for reasonableness, identifies maximum/minimum values correctly, and verifies units
Mathematical Communication and Reasoning (25 points): Shows clear step-by-step work, explains reasoning behind each step, uses proper mathematical notation, and presents solutions in logical sequence
instructions: This assessment consists of four complex calculus problems worth 25 points each. You have 90 minutes to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and completely – partial credit will be awarded based on your process even if final answers are incorrect. Use proper mathematical notation throughout your solutions. For optimization problems, clearly identify what you are maximizing or minimizing, define all variables, state constraints, and verify that your solution represents a maximum or minimum. For related rates problems, clearly identify given information, what you need to find, establish the relationship equation, and show the differentiation process step by step. Each problem should include: (1) Clear identification of given information and what is being asked, (2) Setup of the mathematical model or equation, (3) Complete solution process with all steps shown, (4) Final answer with appropriate units and context, (5) Verification or check of your answer when applicable. You may use a calculator for arithmetic computations, but all calculus work must be shown by hand. If you cannot complete a problem, show as much work as possible to receive partial credit. Clearly label each problem and organize your work neatly. Submit all work on the provided answer sheets with your name and section clearly marked.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct setup and methodology, even with computational errors. Look for evidence of conceptual understanding in problem setup and approach. Deduct minimally (1-2 points) for minor arithmetic errors if the process is correct. Major deductions should be for incorrect problem setup, missing steps in reasoning, or failure to show work. Common issues to watch: students may struggle with identifying the correct relationship equations in related rates problems, forget to check endpoints in optimization problems, or make sign errors in derivatives. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below 70. Students scoring below 60 should be recommended for additional tutoring support.

title: Distributed Web Crawler with Microservices Architecture
description: Students will design and implement a scalable distributed web crawler system using microservices architecture, incorporating containerization, message queues, data persistence, and monitoring. The system must handle concurrent crawling, avoid duplicate URLs, respect robots.txt, and provide real-time analytics through a web dashboard.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement distributed systems using microservices architecture patterns
Apply advanced concurrency and parallel processing techniques in a real-world application
Integrate multiple technologies including containerization, message queues, and databases
Implement comprehensive testing strategies for distributed systems
Demonstrate understanding of system scalability, fault tolerance, and performance optimization
rubric_criteria: System Architecture & Design (25 points): Clear microservices separation, proper API design, scalable architecture documentation, appropriate technology choices, comprehensive system diagram with data flow

Implementation Quality (25 points): Clean, maintainable code following best practices, proper error handling, efficient algorithms, appropriate use of design patterns, comprehensive logging and monitoring

Technical Features (25 points): Functional distributed crawling, duplicate URL prevention, robots.txt compliance, data persistence with proper schema design, real-time dashboard with meaningful metrics

Testing & Documentation (25 points): Unit tests with >80% coverage, integration tests for microservices communication, load testing results, complete README with setup instructions, API documentation, architectural decisions document
instructions: Implement a distributed web crawler system with the following components: (1) URL Frontier Service - manages crawling queue using Redis/RabbitMQ, implements politeness policies, handles URL deduplication; (2) Crawler Service - performs actual web crawling with configurable worker pools, respects robots.txt, extracts links and content; (3) Data Processing Service - processes crawled content, extracts metadata, stores results in database (PostgreSQL/MongoDB); (4) Analytics Dashboard - React/Vue.js frontend displaying real-time crawling statistics, crawled pages count, domain distribution, system health metrics. Technical requirements: Use Docker containers for all services, implement service discovery, include health checks and graceful shutdowns, support horizontal scaling of crawler workers, implement rate limiting per domain, handle failures with retry mechanisms. Deliverables: Complete source code in Git repository with clear commit history, docker-compose.yml for easy deployment, comprehensive README with architecture overview and setup instructions, API documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger), test suite with coverage report, 10-minute video demonstration showing system operation and scalability features. Submit repository link and video URL via course management system. Code must be original work with proper attribution for any libraries used.
grading_notes: Evaluate system architecture first - look for proper service separation and clear interfaces between components. Test the actual deployment using provided docker-compose file; deduct points if system doesn't start properly. Run load tests to verify scalability claims. Common issues: inadequate error handling in distributed components, missing service health checks, poor database schema design, insufficient testing of edge cases. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below 70%. Bonus points (up to 5) for exceptional features like machine learning content classification, advanced monitoring with Prometheus/Grafana, or novel optimization techniques. Schedule individual 15-minute demos during final week to verify understanding and discuss implementation decisions.

title: Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategies Discussion: Real-World Applications
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing different mathematical problem-solving approaches by examining real-world scenarios involving systems of linear equations, quadratic functions, and statistical analysis. Students must demonstrate understanding of multiple solution methods, justify their chosen approaches, and critically evaluate peers' strategies.
estimated_time: 3-4 hours (including initial post, peer responses, and reflection)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply multiple problem-solving strategies to solve systems of linear equations and quadratic functions
Analyze and interpret mathematical solutions in real-world contexts
Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly using appropriate terminology and notation
Evaluate and critique mathematical approaches used by others
rubric_criteria: Initial Problem Analysis (25 points): Correctly identifies mathematical concepts in scenarios, selects appropriate solution methods, shows complete work with proper notation, and arrives at accurate solutions

Real-World Application & Interpretation (25 points): Clearly explains what solutions mean in practical context, discusses limitations or assumptions, and connects mathematical results to real-world implications
Mathematical Communication (25 points): Uses precise mathematical language and notation, explanations are clear and logical, work is well-organized, and reasoning is easy to follow

Peer Engagement & Critical Thinking (25 points): Provides substantive responses to at least two peers, offers alternative approaches or identifies errors, asks thoughtful questions, and demonstrates understanding of others' methods
instructions: You will analyze three real-world scenarios requiring different mathematical approaches: (1) A business optimization problem using systems of linear equations, (2) A projectile motion problem involving quadratic functions, and (3) A data analysis problem using statistical measures. For your initial post (due Wednesday): Choose ONE scenario and provide a complete solution showing all work. Explain your problem-solving approach and why you selected that method. Discuss what your solution means in the real-world context and any limitations. Your post should be 400-500 words with clear mathematical notation. For peer responses (due Friday): Reply to two classmates who solved different scenarios than you. Comment on their approach, suggest alternative methods if applicable, or ask clarifying questions about their reasoning. Each response should be 150-200 words. For your reflection (due Sunday): Write a 200-word reflection on what you learned from seeing different problem-solving approaches and how the discussion enhanced your understanding. Submit all components in the discussion forum using the math equation editor for proper notation. Late posts will lose 10% per day.
grading_notes: Look for evidence that students understand the underlying mathematical concepts, not just procedural completion. Award full points for mathematical accuracy only when work is shown and methods are appropriate. In communication scoring, prioritize clarity and proper use of mathematical terminology over writing style. For peer engagement, quality matters more than quantity - substantive mathematical dialogue should score higher than generic praise. Watch for common issues: incomplete algebraic work, failure to check solutions, misinterpretation of real-world context, and superficial peer responses. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Provide specific feedback on mathematical errors and suggest resources for improvement.

title: Advanced Algorithm Design and Analysis: Technical Presentation
description: Students will design, analyze, and present a novel algorithmic solution to a complex computational problem, demonstrating mastery of algorithm design paradigms, complexity analysis, and technical communication skills.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design efficient algorithms using advanced paradigms (dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, divide-and-conquer, graph algorithms)
Perform rigorous time and space complexity analysis using asymptotic notation
Evaluate trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches and justify design decisions
Communicate complex technical concepts clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences
Implement and validate algorithmic solutions with appropriate testing strategies
rubric_criteria: Algorithm Design and Innovation (25 points): Demonstrates creativity and technical soundness in problem selection and solution approach. Shows clear understanding of chosen algorithm paradigm(s). Solution must be non-trivial and go beyond textbook examples.

Theoretical Analysis (25 points): Provides rigorous mathematical analysis of time/space complexity. Includes best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios where applicable. Compares with alternative approaches and justifies optimality claims.

Implementation and Validation (25 points): Code is well-structured, documented, and demonstrates the algorithm working on test cases. Includes edge cases and performance benchmarks. Shows proper software engineering practices.

Presentation Quality and Technical Communication (25 points): Clear explanation of problem motivation, solution approach, and results. Effective use of visual aids. Handles questions confidently. Presentation flows logically and stays within time limits.
instructions:
Select a computational problem not covered in class that requires advanced algorithmic thinking. Your problem should be practically motivated (e.g., from bioinformatics, network optimization, machine learning, cryptography, or distributed systems). Design and implement an efficient solution, then present your work in a 20-minute technical presentation followed by a 10-minute Q&A session.

Your presentation must include: (1) Problem statement with real-world context and constraints, (2) Overview of existing approaches and their limitations, (3) Detailed explanation of your algorithmic solution with pseudocode, (4) Theoretical analysis including time/space complexity derivations, (5) Implementation details and code walkthrough of key components, (6) Experimental results with performance analysis on various input sizes, (7) Discussion of limitations and potential improvements.

Submit a technical report (8-12 pages) three days before your presentation containing all analytical work, complete source code, and experimental data. Include a bibliography with at least 8 relevant academic sources. Code should be executable with clear setup instructions.

Presentation schedule will be randomly assigned during the final two weeks of the semester. You must be prepared to answer detailed questions about your algorithm's correctness, complexity analysis, implementation choices, and potential extensions. Visual aids should include complexity graphs, algorithm visualizations, and performance comparisons.
grading_notes: Instructors should evaluate the mathematical rigor of complexity proofs, not just stated results. Look for proper use of asymptotic notation and clear reasoning. Code quality matters - check for modularity, documentation, and testing. Common issues include: choosing trivial problems, incorrect complexity analysis, poor time management during presentation, and inability to defend design choices during Q&A. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (exceptional innovation/analysis), 60% B-level (solid technical work), 20% C-level (meets basic requirements), 5% below C (significant technical errors). Deduct points for late submissions: -5 points per day for reports, automatic 10-point penalty for unprepared presentations.

title: Data Collection and Statistical Analysis Lab Report
description: Students will design and conduct a simple statistical survey, collect real data, analyze their findings using basic statistical measures, and present their results in a structured lab report format.
estimated_time: 2-3 hours (including data collection time over 1-2 days)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply basic statistical concepts (mean, median, mode, range) to real-world data
Create and interpret simple data visualizations (bar graphs, histograms)
Demonstrate understanding of data collection methods and potential sources of bias
Communicate mathematical findings clearly using appropriate terminology
rubric_criteria: Data Collection & Methodology (25 points): Survey question is clear and appropriate, sample size meets minimum requirements (20+ responses), data collection method is described, potential sources of bias are identified

Mathematical Calculations (25 points): All statistical measures (mean, median, mode, range) are calculated correctly with work shown, calculations are clearly labeled and organized, appropriate units are used throughout

Data Visualization (25 points): Graph type is appropriate for data collected, graph includes proper title, axis labels, and scale, data is accurately represented visually, graph is neat and professional in appearance

Analysis & Communication (25 points): Results are interpreted correctly in context, conclusions are supported by data, mathematical vocabulary is used appropriately, report follows required format and is well-organized
instructions: You will conduct a statistical investigation by surveying at least 20 people about a topic of your choice. Your lab report must include: (1) Introduction section stating your research question and hypothesis, (2) Methods section describing how you collected data and from whom, (3) Results section showing your raw data in a table, all calculated statistics (mean, median, mode, range), and one appropriate graph, (4) Discussion section interpreting your findings and identifying at least two potential sources of bias in your study, and (5) Conclusion summarizing your key findings. Suggested survey topics include: favorite pizza toppings, hours of sleep per night, number of siblings, or time spent on social media daily. Show all mathematical work clearly. Use graph paper or digital tools for your visualization. Type or write legibly in blue/black ink. Include a cover page with your name, date, and title. Submit all work including your data collection sheets. Reports should be 3-4 pages total. Due date allows 48 hours for data collection plus additional time for analysis and writing.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical accuracy first, then communication clarity. Common errors include: confusing mean vs. median, incorrect graph scaling, insufficient sample sizes, and unsupported conclusions. Expect grade distribution: 20% A-level (90-100), 50% B-level (80-89), 25% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Partial credit available for each criterion - give credit for correct process even with minor calculation errors. Look for evidence of genuine data collection vs. fabricated numbers. Students often struggle with bias identification - accept reasonable examples even if not comprehensive.

title: Programming Languages Discussion: Comparing Python and Java for Beginners
description: Students will engage in a structured online discussion comparing Python and Java programming languages, focusing on syntax, ease of learning, and practical applications. Students must make an initial post and respond meaningfully to two peers' posts.
learning_objectives_assessed: Compare and contrast fundamental characteristics of different programming languages
Analyze the appropriateness of programming languages for specific tasks and beginner learning
Demonstrate understanding of basic programming concepts through written communication
Engage constructively in technical discussions with peers
rubric_criteria: Initial Post Quality (35 points): Demonstrates clear understanding of both languages, includes specific examples of syntax differences, discusses at least 2 practical applications, uses proper technical terminology, meets 250-300 word requirement

Peer Response Quality (25 points): Provides 2 substantive responses (100+ words each) that extend the conversation, asks thoughtful questions or offers additional insights, demonstrates engagement with peers' ideas rather than simple agreement

Technical Accuracy (25 points): Information about both languages is factually correct, code examples (if included) are syntactically accurate, demonstrates understanding of basic programming concepts like variables, loops, or functions

Communication and Professionalism (15 points): Uses clear, professional writing with proper grammar and spelling, organizes ideas logically, responds respectfully to peers, posts within specified timeframe
instructions:
This discussion will help you explore the differences between Python and Java, two popular programming languages. You'll compare their characteristics and consider which might be better for different situations.

Initial Post Requirements (due by Wednesday 11:59 PM):
Create a post of 250-300 words addressing these points:
1. Compare Python and Java syntax using specific examples (e.g., how to print 'Hello World' or create a simple loop in each language)
2. Discuss which language you think is easier for beginners to learn and why
3. Identify at least two real-world applications where each language is commonly used
4. Include your personal opinion on which language you'd prefer to learn first

Peer Response Requirements (due by Sunday 11:59 PM):
Respond to two classmates' posts with substantive comments (100+ words each). Your responses should:
- Build on their ideas or offer a different perspective
- Ask thoughtful follow-up questions
- Share additional examples or experiences
- Avoid simple agreement statements like 'I agree' or 'Good post'

Submission Guidelines:
- Post directly to the discussion forum
- Use clear subject lines for your initial post
- Cite any external sources you reference
- Use code formatting for any programming examples
- Be respectful and constructive in all interactions

Resources: Review course materials on programming language fundamentals and feel free to explore online documentation for both languages.
grading_notes: Grade initial posts first, focusing on technical accuracy and depth of comparison. Look for students who go beyond surface-level observations to discuss specific syntax differences and practical applications. For peer responses, prioritize quality over quantity - two thoughtful responses score higher than multiple shallow ones. Deduct points for late submissions (5 points per day). Common issues include: oversimplified comparisons, lack of specific examples, responses that don't engage meaningfully with peers' ideas, and technical inaccuracies about language capabilities. Expect grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below C-level. Provide specific feedback on technical errors and suggest resources for improvement.

title: Real-World Data Science Project: From Raw Data to Business Insights
description: Students will conduct a complete data science project using a provided messy dataset, performing data cleaning, exploratory analysis, modeling, and presenting actionable business recommendations through a 12-15 minute presentation with supporting materials.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply end-to-end data science workflow including data cleaning, exploration, and modeling
Communicate technical findings effectively to non-technical stakeholders
Make data-driven business recommendations based on analytical results
Demonstrate proficiency with data visualization and statistical analysis tools
rubric_criteria: Data Preparation & Methodology (25 points): Quality of data cleaning process, handling of missing values, feature engineering decisions, and appropriateness of analytical methods chosen
Analysis & Modeling (25 points): Depth of exploratory data analysis, validity of statistical tests/models used, interpretation of results, and acknowledgment of limitations
Visualization & Communication (25 points): Clarity and effectiveness of charts/graphs, logical flow of presentation, appropriate use of technical vs. non-technical language for audience
Business Impact & Recommendations (25 points): Relevance and feasibility of recommendations, clear connection between data insights and business value, consideration of implementation challenges
instructions: You will receive a real-world dataset containing customer, sales, or operational data with typical data quality issues. Your task is to complete a full data science project and present your findings to a simulated business stakeholder audience. DELIVERABLES: (1) 12-15 minute presentation with slides, (2) Jupyter notebook with documented code and analysis, (3) One-page executive summary of key findings and recommendations. REQUIREMENTS: Your analysis must include data cleaning documentation, at least 5 meaningful visualizations, statistical analysis or predictive modeling, and 3-5 specific business recommendations. Address data quality issues explicitly and explain your methodological choices. Your presentation should be accessible to non-technical managers while demonstrating technical competency. Submit all materials 24 hours before your scheduled presentation slot. PRESENTATION FORMAT: 10 minutes presenting + 2-5 minutes Q&A. Use clear, professional slides with a logical narrative flow. Practice timing and prepare for questions about your methodology, assumptions, and alternative approaches. Focus on the 'so what' - why should the business care about your findings?
grading_notes: Evaluate technical rigor while emphasizing communication effectiveness. Look for evidence of critical thinking in methodology choices and honest discussion of limitations. Deduct points for overly technical presentations that lose business focus. Reward creative insights and practical recommendations. Common issues: insufficient data cleaning documentation, poor time management during presentation, recommendations not supported by analysis, overly complex models without business justification. Grade distribution expectation: 15% A-level (90-100), 60% B-level (80-89), 20% C-level (70-79), 5% below 70. Award bonus points (up to 5) for exceptional creativity or insights that go beyond requirements.

title: Distributed Systems Consensus Algorithm Implementation and Performance Analysis
description: Students will implement the Raft consensus algorithm, deploy it across multiple nodes, and conduct comprehensive performance analysis under various failure scenarios. This assessment evaluates advanced distributed systems concepts, algorithm implementation skills, and empirical research methodology.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design and implement fault-tolerant distributed algorithms with proper handling of network partitions and node failures
Analyze and evaluate distributed system performance under varying load conditions and failure scenarios
Apply empirical research methods to validate theoretical concepts in distributed computing
Demonstrate proficiency in concurrent programming and inter-process communication protocols
rubric_criteria: Implementation Quality (25 points): Correct Raft algorithm implementation including leader election, log replication, and safety properties. Code must handle edge cases, demonstrate proper concurrency control, and include comprehensive error handling.

Experimental Design and Execution (25 points): Well-designed experiments testing performance under different scenarios (varying cluster sizes, network delays, failure rates). Proper use of metrics, statistical significance testing, and reproducible methodology.

Analysis and Insights (25 points): Thorough analysis of results with clear explanations of performance characteristics, identification of bottlenecks, comparison with theoretical expectations, and discussion of trade-offs between consistency and availability.

Technical Communication (25 points): Clear, well-structured lab report with proper use of technical terminology, effective visualizations, complete documentation of setup procedures, and professional presentation of findings.
instructions: Implement the Raft consensus algorithm in your choice of programming language (Python, Java, Go, or C++ recommended). Your implementation must support dynamic cluster membership and handle network partitions gracefully. Deploy your system across at least 5 nodes (can be containerized) and conduct experiments measuring: (1) throughput and latency under normal operations, (2) recovery time after leader failures, (3) performance degradation during network partitions, and (4) scalability with cluster size variations. Your lab report must include: executive summary, detailed implementation description with architecture diagrams, experimental methodology section, comprehensive results analysis with statistical tests, performance comparison with published benchmarks, and conclusions with recommendations for production deployment. Submit source code via Git repository with clear README, deployment scripts, experimental data in CSV format, and a PDF report (15-20 pages). Include a 10-minute video demonstration showing your system handling simulated failures. All code must be original work with proper citations for referenced algorithms or techniques. Testing framework should include unit tests achieving >85% code coverage and integration tests validating consensus properties.
grading_notes: Expect 20% of students to struggle with concurrent programming aspects - look for race conditions and deadlocks in code review. Strong implementations should demonstrate understanding of linearizability and handle split-brain scenarios correctly. Grade harshly on experimental rigor - results without proper statistical analysis or insufficient sample sizes should lose significant points. Award bonus points for creative failure injection methods or performance optimizations beyond basic requirements. Common issues: inadequate handling of network timeouts, insufficient logging for debugging, poorly designed experiments with confounding variables. Grade distribution should target: 15% A-level (>90), 25% B-level (80-89), 40% C-level (70-79), with remaining below 70 requiring resubmission.

title: Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Exploring Data Types and Basic Analysis
description: A comprehensive quiz assessing students' understanding of fundamental data science concepts including data types, basic statistical measures, data visualization principles, and introductory data cleaning techniques. Students will demonstrate knowledge through multiple choice questions, short calculations, and scenario-based problem solving.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and classify different types of data (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio)
Calculate basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation)
Recognize appropriate data visualization methods for different data types
Understand fundamental data quality issues and basic cleaning approaches
rubric_criteria: Data Types and Classification (25 points): Correctly identifies qualitative vs quantitative data, distinguishes between discrete and continuous variables, and classifies data using appropriate measurement scales

Descriptive Statistics (25 points): Accurately calculates measures of central tendency and variability, interprets statistical results in context, and identifies when different measures are most appropriate

Data Visualization Principles (25 points): Selects appropriate chart types for different data scenarios, identifies misleading visualizations, and understands basic design principles for effective data presentation

Data Quality and Cleaning (25 points): Recognizes common data quality issues (missing values, outliers, inconsistencies), understands impact of data problems on analysis, and knows basic cleaning strategies
instructions: This quiz consists of 25 questions across four main topic areas in data science fundamentals. You have 45 minutes to complete all questions. The quiz includes multiple choice questions (worth 2-4 points each), short calculation problems (worth 4-6 points each), and scenario analysis questions (worth 6-8 points each). For calculation questions, show your work in the provided space - partial credit will be awarded for correct methodology even if the final answer is incorrect. For multiple choice questions, select the single best answer. For scenario questions, provide clear, concise explanations using appropriate data science terminology. You may use a basic calculator, but no other resources are permitted. Read each question carefully and manage your time effectively - if you get stuck on a difficult question, move on and return to it later. Ensure all answers are clearly marked and legible. Submit your completed quiz by uploading a clear photo or scan if taking remotely, or hand it directly to the instructor if in-person. Late submissions will incur a 10% penalty per day unless prior arrangements have been made.
grading_notes: Grade distribution should typically follow: 90-100% (A), 80-89% (B), 70-79% (C), 60-69% (D), below 60% (F). Award partial credit generously for calculation problems where methodology is correct but arithmetic errors occur. Common issues to watch for: confusion between correlation and causation, misunderstanding of when to use mean vs median, incorrect chart type selections, and oversimplified understanding of data cleaning. Students often struggle with distinguishing interval vs ratio data - provide additional feedback on these concepts. For scenario questions, look for practical understanding rather than memorized definitions. If class average falls below 75%, consider offering a review session and brief makeup quiz on challenging concepts.

title: Community Data Analysis Project: Statistical Investigation and Presentation
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive statistical investigation of a real-world community issue using data collection, analysis, and mathematical modeling. They will present their findings through both written report and visual presentation, demonstrating understanding of statistical concepts and their practical applications.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply statistical measures of central tendency and variability to real-world data sets
Create and interpret various types of graphs and charts for data visualization
Use mathematical modeling to make predictions and draw conclusions from data
Communicate mathematical findings clearly using appropriate terminology and notation
Evaluate the reliability and validity of data sources and statistical claims
rubric_criteria: Data Collection and Organization (25 points): Gathers appropriate, reliable data from multiple sources; organizes data systematically in tables/spreadsheets; clearly documents sources and methodology; demonstrates understanding of sample size and bias considerations

Mathematical Analysis (25 points): Correctly calculates measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and variability (range, standard deviation); creates appropriate graphs/charts with proper labels and scales; applies relevant mathematical concepts accurately with clear work shown

Interpretation and Conclusions (25 points): Makes logical connections between data and real-world context; draws reasonable conclusions supported by mathematical evidence; identifies patterns and trends; discusses limitations and potential sources of error; makes data-driven predictions or recommendations

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Written report is well-organized with clear mathematical explanations; uses proper mathematical vocabulary and notation; visual presentation effectively communicates findings; includes appropriate graphs, charts, and mathematical representations; demonstrates understanding through clear explanations
instructions: Choose a community issue that interests you (examples: local traffic patterns, school lunch preferences, environmental data, sports statistics, or economic trends). Your project must include: (1) A clear research question and hypothesis, (2) Collection of at least 50 data points from reliable sources, (3) Statistical analysis including measures of central tendency, variability, and appropriate graphs, (4) Mathematical modeling or trend analysis with predictions, (5) A 3-4 page written report with proper mathematical formatting, and (6) A 10-minute presentation with visual aids. Your written report should include an introduction explaining your research question, methodology section describing data collection, results section with calculations and graphs, and conclusion discussing findings and implications. All mathematical work must be shown clearly, and graphs must include proper titles, axis labels, and scales. Cite all data sources using proper format. Submit your project as: written report (PDF), spreadsheet with raw data and calculations, and presentation slides. Due dates: Topic approval (Week 1), Data collection complete (Week 2), Draft report (Week 3), Final submission and presentations (Week 4). Projects will be evaluated on mathematical accuracy, depth of analysis, quality of communication, and real-world relevance.
grading_notes: Use the 4-point scale within each criterion: Exemplary (23-25 points), Proficient (20-22 points), Developing (15-19 points), Beginning (0-14 points). Look for evidence of mathematical understanding beyond just correct answers - students should demonstrate conceptual knowledge through explanations. Expect grade distribution around: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below C-level. title: Ethics and Bias in Machine Learning: A Critical Analysis Discussion
description: Students will engage in a structured discussion analyzing real-world cases of algorithmic bias, evaluate ethical frameworks for ML deployment, and propose comprehensive solutions for bias mitigation in data science projects.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (2 hours preparation, 2-3 hours discussion participation and responses)
learning_objectives_assessed: Critically evaluate ethical implications and potential biases in machine learning models and data science workflows
Apply established ethical frameworks to assess real-world AI/ML deployment scenarios
Synthesize technical and ethical considerations to propose actionable bias mitigation strategies
Communicate complex ethical and technical concepts effectively to diverse stakeholders
rubric_criteria: Initial Analysis Post (25 points): Demonstrates deep understanding of algorithmic bias concepts, provides thorough analysis of assigned case study with specific technical details, correctly applies ethical frameworks, and presents well-reasoned conclusions supported by credible sources

Peer Responses and Engagement (25 points): Provides substantive, thoughtful responses to at least 3 peers, asks probing questions that advance discussion, respectfully challenges assumptions with evidence, and builds upon others' ideas constructively

Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Accurately explains technical concepts related to bias sources (data, algorithmic, evaluation), demonstrates understanding of detection methods and metrics, and shows knowledge of current industry practices and tools

Solution Synthesis and Innovation (25 points): Proposes comprehensive, implementable solutions that address both technical and organizational aspects, considers stakeholder perspectives and real-world constraints, and demonstrates creative thinking while maintaining technical feasibility
instructions:
You will participate in a week-long asynchronous discussion analyzing algorithmic bias in machine learning systems. Each student will be assigned one of five real-world case studies: Amazon's hiring algorithm, COMPAS recidivism prediction, facial recognition accuracy disparities, healthcare AI diagnostic bias, or financial lending algorithm discrimination.

Your initial post (due Wednesday, 500-700 words) must: (1) Summarize your assigned case, identifying specific types of bias present; (2) Analyze the case using at least two ethical frameworks (utilitarian, deontological, virtue ethics, or fairness principles); (3) Identify technical factors that contributed to bias (data collection, feature selection, model choice, evaluation metrics); (4) Propose a comprehensive mitigation strategy including technical solutions, process changes, and governance measures; (5) Include at least 4 credible academic or industry sources.

For peer responses (due Friday, minimum 150 words each): Engage with at least 3 classmates' posts by comparing cases, questioning assumptions, suggesting alternative approaches, or connecting concepts across different scenarios. Focus on substantive dialogue that advances understanding rather than simple agreement.

Your final reflection (due Sunday, 200-300 words) should synthesize key insights from the discussion and explain how this analysis would influence your approach to future data science projects. All posts must be professional, evidence-based, and demonstrate respect for diverse perspectives while maintaining critical rigor.
grading_notes: Evaluate initial posts for both breadth and depth - students should demonstrate understanding of multiple bias types and their interconnections. Look for evidence of original thinking rather than superficial coverage of obvious points. Strong responses will connect technical concepts to broader societal implications. For peer engagement, prioritize quality over quantity - substantive responses that advance discussion are worth more than numerous shallow comments. Technical accuracy is crucial; deduct points for misunderstanding of bias detection methods or mitigation strategies. Expect 15-20% of students to earn A-level grades (90-100), with most falling in B range (80-89). Watch for students who focus only on technical solutions without considering organizational or societal factors, or those who make broad ethical claims without supporting evidence.

title: My Favorite Number: A Mathematical Story Presentation
description: Students will create and deliver a 5-7 minute presentation about their favorite number (1-100), exploring its mathematical properties, real-world applications, and personal significance while demonstrating basic mathematical concepts through visual aids and clear explanations.
learning_objectives_assessed: Identify and explain basic mathematical properties (odd/even, factors, multiples)
Connect mathematical concepts to real-world applications and personal experiences
Communicate mathematical ideas clearly using appropriate vocabulary and visual representations
Demonstrate understanding of number relationships and patterns
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Content (25 points): Correctly identifies at least 4 mathematical properties of chosen number (odd/even, factors, prime/composite, place value, multiples). Shows accurate calculations and uses proper mathematical vocabulary.

Real-World Connections (25 points): Provides 2-3 meaningful examples of how the number appears in everyday life, nature, or specific contexts. Explains why these connections are significant and interesting.
Presentation Skills (25 points): Speaks clearly and confidently, maintains eye contact, stays within time limit (5-7 minutes), engages audience appropriately. Shows enthusiasm for the topic.

Visual Aids and Organization (25 points): Uses at least 2 visual elements (poster, drawings, objects, etc.) effectively. Presentation follows logical sequence: introduction, mathematical properties, real-world examples, conclusion.
instructions: Choose your favorite number between 1 and 100 and create a presentation that tells its mathematical story! Your presentation should be 5-7 minutes long and include: (1) An introduction explaining why this number is special to you, (2) Mathematical properties - identify at least 4 characteristics such as whether it's odd or even, what its factors are, if it's prime or composite, what it looks like in different forms (fractions, tally marks, etc.), (3) Real-world examples - find 2-3 interesting ways your number appears in the world around us (sports, nature, holidays, measurements, etc.), and (4) A conclusion summarizing why your number is mathematically interesting. You must create visual aids to support your presentation - this could include a colorful poster, drawings, physical objects to count, or simple charts. Practice your presentation beforehand and be prepared to answer one question from classmates. Remember to speak clearly, look at your audience, and show enthusiasm for your number! Submit a simple outline of your presentation to your teacher the day before presenting.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical accuracy first - verify student calculations and property identification. Look for genuine understanding rather than memorization. Common issues include: confusing factors vs. multiples, incorrect prime/composite identification, and insufficient real-world connections. Encourage creativity in visual aids but ensure they support mathematical content. Grade presentation skills generously for beginners, prioritizing effort and enthusiasm over polished delivery. Expected grade distribution: 85-100 points (meets all requirements with good effort), 70-84 points (missing 1-2 minor elements), below 70 (significant gaps in mathematical content or major presentation issues). Allow re-presentation opportunities for students scoring below 75.

title: Predictive Analytics Pipeline: Customer Churn Analysis Lab Report
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive end-to-end data science project analyzing customer churn data. Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and validation techniques for business classification problems
Communicate technical findings effectively through professional documentation and data-driven recommendations
rubric_criteria: Data Exploration & Preprocessing (25 points): Comprehensive EDA with 8+ meaningful visualizations, proper handling of missing values, outlier detection, feature scaling, and clear documentation of data quality issues and preprocessing decisions

Professional Communication & Business Impact (25 points): Executive summary with clear business recommendations, technical methodology section, results interpretation with visualizations, discussion of limitations, and professional formatting with proper citations
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (telecom_churn.csv), develop a complete predictive analytics solution to identify customers likely to churn. Technical requirements: Use scikit-learn for modeling, implement proper train/validation/test splits (60/20/20), perform hyperparameter optimization using GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV, include feature importance plots, and create ROC curves for all models. grading_notes: Grade using the 4-point scale per criterion: Excellent (23-25 pts), Proficient (20-22 pts), Developing (15-19 pts), Inadequate (0-14 pts). title: Advanced Calculus and Real Analysis Comprehensive Quiz
description: A comprehensive assessment evaluating students' mastery of advanced calculus concepts including multivariable optimization, series convergence, complex integration, and rigorous proof techniques. Students will solve challenging problems requiring deep theoretical understanding and computational proficiency.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply advanced optimization techniques to solve multivariable calculus problems with constraints
Analyze convergence and divergence of infinite series using multiple convergence tests
Evaluate complex line integrals and apply residue theorem for contour integration
Construct rigorous mathematical proofs using epsilon-delta definitions and logical reasoning
rubric_criteria: Problem Setup and Mathematical Modeling (25 points): Correctly identifies problem type, sets up appropriate equations/functions, clearly defines variables and constraints, demonstrates understanding of underlying mathematical concepts

Solution Method and Computational Accuracy (25 points): Selects appropriate solution techniques, executes calculations correctly, shows all intermediate steps, arrives at correct numerical or algebraic answers

Mathematical Reasoning and Proof Structure (25 points): Constructs logically sound arguments, uses proper mathematical notation and terminology, provides clear justification for each step, demonstrates rigorous thinking

Communication and Presentation (25 points): Presents solutions clearly and organized manner, explains reasoning effectively, uses appropriate mathematical language, provides complete and well-formatted responses
instructions:
This quiz consists of 4 multi-part problems covering advanced calculus topics. You have 3 hours to complete all problems. Show all work clearly and provide detailed explanations for your reasoning. Use proper mathematical notation throughout.

Problem 1 (25 points): Solve a constrained optimization problem using Lagrange multipliers, including verification of critical points and interpretation of results in context.

Problem 2 (25 points): Determine convergence/divergence of three given infinite series using different convergence tests. Provide rigorous justification for your choice of test and conclusion.

Problem 3 (25 points): Evaluate a complex contour integral using residue theorem. Identify singularities, calculate residues, and apply the theorem correctly.

Problem 4 (25 points): Prove a given statement about continuity or differentiability using epsilon-delta definitions. Your proof must be complete and logically sound.

Submission requirements: Write solutions legibly in blue or black ink, number all pages, clearly label each problem and sub-part. Partial credit will be awarded based on the rubric criteria. Calculator use is permitted for arithmetic only. No collaboration or external resources allowed.
grading_notes: Award partial credit generously for correct methods even with computational errors. Look for evidence of understanding in problem setup and approach. Deduct points for unclear explanations or missing steps in reasoning. For proofs, require proper logical structure - award credit for correct approach even if proof is incomplete. Common issues include: incorrect application of Lagrange multipliers, confusion between convergence tests, errors in residue calculations, and inadequate rigor in proofs. Expected grade distribution: 15% A-level (90-100), 35% B-level (80-89), 35% C-level (70-79), 15% below 70. Flag for review any student scoring below 60 points.

title: Personal Budget Calculator - Console Application Project
description: Students will design and implement a console-based personal budget calculator that allows users to input income and expenses, categorize transactions, and generate basic financial reports. Deduct points if core features are missing or non-functional. For code structure, look for logical function organization and consistent naming conventions - avoid penalizing minor style variations if code is readable. title: Advanced Calculus Applications: Multi-Variable Optimization in Real-World Contexts
description: Students will engage in structured discussions analyzing complex multi-variable optimization problems from engineering, economics, and physics, demonstrating mastery of partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization while evaluating peer solutions and justifying mathematical approaches.
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply partial derivatives and gradient vectors to solve multi-variable optimization problems
Implement Lagrange multipliers method for constrained optimization scenarios
Analyze and critique mathematical solutions using precise mathematical language
Synthesize optimization techniques to model and solve real-world problems
rubric_criteria: Mathematical Accuracy and Methodology (25 points): Correct application of partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and optimization techniques with proper mathematical notation and step-by-step reasoning
Problem Analysis and Interpretation (25 points): Clear identification of variables, constraints, and objective functions; accurate translation of real-world scenarios into mathematical models

Critical Evaluation and Peer Response (25 points): Thoughtful analysis of at least two peer solutions, identification of errors or alternative approaches, constructive feedback with mathematical justification
Communication and Mathematical Discourse (25 points): Clear, precise mathematical writing using appropriate terminology, logical flow of arguments, and professional discussion forum etiquette
instructions:
You will participate in a week-long discussion analyzing three complex optimization scenarios: (1) minimizing material costs for a cylindrical container with volume constraints, (2) maximizing profit in a two-product manufacturing system with resource limitations, and (3) finding optimal dimensions for a solar panel array with geometric constraints.

Initial Post Requirements (due by Wednesday): Choose ONE scenario and provide a complete mathematical solution including: variable identification, constraint equations, objective function formulation, application of appropriate optimization techniques (partial derivatives and/or Lagrange multipliers), verification of critical points, and interpretation of results in the original context. Your solution must include all mathematical work with clear explanations of each step. Minimum 400 words with proper mathematical notation.

Peer Response Requirements (due by Friday): Analyze TWO peer solutions from different scenarios than your initial post. For each response: verify mathematical calculations, evaluate the approach taken, identify any errors or suggest improvements, and discuss alternative solution methods. If you find errors, provide corrections with full mathematical justification. Minimum 200 words per response.

grading_notes: Evaluate mathematical rigor first - solutions must demonstrate genuine understanding of optimization techniques, not just formula application. Look for proper use of mathematical notation and terminology. In peer responses, assess quality of mathematical critique rather than just agreement/disagreement. title: Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture: Design and Defense Presentation
description: Students design and present a comprehensive distributed system architecture for a real-world scenario, demonstrating mastery of scalability patterns, fault tolerance mechanisms, consistency models, and performance optimization. The presentation includes a technical deep-dive, architectural justification, and defense against expert-level questioning.
learning_objectives_assessed: Design scalable distributed system architectures using appropriate patterns and technologies
Analyze and justify trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Implement fault tolerance and disaster recovery strategies in distributed environments
Evaluate and optimize distributed system performance under various load conditions
Communicate complex technical concepts clearly to expert audiences
rubric_criteria: System Design and Architecture (25 points): Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of distributed systems patterns, appropriate technology selection, clear component interaction diagrams, and scalability considerations with quantified metrics

Technical Depth and Accuracy (25 points): Shows expert-level knowledge of consensus algorithms, consistency models, fault tolerance mechanisms, and performance optimization techniques with accurate technical details and proper terminology

Critical Analysis and Trade-offs (25 points): Provides thorough analysis of CAP theorem implications, justified architectural decisions, comprehensive risk assessment, and alternative approach comparisons with quantified impact analysis

Your presentation must include: (1) Complete system architecture diagram with all components, data flows, and external dependencies clearly labeled, (2) Detailed analysis of chosen consistency model (eventual, strong, or hybrid) with specific implementation strategies, (3) Fault tolerance design including failure scenarios, recovery mechanisms, and disaster recovery procedures with RPO/RTO specifications, (4) Performance optimization strategy covering caching layers, database sharding, load balancing, and CDN implementation with projected performance metrics, (5) Security architecture including authentication, authorization, data encryption, and compliance considerations, (6) Monitoring and observability strategy with specific tools and metrics. grading_notes: Evaluate technical accuracy rigorously - incorrect statements about consensus algorithms, consistency models, or distributed systems principles should result in significant point deductions. Look for depth beyond surface-level understanding; students should demonstrate knowledge of implementation details, not just conceptual awareness. Strong responses show quantified analysis (latency numbers, throughput calculations, cost estimates). During Q&A, assess ability to think on feet and modify design based on new constraints. Common issues: oversimplified fault tolerance, ignoring network partition scenarios, unrealistic performance claims, weak security considerations. Grade distribution expectation: 20% A-level (90+), 40% B-level (80-89), 30% C-level (70-79), 10% below C-level. Deduct points for presentations exceeding time limits or missing required technical components.

title: Linear Regression Analysis Lab Report
description: Students will collect real-world data, perform linear regression analysis, and write a comprehensive lab report documenting their methodology, calculations, statistical analysis, and conclusions about the relationship between two variables.
estimated_time: 4-5 hours (data collection: 1 hour, analysis: 2-3 hours, report writing: 1-2 hours)
learning_objectives_assessed: Apply linear regression techniques to analyze real-world data relationships
Calculate and interpret correlation coefficients and regression equations
Evaluate the validity and limitations of statistical models
Communicate mathematical findings through clear written analysis
rubric_criteria: Data Collection & Organization (25 points): Appropriate variable selection, minimum 20 data points, properly formatted tables, clear data source documentation
Mathematical Analysis (25 points): Correct calculation of correlation coefficient, accurate regression equation derivation, proper use of formulas and statistical methods
Statistical Interpretation (25 points): Meaningful analysis of R² value, discussion of correlation strength, identification of outliers, assessment of model limitations
Report Quality & Communication (25 points): Clear methodology explanation, logical organization, proper mathematical notation, evidence-based conclusions, professional presentation
instructions: Select two quantitative variables that you hypothesize have a linear relationship (e.g., height vs. shoe size, study time vs. test scores, temperature vs. ice cream sales). grading_notes: Expect most students to score 75-85 points. title: Advanced Data Structures and Algorithm Complexity Analysis Quiz

Design optimal algorithms for complex problems using appropriate data structures and algorithmic paradigms
Evaluate trade-offs between different data structure implementations in real-world scenarios
Apply mathematical reasoning to prove algorithm correctness and analyze worst-case, best-case, and average-case performance
rubric_criteria: Complexity Analysis (25 points): Correctly determines and justifies time/space complexity using formal notation, shows all mathematical work, identifies dominant terms, and explains reasoning clearly

Algorithm Design (25 points): Creates efficient, correct algorithms that solve given problems optimally, demonstrates understanding of algorithmic paradigms (divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy), and shows clear logical flow
Data Structure Application (25 points): Selects appropriate data structures for specific use cases, explains implementation details and operations, compares alternatives with valid justifications

Problem-Solving and Communication (25 points): Demonstrates systematic problem-solving approach, provides clear explanations with proper terminology, shows complete work with logical progression, and addresses all parts of multi-step problems
instructions:
This quiz consists of 8 problems covering advanced data structures and algorithms. You have 90 minutes to complete all questions. Show all work for full credit - partial credit will be awarded based on your approach and reasoning even if final answers are incorrect.

For complexity analysis, show mathematical derivations and justify your conclusions. For comparison problems, create tables or lists with explanations.

grading_notes: Grade holistically considering both correctness and approach. Award partial credit generously for correct reasoning with minor computational errors. rubric_criteria: Data Exploration & Feature Engineering (25 points): Comprehensive EDA with statistical insights, creative feature engineering including domain-specific variables, proper handling of missing data and outliers, feature selection using statistical methods

Model Development & Optimization (25 points): Implementation of at least 3 different algorithms (e.g., logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting), proper cross-validation strategy, hyperparameter optimization using grid/random search, ensemble methods or stacking techniques

Model Evaluation & Interpretation (25 points): Appropriate metrics for imbalanced data (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR), statistical significance testing, feature importance analysis, model interpretability using SHAP or LIME, business impact quantification

Technical Implementation & Deployment (25 points): Clean, well-documented code following best practices, reproducible pipeline with version control, model deployment (API endpoint, Docker container, or cloud service), comprehensive technical documentation and testing
instructions: Using the provided telecommunications customer dataset (or acquire from Kaggle/UCI), develop a complete churn prediction system. Your submission must include: (1) Jupyter notebook with full analysis pipeline including data exploration, feature engineering, model development, and evaluation; (2) Python scripts for production-ready model training and prediction functions; (3) Deployed model accessible via REST API or web interface; (4) Executive summary (2-3 pages) presenting business insights and recommendations; (5) Technical documentation explaining model architecture, deployment instructions, and maintenance procedures. Requirements: Handle class imbalance appropriately, achieve minimum 0.75 AUC-ROC score, implement at least one ensemble method, provide model interpretability analysis, and demonstrate statistical rigor in evaluation. Submit all code via GitHub repository with clear README, deployed model URL, and executive summary as PDF. Include requirements.txt and detailed setup instructions for reproducibility.
grading_notes: Expect 15% A grades (90-100 points) for exceptional work with novel approaches and superior business insights. Watch for common issues: inadequate handling of data leakage, inappropriate metrics for imbalanced data, overfitting without proper validation, poor feature engineering, and weak business interpretation. Deduct points for non-reproducible code, missing documentation, or failed deployment. Strong projects will show creativity in feature engineering, sophisticated model interpretation, and clear business value proposition. Average performance should achieve 75-85 points with competent technical execution but limited innovation or insight depth.

title: Fundamentals of Arithmetic Operations and Problem Solving Exam
description: A comprehensive beginner-level mathematics exam covering basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), fractions, decimals, and real-world problem solving. Students will demonstrate computational skills and mathematical reasoning through various question formats including multiple choice, short answer, and word problems.
learning_objectives_assessed: Perform accurate calculations using the four basic arithmetic operations with whole numbers, fractions, and decimals
Apply mathematical reasoning to solve real-world word problems involving money, measurement, and time
Demonstrate understanding of place value, number relationships, and basic mathematical concepts
Show organized work and clear mathematical communication in problem-solving processes
rubric_criteria: Computational Accuracy (25 points): Correct execution of arithmetic operations including addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division with whole numbers, fractions, and decimals. Full credit for 90-100% accuracy, partial credit for 70-89%, minimal credit for 50-69%, no credit below 50%

Problem-Solving Strategy (25 points): Demonstrates logical approach to word problems, identifies relevant information, selects appropriate operations, and shows systematic work. Evaluates quality of mathematical reasoning and strategy selection rather than just final answers

Mathematical Communication (25 points): Shows clear, organized work with proper notation, labels units appropriately, explains reasoning where requested, and presents solutions in understandable format. Assesses clarity of mathematical expression and completeness of explanations

Application and Reasoning (25 points): Successfully interprets real-world contexts, makes connections between mathematical concepts, checks reasonableness of answers, and applies learned concepts to unfamiliar situations. Measures depth of understanding beyond memorized procedures
instructions: This exam consists of 40 questions divided into four sections: multiple choice, computational problems, fraction and decimal operations, and word problems. You have 90 minutes to complete all sections. Show all work for computational problems and word problems, even if the answer seems obvious. For multiple choice questions, clearly mark your selected answer. Use proper mathematical notation and include appropriate units in your final answers. Calculators are not permitted for basic arithmetic sections but may be used for decimal calculations involving more than two decimal places. Read each word problem carefully and identify what information is given and what you need to find. Write your final answer clearly and check that it makes sense in the context of the problem. If you finish early, review your work and ensure all questions are answered. Partial credit will be awarded for showing correct mathematical thinking even if the final answer is incorrect. Organize your work neatly and cross out any work you don't want graded rather than erasing. For fraction problems, you may leave answers in simplified fraction form or convert to decimals as appropriate. Round decimal answers to two places unless otherwise specified.
grading_notes: Focus on mathematical thinking process as much as final answers. Award partial credit generously for correct approaches with minor computational errors. Common issues include: misreading word problems, incorrect operation selection, careless arithmetic mistakes, and failure to include units. Expect grade distribution: 20% A's (90-100), 35% B's (80-89), 30% C's (70-79), 15% D's and F's (below 70). Pay attention to systematic errors that indicate conceptual misunderstandings versus random mistakes. Students showing work but arriving at incorrect answers should receive 50-75% credit if the method is sound. Deduct minimally for minor notation issues but more significantly for unclear or missing work on problem-solving sections.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis and Trade-off Discussion
description: Students will analyze and compare different algorithmic approaches to a common problem, evaluating time/space complexity trade-offs and discussing real-world implementation considerations through structured peer discussion and written analysis.
learning_objectives_assessed: Analyze time and space complexity of algorithms using Big O notation
Compare and contrast different algorithmic approaches to solve the same problem
Evaluate trade-offs between algorithm efficiency and implementation complexity
Communicate technical concepts clearly in both written and verbal formats
rubric_criteria: Complexity Analysis (25 points): Correctly identifies and explains time/space complexity using Big O notation, shows mathematical reasoning, identifies best/average/worst case scenarios

Algorithm Comparison (25 points): Provides thorough comparison of at least 3 different approaches, identifies strengths and weaknesses of each method, demonstrates understanding of when each approach is most suitable

Real-world Application (25 points): Discusses practical implementation considerations, addresses scalability concerns, considers memory constraints and hardware limitations, provides concrete examples of usage scenarios

Communication and Discussion Participation (25 points): Presents ideas clearly and logically, actively engages in peer discussion, asks thoughtful questions, provides constructive feedback to classmates, uses appropriate technical terminology
